t: UK Biobank self-reported ME/CFS heritability analysis gave a low h2 estimate of 0.08 with low confidence.
Increased frequency of HLA-DQA1 alleles and reduced expression of HLA-DRB1 were found associated with ME/CFS.
In CCC-diagnosed ME/CFS patients, HLA-C*07:04 or HLA-DQB1*03:03 alleles were significantly linked to disease status, present in about 10% of patients and associated with a 1.5-2.0-fold altered risk.
GWAS studies using UK Biobank ME/CFS samples found no DNA variant that was repeated across multiple analyses.

Antibodies against herpesvirus dUTPase proteins (HSV-1, EBV, HHV-6) have been identified in ME/CFS patients, hypothesised to promote cellular damage, autoimmune features, and mitochondrial dysfunction via TLR2/NF-κB signalling.
Earlier serological studies using classical EBV antigens found no upregulation of EBV-encoded proteins in ME/CFS, and viral load was generally not significantly increased compared to controls.
Anti-inflammatory gut bacterial species Faecalibacterium and Bifidobacterium are decreased in ME/CFS, leading to reduced anti-inflammatory butyrate production.

Proinflammatory Proteobacteria, particularly Enterobacteriaceae, are found at elevated concentrations in the ME/CFS gut microbiome, potentially contributing to increased transit time and IBS-like symptoms.

Elevated IgM and IgA antibodies to LPS, along with higher blood levels of bacterial LPS, LPS-binding proteins, and soluble CD14, have been observed in ME/CFS, indicating gut bacterial translocation and systemic inflammation.
Seventeen cytokines showed a significant upward linear trend with increasing ME/CFS severity, though they did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and control groups overall.

A meta-analysis of 64 studies found ME/CFS patients have higher resting heart rate, lower maximal/peak heart rate, higher heart rate responses to head-up tilt and standing, lower heart rate at submaximal exercise threshold, higher LF power, and lower HF power of heart rate variability compared to controls, suggesting reduced vagal modulation and increased sympathetic tone.

One cluster analysis of 131 Fukuda-criteria ME/CFS patients found 34% had sympathetic dysautonomia symptoms (linked to more severe disease), 5% sympathetic symptoms alone, 21% parasympathetic symptoms, and 40% sympathovagal imbalance.
The long non-coding RNA myocardial infarction associated transcript (MIAT) was found upregulated in PBMCs of ME/CFS patients, indicating endothelial dysfunction.
Plasma miRNAs modulating the Sirt1/eNOS endothelial signalling axis (miR-21, miR-34a, miR-92a, miR-126, miR-200c) were found elevated in ME/CFS but did not correlate with disease severity.
ME/CFS blood samples showed significant hypercoagulability on thromboelastography, platelet hyperactivation, and larger fibrinaloid microclot area compared to healthy controls.
Reduced plasma coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) levels were found in ME/CFS blood and plasma, and this reduction is inversely associated with fatigue severity.

Reduced mitochondrial respiratory function has been observed in neutrophils and PBMCs of ME/CFS patients, along with reduced ATP production, proton leak, and mitochondrial membrane potential in CD8+ T cells.
One ME/CFS study found significantly lower levels of ACTH/cortisol, consistent with HPA axis hypofunction.
GH peak and IGF-1 were significantly reduced in severe ME/CFS patients compared to controls and to mild ME/CFS patients.
Double-stranded DNA antibodies were found in 12% of ME/CFS patients in one study, while another study found them in only 0.7% of patients, illustrating inconsistent findings.
Antibodies against cardiolipin were found in 92-95% of ME/CFS patients in two studies, but only 4% in another study.

Autoantibodies against neurotransmitter receptors, including muscarinic M1AChR, M3AChR, and adrenergic B2AdR, have been identified in ME/CFS patients, potentially causing receptor dysfunction relevant to dysautonomia.
Some ME/CFS patients show elevated serum BAFF while gene expression of its receptor TNFRSF13C is reduced, suggesting elevated BAFF may be compensatory.
Heightened levels of activin A and B, with elevated ratios of activin to its binding protein follistatin, have been found in ME/CFS, potentially promoting autoimmune and inflammatory processes.
Peak growth hormone and IGF-1 levels were significantly reduced in patients with severe ME/CFS compared to both controls and patients with mild disease.
One study found significantly lower ACTH/cortisol levels in ME/CFS patients, consistent with HPA axis hypofunction.
It has been hypothesised that excessive serotonin levels drive CRH release and chronic HPA axis reactivation, potentially explaining classic ME/CFS symptoms.
Lowered dopamine levels are associated with fatigue, a commonly present symptom of ME/CFS.
ME/CFS patients show dysfunctional hypothalamic function evidenced by up-regulation of hypothalamic 5-HT receptors and abnormal arginine/vasopressin responses to deprivation/water-loading tests.
Antipituitary and antihypothalamic antibodies have been identified in ME/CFS, particularly in more severe cases, suggesting possible hypothalamic/pituitary autoimmunity.
Abnormal immune responses are more pronounced within the first three years of ME/CFS, but as disease duration lengthens these abnormalities subside and T-cell exhaustion becomes evident.
An increased prevalence of the HLA-DQB*01 allele, along with two other HLA-DQB1 variants combined with two RAGE-374A variants, was found in ME/CFS.
Antiviral drug treatment of ME/CFS has been unsuccessful, arguing against the hypothesis that ME/CFS is caused by failure to clear a persistent pathogen.
After EBV infection, some ME/CFS patients show upregulation of EBV-induced gene 2, a gene important for immune and CNS function, which may correlate with neurological and immune symptoms.
Enhanced IgG reactivity against an EBV repeat sequence (EBNA-6) suggests homologous human protein sequences could serve as targets for antigenic/molecular mimicry in ME/CFS.
Double-stranded DNA antibodies were found in 12% of ME/CFS patients in one study, whereas another study found them in only 0.7% of patients, indicating inconsistent evidence for this autoantibody.
Antibodies against cardiolipin were found in 92-95% of ME/CFS patients in two studies, but only 4% in another study, showing marked inconsistency across studies.

Autoantibodies against neurotransmitter receptors, including muscarinic M1AChR and M3AChR and adrenergic B2AdR, have been identified in some ME/CFS patients and are thought to cause receptor dysfunction underlying dysautonomia.

No difference between ME/CFS patients and controls was found for autoantibodies against serotonin, angiotensin, endothelin, mu-opioid, and dopamine receptors, although serotonin autoantibodies have been linked to ME/CFS in other work.
Some ME/CFS patients display elevated serum BAFF alongside reduced gene expression of its receptor TNFRSF13C, suggesting the elevated BAFF is a compensatory response.

Heightened levels of activin A and B, with an elevated ratio to the binding protein follistatin, have been found in ME/CFS, a pleiotropic cytokine family implicated in immune regulation and inflammatory disease.

Dysregulation of IL-21, a pleiotropic cytokine essential for follicular helper T cell differentiation and germinal centre antibody responses, is hypothesised to promote autoimmune and inflammatory processes in ME/CFS, though a causal role is unproven.
30% of ME/CFS patients in one study were found to have antibodies against endothelial cells.
Graded exercise therapy (GET), once recommended in NICE guidelines, was removed from the revised 2021 NICE guideline after being strongly criticised for causing harm to ME/CFS patients.

The 2011 PACE trial, which reported GET/CBT as safe and effective, has been discredited; subsequent review of the raw data showed no significant difference in improvement/recovery rates versus controls, and 54-74% of patients reported experiencing harm after GET.
Energy management (pacing), an individualised approach monitoring energy expenditure to reduce PEM occurrence, duration, and severity, is now emphasised over GET for symptom control.
Vitamin D supplementation can help prevent vitamin D deficiency in ME/CFS patients.
Nutritional supplementation with zinc and magnesium may be beneficial for prophylaxis and therapy in ME/CFS patients with suspected cadmium toxin exposure.
A specialty ME/CFS clinic found that 84% of 960 patients presented with at least one other comorbid condition, often resulting in worsened health.
The DecodeME study, launched September 2022, aims to identify genetic causes of ME/CFS by testing more than 25,000 DNA samples to achieve statistical power for reproducible results.

GWAS studies performed on ME/CFS patient samples from the UK Biobank found no DNA variant repeated across multiple analyses, though uncertainty remains about how many included patients truly met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.
An estimated 38-55% of ME/CFS patients have symptoms that overlap with other autoimmune diseases.

Five weeks of low-dose subcutaneous immunoglobulin treatment produced significant improvements in symptoms, quality of life, and working ability in ME/CFS patients with infection-related symptomatology.

Among the 7 patients who reported the greatest benefit, quality of life scores increased by 35 points on a 0-100 scale after IG treatment, with one patient reporting complete resolution of ME/CFS symptoms.
No serious adverse events were observed with low-dose subcutaneous immunoglobulin treatment in this ME/CFS case series.
Prior to treatment, patients with infection-related ME/CFS reported very poor quality of life (median 25/100) and working ability (median 5/100).
SARS-CoV-2 infection was the most frequent confirmed trigger of ME/CFS onset overall and was far more common in adults than in children/adolescents.
EBV was a more common confirmed trigger of ME/CFS in children/adolescents than in adults.
Influenza virus infection as an ME/CFS trigger was rare and not significantly different between children/adolescents and adults.
Almost all ME/CFS patients recalled an acute viral infection preceding disease onset, with a significantly higher rate in adults than in children/adolescents.

Beyond SARS-CoV-2, EBV, and influenza, other confirmed or probable infectious triggers of ME/CFS onset in the cohort included coxsackieviruses, mycoplasma, Borrelia burgdorferi, respiratory syncytial virus, and Group A streptococci.

A self-report PROM (DSQ-PEM) failed to detect PEM in about 9% of patients who were unequivocally confirmed to have PEM during structured physician interview, indicating that self-assessment underestimates PEM relative to clinical evaluation.
The large majority of ME/CFS patients reported long-lasting post-exertional malaise, with over 80% experiencing PEM lasting more than 24 hours.

ME/CFS patients showed significantly reduced health-related quality of life across all SF-36 domains compared to a healthy German population sample, with the lowest scores in vitality and role-physical domains.
Children and adolescents with ME/CFS reported significantly better mental health, role-physical functioning, and self-reported health change over the past year compared to adult patients.
The median Bell Score of the ME/CFS registry cohort indicated severely impaired functional status, with no significant difference between children/adolescents and adults.
Children and adolescents with ME/CFS reported significantly less fatigue than adult patients on the Chalder Fatigue Scale.
The majority of ME/CFS patients showed autonomic dysfunction on the COMPASS-31 questionnaire, most commonly of moderate severity.
Children and adolescents had significantly lower COMPASS-31 gastrointestinal, bladder, pupillomotor, and total scores than adults, but significantly higher orthostatic intolerance subscores.
The majority of ME/CFS patients, especially adults, were completely unable to participate in previous education or work following disease onset.
Nearly all adult patients tested fulfilled both the Canadian Consensus Criteria and the IOM criteria for ME/CFS, supporting high internal diagnostic concordance in the registry cohort.
ME/CFS respondents scored significantly lower than healthy controls on all FUNCAP55 and FUNCAP27 domain (A-H) sub-scores and total scores, supporting the questionnaire's known-group validity.

FUNCAP domain and total scores showed a monotonic decline in functional capacity with increasing ICC-defined ME/CFS severity, from healthy controls through mild, moderate, severe, to very severe disease.
Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) of FUNCAP55 and FUNCAP27 domain and total scores was good to excellent across all eight domains.
Test-retest reliability of FUNCAP27, assessed two weeks apart, was excellent for all eight domains and the total score.
Floor and ceiling effects for FUNCAP55 and FUNCAP27 domain scores were negligible for the large majority of domains, supporting the instrument's ability to capture the full range of severity.
The shortened FUNCAP27 correlated very highly with the full FUNCAP55 on domain and total scores in both the Norwegian and international samples.
No statistically significant differences were found between male and female respondents on FUNCAP55 domain or total scores in either Round 5 or Round 4.
Across all six survey rounds, ME/CFS respondents were overwhelmingly female (~90%) versus male (~10%).
Nearly all FUNCAP55 items had content compatible with WHO ICF 2001 functional domains, except two items (getting up/staying out of bed, and going on a necessary errand).

The SF-36, widely used in prior ME/CFS studies, fails to incorporate the consequences of post-exertional malaise and lacks items central to ME/CFS functional capacity such as cognitive/social activities, orthostatic tolerance, and sensory hypersensitivity.

The CFS-APQ, previously considered the best available FC tool, has only moderate content and construct validity and does not incorporate consequences of PEM, partly because it was validated in Fukuda-criteria populations that do not require PEM.
In the second development round, three-quarters of ME/CFS respondents rated the questionnaire as highly suitable for describing their functional capacity, supporting early face validity.
In the finalized test-retest rounds, 90% of respondents rated FUNCAP as having good or very good ability to assess their functional capacity, supporting face validity of the final instrument.
The magnitude of ME/CFS versus healthy control differences varied greatly by item, from minimal difference on reading a short text to a very large gap on managing a full non-physical working day.

ANOVA analyses across the eight FUNCAP domains and total score confirmed statistically significant differences in functional capacity between the five ME/CFS severity subgroups, with nearly all post hoc pairwise comparisons also significant.
PregS-evoked TRPM3 current amplitude was significantly smaller in NK cells from GWI participants compared to healthy controls, indicating impaired TRPM3 channel function.

The reduction in current amplitude caused by the TRPM3 antagonist Ononetin (in the presence of PregS) was significantly smaller in NK cells from GWI participants than HC, indicating reduced channel modulation.
A significantly lower proportion of NK cells from GWI participants were sensitive to Ononetin compared to HC, with only 30.8% showing reduced current amplitude.

GWI participants had significantly higher disability scores than healthy controls across all seven WHODAS domains, including communication, mobility, self-care, interpersonal connections, life activities, work participation, and societal participation.
Full blood count parameters did not differ significantly between GWI participants and healthy controls.
All GWI veterans in the study reported fatigue, cognitive difficulties, pain, and sleep disturbances, while respiratory disturbances were the least common symptom (reported by only one patient).
All GWI participants in this study met the Canadian Consensus Criteria (CCC) for ME/CFS, and one participant additionally met the International Consensus Criteria (ICC) for ME/CFS.
There was no statistically significant difference in NK cell purity (CD3-CD56+) between GWI and HC groups.
CFS model rats had significantly lower body weight than control rats.
CFS model rats consumed significantly less food than control rats.
CFS model rats crossed the original platform quadrant fewer times in the Morris water maze, indicating impaired spatial memory, compared with control rats.
CFS model rats had higher general-condition fatigue scores than control rats.
CFS model rats showed increased grid-crossing and center-area-entering counts in the open field test compared with control rats, indicating altered anxiety-related behavior.
CFS model rats showed a longer escape latency in the Morris water maze navigation task than control rats, indicating impaired learning.
Electroacupuncture treatment reversed the CFS-model-induced decrease in original-platform quadrant crossings during the Morris water maze test, indicating improved spatial learning-memory.
Electroacupuncture reversed the elevated semi-quantitative general condition (fatigue) score seen in CFS model rats, indicating reduced fatigue severity after treatment.
Electroacupuncture reversed the CFS-model-induced increase in open field test grid-crossing and center-area entering, indicating reduced anxiety-like behavior after treatment.
Electroacupuncture reversed the prolonged escape latency in the Morris water maze navigation task seen in CFS model rats, indicating improved learning ability.
Hippocampal phosphoproteomic profiling identified 297 differentially expressed phosphopeptides between control and CFS model rats (48 up-regulated, 249 down-regulated).
Proteomic comparison between control and model groups identified 297 differentially expressed phosphorylated peptide segments, with 48 up-regulated and 249 down-regulated in the model group.
Comparison between the EA group and model group identified 245 differentially expressed phosphorylated peptide segments, with 185 up-regulated and 60 down-regulated after EA treatment.
Twenty-five overlapping differentially expressed peptide segments, corresponding to 24 proteins mainly involved in cytoskeletal structure, were reversed by EA treatment.

GO biological process enrichment showed that the top differentially expressed phosphorylated proteins affected by EA were involved in actin filament polymerization, protein depolymerization, and cytoskeletal organization.
GO molecular function enrichment showed EA-affected phosphorylated proteins were involved in actin binding, structural molecule activity, and cytoskeletal protein binding.
GO cellular component enrichment showed EA-affected phosphorylated proteins localized to the cytoskeleton, dendrites, and dendritic trees.

KEGG pathway annotation analysis showed that insulin secretion, axon guidance, the phosphatidylinositol signaling system, and lysine biosynthesis pathways were involved in the effect of EA intervention on hippocampal phosphorylated proteins.
Endoscopy revealed linear esophageal stretch marks (striae) that distended and collapsed with respiration, proposed as a novel endoscopic sign of hypermobile EDS.

High-resolution esophageal manometry showed ineffective esophageal motility per Chicago Classification 4.0, with more than 70% ineffective swallows including fragmented swallows, failed peristalsis, and weak contractions.
The patient was diagnosed with postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and migraine following neurologic workup, co-occurring with her hypermobile EDS diagnosis.

Physical examination showed multiple classic h-EDS features including a Beighton score of 7/9, atrophic scars, hyperextensible skin, thigh stretch marks, and piezogenic papules, supporting the clinical diagnosis of h-EDS despite negative genetic testing.
Hypermobile children showed significantly better lower extremity functional strength (FSM) scores compared to children with normal mobility.
No significant differences were found between hypermobile and normal mobility children on the upper limb items of the FSM.

Children with normal mobility had significantly higher isometric strength of the knee extensors and ankle extensors/flexors than children with hypermobility, while grip strength did not differ between groups.

Children with normal mobility reached significantly further than hypermobile children on the Y-Balance test in posteromedial and posterolateral directions, but no difference was found in the anterior direction.
No significant differences in proprioception (assessed via wedges heel-height discrimination test) were found between hypermobile and normal mobility children.
Pain reporting (18% of children overall) was not significantly associated with joint hypermobility status.

Moderate partial correlations (controlling for age) were found between Y-balance reaching distance and isometric strength of knee and ankle muscles, and with upper extremity explosive power (throw) items of FSM, but lower extremity items (long jump, sit to stand) were not significantly correlated with Y-balance.

The prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility (GJH) using a strict Beighton cut-off of ≥6 was 31% in this Nigerian pediatric sample, higher than previously reported in Caucasian populations despite the stricter cutoff.
Exome sequencing identified a novel pathogenic variant in the CHST14 gene in two Indian siblings clinically diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, confirming musculocontractural EDS (MC-EDS).
The affected siblings presented clinically with craniofacial dysmorphism and distal arthrogryposis, consistent with the musculocontractural subtype of EDS.
Among women with vEDS included in the pooled sample, 30% were infertile.
The pooled miscarriage rate among vEDS pregnancies was 13.8% (57/412).
8.8% of live births to women with vEDS were premature.
Obstetric anal sphincter injuries occurred in 11.3% (23/203) of deliveries in women with vEDS.
The maternal mortality rate per pregnancy in women with vEDS was 5.7%.
Women with vEDS have an elevated risk of uterine rupture, vascular events, digestive events, and death during pregnancy, with the peripartum period being highest risk.
The review recommends scheduling a caesarean section at 37 weeks of gestation to avoid expulsive efforts in women with vEDS.
Women with vEDS have an elevated risk of digestive complications during pregnancy.
The authors recommend scheduling a caesarean section at 37 weeks of gestation to avoid expulsive efforts and peripartum risks in women with vEDS.
Women with vEDS appear to be at greatest risk of complications during the peripartum period.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 gene encoding type III collagen, leading to arterial fragility and predisposition to aneurysm, dissection, or rupture.
The median survival age in patients with vascular EDS is 51 years, with vascular complications being the most common cause of death.
In this vEDS patient, myocardial infarction was caused by spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) involving the left main and left anterior descending arteries.

Percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents in this vEDS patient resulted in iatrogenic complications, including coronary rupture, cardiac tamponade, and aortic dissection, ultimately leading to death.
The patient had a family history of vEDS-related vascular events: his father died suddenly and his brother had vEDS with ischemic heart disease and survived a splenic artery rupture.

The authors recommend that patients with vascular EDS presenting with acute coronary syndrome be immediately transferred to hospitals with cardiac surgery capability given the high risk of vascular complications during endovascular procedures.
The authors suggest that a baseline CT scan prior to coronary angiography could help exclude concomitant vascular dissections and inform treatment planning in vEDS patients with ACS.

Surgical treatment for secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in heritable connective tissue disorders was associated with significantly lower rates of readmission for recurrent pneumothorax compared with nonsurgical management.
Younger age was identified as a risk factor associated with a higher likelihood of pneumothorax recurrence in patients with heritable connective tissue disorders.
Patients with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome had a higher risk of pneumothorax recurrence compared with other heritable connective tissue disorder groups.

The typical age of pneumothorax occurrence differed by underlying heritable connective tissue disorder, being most frequent in teenagers with Marfan syndrome, ages 20-39 with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and ages 40 and older with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome.
A case of a patient presenting with bruising and joint hypermobility highlights the need to consider genetic testing for underlying platelet disorders in such presentations.
38.8% of the 67 college-aged female participants were classified as having generalized joint hypermobility (GJH) based on a Beighton score of ≥5.
Left foot posture (measured via FPI-6) was significantly more often altered (pronated) in participants with GJH (61.5%) compared to those without GJH (31.7%).
Right foot posture was significantly more often altered (pronated) in participants with GJH (73.1%) than those without GJH (39%).
Participants with GJH showed significantly better flexibility (longer sit-and-reach distances) than those without GJH.
Participants with GJH had worse static balance (more attempts needed to maintain position in the flamingo balance test) than those without GJH.
Handgrip strength did not differ significantly between participants with and without GJH.
Explosive strength (standing broad jump distance) did not differ significantly between participants with and without GJH.
Participants with GJH showed significantly worse back muscle static strength endurance than those without GJH.
Abdominal muscle static strength endurance did not differ significantly between participants with and without GJH.
Health-related quality of life, as measured by the SF-36 across all domains, did not differ significantly between participants with and without GJH.
Single-level ACDF at C5-C6 significantly reduced flexion/extension range of motion at the fused level.
No significant change in range of motion was observed at the immediately adjacent C4-C5 segment following C5-C6 ACDF.
No significant change in range of motion was observed at the immediately adjacent C6-C7 segment following C5-C6 ACDF.
In one-third of specimens, compensatory hypermobility after ACDF occurred exclusively at adjacent segments.
In two-thirds of specimens, compensatory hypermobility after ACDF occurred at noncontiguous (nonadjacent) segments rather than adjacent ones.
Hypermobility occurred in 42% of adjacent segments evaluated after ACDF.
Hypermobility occurred in 28% of noncontiguous segments evaluated after ACDF.
Hypermobility occurred most frequently at the cervicothoracic segments (50%, 3 of 6) compared with adjacent (42%) and noncontiguous (28%) segments after single-level ACDF.
Scoliosis is the predominant skeletal complication of Osteogenesis Imperfecta, affecting between 25% and 80% of patients.
Vertebral deformities in OI scoliotic curves include codfish and wedge-shaped vertebrae, platyspondyly, craniocervical junction abnormalities, and lumbosacral spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis.
BMD Z-score measurements show a significant reduction indicating osteoporosis in OI, correlating with progression of scoliotic curves.

Factors such as increased mechanical strains, joint hypermobility, lower leg length discrepancy, pelvic obliquity, spinal ligament hypermobility, and vertebral microfractures may contribute to the severity of scoliosis in OI.
Histological vertebral analysis in OI confirms changes in trabecular microarchitecture associated with inadequate bone turnover, reflecting generalized bone metabolic defects.
Upregulation of TGFβ signaling in OI is proposed to disturb bone turnover and alter muscle mass and strength.
Pectus excavatum is reported to frequently co-occur with heritable connective tissue disorders and joint hypermobility.
Rib flare in pectus excavatum is proposed to result from diaphragmatic anomalies producing posterior traction on the sternum.
Forced vital capacity (percent predicted) improved substantially from baseline to treatment #7 during the OMT course.
Forced expiratory volume in one second (percent predicted) improved from baseline to treatment #7 during the OMT course.
The FEV1/FVC ratio remained essentially unchanged across the OMT treatment course despite absolute increases in FEV1 and FVC.
Resting respiratory rate decreased markedly over the course of OMT treatment.
Chest wall maximal excursion (diaphragm, sternal angle, and xiphoid process) increased from baseline to treatment #14 following OMT.
Abdominal wall maximal excursion at the umbilicus increased with OMT, while the lower rib angle remained unchanged.

By the 14th OMT treatment the patient reported improvement in chest wall pain, exertional dyspnea, and cough, alongside resolution of thoracic kyphosis and a type I group curve and significant improvement in sternal and diaphragmatic mobility.
At 10-month follow-up after completing the 14-week OMT course, chest pain improvement was sustained, but cough and dyspnea on exertion returned at decreased severity.
Rib-raising technique is reported to transiently increase and then produce a longer-lasting inhibitory effect on sympathetic nervous system activity, per a cited pilot study.

Exercise intolerance in pectus excavatum is proposed to primarily reflect cardiovascular compression of the anterior chest wall reducing cardiac output, rather than reduced lung capacity, consistent with limited pulmonary gains despite symptomatic improvement in this patient.
Pain threshold for Aδ-fiber stimulation was similar between fibromyalgia groups and controls.
Perceived pain (VAS) on Aδ-fiber stimulation at the knee was increased in both FM subgroups compared to controls.
The presence of ULEPs (C-fiber cortical responses) differed significantly across the three groups, being least frequent in the abnormal-biopsy FM group.
None of the 13 patients with abnormal skin biopsy showed ULEPs upon foot stimulation, significantly differing from controls.

At the hand, Aδ N2 amplitude was slightly reduced centrally in FM patients with normal biopsy, while FM patients with abnormal biopsy showed reduced N2 and P2 amplitude over fronto-central and parietal electrodes compared to controls.
ULEP amplitude at the hand was reduced at the vertex in FMN patients and over parietal/frontal regions in AFM patients compared to controls.
Knee stimulation showed reduced centro-parietal N2 amplitude in FMN patients and diffuse N2 and P2 amplitude reduction in AFM patients compared to controls.
ULEPs elicited by knee stimulation were reduced over centro-frontal leads in the AFM group compared to controls, with no significant difference in the FMN group.
Foot stimulation produced a reduced P2 amplitude in bilateral central leads in AFM patients compared to controls.
ULEPs from foot stimulation were completely absent in the AFM group and reduced in a limited central/parietal zone in the FMN group.
Fibromyalgia patients with reduced IENFD (AFM) had significantly higher WPI scores and longer disease duration than those with normal skin biopsy (NFM).
A significant correlation was found between the amplitude of knee-evoked ULEPs and fatigue severity measured by the MAF scale in the fibromyalgia sample.
No significant correlation was found between IENFD values and LEP/ULEP latencies and amplitudes.
Heat threshold appeared slightly increased in FM patients with small fiber involvement at hand and knee, but this did not reach statistical significance.
Absence of LEPs at stimulation sites was more common in AFM patients (30.7%) than NFM patients (7.6%), though the difference was not statistically significant.
The presence of small fiber involvement (abnormal IENFD) did not correspond to a more severe overall fibromyalgia clinical phenotype, consistent with prior studies.
Structured, personalised exercise programmes starting with low demand and gradually progressing improve compliance, reduce adverse effects, and mitigate core pathogenetic mechanisms of fibromyalgia.
Regular physical activity in fibromyalgia patients also confers benefits for preventing other chronic diseases and promoting healthy ageing and general well-being.
Effective fibromyalgia management requires a patient-centred approach integrating both pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments, with exercise playing a pivotal role.
The reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model showed important mitochondrial dysfunction in the central nervous system.
Oral Boswellia serrata (100 mg/kg for 21 days) reduced pain-like behaviors in reserpine-injected rats.
BS treatment reduced astrocyte activation in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and prefrontal cortex of the fibromyalgia model.
BS administration increased nuclear PGC-1α expression in spinal cord and brain tissues.
BS increased expression of NRF-1, a regulatory gene for mitochondrial biogenesis, in spinal cord and brain.
BS increased Tfam expression, supporting mitochondrial biogenesis in the CNS of the fibromyalgia model.
BS increased UCP2 expression, part of the mitochondrial biogenesis regulatory response in CNS tissues.
Boswellia serrata treatment increased SOD activity in spinal cord and brain tissue of reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model rats.
BS administration mitigated cytochrome-c leakage from mitochondria, indicating improved mitochondrial function.
BS supported nuclear translocation of PGC-1α protein, restoring mitochondrial quality control mechanisms.
BS reduced expression of Drp1 and Fis1, preventing excessive mitochondrial fission and cell death in the fibromyalgia model.
BS increased expression of Mfn2 protein, facilitating mitochondrial fusion in the fibromyalgia model.
Women with fibromyalgia reported higher levels of depression than healthy control participants.
Women with fibromyalgia reported higher levels of anxiety than healthy control participants.
Women with fibromyalgia demonstrated lower levels of body appreciation compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia had a significant indirect effect on depression through self-criticism, mediated in a serial pathway from body appreciation.

Self-compassion significantly moderated the relationship between body appreciation and self-criticism, such that the indirect effect of FM on depression through body appreciation and self-criticism was significant only at lower levels of self-compassion.
Fibromyalgia had a significant indirect effect on anxiety through self-criticism.
The moderated mediation effect of FM on anxiety via body appreciation and self-criticism was significant only at lower levels of self-compassion.
Age and having children were not significantly correlated with depression when tested separately within each group, ruling them out as confounding variables.

Mast cell counts (CD117+ staining) in capsules of breast implant illness (BII) patients were significantly higher than in non-BII implant patients (CG1) and healthy prophylactic mastectomy breast tissue (CG2).

Non-BII implant patients (CG1) who did not self-identify as having BII nevertheless had higher capsule mast cell counts than healthy prophylactic mastectomy tissue (CG2), mirroring their intermediate symptom scores.
BII patients showed a statistically significant, rapid, and sustained reduction in symptom questionnaire scores following explant surgery with total capsulectomy.
Non-BII implant patients (CG1), who did not believe they had BII preoperatively, also showed marked and significant improvement in BII symptom scores after explantation and capsulectomy.

Histological analysis found silicone fragments with associated giant cell reaction and granuloma formation in the majority of BII patient capsules despite no macroscopic implant rupture on preoperative imaging.

The authors propose that mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), a prevalent but underrecognized multisystem disease, may be an antecedent condition that is antigenically worsened by breast implant materials (particularly silicone), fundamentally underlying breast implant illness (BII).
MCAS is cited as having a preliminary estimated prevalence of 17%-20% in the general population, based on prior epidemiologic research.
MCAS is described as having a strong female predilection (approximately 4-5:1 female:male), possibly due to estrogen receptors on mast cells promoting activation upon ligand binding.
Between attacks, the patient's plasma prostaglandin D2 was elevated above the normal range, supporting an MCAS mediator abnormality.
Repeat serum tryptase drawn 6 hours after attack onset was normal, though the authors note it ideally should be checked within 4 hours for optimal sensitivity.

Oral imatinib 200 mg daily, started after his last hospitalization, prevented severe attacks requiring hospitalization, emergency department, or urgent care within 1 month, though mild attacks continued at home.

Identification and avoidance of prolonged occupational paint fume exposure led to complete cessation of attacks, with maintained remission of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, heartburn, and cognitive dysfunction for 2 years after retirement.

A 2-year regimen of standard oral MC-directed therapies (gluten/dairy-free diet, H1/H2 blockers, vitamins C and D, quercetin, low-dose naltrexone, aspirin, cromolyn, and lorazepam) provided minimal benefit in this patient.
Two courses of rifaximin given 18 months apart for presumed small intestinal bacterial overgrowth reduced gas symptoms and appeared to temporarily reduce the frequency of attacks.

A standardized intravenous regimen of diphenhydramine 50 mg, famotidine 20 mg, methylprednisolone 40 mg, and lorazepam 1 mg reduced the severity of and/or aborted attacks when given in the emergency department, urgent care, or hospital.

The patient fulfilled consensus-2 diagnostic criteria for MCAS based on symptoms in 2 or more systems (gastrointestinal, dermatologic, neuropsychiatric), an abnormal mast cell mediator (prostaglandin D2), and ultimate response to MC-directed therapy.

In a retrospective cohort of 23 drug-refractory MCAS patients treated with imatinib, 11 had clinical improvement and remained on maintenance therapy for up to 4 years, with benefits including gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, bone pain, myalgia, flushing, migraines, and reduced anaphylaxis; one jejunal-tube-dependent patient returned to an oral diet.
Six of the 23 imatinib-treated MCAS patients did not improve and discontinued treatment.

Eight of the 23 imatinib-treated MCAS patients had adverse events (fatigue in 3, hand edema in 1, nausea in 2, headaches in 1, alopecia in 1, myalgias in 1, increased liver enzymes in 1), and 6 of these patients stopped therapy as a result.

In a gastroenterology cohort of 175 newly diagnosed MCAS patients with refractory GI symptoms, abdominal pain occurred in 86%, bloating in 68%, diarrhea in 65%, nausea in 63%, constipation in 63%, heartburn in 55%, and dysphagia in 33%.

In contrast, a hematology-based case series of 413 newly diagnosed MCAS patients with obscure multisystemic disorders reported nausea in 57%, heartburn in 50%, abdominal pain in 48%, alternating constipation/diarrhea in 36%, dysphagia in 35%, diarrhea in 27%, and constipation in 14%.

MCAS is described as a common mast cell activation disease with an estimated prevalence of 17%-20% in Western populations, in contrast to mastocytosis which is rare (incidence 0.89 cases/100,000 persons-per-year).
Vitamin K3 (VK3) inhibited Substance P-induced activation of LAD2 mast cells, reducing release of β-hexosaminidase, histamine, and cytokines.

In mouse models of cutaneous and systemic pseudo-allergy, VK3 inhibited Substance P-induced pseudo-allergic reactions and decreased serum histamine and TNF-α levels, with reduced skin mast cell degranulation.
Proteome microarray, biolayer interferometry, and immunoprecipitation showed that VK3 stably binds GAB1 protein in mast cells.

GAB1 knockdown via RNA interference in LAD2 cells prevented Substance P-induced β-hexosaminidase release, calcium mobilization, and cytoskeletal remodeling, indicating GAB1 is required for SP-induced mast cell activation.
VK3 directly binds to GAB1 and reduces its expression, thereby inhibiting Substance P-induced LAD2 cell activation.

In children with cerebral palsy and constipation, the osteopathic manipulative treatment home program (OMT-H) produced a significant reduction in Modified Constipation Assessment Scale (MCAS) scores as early as the first week of treatment.
In the abdominal massage home program (AMHP) group, a significant reduction in MCAS score was observed only at the end of Week 3, later than the OMT-H group.
When individual MCAS sub-parameters were compared, the OMT-H group showed improvement in more parameters (7 of 9) than the AMHP group (2 of 9).
After treatment, all children (9/9) in the OMT-H group no longer met Rome III criteria for constipation, a statistically significant resolution.
In the AMHP group, only 3 of 10 children were no longer diagnosed with constipation by Rome III criteria after treatment, which did not reach statistical significance.
Stool consistency, measured by the Bristol Stool Form Scale, returned to normal in 6 of 9 children in the OMT-H group at end of treatment, a significant change.
In the AMHP group, stool consistency normalized in 2 of 10 children, a borderline (non-significant) result.
The control group, which received no constipation intervention while continuing routine physical therapy, showed no change in constipation status.

At baseline, the majority of children with CP and constipation reported inability to pass stool (86%), rectal fullness/pressure (79%), abdominal pain/bloating (65%), high-volume stools (58%), and low-volume stools (37%).

Constipation occurred even in children with CP who were more independently ambulatory (GMFCS levels I-III, 76% of the sample), suggesting constipation in CP is multifactorial rather than solely due to immobilization.
Natural resolution of cow's milk allergy in children correlates with rising allergen-specific IgG levels, particularly IgG4.
Presence of peanut-specific IgG4 in patients who also have peanut-specific IgE is associated with oral tolerance to peanut.
After a 24-week peanut OIT regimen, 67.5% of participants could tolerate six times more peanut protein without dose-limiting symptoms than at baseline.
In a study of 29 subjects, peanut-specific IgG4 levels rose immediately after starting OIT, reaching statistical significance vs. baseline at three months and remaining elevated through study end.
OIT increases both the diversity and binding intensity of allergen-specific IgG epitope recognition, while IgE epitope specificity remains largely unchanged.
Depletion of IgG from IgE-deficient sensitized mouse sera abrogated its suppressive activity on mast cell activation, showing IgG mediates the inhibitory effect.
Post-OIT serum reduced basophil CD63 activation (indirect basophil activation test), and this suppressive effect was diminished when IgG was depleted from post-OIT sera.
Children receiving peanut OIT (vs. placebo) experienced a marked increase in peanut-specific IgA alongside peanut-specific IgG4.
IgA immune complexes bound to dendritic cells increased production of the immunomodulatory cytokines IL-10 and TGFβ, promoting T cell regulatory responses.
Food-allergic infants and mice show decreased fecal IgA and increased fecal IgE binding to commensal bacteria compared to non-allergic counterparts, indicating dysbiosis-linked antibody imbalance.
Oral administration of human-origin Clostridiales species protected Il4raF709 mice against food allergy, normalizing SIgA levels and suppressing IgE responses to gut commensals.
After 42 days of daily peanut exposure, peanut-specific IgA was detectable only at low levels or not at all in wild-type mice, challenging the idea that IgA reliably tracks natural tolerance.
In a cohort of 441 atopic children, fecal peanut-specific IgA in childhood was not a good predictor of protection from allergy later in life.

The IgG concentration needed to achieve 50% inhibition of IgE-mediated mast cell activation is more than 10-fold higher in FcγRIIb-deficient mast cells than in FcγRIIb-sufficient cells, confirming a steric-blockade component independent of the inhibitory receptor.

Antigen-specific IgG reduced LAMP-1 surface expression (a marker of mast cell degranulation) in FcγRIIb-sufficient BMMCs following IgE-mediated activation, but this inhibitory effect was lost in FcγRIIb-deficient BMMCs.
IgG colligation via FcγRIIb inhibited IgE-mediated secretion of proinflammatory cytokines CCL2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-13, and TNFα by mast cells, and this effect was lost in FcγRIIb-deficient cells.
Mice with a germline deletion of FcγRIIb experience more severe anaphylaxis in response to allergen challenge.

Antigen-specific IgG failed to suppress IgE-induced hypothermia (anaphylaxis surrogate) in mice with mast-cell-specific deletion of FcγRIIb, demonstrating that IgG's anti-anaphylactic effect depends specifically on mast-cell FcγRIIb expression.

RNA sequencing showed IgG:FcγRIIb selectively downregulates SYK-target transcripts (proinflammatory) induced by FcεRI activation, while STAT5a-associated pro-survival/homeostatic transcripts (e.g., MCL1, BCL2) remain unaffected.
Intravenous antigen-specific IgA pretreatment reduced hypothermia severity following oral allergen challenge compared to untreated mice in a passive sensitization model.
Antigen-specific IgA treatment considerably reduced serum MMCP-1 (a marker of mast cell degranulation) in response to oral allergen challenge.

Removal of calcium or desialylation of antigen-specific IgA abolished its binding to bone-marrow-derived mast cells and eliminated its ability to suppress IgE-mediated degranulation, showing IgA-MC binding is calcium- and sialic-acid-dependent.
Antigen-specific IgA inhibited phosphorylation of SYK following IgE-receptor crosslinking in mast cells, indicating a receptor-proximal inhibitory mechanism.

IgA-mediated inhibition of IgE-activated mast cells remains intact in mice lacking SIGN-R1, CD33, Siglec F, or FcγRIIb, indicating the receptor mediating IgA's inhibitory effect on mast cells is still unidentified.
Addition of antigen-specific IgA to sensitized mast cells completely suppressed production of proinflammatory cytokines IL-13, TNF-α, and IL-6 following IgE-mediated stimulation.

Il4raF709 mice with a disinhibited IL-4 receptor develop mast cell expansion in the small intestine, peanut sensitization, and anaphylaxis upon peanut challenge; these phenotypes are lost in mast-cell-deficient (KitW-sh) mice carrying the same mutation.
SYK inhibitor treatment of peanut-fed Il4raF709 mice significantly reduced peanut-specific Th2 cell responses and IgE levels while inducing robust peanut-specific FoxP3+ Treg expansion.

In a study of 29 subjects undergoing peanut OIT, peanut-specific IgG4 levels increased immediately after treatment start, reached statistical significance versus baseline at three months, and remained elevated through the end of the study.

During OIT, the allergen-specific IgG repertoire diversifies with an increase in the number of bound IgG epitopes and increased binding intensity to many pre-existing epitopes, while IgE epitope specificity remains largely unchanged.
IgG epitopes that emerge during OIT overlap with pre-existing IgE epitopes down to the amino acid level.
In a 24-week peanut OIT regimen, 67.5% of participants tolerated ingesting six times more peanut protein without dose-limiting symptoms than at treatment start.

Sera from IgE-deficient, OIT-treated Il4raF709 mice suppressed OVA-induced activation of bone marrow-derived mast cells, and this suppression was abolished by depleting IgG from the sera, implicating IgG as the suppressive factor.

Using an indirect basophil activation test, serum from peanut-allergic patients after OIT reduced basophil CD63 activation compared with pre-OIT sera, and this suppressive effect was diminished when IgG was depleted from post-OIT sera.

The IgG concentration required to achieve 50% inhibition of IgE-mediated activation was more than 10-fold higher for mast cells lacking FcγRIIb, demonstrating both a steric-blocking effect independent of FcγRIIb and a much more potent FcγRIIb-dependent inhibitory mechanism.
Antigen-specific IgG treatment reduced surface LAMP-1 expression (a marker of degranulation) on IgE-activated FcγRIIb-sufficient BMMCs, but this inhibitory effect was absent in BMMCs lacking FcγRIIb.
IgG colligation via FcγRIIb inhibits IgE-mediated secretion of proinflammatory cytokines (CCL2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-13, TNFα) from mast cells, an effect lost in FcγRIIb-deficient BMMCs.
Mice with germline deletion of FcγRIIb experience more severe anaphylaxis in response to allergen challenge compared to FcγRIIb-sufficient mice.

In a murine food allergy model, IgG administration decreased serum IL-4 levels and mast cell burden and increased Treg frequency post-challenge in WT mice, but these effects were absent in FcγRIIb-deficient mice, where Treg frequencies were instead reduced.

In a murine model of passive systemic anaphylaxis, antigen-specific IgG failed to suppress IgE-induced hypothermia in mice with a mast cell-specific deletion of FcγRIIb, confirming that IgG suppression of anaphylaxis depends specifically on mast cell-expressed FcγRIIb.

RNA sequencing of BMMCs showed that IgG:FcγRIIb selectively downregulates SYK-target transcripts (proinflammatory cytokines/chemokines/growth factors) induced by IgE-receptor crosslinking, while STAT5a-associated pro-survival transcripts (including MCL1 and BCL2) remain unaffected.

In a passive sensitization mouse model, intravenous antigen-specific IgA pretreatment reduced hypothermia severity and reduced serum levels of mast cell protease MMCP-1 following oral allergen challenge compared to untreated mice.

Strait et al. found that the suppressive effect of antigen-specific IgA on anaphylaxis persisted in mice lacking the IgA receptor Fcα/μR, concluding that IgA protects via steric blockade rather than a receptor-mediated mechanism.

IgA binding to bone marrow-derived and peritoneal mast cells is dependent on extracellular calcium and on sialylation of the IgA antibody, since calcium removal or neuraminidase-mediated desialylation abolished IgA binding.

Desialylated antigen-specific IgA lost the ability to suppress IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation (measured by LAMP-1 surface expression), indicating sialylation is required both for IgA-mast cell binding and for its inhibitory function.
Antigen-specific IgA inhibits SYK phosphorylation following IgE-receptor crosslinking in BMMCs, indicating a receptor-proximal inhibitory effect on FcεRI signaling.

IgA-mediated inhibition of IgE-activated mast cells remained intact in mice with targeted deletions of the C-type lectin receptors SIGN-R1, CD33, and Siglec F, as well as in FcγRIIb-deficient mice, indicating none of these receptors are required for the IgA inhibitory effect.
Addition of antigen-specific IgA to sensitized BMMCs completely suppressed production of the proinflammatory cytokines IL-13, TNF-α, and IL-6 following stimulation.

In wild-type C57BL/6 mice fed peanut daily for 42 days, peanut-specific IgA was detectable at only low levels or not at all, challenging the assumption that IgA production accompanies natural tolerance.
In a cohort of 441 atopic children, the presence of fecal peanut-specific IgA in childhood was not a good predictor of protection from allergy later in life.

Food-allergic infants and mice showed decreased IgA and increased IgE binding to fecal bacteria compared to non-allergic controls, suggesting dysbiosis in food allergy is linked to reduced secretory IgA responses and heightened IgE responses to commensal flora.
Oral administration of human-origin Clostridiales species protected against food allergy in Il4raF709 mice, normalizing secretory IgA and suppressing IgE responses to gut commensals.

IgA immune-complexed to TNP/OVA protected against Th2 responses in the gut and lung, and IgA bound dendritic cells in vitro to increase production of the immunomodulatory cytokines IL-10 and TGFβ, promoting tolerance.
In a cohort of peanut-allergic children, those receiving peanut OIT experienced a marked increase in peanut-specific IgA and IgG4 compared to those receiving placebo OIT.

The prevalence of allergic symptoms among selective IgA deficiency (SIgAD) patients varies markedly across populations, with 45.7% of Turkish IgA-deficient patients showing eczema, asthma, rhinitis, or atopic dermatitis, versus 17% in a Chinese SIgAD cohort.
Low levels of salivary IgA are associated with allergic sensitization, allergic rhinitis, and atopic eczema, while high salivary IgA confers protection against allergy in sensitized infants.
High fecal IgA is associated with reduced risk of atopy.
pIgR-deficient mice lacking secretory IgA exhibit increased uptake of both food antigens and commensal intestinal bacteria across the epithelial surface.

IgA-deficient mice showed increased translocation of live commensal bacteria to the mesenteric adipose tissue compared to IgA-sufficient littermates, suggesting IgA restrains systemic anti-commensal IgG responses by preventing microbial translocation.
Mechanical stimulation (cyclic stretching) of human tenocytes induces release of substance P.
Substance P activates mast cells via the MRGPRX2 receptor, leading to mast cell degranulation and migration.
Mast cell degranulation (measured via beta-hexosaminidase activity) and migration increase in response to MRGPRX2 activation by substance P.
Mast cell activation causes human tenocytes to increase expression of inflammatory factors, matrix proteins, and matrix metalloproteinase enzymes.
Mast cells are more abundant in tendinopathy biopsies and at sites of tendon injury, particularly in patients with chronic symptom duration and history of intensive mechanical loading.
Uterine fibroid tissue had significantly higher numbers of NK cells compared with matched myometrium from the same patient.
Total macrophage numbers were significantly higher in fibroid tissue compared with matched myometrium.
M2 macrophage numbers were significantly higher in fibroid tissue than matched myometrium.
Conventional dendritic cell numbers were significantly higher in fibroid tissue compared with matched myometrium.
CD3+ T cells were significantly fewer in fibroid tissue compared with matched myometrium.
CD4+ T cells were significantly fewer in fibroid tissue compared with matched myometrium.
Mass cytometry showed no significant difference in the number of resting mast cells between fibroid tissue and matched myometrium.

Immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry confirmed a significantly higher number of tryptase-positive (activated) mast cells in uterine fibroids compared with matched myometrium, despite no difference in resting mast cell numbers by mass cytometry.
Cytokine assay showed significantly higher levels of human interferon α2 in uterine fibroid tissue compared with matched myometrium.
Cytokine assay showed significantly higher levels of IL-1α in uterine fibroid tissue compared with matched myometrium.
Cytokine assay showed significantly higher levels of platelet-derived growth factor AA in uterine fibroid tissue compared with matched myometrium.
Cytokine assay showed significantly lower levels of macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) in uterine fibroid tissue compared with matched myometrium.
Cytokine assay showed significantly lower levels of IL-1 receptor antagonist in uterine fibroid tissue compared with matched myometrium.
Peanut skin prick test (SPT) wheal size was significantly larger in peanut allergic (PA) children compared to peanut sensitised but tolerant (PS) children at 12 months, 36 months and 7-12 years.
Median peanut-specific IgE (sIgE) levels were significantly higher in the PA group compared to the PS group from 3 months of age onward.
Ara h 2-specific IgE was already significantly higher in PA children compared to PS children at 12 months of age and continued to increase and remain elevated through 36 months and 7-12 years.
Peanut allergic children had significantly higher Ara h 1-sIgE, Ara h 3-sIgE at all time points and Ara h 6-sIgE (measured only at 7-12 years) compared to peanut-sensitised tolerant children.

The percentage of CD63-positive LAD2 mast cells following peanut stimulation (mast cell activation test, MAT) was higher in the peanut allergic group at all time points compared to peanut-sensitised tolerant children.
In children with persistent peanut allergy, mast cell activation (MAT) was already detectable at 12 months of age and was highest at the 36-month time point.

In the two children who developed new peanut allergy after 36 months, mast cell activation (MAT) remained low at all time points despite rising sIgE levels, in contrast to persistent PA children who had elevated MAT from 12 months onward.

Children who developed new peanut allergy between 36 months and 7-12 years showed a significant increase in Ara h 8-specific IgE over that period, higher than the other three phenotype groups, possibly reflecting pollen cross-reactivity.

The single child who outgrew peanut allergy by 7-12 years showed decreasing peanut-sIgE beginning at 36 months (undetectable by 7-12 years) despite initially high SPT, and had low MAT at all time points, consistent with resolving allergy.
Peanut-specific IgG4:IgE ratio was significantly higher in peanut-sensitised tolerant (PS) children compared to peanut allergic (PA) children at 12 months, 36 months and 7-12 years.

Children with peanut allergy were significantly more likely to have a history of eczema, and to have eczema, asthma or allergic rhinitis at 7-12 years, compared to peanut-sensitised tolerant children.

In multivariable logistic regression models, no individual peanut biomarker (SPT, sIgE, Ara h 2-sIgE, MAT) was independently significantly associated with peanut allergy status at 7-12 years, likely due to high collinearity between biomarkers, although the models overall had excellent discriminatory power (ROC AUC ≥0.9).

The prevalence of peanut allergy in the EAT-On cohort at 7-12 years was 2.1% (20/947), similar to the 1.9% (22/1189) prevalence at the end of the original EAT study, and only 1/18-22 children (4.5-5.5%) outgrew their peanut allergy over the decade of follow-up.
Freshly extracted human lung mast cells failed to degranulate in response to IgE-crosslinking and required several days of resting culture before they could respond.
Culturing HLMCs in serum-free StemPro-34 SFM media resulted in significantly higher IgE-mediated degranulation than culturing in RPMI 1640 with either of two FBS batches.
FcεRI surface expression (MFI) was similar across the different culturing media conditions despite differing degranulation percentages.
Degranulation of HLMCs peaked at an anti-IgE concentration of 2 µg/mL.

At timepoints of 90 minutes down to 2 minutes of activation, cells crosslinked in StemPro-34 SFM media had substantially higher degranulation than those in PIPES-BSA buffer, while at 120 minutes there was no difference.
Pre-incubating HLMCs in PIPES-BSA buffer for 30 minutes prior to IgE crosslinking significantly lowered degranulation compared to crosslinking immediately after media change.
Surface expression of CD203c did not increase in degranulated HLMCs, indicating it is not a useful degranulation marker for these cells.
Surface expression of CD13 did not increase in degranulated HLMCs, indicating it is not a useful degranulation marker for these cells.

CD63 surface staining increased upon IgE crosslinking, reached maximum at 10 minutes, remained stable up to 120 minutes, and showed the clearest distinction between degranulated and non-degranulated HLMCs.
CD107a surface staining increased and peaked at 10 minutes after anti-IgE activation but began declining thereafter, indicating instability over time as a degranulation marker.
CD164 surface staining increased upon activation, peaked at 10 minutes, and remained stable up to 120 minutes, correlating well with CD63 as a degranulation marker.
Avidin staining increased and peaked at 10 minutes after anti-IgE activation but began declining thereafter, indicating instability over time.
Varying SCF concentration (10 ng/mL vs 100 ng/mL) during culture for 1 day showed no significant difference in HLMC degranulation.
Degranulation response was stable regardless of which day (within a 7-8 day culture cycle) after media change the IgE-crosslinking experiment was performed.

Pre-incubating HLMCs in fresh StemPro-34 SFM media for 30 minutes before IgE crosslinking significantly increased degranulation compared to activating immediately after media change, an effect independent of SCF or nutrient supplement presence.
Pre-incubating HLMCs in serum-free RPMI media for 30 minutes also increased degranulation to a similar extent as StemPro-34 SFM media.
Pre-incubating HLMCs in RPMI media with 10% serum significantly reduced degranulation compared to serum-free pre-incubation, suggesting an inhibitory factor present in serum.

HLMCs did not degranulate significantly in response to the MRGPRX2 agonist compound 48/80, consistent with prior reports that lung mast cells lack MRGPRX2 expression, whereas the LAD-2 mast cell line readily degranulated.
GSEA of IL-17-secreting PBMCs showed that the mast cell activation gene set was more strongly enriched in male AS patients than in female AS patients.
Multiple mast-cell-activation-associated genes (IL13, PTPN6, VAMP8, LAT2) were upregulated in IL-17-secreting PBMCs from male AS patients compared with female patients.

Among healthy control subjects, GSEA showed no sex difference in T-cell or mast-cell activation pathways despite differing IL-17 secretion levels, suggesting the AS patients' sex-specific mast cell/TCR signaling differences are disease-specific rather than baseline sex differences.
Deconvolution-based immune infiltration analysis showed CD4+ T cells constituted the majority of IL-17-secreting PBMCs in AS patients, followed by CD8+ T cells.
GSEA showed the TCR signaling pathway was more activated in female AS patients than males, with upregulation of PTPRC indicating stronger T-cell activation in females.
Immune infiltration analysis showed a decreased proportion of CD4+ T cells in AS patients compared with healthy controls, while CD8+ T cell infiltration did not differ significantly.

KEGG and GSEA analyses showed the TNF signaling pathway was the most enriched pathway and was significantly more activated in female AS patients, with TNF expression itself significantly increased in women.

Despite higher TNF pathway activation in female AS patients, this does not correlate with clinical TNF-inhibitor efficacy, which is reported to be lower in women, suggesting additional pathways (e.g., IL-17, Wnt) contribute to disease and treatment response.
GSEA showed pathways related to MTA3, the proteasome, NK cells, and NDK/dynamin were more highly activated in male AS patients compared with female patients.

GSEA showed male AS patients had greater enrichment of carbohydrate metabolism and oxidative phosphorylation pathway genes, including upregulated respiratory chain complex I-V genes, compared with female patients.
GSEA showed enrichment of upregulated fatty-acid-oxidation genes (PCK2, BDH2, ACADS, ECHDC2, ACAA1, AKT1, ABCD4, CRAT, ECH1) in male AS patients compared with female patients.

Compared with healthy male controls, male AS patients showed increased expression of oxidative phosphorylation genes, while fatty acid oxidation gene expression was unchanged, suggesting oxidative phosphorylation changes specifically contribute to AS onset.
Transcripts encoding the pro-inflammatory secreted proteins IL-6 and CCL24 were more highly expressed in female AS patients than in male patients.
Transcripts encoding osteogenesis-promoting secreted proteins FGF2, WNT, and DLL1 were highly expressed in male AS patients relative to female patients.
XGBoost machine learning modeling across five GEO datasets identified METRN and TMC4 among the top differentially expressed genes potentially explaining the higher incidence of AS in males.
DEGs CXCL5, MMP11, and CCL17, previously reported to promote inflammation, were identified as elevated secreted-protein-encoding genes in male AS patients via XGBoost feature-importance analysis.
DEGs WNT7A, WNT11, and FGF2, documented to enhance osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells, were elevated in male AS patients, implicating them in new bone formation pathogenesis.

CMAP analysis combined with prior literature suggested statins may attenuate CXCL5-driven inflammation and oxidative-phosphorylation-derived ROS, proposed as a possible mechanism underlying statin efficacy in AS treatment.
CMAP-based analysis and prior literature suggest ACE inhibitors such as benazepril may suppress CXCL5 production and ROS, potentially alleviating inflammation in AS patients.

Genes overexpressed in male AS patients were predominantly located on the Y chromosome, whereas genes with higher expression in female patients were more frequently located on chromosome 12 rather than the X chromosome.
Machine learning (XGBoost) identified CXCL5, MMP11, and CCL17 as pro-inflammatory secreted-protein-encoding genes elevated in IL-17-secreting cells from male AS patients.

WNT7A, WNT11, and FGF2, upregulated in male AS patients' secreted-protein gene set, have been documented to enhance osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells, a process central to new bone formation in AS.

The authors propose that statins could attenuate the pro-inflammatory effects of CXCL5 and reduce ROS from oxidative phosphorylation, potentially explaining reported therapeutic efficacy of statins in AS.
ACE inhibitors such as benazepril are proposed to suppress CXCL5 production and ROS, suggesting they may help alleviate inflammation in AS patients.
Hesperidin, a flavanone glycoside known to reduce intracellular ROS and cartilage destruction in osteoarthritis, is proposed as a potential agent to reduce cartilage damage in AS patients.

CMAP analysis identified alisertib, an aurora kinase inhibitor, as a candidate drug that may reduce ectopic bone formation in AS by promoting osteoblast apoptosis via mitochondrial and p38 MAPK/PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway inhibition.

CMAP analysis identified atorvastatin, an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor, as a candidate AS drug based on its reported ability to alleviate bone loss and aortic valve atherosclerosis in LDLR-deficient mice.
GNLY (granulysin), a saposin-like protein stored in T cell cytotoxic granules, was identified as a differentially expressed gene in IL-17-secreting cells with no prior reported connection to AS.

Despite higher transcriptomic TNF pathway activation in female AS patients, this does not correlate with TNF inhibitor efficacy, which is less pronounced in women, leading the authors to hypothesize that women might require higher TNF inhibitor dosages for therapeutic parity with men.
The authors propose that MTA3 signaling, more highly activated in male AS patients, may contribute to ligament osteogenesis by activating the Wnt signaling pathway.

The authors suggest that the observed stronger TCR-pathway activation in female AS patients and stronger mast cell activation in male AS patients may help explain the previously reported higher BASFI functional index in female AS patients.

The review describes small-fiber neuropathy, nerve compression syndromes, post-herpetic neuralgia, scars and burns as peripheral causes of neuropathic itch, and spinal cord lesions and stroke as central causes.

Neuropathic itch is characterized by onset on normal-appearing skin, association with pain and other dysesthesias, distribution following the affected somatosensory pathway, and relief with local cold application.
Diagnostic workup for neuropathic itch includes comprehensive medical history, skin biopsies to assess cutaneous neuromorphological alterations, and medical imaging to rule out nerve impingement.
Topical capsaicin and local anesthetics, along with systemic gabapentinoids, antidepressants, and opioid receptor modulators, are used to treat neuropathic itch.
Only 55% of surveyed healthcare providers reported excluding hypermobility during clinical assessment of possible bleeding disorders.
80% of respondents reported using bleeding assessment tools when evaluating possible bleeding disorders.
Among hemostatic tests, only prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time received universal support among survey respondents for evaluating BDUC.
Tranexamic acid was the preferred prophylactic agent for minor surgery (71%), major surgery (59%), and pregnancy (58%) in people with BDUC among surveyed providers.
Advice on treatment for active bleeding events (as opposed to prophylaxis) in people with BDUC was heterogeneous among surveyed healthcare providers.

Management of heavy menstrual bleeding in women with BDUC who fail combined oral contraceptive pill therapy was found to be challenging, with providers selecting multiple differing alternative strategies.

The vagus nerve innervates most of the digestive tract, is a key component of the microbiota-gut-brain axis, has anti-inflammatory and prokinetic properties, modulates intestinal permeability, and shows capacity for plasticity and regeneration.
Lymphocytic ganglionitis (immune-mediated inflammation of enteric ganglia) is observed in about 30% of patients with chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction.
Low cardiac vagal tone correlates with gut dysmotility, and in type 1 diabetes patients low vagal tone is associated with increased gastric motility index and colonic transit time.
Vagally-mediated cephalic stimulation via chewing gum can normalize meal-induced antral motility in functional dyspepsia, suggesting hypomotility is due to insufficient vagal activation.
Butyrate protects intestinal barrier function via upregulation of tight junction protein claudin-1 and inhibition of histone deacetylases, and can directly act on vagal afferents.
Acetylcholine mediates the vagal anti-inflammatory reflex by binding alpha7 nicotinic ACh receptors on macrophages, dampening release of TNF, IL-6, and IL-1beta but not IL-10.
In 16 healthy volunteers, brief noninvasive transcutaneous auricular VNS consistently reduced paracellular small intestinal permeability increased by CRF administration.

Enteric glial cells protect the epithelial barrier against bacterial injury by increasing occludin and ZO-1 tight junction protein expression via release of S-nitrosoglutathione, and inflammation is decreased by VNS only in areas with intact EGCs.

In chronic constipation, there is a significant decrease in size/number of enteric ganglia, decreased amounts of EGCs and neurons, lymphocyte invasion, decreased interstitial cells of Cajal, neuronal dysplasia, and reduced expression of VIP and Substance P.

A 4-week course of noninvasive cervical VNS improved cardinal symptoms and gastric emptying in patients with idiopathic gastroparesis, without restoring overall autonomic function but modulating reflex parasympathetic activity.

In patients with severe drug-refractory gastroparesis (idiopathic, diabetic, postsurgical), noninvasive cervical VNS achieved a 35% response rate at 3 weeks and 43% by 3-6 weeks, with improvement in gastroparesis cardinal symptom index scores and no severe adverse events.
Compared with sham stimulation, taVNS increased the number of complete spontaneous bowel movements per week in IBS patients, with vagal activity weakly correlated with bowel movement frequency.
In a pilot study of nine IBS women, 6 months of taVNS decreased colonic transit time in all but two patients.

In a randomized double-blind pilot study of Parkinson's disease patients with GI complaints, taVNS improved GI symptom rating scale scores versus sham but did not significantly alter gastric emptying measured by 13C-octanoic acid breath test.
In patients with systemic sclerosis, taVNS significantly reduced chronic (including abdominal) pain compared to active control.
In systemic lupus erythematosus patients, taVNS increased vagal tone and, in a randomized double-blind sham-controlled pilot trial, decreased pain and fatigue.

In a pilot study of invasive VNS in 9 Crohn's disease patients naïve to biologics, at 6 months five of seven included patients achieved clinical, biological, and endoscopic remission with normalization of vagal tone.

At 1 year in 9 Crohn's disease patients treated with invasive VNS, five and six of nine were in clinical and endoscopic remission respectively, with decreased CRP and fecal calprotectin, normalized vagal tone in seven of nine, and altered IL-6, IL-12, IL-23, and TNF cytokine profiles.

In a 16-week open-label multicenter pilot study of invasive VNS in 16 patients with moderately-to-severely active, biologic-refractory Crohn's disease, there was a significant decrease in clinical index of activity, fecal calprotectin, mucosal inflammation, and blood cytokines at week 16, with quality of life improvement in patients treated without biologics; VNS was well tolerated and safe.
Low vagal tone is a pro-inflammatory state associated with increased circulating TNF.
In a rodent model, taVNS improved opioid-induced constipation by increasing colonic motility and re-establishing enteric neuronal function through central and vagal efferent pathways.
taVNS improves constipation in IBS patients, in whom low-grade infiltration of lymphocytes was observed in myenteric ganglia.
Vagus nerve atrophy has been detected ultrasonographically in Parkinson's disease patients, which can be used as a marker of vagal neuronal lesion or neuropathy.

Pyridostigmine, a peripheral acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, enhances HRV and vagal tone in normal and spontaneously hypertensive rats, and in a myocardial infarction model increased parasympathetic tone and lowered the M1/M2 macrophage ratio toward an anti-inflammatory profile with decreased TNF in heart and spleen.

Galantamine, a cholinesterase inhibitor and nicotinic receptor agonist, decreases circulating TNF and IL-6 and improves survival in a murine endotoxemia model, but has only been used experimentally, not clinically.

Activated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (aPBMC) or their secretome induced adipose stromal cells (ASC) to upregulate smooth muscle/myofibroblast markers alpha smooth muscle actin (αSMA), SM22α, and Calponin I, along with increased contractility.
IL-1β alone was sufficient to replicate the aPBMC-induced myofibroblast phenotype in ASC, and blocking IL-1β eliminated the effects of aPBMC.
ASC-derived Activin A (ActA) stimulated connective tissue growth factor (CTGF) and αSMA expression in ASC, with the αSMA effect being independent of CTGF.
Induction of αSMA in ASC by IL-1β or Activin A-enriched media depended on extracellular enzymatic activity, indicating ActA requires extracellular processing to exert its effect.

Activin A upregulated mRNA levels of several extracellular matrix proteins in ASC, though to a lesser extent than TGF-beta, and only marginally increased cell contractility, suggesting weak fibrotic activity.
Genetically predicted insomnia was causally associated with an increased risk of chronic widespread pain using Mendelian randomization.
Genetically predicted short sleep duration (≤6 hours per 24 hours) was causally associated with an increased risk of chronic widespread pain.
There was no evidence supporting a causal association between long sleep duration and risk of chronic widespread pain.
There was no evidence supporting a causal association between chronotype (morning vs evening preference) and risk of chronic widespread pain.
There was limited evidence for reverse causation, i.e. chronic widespread pain causing insomnia or short sleep duration.
ME/CFS patients had significantly higher plasma NfL levels than healthy controls, even after adjusting for age and sex.
ROC curve analysis showed plasma NfL alone had limited discriminative ability for distinguishing ME/CFS patients from healthy controls.
Plasma NfL levels increased significantly with age in both ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, with a steeper increase in HC than in patients.

ME/CFS patients showed significantly worse cognitive performance than HC across general cognition, verbal fluency, processing speed, attention, verbal memory, visual memory, visuospatial perception, and abstraction.
ME/CFS patients reported significantly greater fatigue, poorer general health, worse sleep quality, and more severe depressive, anxiety, and suicidal ideation symptoms than HC.
ME/CFS patients had significantly greater autonomic symptom burden on the COMPASS-31 questionnaire than HC, even after adjusting for age and sex.
Cardiovascular autonomic testing showed abnormal heart rate responses in ME/CFS patients at rest and during tilt table testing, with 31.3% meeting diagnostic criteria for POTS.
No significant differences were found between ME/CFS patients and HC in sympathetic (Valsalva maneuver) and parasympathetic (deep breathing) responsiveness tests.

ME/CFS patients showed significantly greater small fiber neuropathy symptoms and objective evidence of impaired heat detection, including increased CHEP latencies and higher heat pain thresholds on QST, compared to HC.

Higher plasma NfL levels correlated with worse cognitive performance in ME/CFS patients, including processing speed, verbal memory, visual memory, visuoconstructive ability, and total cognitive score.
No significant correlations were found between plasma NfL levels and cognitive performance in healthy controls, in contrast to the ME/CFS group.
In ME/CFS patients, higher plasma NfL levels correlated with greater autonomic symptom burden (COMPASS-31) and worse parasympathetic function (deep breathing index and E/I ratio).

Higher NfL levels in ME/CFS patients were associated with lower extracellular cardiac volume, higher total peripheral resistance, worse palmar electrochemical skin conductance, and worse cold detection thresholds.
In healthy controls, higher plasma NfL levels correlated with higher systolic and diastolic blood pressure, lower extracellular cardiac volume, and higher total peripheral resistance.
No statistically significant correlations were found between plasma NfL levels and neuropathy indicator variables.

ME/CFS patients with pathological NfL levels (>15 pg/mL) showed significantly worse parasympathetic function (deep breathing index, E/I ratio) and reduced extracellular cardiac volume compared to those with normal NfL levels.

Stepwise linear regression identified age, years of education, anxiety symptoms, and NfL levels as predictors of cognitive performance in ME/CFS; NfL alone explained up to 17.2% of cognitive test variance in patients but had no significant contribution to cognition in HC.
