During the second half of the second SDMT task block, healthy controls showed a decline in BOLD signal (BOLD adaptation) whereas ME/CFS patients showed no such decline, resulting in significantly higher BOLD responses in ME/CFS in bilateral pre/postcentral gyrus, inferior parietal lobule, and right superior temporal gyrus.

BOLD response changes in the left pre- and post-central gyrus during the second half of the second task block were significantly associated with long-term (past 6-month) fatigue severity scores, controlling for age, sex, BMI, depression, and anxiety.

No significant relationship was found between the absence of BOLD adaptation and current fatigue levels as measured by the Fatigue State Questionnaire (FSQ), unlike the correlation seen with long-term fatigue severity.
An initial multiple regression analysis found no significant correlations between overall SDMT-related BOLD changes and behavioural measures in either the ME/CFS or HC group.
ME/CFS participants achieved similar SDMT accuracy to healthy controls but required significantly more time to respond correctly.

Learning effects differed between groups: ME/CFS patients' accuracy and response time improvements plateaued after the second set of trials in Block 1, whereas HCs' response time improvements (learning effect) continued into the first set of Block 2.

Within-group analysis showed ME/CFS patients tended to recruit broader brain areas in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and left somatosensory cortex than HCs during the SDMT, though the formal between-group comparison was not statistically significant.

Citing prior studies, the authors note impaired Ca2+-mobilisation has been observed in ME/CFS, supporting their postulation that impaired glutamate-Ca2+ neurovascular coupling pathways underlie the absent BOLD adaptation.

A sensitivity analysis including all 54 diagnosed ME/CFS patients (versus the matched 34) showed similar within-group BOLD activation patterns but slightly larger activated brain areas, while between-group comparisons versus HCs remained unchanged.
Anti-flagellin antibody responses were significantly overrepresented in patients with Crohn's disease compared to matched healthy controls (HC-NL).
Anti-flagellin antibody responses were significantly overrepresented in patients with ME/CFS compared to matched healthy controls (HC-UK).
Anti-flagellin antibody response patterns were highly concordant between patients with CD and patients with ME/CFS, though a distinct subset of peptides was more prevalent in ME/CFS.

A distinct set of anti-flagellin antibody responses, almost exclusively targeting pathogenic bacteria (e.g., Salmonella enterica, E. coli O157:H7, Shigella flexneri, Shigella sonnei, Listeria monocytogenes, Legionella pneumophila, Yersinia enterocolitica), was more commonly present in ME/CFS patients than in CD patients.
Anti-flagellin antibody response patterns were highly concordant between the two independent matched healthy control cohorts (HC-NL and HC-UK) despite differing geography and sample size.

In CD patients, highly overrepresented antibody-bound flagellin peptides (>15-fold vs. HC-NL) were more commonly directed against the C-terminal region of the flagellin protein, whereas overall responses targeted both N- and C-terminal regions.

C-terminal domain-directed antibody responses in CD were exclusively directed toward flagellins from commensal Lachnospiraceae bacteria (Roseburia, Clostridium, Butyrivibrio) and Eubacterium, not pathogens.
In ME/CFS patients, unlike CD, highly overrepresented antibody-bound flagellin peptides did not show a preferential N- or C-terminal binding region relative to matched controls.

Full-length antibody-bound flagellin sequences overrepresented in both CD and ME/CFS showed significantly higher sequence similarity to stimulator- and silent-type flagellins than to evader-type flagellins.

N-terminal domains of antibody-bound flagellins overrepresented in both CD and ME/CFS closely resembled stimulator- and silent-type flagellin N-terminal (TLR5 motif-containing) domains but not evader-type domains.
In CD, C-terminal domains of antibody-bound flagellins showed significantly higher resemblance to stimulator-type than to silent-type flagellin reference sequences.
In ME/CFS, C-terminal domains of antibody-bound flagellins showed similar resemblance to both stimulator- and silent-type flagellin reference sequences, unlike the CD-specific stimulator preference.

A distinct subset of antibody-bound flagellins, exclusively found in 10-20% of CD patients and overrepresented more than 20-fold, was identified, suggesting a potential CD pathophysiologic subtype not seen in ME/CFS.

Using a broader set of 44 reference flagellins, the C-terminal domain similarity difference between stimulator- and silent-type classification was significant in both CD and ME/CFS, but approximately 1000-fold more statistically significant in CD.

Flagellins present in the antigen library but NOT bound by antibodies in either patients or controls ('unbound' flagellins) showed no significant sequence similarity difference between stimulator- and evader-type classes, in contrast to the pattern seen for antibody-bound flagellins, indicating the disease-associated pattern is not simply a library-composition artifact.

Citing two prior microbiome studies, the authors note reduced abundance of Lachnospiraceae bacteria and reduced short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) levels in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, raising the hypothesis that anti-flagellin antibodies could contribute to reduced abundance of these SCFA-producing commensals.
Functional disorders (fibromyalgia, ME/CFS, IBS) and internalizing disorders (MDD, GAD) were found to be highly comorbid, with odds ratios ranging from 3.2 to 12.6.
The strength of comorbidity associations between functional disorders and internalizing disorders differed by sex, being stronger among men than women.
Individuals with three or more comorbid disorders/diagnoses among the assessed FDs and IDs occurred more often than would be expected by chance based on observed-to-expected frequency ratios.
Most PACVS patients met symptom criteria for more than one dysautonomia syndrome (ME/CFS, POTS, MCAS, SFN), with only a minority uniquely assignable to a single syndrome or none.
Hierarchical Jaccard clustering of symptoms identified eight clusters, with cluster 3 (chronic fatigue and malaise) representing a near-universal, cross-cohort symptomatology in PACVS.
Serum IL-6 was elevated above reference range in 60% of PACVS study participants.
Serum IL-8 (free or total) was elevated in the large majority of PACVS patients, with a third showing >100-fold increases.
PACVS patients showed increased angiotensin II type 1 receptor autoantibodies compared to the normal post-vaccination state, as previously reported by the authors.
PACVS patients showed decreased alpha-2B adrenergic receptor autoantibodies compared to the normal post-vaccination state, as previously reported by the authors.
A subset of PACVS patients showed abnormally high eGFR combined with abnormally low serum urea, potentially indicating diabetes insipidus/hypopituitarism.
All PACVS participants had fT3 values below the 95% confidence limit or in the lower half of the normal range, consistent with 'low-T3-syndrome'.

The majority of PACVS patients exhibited low ferritin index and subnormal transferrin, soluble transferrin receptor, and transferrin saturation, suggesting disturbed iron metabolism/storage, though not hyper-ferritinemia as seen in severe/chronic COVID-19.
About a quarter of PACVS patients had sNFL above the 90th percentile, indicating possible neuroaxonal damage, though not significantly linked to neurological symptom clusters.
Nearly half of PACVS patients showed IgG subclass imbalances, mainly decreased IgG-2 and increased IgG-3, though this was not associated with specific symptoms or clusters.
Decreased IgG-3 observed in PACVS parallels similar decreases reported in ME/CFS, influenza, and long COVID/PACS, where IgG-3 is considered a protective factor against these conditions.

A subset of PACVS patients showed increased total cholesterol and triglycerides, likely reflecting non-fasting sampling rather than a genuine lipid disorder since LDL and LDL/HDL ratio were not correspondingly elevated.
Cardiac markers and liver function parameters were normally distributed in the PACVS cohort.
None of the abnormal blood markers (ferritin index, fT3, IgG3, IgG4, sNFL z-score) were significantly associated with any of the eight symptom clusters.
Symptoms and symptom clusters were not correlated with altered receptor antibodies, COVID-19 reconvalescence, vaccination regimen, or SARS-CoV-2 spike antibody reactivity.

Pathogen reactivation was reported by about a quarter of PACVS patients and was associated with sleep disturbance/cutaneous symptoms (cluster 7) but not with chronic fatigue, contrasting with long COVID/PACS where such reactivation is linked to chronic fatigue.
None of the 191 PACVS cases presented with Guillain-Barré syndrome despite explicit questioning, distinguishing PACVS from reported post-vaccination GBS reactivation.

The predominant PACVS clinical phenotype comprised a symptomatic triplet of malaise/chronic fatigue, cognitive impairment, and peripheral neuropathic symptoms, leading the authors to propose PACVS may be a sub-form of ME/CFS.

Symptom clusters 2 (peripheral neuropathy/dysesthesia/vasomotor dysfunction), 4 (cardiovascular impairment), and 5 (cognitive impairment, headache, visual/acoustic dysfunction) were also frequently represented and largely overlapped with the chronic fatigue cluster, characterizing PACVS subgroups.
Symptom clusters 1 (general unwellness/B-symptoms) and 8 (dysphagia/breathing impairment) were rarely represented among participants, suggesting these are nonspecific and not characteristic of PACVS.

Among 8 MMF patients with biopsy-proven macrophagic myofasciitis, chronic fatigue and widespread myalgia were universal (8/8) and cognitive impairment was present in 6/8; 5/8 (62.5%) fully met CDC1994 ME/CFS criteria, consistent with previously reported prevalence.
MMF and healthy control macrophages showed similar intracellular uptake and lysosomal co-localization of aluminum oxyhydroxide particles within the first 4 hours of exposure.

Unlike control cells, which showed a decrease in LC3-II and p62 (efficient autophagic flux) after rapamycin, MMF cells responded to the autophagy activator with an increase in the LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, suggesting a propensity to activate an additional LC3-dependent pathway.
Exposure to AH particles increased LC3-II and reduced p62 in both groups, indicating autophagic flux activation, but the increase in the LC3-II/LC3-I ratio was restricted to MMF cells.

Unlike controls, MMF cells did not show an increase in LC3-II or the LC3-II/LC3-I ratio when AH was combined with the autophagy inhibitor chloroquine, suggesting an interfering phenomenon in canonical autophagy in MMF cells.

Whole adjuvanted vaccine (V) induced autophagic flux activation in MMF cells similar to AH alone (LC3-II/LC3-I ratio increase, p62 decrease, alleviation of CQ inhibition, potentiation of rapamycin effect), whereas in controls V produced a weaker LC3-II increase than AH.
At baseline (unexposed cells), MMF macrophages expressed markedly greater amounts of Rubicon, a key LAP protein and negative regulator of canonical autophagy, than healthy control macrophages.
Both AH and whole vaccine exposure decreased Rubicon levels in both MMF and control cells, consistent with consumption of Rubicon during LAP-mediated capture of the adjuvant.

Nox2 was decreased by AH in both groups, but unlike controls, MMF cells failed to show a Nox2 decrease after whole vaccine exposure, resulting in higher Nox2 levels in MMF than controls under that condition, suggesting a defect in the terminal steps of LAP-mediated vaccine handling.

MMF cells released systematically higher levels of the pain-inducing chemokine GROα/CXCL1 than healthy control cells after vehicle, adjuvant, and vaccine exposure, indicating this is a basal characteristic of MMF cells not induced by treatment.
GROα/CXCL1 levels decreased with age among MMF patients, though they remained higher than in healthy controls at all ages tested.
IL-8/CXCL8 levels were higher in MMF patient cells than in healthy control cells after adjuvant (AH) treatment.

Unlike a prior report of elevated serum MCP1/CCL2 in MMF patients, in this short-term ex vivo experiment MCP1/CCL2 release was not increased in MMF cells after any exposure, whereas healthy control cells showed significantly increased MCP1/CCL2 release specifically after whole vaccine exposure (not adjuvant alone).

MMF cells released significantly lower amounts of TNF-α than healthy control cells after exposure to both AH particles and whole adjuvanted vaccine, a blunted response attributed to intrinsically high Rubicon expression.
There was a non-significant trend toward lower oxygen consumption rate (a proxy for aerobic mitochondrial metabolism) in MMF cells compared to controls at baseline (vehicle) exposure.

MMF cells, unlike controls, showed a significant increase in basal and ATP-linked OCR after vaccine (and adjuvant) treatment compared to vehicle, suggesting a systemic metabolic adaptation to vaccine stress.

Despite the acute OCR increase, MMF cells showed a significant decrease in spare respiratory capacity and a significant increase in proton leak after vaccine exposure compared to vehicle, indicating poor coupling between proton production and ATP generation and reduced mitochondrial reserve capacity.

Vaccine exposure produced a small but statistically significant increase in ROS in control cells but not in MMF cells; AH alone did not increase ROS in either group, indicating limited and similar oxidative stress responses overall between MMF and control cells in this short exposure.
Among all SARS-CoV-2 PCR-positive patients, females had a higher rate of long COVID diagnosis than males.
The median age of long COVID patients was significantly higher than that of control patients in the unmatched cohort.
Patients with pre-existing chronic pulmonary disease (asthma, COPD, emphysema, bronchiectasis) had higher odds of developing long COVID.
Individuals with pre-existing renal disease had higher odds of long COVID diagnosis.
Pre-existing migraine was more common among patients who went on to be diagnosed with long COVID than in matched controls.
Pre-existing fibromyalgia was more common among patients who developed long COVID than in matched controls.
Hospital admission within 14 days of infection was significantly more frequent in patients who later developed long COVID.
ICU admission rates during acute infection were significantly higher in patients who later developed long COVID.
During acute COVID-19, patients who later developed long COVID had a higher mean neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio than matched controls, exceeding the normal range.
During acute COVID-19, patients who later developed long COVID had higher mean ALT levels than matched controls, exceeding the normal range.
During acute COVID-19, patients who later developed long COVID had markedly higher mean serum triglyceride levels than matched controls.
During acute COVID-19, patients who later developed long COVID had markedly lower mean serum HDL cholesterol levels than matched controls.
Both long COVID and control patients showed elevated serum glucose levels during the acute COVID-19 phase, suggesting a metabolic dysfunction signal associated with acute infection generally.
Unlike most phenotypes, reported brain fog increased from the acute to the post-COVID-19 phase in the long COVID cohort.
Reported sleep problems increased from the acute to the post-COVID-19 phase in the long COVID cohort.
During the post-COVID-19 phase, the most commonly reported phenotypes in the long COVID cohort were cough, difficulty breathing, and tiredness.

Overall symptom/phenotype reporting remained above baseline throughout follow-up in the long COVID cohort, whereas control patients' symptom reporting returned to baseline within 20 days of a positive PCR test.
Antiviral medications were administered at significantly higher rates in the long COVID cohort during the acute and post-acute phases, consistent with more severe acute disease.
Anticoagulant medications were administered at significantly higher rates in the long COVID cohort during the acute and post-acute phases, consistent with more severe acute disease.
Steroid medications were administered at significantly higher rates in the long COVID cohort during the acute and post-acute phases, consistent with more severe acute disease.
No significant difference in monoclonal antibody administration rates was observed between the long COVID and control cohorts.
Albuterol administration was already elevated at baseline (pre-infection) in the long COVID cohort, consistent with a higher baseline prevalence of chronic pulmonary disease in this group.

In fibromyalgia patients, lower tryptophan levels correlated with greater pain intensity while a higher kynurenine/tryptophan ratio correlated with pain intensity and (inversely) with anxiety symptoms.
The kynurenic acid/quinolinic acid ratio, a neuroprotective index, was lower in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome compared to healthy controls.
In fibromyalgia patients, the kynurenic acid/3-hydroxykynurenine ratio was lower and associated with increased pain, and KAT II enzymatic activity was reduced compared to healthy controls.

CFS patients showed increased kynurenine production correlating with symptom severity, alongside decreased 3-hydroxykynurenine, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, quinolinic acid, and picolinic acid, potentially affecting cellular energy metabolism.
An IFN-α-induced model of CFS was associated with increased kynurenine, 3-hydroxykynurenine, and kynurenine/tryptophan ratio, alongside decreased kynurenic acid and quinaldic acid.

CFS patients showed reduced kynurenine and serotonin with elevated IL-17A, FABP-2, and 3-hydroxykynurenine compared to healthy controls, along with an increased kynurenic acid/kynurenine ratio and 3-hydroxykynurenine/kynurenine ratio.
Among CFS patients, those whose illness onset followed an infection had lower kynurenine levels than those with non-infection-triggered onset.
Microglial activation was found to extend across extensive brain regions in individuals with ME/CFS, suggesting widespread neuroinflammation.
Neuroinflammation observed across brain regions in ME/CFS patients correlates with the severity of neuropsychological symptoms.
CRP, the kynurenine/tryptophan ratio, and insulin resistance were correlated with CFS symptoms, including psychosomatic symptoms in patients recovering from COVID-19.
Chronic fatigue syndrome affects an estimated 0.5-2.5% of the population and fibromyalgia up to 5%.

Quinolinic acid acts as a weak NMDA receptor agonist with neurotoxic potential, while kynurenic acid is a nonselective antagonist of glutamatergic receptors (NMDA, kainate, AMPA) implicated in pain transmission.
IBS is associated with heightened kynurenine, kynurenine/tryptophan ratio, and quinolinic acid, along with reduced kynurenic acid and kynurenic acid/kynurenine ratio.
Neopterin, a marker of immune activation, is elevated in IBS patients compared to controls, suggesting heightened IDO activity.
IBS symptom severity positively correlated with the kynurenine/tryptophan ratio, particularly in patients with severe symptoms who also showed increased likelihood of depression or anxiety.
IBS patients displayed lower mucosal but higher systemic concentrations of kynurenic acid and serotonin compared to healthy controls, with mucosal levels associated with disease physiological state.
In patients with recurrent functional abdominal pain, reducing dietary tryptophan consumption significantly decreased quinolinic acid levels.
In episodic cluster headache patients, plasma l-kynurenine was decreased and quinolinic acid increased during interbout periods compared to controls, with a further drop in kynurenine during attacks.

Migraine patients had significantly lower plasma concentrations of tryptophan, kynurenine, kynurenic acid, quinolinic acid, anthranilic acid, xanthurenic acid, and picolinic acid during the interictal phase versus healthy controls, most evident in migraine without aura.

Cluster headache patients showed reductions in kynurenine, kynurenic acid, 3-hydroxykynurenine, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, and quinolinic acid, with elevated tryptophan and anthranilic acid, suggesting NMDA receptor overactivity.

Chronic migraine patients showed reduced kynurenine, kynurenic acid, 3-hydroxykynurenine, and quinolinic acid, with increased tryptophan, anthranilic acid, and xanthurenic acid, suggesting a shift of kynurenine metabolism toward anthranilic acid at the expense of neuroprotective kynurenic acid.
Intraperitoneal nitroglycerin (10 mg/kg) in rats downregulated KAT, lowering brain kynurenic acid levels, modeling migraine-like kynurenine pathway changes.

NTG injection in rats reduced expression of IDO1, TDO2, kynurenine hydrolase, and KMO in the caudal trigeminal nucleus, indicating pathway downregulation potentially affecting glutamatergic transmission in migraine models.

Pediatric migraine patients showed decreased gut microbiota diversity along with decreased kynurenic acid and increased quinolinic acid and serotonin; the kynurenic acid/quinolinic acid ratio had good diagnostic efficacy for pediatric migraine.

Across multiple IBS studies, IBS is associated with heightened kynurenine, kynurenine/tryptophan ratio, quinolinic acid, and neopterin, alongside reduced kynurenic acid and kynurenic acid/kynurenine ratio, suggesting increased IDO activity.

Heitkemper et al. found a non-significant decrease in kynurenine/tryptophan ratio and a decreased melatonin/tryptophan ratio in IBS-D patients versus IBS-C and controls, suggesting a possible sleep-quality impact.

One study found reduced 3-hydroxykynurenine, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, and kynurenic acid in IBS-D patients, with no significant differences in kynurenine, xanthurenic acid, or anthranilic acid versus controls.

IBS patients had lower mucosal but higher systemic concentrations of kynurenic acid and serotonin compared to healthy controls, with mucosal serotonin and kynurenic acid concentrations associated with disease state.

In mixed-type IBS, urinary excretion of tryptophan metabolites, particularly 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid and indican, was higher and significantly increased during diarrheal periods, coinciding with gut microbiome alterations.

In recurrent functional abdominal pain patients, ratios of 5-HIAA/tryptophan and kynurenine/tryptophan and quinolinic acid levels were significantly higher than controls, and reducing dietary tryptophan intake significantly decreased quinolinic acid levels.

Children with recurrent abdominal pain had higher serum TNF-α, lower IL-10, IL-6, and BDNF, increased 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, and decreased anthranilic acid, though tryptophan, kynurenine, and KYN/TRP ratio did not differ from controls.

IBS patients had elevated kynurenine/tryptophan ratios and showed differential kynurenine production profiles following toll-like receptor activation (TLR1/2, TLR2, TLR3, TLR5, TLR7, TLR8) compared to controls, suggesting a potential IBS biomarker.

IBD patients, especially those with Crohn's disease, had significantly lower serum tryptophan correlating with disease activity and CRP; colonic biopsies showed reduced TDO mRNA, elevated IDO1 mRNA, and increased quinolinic acid during active disease.
Elevated serum kynurenine levels in IBD patients have been proposed as a potential factor distinguishing Crohn's disease from ulcerative colitis.

Both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis patients showed elevated kynurenine pathway activity and oxidative stress with increased kynurenic acid even during quiescent disease phases, despite unchanged neopterin.

IBD pathway dysregulation involves increased expression of IDO1, KMO, and kynureninase, raising kynurenine metabolite levels; kynurenic acid is decreased in Crohn's disease while quinolinic acid is increased in IBD.

Intestinal inflammation severity in IBD negatively correlated with xanthurenic and kynurenic acid levels in mice and humans; supplementing these metabolites alleviated colitis severity via AhR activation and modulation of cellular energy metabolism.

A positive feedback loop of IL-6, IDO1, and AhR accelerates kynurenine metabolism in the gut; the GPR35 agonist vardenafil and AhR agonist linagliptin, identified via drug screening, significantly mitigated chemotherapy-induced intestinal toxicity in vivo.
Patients with episodic cluster headache showed decreased L-kynurenine levels during interbout periods compared to healthy controls, with a further reduction during ictal phases.
Quinolinic acid was elevated during interbout periods in cluster headache patients and negatively correlated with disease duration and inversely with total attack number for kynurenine.

Migraine patients (especially without aura) showed significantly lower plasma tryptophan, kynurenine, kynurenic acid, quinolinic acid, anthranilic acid, xanthurenic acid, and picolinic acid during the interictal phase compared to healthy controls, with anthranilic acid, 5-HIAA and melatonin rising during the ictal phase.

Cluster headache patients showed reduced kynurenine, kynurenic acid, 3-hydroxykynurenine, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, and quinolinic acid, with increased tryptophan and anthranilic acid, suggesting NMDA receptor overactivity.

Chronic migraine patients showed reduced kynurenine, kynurenic acid, 3-hydroxykynurenine and quinolinic acid, with increased tryptophan, anthranilic acid, and xanthurenic acid, suggesting a shift of metabolism toward anthranilic acid at the expense of kynurenic acid.

In pediatric migraine patients, gut microbiota richness/evenness were reduced, and kynurenic acid was decreased while quinolinic acid and serotonin were elevated, with the kynurenic acid/quinolinic acid ratio showing excellent diagnostic efficacy.
In an NTG-induced rodent migraine model, intraperitoneal nitroglycerin (10 mg/kg) downregulated kynurenine aminotransferase, decreasing brain kynurenic acid levels.

NTG injection in rats reduced expression of IDO1, TDO2, kynurenine hydrolase, and KMO in the caudal trigeminal nucleus, suggesting downregulation of the kynurenine pathway influences the glutamatergic system in migraine.

Kynurenic acid analogs KA1 and KA2, and co-administration of kynurenine with probenecid, prevented NTG-induced behavioral and morphological changes and attenuated aberrant CGRP, c-fos, nNOS and CamKIIα expression, likely by targeting NMDA receptors.

Systemic treatment with kynurenine plus probenecid, which enables kynurenine (but not kynurenic acid) to cross the BBB, significantly mitigated the NTG-induced surge in c-fos immunoreactivity within the brainstem.
Probenecid demonstrated an anti-nociceptive effect in a trigeminal inflammatory pain (orofacial formalin) model in rats, potentially via increasing CNS kynurenic acid levels.
Kynurenic acid reduces the number of cortical spreading depression (CSD) waves and decreases blood-brain barrier permeability during CSD, a phenomenon believed to underlie migraine aura.

L-kynurenine (alone or with probenecid) decreased cortical spreading depression frequency in a sex-dependent manner, being significant in females during the diestrus phase, while in males only the kynurenine+probenecid combination was effective.

Estradiol and progesterone increase cortical spreading depression frequency after ovariectomy, and the suppressive effect of L-kynurenine on CSD frequency present in cycling females disappears after ovariectomy but reappears with progesterone replacement.

While sumatriptan decreased CSD number with minimal effect on propagation failure, novel kynurenic acid analogues SZR-105 and SZR-109 restored CSD propagation to control levels after NTG administration.

In a rat model of orofacial pain (CFA), glutamate, kynurenic acid and kynurenine were significantly elevated in the caudal trigeminal nucleus at 24h post-treatment, diminishing by 48h, with increases in kynurenic acid and serotonin also seen in the somatosensory cortex.

Pretreatment with the kynurenic acid analogue SZR72 reduced pERK1/2 and IL-1β immunoreactivity in the trigeminal ganglion and prevented increased c-fos and glutamate immunoreactivity in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis and C1-C2 following CFA application.

TLR4 plays a role in migraine-like behavior and nucleus caudalis neuronal activation through the MyD88 pathway in mice, suggesting TLR activation may contribute to migraine via neuroinflammatory routes linked to the kynurenine pathway.

IBS patients showed elevated kynurenine/tryptophan ratios and differential kynurenine production following toll-like receptor activation (notably TLR1/2, TLR2, TLR3, TLR5, TLR7, TLR8) compared to controls.
Fitzgerald et al. found increased kynurenine in the blood of patients with IBS.
Clarke et al. found increased kynurenine and decreased kynurenic acid in the blood of IBS patients.
Li et al. reported increased quinolinic acid and kynurenine, and decreased kynurenic acid, in blood of patients with diarrhea-type IBS (IBS-D).
Clarke et al. (2009) found increased kynurenine and neopterin, and decreased kynurenic acid, in patients with IBS, suggesting heightened IDO activity.

Heitkemper et al. reported a non-significant decrease in kynurenine/tryptophan ratio and a decreased melatonin/tryptophan ratio in IBS-D patients versus IBS-C and healthy controls, hinting at impaired sleep quality.

Christmas et al. found no significant differences in kynurenine, xanthurenic acid, or anthranilic acid between IBS-D patients and controls, but observed reduced 3-hydroxykynurenine, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, and kynurenic acid in IBS-D patients.

In IBS-C and IBS-D patients, serum quinolinic acid levels positively correlated with depression scale scores, while kynurenic acid levels showed a negative correlation with both intestinal symptoms and depression scale scores.
In fibromyalgia and TMD myalgia patients, lower serum tryptophan levels correlated with higher pain intensity, with a trend toward significantly lower tryptophan compared to healthy controls.
The kynurenine/tryptophan ratio was positively correlated with pain intensity in fibromyalgia and TMD myalgia patients.
In fibromyalgia patients, the kynurenine/tryptophan ratio was negatively correlated with anxiety symptoms.
The kynurenic acid/quinolinic acid ratio was lower in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
The kynurenic acid/3-hydroxykynurenine ratio was lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls, and this decreased neuroprotective ratio was associated with increased pain symptoms.
KAT II enzymatic activity, measured as the xanthurenic acid/3-hydroxykynurenine ratio, was lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Kavyani et al. reported increased kynurenine production in CFS patients compared to healthy controls, correlating with symptom severity.

Kavyani et al. observed decreased levels of 3-hydroxykynurenine, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, quinolinic acid, and picolinic acid in CFS patients, potentially negatively impacting cellular energy levels.
In an IFN-alpha-induced model of CFS, increases in kynurenine, 3-hydroxykynurenine, and the kynurenine/tryptophan ratio were observed alongside decreases in kynurenic acid and quinaldic acid.
Simonato et al. found elevated IL-17A, FABP-2, and 3-hydroxykynurenine, alongside reduced kynurenine and serotonin, in CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
In CFS patients, the kynurenic acid/kynurenine ratio (KAT activity) and 3-hydroxykynurenine/kynurenine ratio (KMO activity) were increased.
Among CFS patients, those whose illness onset followed an infection exhibited lower kynurenine levels than those with non-infection-triggered onset.
Microglial activation and neuroinflammation are evident across extensive brain regions in ME/CFS patients and correlate with severity of neuropsychological symptoms.
CRP, the kynurenine/tryptophan ratio, and insulin resistance were correlated with CFS symptoms, including psychosomatic symptoms in COVID-19 recovery patients.
ME/CFS and fibromyalgia are prevalent conditions, with CFS affecting an estimated 0.5-2.5% of the population and fibromyalgia affecting up to 5%.
Findings on kynurenine levels in CFS are conflicting, with some studies reporting increased kynurenine production and others reporting decreased levels compared to healthy controls.

In a retrospective study of 86 patients with diagnosed or suspected connective tissue disorders evaluated for cerebral venous outflow disorders, high prevalences of IIH, CSF leaks, dysautonomia, EDS, MCAD, and systemic venous compression syndrome were observed.
The same cohort of 86 CTD/CVD patients showed high rates of POTS, dysautonomia, craniocervical instability, MCAD, and tethered cord syndrome.
A separate large study of 2,149 hEDS patients found that the majority had dysautonomia/POTS, with substantial minorities having CCI/AAI, Chiari malformation, or tethered cord syndrome.
A review of 37,665 MCAD patients found that nearly one-third also carried a comorbid diagnosis of hEDS.

Patients with suspected/diagnosed CTDs and IIH differ demographically and clinically from typical IIH patients, presenting with lower BMI, lower lumbar puncture opening pressures, lower sagittal sinus pressures, more severe headaches, and worse quality of life.
A 1997 study of 51 individuals with EDS found that 30-40% reported neck pain and headache.
A 2011 study reported migraines with or without aura in 75% of patients with joint hypermobility spectrum.
In a small study of 11 patients presenting with postural headaches and other neurological complaints, all participants were found to have a spontaneous CSF leak.
An observational study found an elevated percentage of meningeal (arachnoid) diverticula in CSF leak patients and classified these diverticula as a type of CSF leak.
Another study found no difference in the prevalence of meningeal diverticula between patients with spontaneous intracranial hypotension and controls, contradicting the earlier association.
Chiari malformation animal/model studies showed significantly higher peak CSF pressure compared to healthy controls.
A 2013 study comparing 10 healthy volunteers and 18 Chiari malformation patients found significantly faster and earlier caudal CSF flow in CM patients.
The same 2013 study found no significant differences in CSF velocities between healthy volunteers and patients with syringomyelia.
A study of over 250 patients with vascular compression syndromes found a strong correlation between EDS and having three or more concurrent vascular compression syndromes.
Nearly 97% of mast cells are located on the brain side of blood vessels, positioning them to interact with the ECM, neurons, astrocytes, and blood vessels of the BBB.

In a cuprizone administration model, tight junction protein expression changed alongside increased mast cell presence and tryptase expression in the cortex and corpus callosum, indicating mast cell activation may alter BBB permeability.
In a Japanese encephalitis virus mouse model, inhibiting chymase reversed BBB leakage, suggesting chymase contributes to BBB permeability.
Mast cell stabilizers were shown to block mast cells' effects on vascular permeability in W/Wv mice.
In a dove model, compound 48/80-induced mast cell degranulation increased BBB permeability, suggesting mast cell activation can locally alter BBB integrity.
In a sepsis-associated encephalopathy study, mast cell activation weakened the BBB, and early treatment with the mast cell stabilizer cromolyn reduced the inflammatory cascade.
Cranio-cervical instability/cervical instability (CCI/CI) is reported in up to 31.6% of hEDS patients based on a large survey cohort.
Tethered cord syndrome (TCS) prevalence in hEDS is estimated at 6.65%, based on a self-reported survey of 2,149 clinically diagnosed hEDS patients.
In a retrospective cohort of 67 EDS patients who underwent neurosurgery, 17.9% had a diagnosis of tethered cord syndrome.
The same retrospective cohort of 67 EDS neurosurgical patients showed 85.1% had craniocervical instability and/or atlantoaxial instability.

Phenotypic clustering of 2,149 hEDS patients identified three clusters, one comprising 11.5% of the cohort with increased spinal/neurological manifestations and a disease burden of over 14 conditions.

In the index case, upright cervical flexion/extension MRI confirmed craniocervical instability with a clivo-axial angle of 116 degrees (pathologic <130 degrees) and medullary kinking, despite a prior unremarkable supine MRI.

Occipital-cervical fusion (C0-C3) for craniocervical instability led to significant improvement in headaches, neck pain, and myelopathic complaints, along with subjective improvement in POTS and dysautonomia symptoms.

Surgical release of occult tethered cord syndrome (L1-L2 partial laminectomy with filum terminale resection) resulted in 90% resolution of preoperative urinary incontinence/retention and resolved low back and sacral pain at 6-month follow-up.

A published 15-item scale for occult TCS surgical criteria showed clinical improvement in 89% of patients at 3-month follow-up and 68% at 12-month follow-up, and correctly predicted surgical outcome in 82% of cases.
A preoperative score greater than 8 on the 15-item TCS scale was associated with an over 80% likelihood of surgical improvement.
Surgical outcomes of filum sectioning for TCS in EDS patients were reported as comparable to or better than outcomes in classical (non-EDS) TCS patients.

Spinal instability in hEDS is thought to arise from ligament laxity, whereas TCS results from impaired elasticity and disorganized collagen with inflammatory infiltration in the filum terminale, increasing mechanical stress on the conus medullaris.

Patients in the hEDS phenotypic cluster with higher incidence of spinal instability and TCS also have higher rates of mast cell activation disorder (MCAD), potentially linked to the inflammatory infiltration seen in TCS.
The risk of hardware or fusion failure after cervical fusion surgery is elevated in individuals with EDS compared to the general surgical population.
hEDS patients can present with co-existing tethered cord syndrome and cranio-cervical/cervical instability, with substantially overlapping neurological symptoms, complicating diagnosis and treatment.

A 52-year-old woman with HSD-related bilateral shoulder microinstability had her DASH score improve from 50.0 to 19.2 after two rounds of US-guided dextrose prolotherapy injections into the glenohumeral joints, with symptomatic improvement in pain and subluxations.
In the same 52-year-old patient, DASH score increased from 19.2 to 33.3 measured 7 weeks after her most recent DPT injection, suggesting waning therapeutic effect over time.

A 25-year-old woman with HSD-related shoulder microinstability and infraspinatus tendinopathy had her DASH score improve from 15.0 to 5.8 after two rounds of dextrose prolotherapy targeting the glenohumeral joints, with reported reduction in spontaneous subluxations and neck pain.

A 20-year-old woman with hEDS, associated Chiari malformation, craniocervical instability, cervical dystonia, MCAS, and POTS, with bilateral shoulder labral tears and rotator cuff tendinopathy, had her DASH score improve from 41.6 to 19.2 after a course of DPT injections following an 8-week treatment hiatus, though improvement plateaued after four sessions.

In the third case, after DPT effects plateaued across four sessions, platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections using the same technique yielded superior results compared to DPT, though PRP was more painful.

The authors describe the mechanism of dextrose prolotherapy as inducing local tissue trauma and low-grade inflammation via glucose transport (GLUT 1-4 channels) and osmotic changes, which upregulate pro-inflammatory cytokines and growth factors, activating macrophages, fibroblasts, chondrocytes, and nerve cells to stimulate connective tissue repair.
None of the three hEDS/HSD patients experienced adverse reactions from repeated dextrose prolotherapy injections across the course of treatment.
The Spider neuromusculoskeletal domain showed a strong positive correlation with select questions from the Bristol Impact of Hypermobility (BIoH) questionnaire.
The Spider gastrointestinal domain showed a strong positive correlation with the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS).
The Spider cardiac dysautonomia domain showed a strong positive correlation with select questions from the COMPASS-31.
The Spider anxiety domain showed a strong positive correlation with the GAD-7.
The Spider depression domain showed a strong positive correlation with the PHQ-9.
The Spider urogenital domain showed a strong positive correlation with the LURN Symptom Index-29.
The Spider fatigue domain showed a moderate positive correlation with the combined CIS and PSQI scores.
The Spider anxiety domain showed a moderate positive correlation with the HADS anxiety subscale in a subsample of 300 participants.
The Spider depression domain showed a moderate positive correlation with the HADS depression subscale in a subsample of 300 participants.
The Spider pain domain showed a moderate positive correlation with the Multidimensional Pain Inventory (MPI).
The Spider pain domain showed a moderate positive correlation with select questions from the BIoH.
Adults with symptomatic hypermobility scored much higher on the Spider neuromusculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, and fatigue domains than healthy controls.
Adults with symptomatic hypermobility scored much higher on the Spider depression, cardiac dysautonomia, and pain domains than healthy controls.
Adults with symptomatic hypermobility scored moderately higher on the Spider anxiety and urogenital domains than healthy controls.
A secondary sensitivity analysis excluding white participants found similarly strong convergent validity correlations across Spider domains, suggesting generalisability across ethnic groups.
Orthostatic intolerance, including POTS, is reported to affect 60-80% of patients with HSD/hEDS, and about a quarter of POTS patients are also diagnosed with HSD/hEDS.
Gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, constipation, and diarrhoea are reported far more frequently in people with HSD/hEDS than in those without.
Approximately 70% of individuals with HSD/hEDS have an anxiety disorder, and they have a 4.1-4.4 times greater probability of depression and anxiety compared to the general population.
Chronic fatigue is reported to affect 77% of individuals with HSD/hEDS.
Joint instability with dislocations is reported by 78% of people with HSD/hEDS.
Urinary incontinence and genital pain/discomfort are reported at much higher rates among women with HSD/hEDS compared with the general population.
HSD/hEDS is estimated to affect around 1 in 500 patients in the UK, suggesting it is a common rather than rare condition.
The letter addresses craniocervical instability in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome patients and discusses outcomes following occipitocervical fusion surgery.
The authors report a case of myopathic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome caused by a novel homozygous nonsense variant in the COL12A1 gene.
Patients with EDS show a strong correlation with having three or more types of abdominopelvic vascular compression syndromes simultaneously.
Over 90% of patients with multiple vascular compression syndromes who were treated for only one syndrome had poor outcomes, because correcting one compression worsened the uncorrected ones.
Correcting multiple or all vascular compression syndromes concurrently improves or resolves symptoms in patients with multiple VCS.

The reported patient had EDS with comorbid mast cell activation, Chiari malformation, tethered cord syndrome (post occipital decompression and sacral laminectomy with cord untethering), and nonepileptic seizures with multiple negative EEGs.
The patient's syncopal episode, initially suspected to be seizure activity, was ultimately attributed to postural hypotension with associated bradycardia and hypotension responsive to IV fluids.

Nutcracker syndrome results from compression of the left renal vein between the superior mesenteric artery and abdominal aorta, causing increased venous pressure and symptoms such as hematuria, flank pain, and pelvic congestion.
Connective tissue laxity in EDS may diminish the aortomesenteric angle, increasing the likelihood of duodenal compression and development of superior mesenteric artery syndrome (SMAS).
An aortomesenteric angle less than 22° and aortomesenteric distance less than 8 mm on CT scan are positive diagnostic indicators of SMAS.
Up to 85% of SMAS patients succeed with conservative treatment, particularly when symptoms have lasted less than a month.
Duodenojejunostomy, the surgical procedure of choice for severe SMAS, shows favorable outcomes in 80%-90% of cases.

Connective tissue laxity and fragility in EDS may cause excessive movement or displacement of the median arcuate ligament, increasing the risk of celiac artery compression (median arcuate ligament syndrome, MALS).
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has an estimated frequency of 1 in 5,000 in the general population.
Median arcuate ligament syndrome has an incidence of 2 in 100,000 patients.
The case patient presented with a documented history of four concurrent abdominopelvic vascular compression syndromes — MALS, SMAS, NCS, and MTS — alongside EDS.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by mutations in COL3A1, which encodes type III procollagen, leading to tissue fragility and vascular rupture risk.
Endovascular and surgical treatments have poor outcomes in vEDS, with complication rates as high as 46%.
Major vascular/organ complications occur in up to 85% of vEDS patients by age 43.
The BBEST randomized trial found that celiprolol reduced the risk of arterial rupture or dissection by roughly threefold compared with usual treatment in vEDS patients.
A 2000 study by Pepin et al. found vEDS patients had a median survival of 48 years, with over 80% experiencing at least one complication by age 40.
A study of more than 1200 vEDS patients found median survival was particularly low in males, mainly due to higher rates of death from vascular rupture by age 20 compared with females.
A French referral center study of 144 vEDS patients (2000-2017) found overall survival of 71.6% over 5.3-year follow-up and over 80% survival by age 50, indicating improved prognosis over time.
A recent multicenter UK observational study found 5-year survival of approximately 90% in vEDS patients.
In the Frank et al. cohort, vEDS patients treated with celiprolol had significantly better survival than untreated patients (72.4% vs 52.2%).
In a UK cohort, vEDS patients on any cardiovascular medication (celiprolol, other beta-blockers, and/or ARBs) had markedly higher 5-year survival than untreated patients (96.53% vs 42.69%).
In a vEDS mouse model, celiprolol but not losartan improved the biomechanical integrity of the aortic wall; doxycycline (an MMP inhibitor) also improved aortic mechanical properties.
vEDS patients showed significantly higher carotid distensibility and circumferential/pulsatile wall stress compared with healthy controls.
Within BBEST participants, celiprolol selectively increased carotid Young's elastic modulus by reducing carotid distensibility, a proposed mechanism of vascular protection.
A later study using a different mouse model failed to demonstrate the protective effect of celiprolol on aortic outcomes seen in the Dubacher et al. model.
Another study suggested celiprolol could accelerate rather than reduce death from aortic rupture in two different vEDS mouse models.

A case report found that after 3 years of celiprolol therapy, a vEDS patient's skin collagen fibril size normalized and ER dilatation (marker of ER stress) resolved, though procollagen III expression was unchanged.
Celiprolol's mortality reduction in vEDS patients was dose-dependent, with 400 mg daily providing the greatest protection compared with lower doses.
A Swedish cohort of 40 vEDS patients on celiprolol had an annual major vascular event risk of 4.7%, comparable to the BBEST celiprolol arm (5%) and lower than untreated patients (12%).

In a Brescia cohort of 26 vEDS patients on celiprolol (80% at max dose of 400mg/day), the yearly risk of symptomatic vascular events remained non-negligible at 8.8%, with most events occurring after reaching the maximum dose.

In a Col3a1 mouse model, bisoprolol (a β1-selective antagonist) did not improve thoracic aortic biomechanical integrity compared with controls, suggesting celiprolol's benefit may not extend to other beta-blockers.
Patients with vEDS showed significantly higher carotid arterial distensibility and circumferential/pulsatile wall stress compared with healthy controls.
Among BBEST participants, celiprolol selectively increased carotid Young's elastic modulus while reducing carotid distensibility, suggesting increased arterial stiffness with treatment.
A later study using a different mouse model failed to reproduce the protective effect of celiprolol on aortic biomechanical integrity seen in earlier work.
Another study suggested that celiprolol could accelerate rather than reduce death from aortic rupture in two different mouse models.

In a case report, skin biopsy before and after 3 years of celiprolol therapy showed unchanged procollagen III expression but improved collagen fibril size uniformity and resolution of ER dilatation (a marker of ER stress) in fibroblasts.
In the Frank et al. cohort, celiprolol's mortality-reducing effect was dose-dependent, with the maximum recommended dose of 400 mg/day providing significantly better protection than lower doses.
In a Swedish cohort of 40 vEDS patients on celiprolol, the annual risk of major vascular events was 4.7%, comparable to BBEST celiprolol-treated patients (5%) and lower than untreated patients (12%).

In an Italian cohort of 26 vEDS patients on celiprolol (80% at maximum dose), the yearly risk of symptomatic vascular events remained non-negligible at 8.8%, with most events occurring after reaching the maximum recommended dose.

In a Col3a1 mouse model, bisoprolol (a β1-selective antagonist) did not improve thoracic aortic biomechanical integrity compared with controls, suggesting celiprolol's benefit may not extend to bisoprolol.

Angiotensin II infusion increased systolic blood pressure similarly in Col3a1+/- and Col3a1+/+ mice, but caused markedly higher premature mortality in Col3a1+/- mice (55% vs 0%), especially in the first week of infusion.
Reducing the angiotensin II infusion dose significantly reduced mortality rates in Col3a1 haploinsufficient mice.
Among several antihypertensive drugs tested in Col3a1+/G182R knock-in mice, only losartan significantly reduced the risk of death from spontaneous thoracic aortic rupture.
Discontinuation of losartan in the mouse model reversed protection, restoring mortality similar to untreated mice, whereas initiating losartan after weaning still conferred strong benefit.

Administration of angiotensin II at doses with minimal effect on systolic blood pressure still induced aortic rupture with 100% mortality within 10 days, suggesting a blood-pressure-independent deleterious mechanism.

Celiprolol is hypothesized to enhance TGFβ-mediated pro-fibrotic mechanisms and collagen synthesis through combined β1 antagonism and β2 stimulation, potentially increasing arterial stiffness protectively.
In two Col3a1 mutant mouse models, the PKCβ inhibitor ruboxistaurin increased 45-day survival compared with controls (94% vs 52%), implicating PKC-dependent ERK activation in aortic rupture.
The MEK inhibitor cobimetinib resulted in 90% survival at 45 days in Col3a1 mutant mice.
Hydralazine initiated at birth improved survival in mutant mice, but this protection from aortic rupture was abruptly lost around sexual maturity, particularly in males.
Concomitant treatment with the androgen receptor antagonist bicalutamide increased survival in both sexes, suggesting androgens influence the PLC/IP3/PKC/ERK pathway distal to IP3.
Combination treatment with hydralazine and spironolactone produced similar survival benefits as hydralazine plus bicalutamide in the vEDS mouse model.

A subsequent study using a different knock-in mouse model (Col3a1+/G182R) did not confirm the PKCβ/ERK pathway-related survival benefits seen with ruboxistaurin, cobimetinib, hydralazine, and bicalutamide.

RNA interference targeting the mutant COL3A1 allele carrying a glycine substitution (p.Gly252Val) in patient dermal fibroblasts selectively suppressed mutant mRNA, preserved the wild-type allele, and was associated with enhanced collagen fibril formation and reduced unfolded protein response effects.

In vEDS mouse models, concomitant treatment with the androgen receptor antagonist bicalutamide (combined with hydralazine) increased survival in both male and female mice, suggesting androgens modulate the PKCβ/ERK-related aortic rupture pathway.
Combination treatment with hydralazine and spironolactone produced similarly improved survival results in the vEDS mouse model as hydralazine plus bicalutamide.

A subsequent study using a different knock-in mouse model (Col3a1+/G182R) failed to confirm the protective effects of PKCβ/ERK pathway inhibition and hydralazine/androgen-modulating combinations previously reported by Bowen et al.

The PREVEnt trial testing enzastaurin (AR101), a PKCβ/PI3K/AKT signaling inhibitor, for prevention of arterial events in vEDS was indefinitely suspended by the sponsoring company in October 2022 for commercial reasons before results were available.

RNA interference (RNAi) technology successfully suppressed expression of a mutant COL3A1 allele carrying a glycine substitution (p.Gly252Val) in patient-derived dermal fibroblasts while preserving the wild-type allele, improving collagen fibril formation and reducing unfolded protein effects.

A-to-I RNA editing is proposed as a therapeutic strategy to correct pathogenic G-to-A point mutations in COL3A1 (which cause many glycine substitutions in vEDS) at the transcript level, offering lower off-target genomic risk than DNA editing.

An integrative multi-omics (transcriptomics and miRNomics) study of patient-derived dermal fibroblasts revealed disrupted extracellular matrix organization, altered endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis, and defective autophagy as interconnected pathological features of vEDS, along with the first disease-specific miRNA expression signature.

miR-29a-3p and miR-29b-3p were found to be upregulated among a panel of dysregulated miRNAs in vEDS fibroblasts, disrupting ECM turnover, ER proteostasis, and the autophagy-lysosome pathway important for vascular integrity.

Increased expression of miR-29a/b was strongly associated with downregulation of several genes involved in vascular ECM structure and turnover, including collagens, elastin, and ECM-modifying enzymes, contributing to aortic damage and aneurysm development.

The BBEST trial had important methodological limitations: investigators were not blinded to treatment because a matching placebo was prohibitively expensive, and only 33 of the 53 enrolled participants had molecularly proven COL3A1 mutations.
Genetic sequencing identified a heterozygous COL3A1 mutation (c.628G>C, p.Gly210Arg) confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS type IV).
The patient presented with spontaneous sigmoid colon perforation as the initial manifestation, later attributed to underlying vascular EDS.

Postoperatively the patient developed ileal subserosal hematomas, many of which ruptured leaving a distinctive 'zebra pattern' of residual hematoma lines, a complication not previously reported after SCP surgery in vEDS.

Spontaneous intestinal perforation occurs in 10.7% of vascular EDS patients, the second-highest incidence among connective tissue diseases after polyarteritis nodosa (13%), compared with 9% in Churg-Strauss syndrome, 3.6% in SLE, and 0.09% in rheumatoid arthritis.
GI perforations in vEDS patients are significantly more common in males than females.
Nearly half (47%) of vEDS patients with a spontaneous colonic perforation are at risk of early reperforation of the remaining colon within 20 months without adequate therapeutic management.

Celiprolol, a selective β1 receptor antagonist and β2 receptor partial agonist, was prescribed at 200 mg to reduce heart rate and mean/pulsatile pressures, potentially lowering the risk of aortic dissection and rupture in vEDS.

The patient was prescribed 1500 mg daily ascorbic acid for collagen synthesis support and antioxidant effect; literature cited indicates a 500 mg daily dose reduces the risk of aortic dissection and rupture in vEDS.

A retrospective study found that cumulative survival after surgery for colorectal perforation is significantly worse in patients with connective tissue disease compared to those without, although no EDS patients were included in that cohort.
Vascular EDS accounts for 3-6% of all EDS cases, has an estimated prevalence of 1/50,000 to 1/20,000, and is considered the most severe EDS subtype, arising from COL3A1 mutations (rarely COL1A1).

The patient exhibited multiple minor EDS diagnostic criteria (skin hyperelasticity, joint hypermobility, easy bruising) alongside major vEDS features (two spontaneous pneumothoraces, colonic perforation), which together prompted clinical suspicion of EDS prior to genetic confirmation.
Most spontaneous GI perforations in vEDS occur in the sigmoid colon, followed by the small bowel, while gastric perforations are exceptional.

The first spontaneous colonic perforations in vEDS typically begin in the late teenage years extending into the late twenties, and most occur before the molecular diagnosis of vEDS is established, as in this case.
Patients with developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) had a significantly higher prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility than healthy controls.
Among DDH patients, those with concomitant generalized joint hypermobility had a lower lateral center-edge angle, indicating more severe radiographic dysplasia, than those without hypermobility.
DDH patients with generalized joint hypermobility had greater lateralization of the femoral head than those without hypermobility.
DDH patients with generalized joint hypermobility reported lower iHOT-12 (hip-related quality of life) scores than those without hypermobility.
Multivariable linear regression found that higher Beighton scores and younger age independently predicted more severe hip dysplasia.
In multivariable regression, the Beighton score was not independently associated with patient-reported outcomes (iHOT-12, HHS, WOMAC) in DDH patients.
Exome sequencing identified a novel homozygous missense variant in the CAT gene (c.635T>G, p.Met212Arg) segregating with acatalasemia in two affected siblings from a consanguineous Egyptian family.
Sanger sequencing of C1S and C1R, the genes causative for periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, did not detect pathogenic variants in the affected siblings, prompting further exome sequencing.
The clinical phenotype of acatalasemia, including joint hyperlaxity and dental/periodontal disease, closely mimicked periodontal-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, leading to initial misdiagnosis.
Premature loss of teeth is described as an emerging clinical finding associated with acatalasemia, highlighting broader systemic manifestations of the disorder.
Substance P levels in cerebrospinal fluid are elevated up to three times above normal in fibromyalgia patients, contributing to central sensitization.
Glutamate levels increase in fibromyalgia patients following nociceptive stimulation, consistent with enhanced excitatory neurotransmission.
A systematic review and meta-analysis found small nerve fiber loss in approximately 50% of fibromyalgia patients, supporting a peripheral neuropathic contribution to pain.
Elevated IL-8 chemokine levels are found in serum and cerebrospinal fluid of fibromyalgia patients and may directly contribute to nociception via chemokine receptors on pain pathways.
The TAAR1 gene, which mediates dopamine availability, may be involved in fibromyalgia, with reduced function potentially increasing pain sensitivity.
The RGS4 gene, which modulates inhibition of descending pain pathways in the spinal dorsal horn, is associated with fibromyalgia pain disorders.
CNR1, encoding the cannabinoid CB1 receptor, is a candidate gene associated with fibromyalgia pain regulation.
GRIA4, an AMPA glutamate receptor subunit gene, is implicated in central sensitization via increased excitatory nociceptive transmission in fibromyalgia.
HPA axis dysfunction in fibromyalgia results in increased basal ACTH levels and exaggerated ACTH secretion in response to stress.

A study found a direct, linear relationship between salivary cortisol levels and pain symptom severity in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting elevated cortisol reflects high stress levels contributing to disease impact.
The percentage of mu-opioid receptor-positive B lymphocytes is lower in fibromyalgia patients than healthy individuals, proposed as a specific diagnostic biomarker.
Neutrophil/lymphocyte, lymphocyte/monocyte, and monocyte/high-density lipoprotein ratios in fibromyalgia patients relate to disease activity, pain, and depression levels.

The authors' own laboratory found higher serum levels of numerous amino acids (aspartic acid, glutamic acid, histidine, taurine, BCAAs, EAAs, NEAAs, etc.) and higher EAA/NEAA, phenylalanine/tyrosine, and arginine bioavailability ratios in fibromyalgia patients compared with controls, indicating a metabolic disturbance.

Serum alanine was lower in fibromyalgia patients than controls, and logistic regression showed the combination of glutamic acid, histidine, and alanine had the greatest predictive ability for diagnosing fibromyalgia.

Women with fibromyalgia had higher norepinephrine and lower dopamine, serotonin (5-HT), 5-HIAA, and 5-HTP than age-matched healthy controls, and plasma norepinephrine >694.69 pg/mL may accurately predict fibromyalgia; higher norepinephrine was associated with worse physical health status.

Serum oxytocinase activity is increased in fibromyalgia patients compared with controls and may be a good marker differentiating patients from healthy subjects, potentially altering the metabolism of analgesic peptides such as oxytocin and enkephalins.
A subgroup of fibromyalgia patients showed abnormally low serum EDA activity compared with healthy controls and other fibromyalgia patients.

No significant differences were found between fibromyalgia patients and controls in activity levels of aminopeptidase A, aminopeptidase B, aspartyl aminopeptidase, insulin-regulated aminopeptidase, pyroglutamyl aminopeptidase, or aminopeptidase N.

In an observational case study of women with fibromyalgia, serum nitric oxide levels, oxytocinase, and EDA activity were significantly associated with specific regional pressure pain thresholds, daily activity level, and global pain intensity.

Portable FT-IR spectroscopy of bloodspot samples, using OPLS-DA pattern recognition, achieved high classification accuracy differentiating fibromyalgia from SLE, osteoarthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis based on aromatic amino acid and peptide backbone spectral features.
In a subgroup of fibromyalgia patients, treatment with NMDA receptor antagonists improved symptoms and pain perception, though tolerability limits clinical use.
Tramadol, the most commonly used opioid for fibromyalgia, reduced pain levels in patients but has adverse effects that limit its use to more refractory cases.
Pregabalin, the most commonly used gabapentinoid for fibromyalgia, has demonstrated clinical utility for reducing pain in numerous studies by reducing sensory/neuropathic pain perception.
Mirtazapine, which increases serotonin and noradrenaline release, appears to help fibromyalgia patients improve sleep, pain, and quality of life.
Duloxetine produces greater pain relief than placebo in fibromyalgia patients.

Amitriptyline, the most prescribed TCA for fibromyalgia, enhances central pain modulation via norepinephrine/serotonin reuptake inhibition and improves pain and sleep quality, though evidence is limited.
Exercise therapy improves pain intensity, sleep disturbances, fatigue, and depression in fibromyalgia patients and enhances quality of life and ability to perform daily activities.
Aquatic aerobic exercise significantly improved sleep quality and pain perception scores on the FIQ scale in fibromyalgia patients.

Tramadol, the most commonly used opioid in fibromyalgia, reduced reported pain levels in patients but is limited by adverse effects such as dizziness, drowsiness, anxiety, and constipation.

Fentanyl, a potent opioid stronger than morphine, is considered as a last-resort treatment for extremely acute fibromyalgia pain crises and has been shown in clinical studies to inhibit onset of severe secondary pain.
Pregabalin, the most commonly used gabapentinoid for fibromyalgia, has demonstrated clinical utility in reducing pain by decreasing perception of sensory/neuropathic pain.

Nortriptyline shows a similar pharmacological profile to amitriptyline in fibromyalgia but with potentially better tolerability due to lower anticholinergic effects.
TCAs offer benefits for pain and sleep in fibromyalgia but their use is limited by adverse effects including dry mouth, constipation, and potential cardiac complications.
Exercise therapy improves pain intensity, sleep disturbances, fatigue, and depression in fibromyalgia and enhances quality of life and ability to perform daily activities.
Physical exercise restores HPA axis output and increases hippocampal dendritic complexity and BDNF expression, mechanisms thought to underlie its benefit in fibromyalgia.
Stretching exercises improved physical function and pain, significantly impacting patients' quality of life.
Resistance training reduces depression symptoms in fibromyalgia patients.
Aerobic exercise showed weak evidence for reducing pain intensity and depression and increasing motor function, but moderate evidence for improving quality of life on the FIQ scale.
Flexibility exercises effectively reduce pain, fatigue, and sleep disturbances, improving quality of life, though protocol inconsistency may limit results.
Muscle strength training showed weak evidence for improving physical function, pain, muscle strength, and sensitivity on the FIQ scale, with variability between protocols affecting results.
Therapeutic Pilates significantly improved vitality, pain modulation, and functional capacity on the FIQ scale in fibromyalgia patients.
A combined strength, flexibility, and aerobic exercise program improved range of motion of shoulder and hip joints and increased grip strength in fibromyalgia patients.
A long-term individualized training program (3x/week, 30-60 min sessions) improved leg strength, grip strength, balance, cardiorespiratory capacity, and quality of life compared to controls.
Aquatic aerobic exercise (hydrotherapy) showed significant improvements in sleep quality and pain perception on the FIQ scale.
Occipital nerve stimulation via subcutaneous electrodes is an invasive electrotherapy technique linked to inhibition of the descending pain pathway in fibromyalgia.
Transcranial direct current stimulation applied at the primary motor cortex can induce changes in cortical excitability and neuroplasticity in fibromyalgia patients.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex has effects on excitatory modulation of cortical and deep brain areas via current pulses.

A manual therapy technique using moderate digital pressure significantly decreased pain perception and improved muscle fatigue and tension-anxiety state compared to a placebo group in women with fibromyalgia.

A systematic review of RCTs found improvements in quality of life with manual lymphatic drainage and myofascial therapy in fibromyalgia patients, but evidence quality ranged from very weak to moderate.
A broader systematic review of randomized clinical trials found current evidence insufficient to support widespread use of manual therapy for fibromyalgia.
General osteopathic treatment was the sole manual therapy intervention demonstrating clinically relevant improvements in pain relief compared to control in fibromyalgia patients.
The review states that virtual reality interventions have shown effectiveness in reducing pain both during and after use in chronic conditions including fibromyalgia and back pain.

The paper describes central hypersensitization, neurotransmitter dysregulation, and autonomic nervous system abnormalities as key pathomechanisms underlying chronic musculoskeletal pain syndromes such as fibromyalgia.

The proposed mechanisms behind VR's analgesic effectiveness include distraction, immersion, and coupling with cognitive behavioral therapy, which are thought to promote neuroplasticity and alter pain perception, with functional MRI studies showing effects on specific brain regions.

In 2017 the IASP formally recognized nociplastic pain as a third pain mechanism distinct from nociceptive and neuropathic pain, reflecting evidence that pain in conditions like fibromyalgia arises from CNS processing rather than peripheral nociceptive input.

The first fMRI study of fibromyalgia (Gracely et al, 2002) showed that low-intensity stimuli perceived as painful by FM patients but not controls activated multiple pain-processing brain regions including primary and secondary somatosensory cortices.
Quantitative sensory testing showed FM patients experience diffuse hyperalgesia/allodynia beyond originally defined tender points, leading to abandonment of tender points from later FM criteria.

Individuals with FM and other nociplastic pain states show polysensory hyper-responsiveness, being as sensitive to light and noise as they are to painful stimuli, indicating a CNS mechanism since visual/auditory input bypasses the spinal cord.
Early brain imaging in nociplastic pain states identified hyperactivity of the insula, a region implicated in sensory integration and interoception.
Comorbid (secondary) fibromyalgia is very common across nearly every autoimmune disorder, a phenomenon also termed central sensitization or centralized pain.

Higher FM Survey scores (used as a surrogate for central sensitization/nociplastic pain) in OA patients are associated with reduced response to lower extremity arthroplasty and to perioperative opioids.
Nearly identical findings of nociplastic-pain-related poor treatment response were observed in women undergoing hysterectomy for chronic pelvic pain.
fMRI findings could predict poor analgesic response to surgery in OA patients.
QST-assessed function of descending analgesic pathways predicted response to knee arthroplasty.
In RA, the FM measure identifies a subset of patients with QST and functional neuroimaging evidence of central sensitization/nociplastic pain who are less likely to respond to biologics and DMARDs.
SNRIs (duloxetine, milnacipran) are more likely to be effective in the subset of OA and RA patients with more widespread/nociplastic pain.
The spatial distribution (widespreadness) of pain is described as the best single determinant of whether a pain mechanism is nociplastic.

Longitudinal studies show non-pain symptoms such as fatigue, sleep problems, memory issues and mood problems predict the subsequent development of nociplastic pain, supporting them as CNS-driven symptoms and treatment targets.
Females are 1.5-2 times more likely than males to develop nociplastic pain, with the sex difference emerging after puberty.
Adverse childhood experiences increase risk of nociplastic pain, but only about 10% of people who develop nociplastic pain do so via this pathway.
Brain imaging studies suggest a pre-existing diathesis for nociplastic pain may be identifiable before pain develops.
Widespreadness of pain is associated with increased functional connectivity between the default mode, salience and sensorimotor brain networks in nociplastic pain conditions.

Individuals with nociplastic pain show abnormal descending pain modulatory system function, with decreased inhibitory and increased facilitatory influences causing net disinhibition and decreased threshold for peripheral nociceptive firing.
Immune activation in nociplastic pain (FM) differs from autoimmune-type inflammation, being best detected via assays that stimulate whole blood to reveal a primed immune system.
Decreased intraepidermal nerve fiber density has been observed in nociplastic pain but is considered a non-specific finding likely reflecting neuroplasticity rather than a distinct pathology.
Low-dose naltrexone, which blocks the endogenous opioid system, has some evidence for therapeutic benefit in nociplastic pain, though other mechanisms may also be involved.
Opioids may worsen nociplastic pain via opioid-induced hyperalgesia if the endogenous opioid system is involved in disease pathogenesis, supporting caution against opioid use.
In studies of new-onset nociplastic pain in children, symptom onset order was sleep/memory issues first, followed by pain, then mood problems.
In children, baseline mood disorder did not predict subsequent development of pain, suggesting pain-related disability drives later mood problems rather than the reverse.
Catastrophising has been shown in multiple recent studies to markedly improve when patients are given effective pain treatment.
In a study of emotional awareness and expression therapy (EAET), the best treatment responders had relatively normal QST profiles, suggesting multiple distinct endophenotypes of nociplastic pain.
The author states there is no evidence that fibromyalgia is an autoimmune disease, and considers it unlikely that animal or in vitro studies will change that conclusion.

Wolfe showed that in rheumatic disorders, higher FM Survey Questionnaire scores (fibromyalgianess) were associated with more pain and disability and were a more powerful predictor of outcomes than objective measures like ESR or joint space.
Familial/genetic contribution to nociplastic pain is highest in 'top-down' individuals who develop primary pain symptoms earlier in life, typically starting with sleep/memory problems in adolescence.
Concomitant fibromyalgia is reported in 4.9-52.4% of rheumatoid arthritis patients, far exceeding the 1-5% prevalence of fibromyalgia in the general population.
Fibromyalgia pathophysiology is theorized to involve central sensitization to pain along with deficits in endogenous pain-inhibitory mechanisms.
Compared with healthy individuals, fibromyalgia patients show lowered pain thresholds and tolerance along with hyperalgesia and allodynia.

EULAR/ACR fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria require a Widespread Pain Index (WPI) of 7 with Symptom Severity (SS) score of 5, or WPI 3-6 with SS score of 9, with symptoms present at a similar level for at least 3 months and no other disorder better explaining the pain.
RA patients with concomitant fibromyalgia rarely achieve remission or low disease activity and switch treatments more often due to non-response.
The Fibromyalgia Rapid Screening Tool (FiRST), a self-administered questionnaire, has reported sensitivity of 90.5% and specificity of 85.7% for identifying fibromyalgia.

Nociplastic pain, defined as pain arising from altered nociception without clear tissue damage or somatosensory lesion, is described as a component of fibromyalgia as well as localized conditions including temporomandibular disorders, bladder pain syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, tension headache and chronic migraine, often co-occurring with fatigue, memory issues, poor sleep and mood disturbance.

The Central Sensitization Inventory is a multidimensional, patient-appropriate tool for fibromyalgia but was originally developed to measure central sensitivity syndromes broadly (including fibromyalgia, IBS, and chronic fatigue syndrome) and is not specific to central sensitization alone nor adapted specifically for RA patients.
Standard RA pain assessment tools (MDHAQ, painDETECT, DN4, RAPID3, PAS-II) are noted as not appropriate for patients with fibromyalgia because of their distorted perception of pain.
In cross-sectional univariable analysis, CPM was not associated with demographic or clinical variables in fibromyalgia patients.
In multivariable regression controlling for age, sex, and symptom duration, CPM was significantly associated with baseline Quality of Life Scale (QOLs) scores.

Longitudinal mixed-effects modeling showed CPM acts as an effect modifier for changes over time in pain VAS, QOLs, and FIQR, with low-efficient CPM at baseline associated with greater improvement over time compared to high-efficient CPM.
The authors conclude that CPM is not a reliable cross-sectional biomarker of clinical manifestations in chronic pain/fibromyalgia patients, though it may predict longitudinal pain evolution.
Among 97 RA patients screened with the FAST 4 index, the prevalence of comorbid fibromyalgia was 30.9%.
The FAST 4 index showed 78.6% sensitivity and 87.1% specificity for detecting fibromyalgia defined by the FiRST score, with PPV 73.3%, NPV 90%, LR+ 6, and LR- 0.246.
A positive FAST 4 index (fibromyalgia screen) was associated with higher numbers of painful and swollen joints in RA patients.
Patients with a positive FAST 4 index (fibromyalgia) had significantly higher DAS28-ESR disease activity scores.
Depression and anxiety, as assessed in the MDHAQ, were significantly associated with a positive FAST 4 (fibromyalgia) screen in RA patients.
No significant association was found between fibromyalgia (FAST 4 positive) status and CRP, ESR, biological treatment use, or corticosteroid use.
In multivariate logistic regression, depression remained the only independent risk factor for a positive FAST 4 (fibromyalgia) screen, increasing risk approximately sixfold.
Myricitrin treatment significantly improved reserpine-induced nociceptive hypersensitivity assessed by the hot plate test.
Myricitrin treatment corrected the reserpine-induced imbalance in brain monoamine neurotransmitter levels.
Myricitrin attenuated reserpine-induced oxidative stress by up-regulating Nrf2 and HO-1 protein expression in the brain.
Myricitrin enhanced SOD and CAT antioxidant enzyme activities in the brain of reserpine-treated rats.
Myricitrin reduced brain malondialdehyde content, indicating decreased lipid peroxidation, in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model.
Myricitrin treatment decreased NLRP3 inflammasome expression that was elevated by reserpine.
Myricitrin reduced brain IL-1β levels that were elevated by reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model.
Myricitrin reduced NF-κB levels elevated by reserpine in the fibromyalgia model.
Myricitrin demonstrated anti-apoptotic activity by increasing the BAX/Bcl-2 ratio through lowering Bcl-2 and increasing BAX levels.
Myricitrin treatment significantly boosted SIRT1 deacetylase expression in reserpine-treated animals and molecular docking showed MYR forms a stable complex at the SIRT1 binding site.
Myricitrin effectively ameliorated reserpine-induced changes in miR-320 gene expression in the fibromyalgia model.
