Myricitrin treatment reduced reserpine-induced elevation of brain interleukin-1 beta levels.
Myricitrin reduced reserpine-induced increases in nuclear factor-κB in the brain.
Myricitrin treatment increased BAX protein levels as part of an altered apoptotic balance in the reserpine model.
Myricitrin treatment significantly increased SIRT1 deacetylase expression in reserpine-treated rats relative to untreated fibromyalgia model animals.
Molecular docking analysis showed that myricitrin can form a stable complex within the binding site of SIRT1, suggesting direct molecular interaction as a mechanism of activation.
Myricitrin treatment ameliorated reserpine-induced changes in brain miR-320 expression in the fibromyalgia model.
Myricitrin treatment ameliorated reserpine-induced changes in brain miR-107 expression in the fibromyalgia model.
IL-18BP treatment suppressed proliferation of activated tryptase+chymase+c-kit+FcεR1+ mast cells in a dose-dependent manner.
RNA expression levels of tryptase and chymase in mast cells were reduced by treatment with 100 ng/mL IL-18BP.
Levels of MMP-3/9, IL-17A, IL-6, TNF-α, and sRANKL secreted by activated mast cells were significantly inhibited by 100 ng/mL IL-18BP.
Annexin V+ (apoptotic) and annexin V-PI+ (necroptotic) mast cells were reduced following incubation with 100 ng/mL IL-18BP.
IL-33 stimulation of mast cells increased TRAP+ multinucleated osteoclast formation and bone resorption area, and these IL-33-driven effects were suppressed by co-treatment with IL-18BP.
Expression of osteoclast differentiation-related genes (TRAP, ATP6v0d2, RANK, and cathepsin K) was suppressed by IL-18BP treatment.
Patients with severe aplastic anaemia had shorter peripheral blood telomere length than expected for their age.
Mosaic chromosomal alterations were detected in 28.6% of patients with severe aplastic anaemia.
Chromosome 6p copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (6p-CNLOH) was found in 15.9% of patients with severe aplastic anaemia.
Loss of chromosome 7 was detected in 3.0% of patients with severe aplastic anaemia and was associated with markedly worse post-transplant survival.
Loss of chromosome X was detected in 4.1% of female patients with severe aplastic anaemia.
The fraction of blood cells carrying mosaic chromosomal alterations was negatively correlated with measured telomere length.
A weaker, borderline-significant negative correlation was observed between mCA cell fraction and genetically predicted telomere length.
Patients with chromosome 7 loss had markedly lower 3-year post-HCT survival probability (39%) compared to those with chr6-CNLOH (72%), other mCAs (60%), or no mCAs (70%).
In multivariable analysis, short telomere length was significantly associated with worse post-HCT survival.
In multivariable analysis, chromosome 7 loss was not significantly associated with post-HCT survival after adjusting for telomere length.
Human peanut-specific IgE monoclonal antibodies derived from allergic individuals predominantly target immunodominant epitopes on the peanut allergens Ara h 2 and Ara h 6.

Class-switched recombinant IgG4 monoclonal antibodies (a mixture called IGNX001) effectively blocked Ara h 2/Ara h 6 epitopes and provided robust protection against peanut-mediated mast cell activation in vitro.
In a peanut allergy mouse model, IGNX001 provided protection against anaphylaxis following intragastric peanut challenge.
Dupilumab produced a significantly greater reduction in median serum total IgE than placebo at both week 12 and week 24 in patients with H1-antihistamine-resistant CSU.
The magnitude of dupilumab-induced IgE reduction was similar regardless of baseline IgE level, with greater reduction seen at week 24 than week 12.
Dupilumab improved Itch Severity Score (ISS7) versus placebo at week 12 and week 24, and this improvement was independent of baseline serum IgE level.
Dupilumab improved Urticaria Activity Score (UAS7) versus placebo at week 12 and week 24, independent of baseline serum IgE level.
Dupilumab improved Hives Severity Score (HSS7) versus placebo at week 12 and week 24, independent of baseline serum IgE level.

Change in serum IgE only weakly correlated with changes in itch, urticaria activity, and hive severity scores in dupilumab-treated patients, suggesting dupilumab's clinical efficacy is largely IgE-independent.
Using a 100 IU/mL cutoff, baseline total IgE level did not predict clinical response to dupilumab in CSU patients.
Overall rates of treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between placebo- and dupilumab-treated CSU patients, consistent with dupilumab's known safety profile.

Per cited literature, higher baseline serum total IgE (>100 IU/mL) in CSU patients is associated with higher disease activity, longer disease duration, greater likelihood of omalizumab response, faster relapse after omalizumab discontinuation, and poorer cyclosporine response.

IL-4/IL-13 signaling in CSU may act via multiple IgE-independent mechanisms, including direct mast cell activation through IL-4Rα expressed on mast cells, immune-cell trafficking into skin, and neuronal sensitization causing itch, in addition to promoting B-cell IgE isotype switching.

The anti-membrane-IgE antibody quilizumab reduced IgE levels versus placebo in CSU but failed to produce clinically meaningful symptomatic improvement, supporting an IgE-independent component of CSU pathogenesis.
Paired acute and baseline tryptase measurement serves as a diagnostic criterion confirming systemic mast cell activation in drug-induced anaphylaxis.
Paired tryptase levels also function as a differential diagnostic criterion to distinguish mast-cell-mediated drug reactions from immediate hypersensitivity reactions involving other mechanisms.
Baseline tryptase determination can help identify underlying mast cell conditions such as hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, including in familial clusters, following drug-induced anaphylaxis.

The review identifies a persistent unmet need in implementing existing guidelines for paired tryptase measurement, and a lack of standardized recommendations for hereditary alpha-tryptasemia testing and counselling.

Administration of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum D266 modulated intestinal peristalsis, enteric neuron activity, visceral hypersensitivity, colonic inflammation, gut barrier function, and mast cell activation in an IBS model.
Lp D266 reshapes gut microbiota composition and enhances tryptophan metabolism in the gut.
Enhanced tryptophan metabolism from Lp D266 activates AhR signaling, leading to increased IL-22 production and maintenance of gut homeostasis.
IL-22 production is increased downstream of AhR activation following Lp D266-driven tryptophan metabolism, contributing to gut homeostasis.
Lp D266 administration reduced colonic mast cell activation in the IBS model.
Combining Lp D266 with tryptophan supplementation synergistically ameliorated IBS symptoms compared to either alone.

Nearly half of spongiotic dermatitis/urticaria cases showed at least 20 mast cells per high-power field, similar to a criterion used for diagnosing cutaneous mastocytosis, indicating this threshold is nonspecific.
Only a minority of spongiotic dermatitis/urticaria cases showed clusters of 15 mast cells, suggesting this criterion is more specific but not highly sensitive for mastocytosis.
Most cutaneous mastocytosis cases met the 20 mast cells per high-power field criterion, but this was not universal.
Clusters of 15 mast cells were found in over half of mastocytosis cases, but this criterion missed a substantial proportion of confirmed cases, indicating limited sensitivity.
Conditioned media from canine adipose-derived MSCs significantly inhibited splenocyte proliferation in vitro.
MSC conditioned media induced the generation of regulatory T cells.
MSC conditioned media decreased mast cell degranulation, a mechanism relevant to atopic dermatitis pathology.
The soluble factor TGF-beta 1, known to reduce atopic dermatitis symptoms, was detectable in the MSC secretome after sequential concentration and lyophilization.
Nano-villi chitosan microspheres (CS-MS) produced by a phase inversion regeneration method achieved high loading capacity and sustained release of the MSC secretome.
Local injection of secretome-loaded chitosan microspheres (ST/SC-MS) reduced clinical severity of atopic dermatitis more effectively than treatment with secretome alone.
Histological analysis showed that ST/SC-MS treatment potently suppressed epidermal hyperplasia, immunocyte infiltration, and mast cell activation in atopic dermatitis skin lesions.
The rate of de-novo headache was significantly higher in healthcare workers wearing N95 respirator masks compared to other groups.
Baseline mean flow velocity of the right middle cerebral artery was significantly lower in the N95 mask group compared to the control and surgical mask groups.
Mean breath-holding index (BHI), a measure of cerebrovascular reactivity, was significantly lower in the N95 mask group compared to control and surgical mask groups.

Despite the lower mean BHI in the N95 group, only one N95 mask user had a BHI value below the 0.69 threshold indicating impaired cerebrovascular reactivity, meaning overall reactivity remained within normal limits.
Surgical mask use did not significantly affect cerebral hemodynamic parameters compared to controls.
The development of de-novo headache was not directly associated with low cerebrovascular reactivity despite the observed decrease in BHI with N95 mask use.
Patients with chronic idiopathic axonal polyneuropathy (CIAP) had significantly reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy compared with healthy controls.
Patients with painful diabetic neuropathy (PDN) had significantly reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy compared with healthy controls.
Diabetic patients without overt neuropathy (DM) also showed significantly reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density compared with healthy controls.

Corneal confocal microscopy nerve parameters (fiber density, branch density, fiber length) in CIAP patients were not significantly different from healthy controls, despite documented skin nerve fiber loss.
In patients with painful diabetic neuropathy, corneal nerve fiber density and fiber length were significantly reduced compared with healthy controls.
In patients with CIAP, corneal confocal microscopy parameters did not correlate with intraepidermal nerve fiber density from skin biopsy.
Inter-center intraclass correlation coefficient for corneal nerve fiber density measurement was 0.77, indicating good reliability.
Inter-center intraclass correlation coefficient for corneal nerve fiber length measurement was 0.87, indicating good reliability.
The authors conclude that CCM is not a good biomarker for small nerve fiber loss specifically in CIAP patients, in contrast to its utility in diabetic neuropathy.
In a prior linked study, 100 µM resveratrol was identified as the optimal dose for inhibiting JHF fibroblast proliferation up to 60 hours by real-time impedance analysis.
In a wound-healing model, all resveratrol doses (50, 75, 100 µM) reduced JHF fibroblast proliferation compared to untreated control, with the 100 µM dose showing the strongest effect.
Unlike JHF fibroblasts, healthy gingival fibroblasts (GF) showed no significant proliferation difference across resveratrol doses at any time point.
By MTT assay at 24 hours, 100 µM and 200 µM resveratrol produced significantly less JHF fibroblast proliferation than 50 µM, with no difference between 100 and 200 µM.
By MTT assay at 48 hours, all three resveratrol doses (50, 100, 200 µM) significantly reduced JHF fibroblast proliferation compared to untreated control.
At 72 hours, 100 µM and 200 µM resveratrol significantly reduced JHF fibroblast proliferation versus control, but the 50 µM dose no longer differed significantly from control.
At 72 hours, the 200 µM resveratrol dose produced significantly lower JHF fibroblast proliferation than the 100 µM dose, indicating a dose-dependent effect.
Resveratrol at 100 µM and 200 µM significantly suppressed TGF-β synthesis by JHF fibroblasts at 48 hours compared to untreated control, with no difference between the two doses.
Resveratrol at 100 µM and 200 µM significantly suppressed CTGF synthesis by JHF fibroblasts at 48 hours compared to untreated control, with no difference between the two doses.
Resveratrol at 100 µM and 200 µM significantly reduced collagen (COL-1) synthesis by JHF fibroblasts at 48 hours compared to untreated control.
Women with vulvodynia have a 2- to 4-fold increased likelihood of also being diagnosed with IBS compared to those without vulvodynia.
Across the reviewed studies, mast cell involvement was identified as a common pathophysiological mechanism shared between vulvodynia and IBS.
Visceral hypersensitization was identified as a shared pathophysiological feature underlying the co-occurrence of vulvodynia and IBS.
A significant diagnostic delay for vulvodynia was consistently reported across the included studies, contributing to underdiagnosis.
During ganglionic (autonomic) blockade with trimethaphan, heart rate increased significantly more in Black women than in White women.
The decrease in systolic blood pressure during ganglionic (autonomic) blockade with trimethaphan did not differ significantly between Black and White women.
The decrease in diastolic blood pressure during ganglionic blockade did not differ significantly between Black and White women.

Under complete autonomic blockade, NO synthase inhibition with L-NMMA produced a significantly greater rise in systolic blood pressure in Black women than in White women, indicating a larger tonic contribution of endothelial NO to blood pressure in Black women.
NO synthase inhibition with L-NMMA during autonomic blockade produced a significantly greater rise in diastolic blood pressure in Black women compared to White women.
Heart rate change with L-NMMA-induced NO synthase inhibition during autonomic blockade did not differ significantly between Black and White women.
During ganglionic blockade, high-frequency heart rate variability (a marker of parasympathetic/vagal modulation) was significantly lower in Black women than in White women.
Low-frequency heart rate variability decreased to similar values in both groups during ganglionic blockade, with no significant between-group difference.
Total cholesterol was lower (borderline significance) in Black obese women compared with White obese women at baseline.

Changes in cardiac output, stroke volume, and systemic vascular resistance during autonomic blockade were not significantly different between Black and White women, indicating equivalent systemic hemodynamic responses despite differing heart rate and pressor responses.
Baroreflex sensitivity declined significantly from baseline after trimethaphan-induced ganglionic blockade in both Black and White women, confirming effective autonomic blockade.
Baroreflex sensitivity did not differ significantly between Black and White women either at baseline or after autonomic blockade.
Other heart rate variability parameters (SDRRI, RMSSD) during autonomic blockade did not differ significantly between Black and White women.
Col4a1+/Δex41 mice have reduced body size and weight compared to wild-type littermates.
Col4a1+/Δex41 mice show reduced ossification during embryogenesis and early postnatal life, predominantly in calvaria, ribs, and vertebrae, based on Alcian blue/Alizarin red skeletal staining.

In P7 calvaria, Col4a1+/Δex41 mice show reduced expression of bone formation genes Col1a1 and Bglap, and increased expression of Sost (inhibitor of bone formation) and Acp5 (bone resorption marker) compared to wild-type littermates.
Both Tnfsf11 (RANKL) and Tnfrsf11b (OPG) expression were increased in P7 Col4a1+/Δex41 calvaria, but the Tnfsf11/Tnfrsf11b ratio was reduced compared to wild-type.
A general reduction in bone marker gene expression was observed in P7 Col4a1+/Δex41 femurs compared to wild-type littermates, consistent with reduced bone turnover.
Femur length was significantly reduced in 3-4 month old Col4a1+/Δex41 mice compared to wild-type littermates.
μCT analysis showed cortical bone thickness was significantly decreased in adult Col4a1+/Δex41 femurs, while cortical area fraction and cortical BMD were unchanged.
Femoral trabecular bone volume fraction and trabecular number were significantly reduced, and trabecular spacing significantly increased, in Col4a1+/Δex41 mice of both sexes.
Trabecular thickness was significantly reduced in male but not female Col4a1+/Δex41 mice compared to sex-matched wild-type littermates.
3-point bending flexural testing showed decreased stiffness and maximal load in Col4a1+/Δex41 femurs, consistent with the reduced cortical thickness.

Skeletal defect severity differs by mutation: Col4a1+/G1344D mice show mild reduced ossification and developmental delay while Col4a1+/G394V mice show no gross developmental skeletal abnormality, though both show trabecular microarchitecture alterations in adulthood.
Two bona fide TGFβ target genes were increased in calvaria and femurs of P7 Col4a1+/Δex41 mice, suggesting elevated TGFβ signaling may contribute to skeletal manifestations.

4PBA treatment (50 mM in drinking water from E9.5) had mixed effects on skeletal parameters in Col4a1+/Δex41 mice: it improved trabecular number and separation but significantly decreased trabecular thickness and BMD, and exacerbated reductions in femoral mechanical stiffness without affecting material bone parameters.

Genetically reducing TGFβ signaling via Tgfb1 heterozygosity significantly improved trabecular number and separation and tended to improve trabecular bone density in Col4a1+/Δex41 mice, though it had detrimental trabecular effects in wild-type mice.

Tgfb1 heterozygosity did not improve femoral bone mechanical or material properties (stiffness, maximal load, elastic modulus) in Col4a1+/Δex41 mice, despite reducing maximal load and increasing elastic modulus in wild-type mice.
Col4a1+/Δex41 mice exhibit a significant increase in femoral bone elastic modulus (a material property) despite unchanged cortical bone mineral density.

Synchrotron radiation μCT revealed reduced vascular canal density and a trend towards decreased cortical bone porosity in femurs of Col4a1+/Δex41 mice, suggesting vascular abnormalities contribute to skeletal phenotype.

Selective expression of the Col4a1Δex41 mutation in vascular endothelial cells (TekCre;Col4a1Flex41/Flex41) was not sufficient to fully recapitulate the skeletal defects seen in global Col4a1+/Δex41 mice, showing only reduced total area and trabecular bone surface/volume with no other cortical/trabecular abnormalities.
TekCre;Col4a1Flex41/Flex41 mice showed increased elastic modulus, mirroring the global Col4a1+/Δex41 phenotype, suggesting a partial vascular contribution to skeletal material property changes.

The authors note that abnormal/elevated TGFβ signaling has also been reported in osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), suggesting a possible convergent pathogenic mechanism shared among Gould syndrome, OI, and EDS.
In a propensity-matched comparison, 10-kHz spinal cord stimulation produced a significantly greater reduction in pain scores than splanchnic nerve radiofrequency ablation at 12 months.
The proportion of patients achieving at least 50% pain relief at 12 months was significantly higher with SCS than with snRFA.
Opioid usage decreased at 12 months in patients treated with SCS but remained unchanged in those treated with snRFA.

Spontaneously hypertensive rats (model group) showed increased sympathetic irritation scores and increased systolic and diastolic blood pressure compared with normal Wistar Kyoto controls at every time point.

Acupuncture at the 'antihypertensive acupoint prescription' reduced sympathetic irritation scores after 3-4 weeks and reduced systolic/diastolic blood pressure after 2-4 weeks compared with the untreated model group.
Serum CGRP levels were decreased in the spontaneous hypertension model group compared with normal controls.
Acupuncture increased serum CGRP levels compared with the untreated model group.
Acupuncture increased serum CGRP and NO levels in spontaneous hypertension rats compared with the untreated model group.
Acupuncture decreased serum ET-1 and NPY levels compared with the model group.
Acupuncture reduced epinephrine and norepinephrine levels in the anterior paraventricular nucleus (PVA) compared with the model group.
eNOS mRNA expression in the internal carotid artery and arcuate nucleus (ARC) was decreased in the model group compared with normal controls.
Acupuncture increased eNOS mRNA expression in the internal carotid artery and ARC compared with the model group.
CGRP mRNA expression in the posterior paraventricular nucleus (PVP) and ventrolateral medulla (VLM) was decreased in the model group compared with normal controls.
Acupuncture treatment increased serum CGRP levels in spontaneous hypertension rats compared with the untreated model group.
Acupuncture increased serum NO levels compared with the model group.
Acupuncture reduced serum ET-1 levels compared with the model group.
Acupuncture reduced serum NPY levels compared with the model group.
Acupuncture reduced epinephrine and norepinephrine levels in the anterior paraventricular nucleus compared with the model group.
In the model group, the media of the internal carotid artery exhibited thickening and remodeling compared with normal structure.

Participants often self-managed their CFS/ME or fibromyalgia independently, delaying contact with healthcare services until reaching a 'crisis point', partly due to fear of wasting clinicians' time or having a negative healthcare encounter.

Some participants perceived that clinicians did not believe in the legitimacy of CFS/ME and fibromyalgia, compounded by the hidden nature of symptoms, reflecting an imbalance of clinician 'power-knowledge'.
Telephone consultations were viewed as convenient for avoiding travel to surgeries but were often experienced as challenging and unpredictable when no set appointment time was given.

Video consulting allowed some participants to visually demonstrate physical symptoms (e.g., twitching) to clinicians and mitigated concerns about lack of non-verbal cues, but was used infrequently in practice.

Reliance on verbal communication in telephone consultations, including loudspeaker use and background typing noise, was particularly difficult for participants with sensory disturbance or sensitivities.
Consulting with the same, familiar clinician (continuity of care) was consistently perceived positively and associated with feeling understood at an individual level.
Remote consulting was generally felt to be less conducive to addressing the wider, holistic complexity and comorbidities of CFS/ME and fibromyalgia, being better suited to single, distinct issues.

A positive therapeutic relationship with a clinician was reported as achievable across all consultation modalities (telephone, video, and face-to-face), suggesting the clinician's approach could outweigh some limitations inherent to remote consulting.

Both video and face-to-face appointments were felt by participants to reinforce the legitimacy of their symptoms by allowing clinicians to visually perceive pain or distress, more so than telephone consultations.
Informal telephone 'check-in' consultations, used to follow up after a consultation or conduct routine review, were viewed positively by participants for building ongoing clinician relationships.
Plasma BH4 levels, normalized to protein and molecular weight, were strongly elevated in ME+OI subjects compared to age-/gender-matched healthy controls.
Plasma BH2, the oxidized metabolite of BH4, was significantly elevated in ME+OI subjects compared to healthy controls.
Protein expression of GTPCH1, the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo BH4 biosynthesis, was strongly elevated in PBMCs of ME+OI subjects compared to HC.
DHPR protein, which regenerates BH4 from qBH2, was strongly upregulated in PBMCs of ME+OI subjects compared to controls.

A 46-gene microarray screen of PPP and BH4 pathway genes identified 20 upregulated genes (including ptps, g6pd, dhpr, ldh, cr, pah, gtpch1, dhfr, nos3, and pcd), 5 downregulated genes, and the remainder unaltered in ME+OI subjects versus healthy controls.
G6PDH mRNA, encoding the rate-limiting PPP enzyme, was significantly upregulated in ME+OI subjects vs HC by real-time PCR.
TALDO1 mRNA, a key non-oxidative PPP enzyme, was significantly upregulated in ME+OI subjects vs HC.
mRNA expression of 6PGL was not significantly different between ME+OI subjects and HC despite being flagged in the initial microarray.
LDH mRNA, indicating anaerobic glycolysis, was significantly upregulated in ME+OI subjects compared to HC.
HK mRNA, an aerobic glycolysis enzyme, was significantly downregulated in ME+OI subjects compared to HC.
GAPDH mRNA, an aerobic glycolysis enzyme, was significantly downregulated in ME+OI subjects compared to HC.
GTPCH1 mRNA was upregulated in ME+OI subjects vs HC by real-time and semi-quantitative PCR.
G6PDH enzymatic activity was significantly and consistently higher in PBMCs of ME+OI subjects compared to controls, along with an elevated NADP/NADPH ratio.
The NADP/NADPH ratio, indicative of G6PDH activity, was significantly higher in PBMCs of ME+OI cases compared to HC.
TALDO protein was significantly upregulated by ELISA in PBMCs of ME+OI cases compared to healthy controls, while transketolase (TK) protein was not significantly changed.
Although TK protein expression was unchanged, TK enzymatic activity was significantly elevated in PBMCs of ME+OI subjects compared to controls.

In C20 microglial cells, exogenous R5P treatment under hypoxic (but not regular) conditions dose-dependently upregulated TALDO1 expression and increased TK enzymatic activity, modeling the non-oxidative PPP induction seen in ME+OI subjects.
R5P treatment under hypoxia elevated PRPP levels and upregulated IMPDH2 and GMPS expression in C20 microglial cells, indicating induction of purine biosynthesis downstream of non-oxidative PPP.
Induction of non-oxidative PPP by R5P under hypoxia upregulated GTPCH1, BH4, and BH2 expression in C20 microglial cells, whereas no change occurred under regular (non-hypoxic) conditions.

siRNA-mediated knockdown of taldo1 attenuated R5P-induced PRPP, IMPDH2, GMPS, GTPCH1, and BH4 expression in hypoxic C20 microglia, directly implicating non-oxidative PPP flux through TALDO1 in driving BH4 biosynthesis.
siRNA knockdown of taldo1 attenuated R5P-stimulated iNOS expression and nitric oxide production in C20 microglia, indicating non-oxidative PPP-derived BH4 drives iNOS activation.

Supplementation with high-BH4 ME+OI plasma (>15 pmol/mg), but not low-BH4 healthy control plasma (<5 pmol/mg), restored iNOS expression and nitric oxide production in taldo1-silenced, R5P-treated hypoxic microglia.
Plasma BH4 levels positively correlated with NO-inducing capacity across ME+OI and healthy control plasma samples.
In C20 microglial cells, ribose-5-phosphate (R5P) treatment dose-dependently increased TALDO1 expression under hypoxic conditions but not under regular oxygen conditions.
TK enzymatic activity was significantly increased in C20 microglia treated with 10 μM R5P under hypoxic conditions but not under regular conditions.
PRPP levels were highly elevated in C20 microglial cell lysates treated with 5 and 10 μM R5P under hypoxic but not regular conditions.
IMPDH2 protein expression was strongly elevated in C20 microglia treated with 10 μM R5P under hypoxic but not regular conditions.
GMP synthase (GMPS) expression was strongly elevated in C20 microglia under hypoxic conditions with R5P treatment but not under regular conditions.
Plasma BH4 levels were strongly elevated in ME+OI subjects compared to age-/gender-matched healthy controls, confirming a prior finding.
GTPCH1 protein expression was strongly elevated in PBMCs of ME+OI subjects compared to healthy controls, confirming mRNA-level findings.
Plasma BH2, a metabolite/precursor of BH4, was strongly upregulated in ME+OI subjects compared to healthy controls.
DHPR, the enzyme that converts qBH2 to BH4 in the regenerative pathway, was strongly upregulated in PBMCs of ME+OI subjects compared to healthy controls.
Despite both BH4 and BH2 being elevated in ME+OI plasma, BH2 levels were much higher than BH4, suggesting disturbed BH4 cellular homeostasis and possible nitrosylative stress.

Induction of non-oxidative PPP by R5P treatment under hypoxia upregulated GTPCH1, BH4, and BH2 expression in C20 microglia in a dose-dependent manner, with no change under regular (non-hypoxic) conditions.
In R5P/hypoxia-treated C20 microglia, BH2 levels were approximately 1.5-fold higher than BH4, mirroring the plasma finding and suggesting dysregulated nitric oxide synthesis.
siRNA-mediated knockdown of taldo1 significantly attenuated the R5P-induced elevation of PRPP in C20 microglia, confirming TALDO1's role in driving non-oxidative PPP flux toward purine precursors.

siRNA knockdown of taldo1 strongly suppressed R5P-induced expression of IMPDH2 and GMPS in hypoxic C20 microglia, demonstrating that non-oxidative PPP directly facilitates R5P utilization in purine biosynthesis.
siRNA knockdown of taldo1 strongly attenuated BH4 and GTPCH1 expression induced by R5P treatment in hypoxic C20 microglia, directly linking non-oxidative PPP activity to BH4 biosynthesis via GTPCH1.
R5P treatment under hypoxia strongly induced nitrite/NO production in C20 microglia, linking non-oxidative PPP activation to nitric oxide synthesis.
siRNA knockdown of taldo1 significantly attenuated R5P-stimulated iNOS expression in C20 microglia, indicating that non-oxidative PPP-derived BH4 drives iNOS induction.

Supplementation with high-BH4 ME+OI plasma, but not low-BH4 HC plasma, restored iNOS expression and nitric oxide production in taldo1-silenced, R5P-treated C20 microglia, demonstrating a functional role for plasma-derived BH4 in inflammatory iNOS induction.
Plasma BH4 levels positively correlated with NO-inducing ability across ME+OI and healthy control plasma samples, supporting a direct link between elevated BH4 and iNOS/NO induction in ME+OI.

An analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov entries for Long COVID found wide variability in trial rigor and focus, with most trials testing non-pharmacological interventions lacking sufficient supporting evidence.
The authors recommend prioritizing pharmaceutical trials with potentially curative primary interventions, pursuing both drug repurposing and new drug development for Long COVID.

The authors recommend that Long COVID trials use rigorous yet accessible designs, such as triple-blinded randomized trials that can be conducted remotely without requiring participants to leave their homes.

The authors recommend that Long COVID studies include multiple illness comparator cohorts, such as ME/CFS and dysautonomia, and screen for the full spectrum of symptoms and pathologies of these infection-associated chronic conditions.

The authors recommend that Long COVID trials design inclusion/exclusion criteria with equity and breadth of representation in mind, including participants across all races, ethnicities, genders, and illness severity levels most impacted by COVID-19.

The authors recommend involving patient-researchers in all aspects of Long COVID studies to bring valuable perspectives and increase trial impact, and encourage efficient trial designs that allow studying several therapies in parallel.
The frequency of detectable circulating EBV DNA by qPCR was similar between stroke survivors with low fatigue (24%) and high fatigue (27%).
Among participants positive for circulating EBV, viral load did not differ between low and high fatigue groups.
Initial stroke severity (NIHSS) did not differ between participants with and without detectable circulating EBV.
IgM antibody titres against the EBV lytic viral capsid antigen (VCA) were lower in participants with high post-stroke fatigue compared to those with low fatigue.
IgG antibody titres against EBV VCA did not differ between high and low post-stroke fatigue groups.
Participants with detectable EBV viremia by qPCR had higher anti-VCA IgG titres than those without detectable virus, consistent with an active/reactivated infection response.
IgG antibody titres against EBV latency antigen EBNA1 did not differ between low and high post-stroke fatigue groups.
A lower proportion of the high fatigue group was seropositive for anti-EBNA1 IgG (75%) compared to the low fatigue group (90%).
Among individuals seropositive for anti-EBNA1 IgG, titre did not correlate with fatigue severity.
Anti-VCA IgM titre negatively correlated with self-reported fatigue score (FACIT-F) across the cohort.
Anti-VCA IgM titre was not associated with age, biological sex, days from stroke to baseline, mood, or infarct volume.
Anti-VCA IgM titre was not associated with cognitive domains including working memory, processing speed, memory, visual spatial, or language.
Total circulating IgM and total IgG levels did not differ between low and high post-stroke fatigue groups, indicating the reduced anti-VCA IgM was not due to global antibody deficiency.
Circulating CRP levels did not differ between low and high post-stroke fatigue groups, suggesting fatigue is not associated with generalized systemic immune/inflammatory alteration post-stroke.
No differences in anti-EBV antibody titres or CRP levels were observed between participants with detectable EBV viremia versus those without, apart from the anti-VCA IgG elevation already noted.
Participants with higher post-stroke fatigue had worse mood (lower Stroke Impact Scale domain 3 scores), and fatigue was associated with mood.
IgA reactivity to lipopolysaccharides (bacterial translocation marker) was identified by neural network analysis as an important variable distinguishing Long COVID patients from controls.
IgG reactivity to the tight junction proteins zonulin and occludin (ZOOC) was identified as an important variable associated with Long COVID diagnosis in a neural network model.
CRP, together with IgA-MBP and IgG-MBP, explained 40.9% of the variance in the physio-affective phenome of Long COVID.
Autoimmune responses (IgA and IgG) against myelin basic protein (MBP) were among the top variables explaining the variance in the Long COVID physio-affective phenome.
Autoimmunity against ZOOC (tight junction proteins) strongly predicted the variance in autoimmune responses to myelin basic protein.
Indicants of HHV-6 reactivation were strongly associated with autoimmunity against tight junction proteins (ZOOC) in Long COVID patients.
Increased IgM directed against SARS-CoV-2 was associated with indicants of HHV-6 reactivation in Long COVID patients.
Elevated CCL19 chemokine levels one month after Lyme disease treatment predicted a markedly higher subsequent risk of developing PTLDS.
A muted acute-infection B-cell response, indicated by lower circulating plasmablast levels, was associated with subsequent development of PTLDS.
Infection with RST1-genotype B. burgdorferi strains generates a heightened inflammatory response and is linked to greater symptom severity and increased risk of antibiotic-refractory arthritis.
PTLDS patients showed reduced regional cerebral blood flow in discrete white matter areas compared to healthy subjects, correlating with memory and visuospatial deficits.
A meta-analysis of five studies found PTLDS patients had impaired verbal memory and diminished ability to formulate ideas.
The same meta-analysis found no increased problems in judgment, conceptual thinking, or naming objects among PTLDS patients.
Antibiotic-refractory Lyme arthritis patients showed consistently elevated proinflammatory cytokines in joint/synovial fluid despite negative PCR for Borrelia DNA.

CSF transcriptomic profiling showed roughly 1,000 genes altered at Lyme disease diagnosis versus uninfected transcriptomes, with nearly 700 genes still altered six months after antibiotic treatment (about half upregulated), reflecting decreased but persistent immune/inflammatory gene dysregulation.

In a cohort of 30 patients who developed post-Lyme autoimmune joint diseases, 10 of 27 tested had Lyme-associated autoantibodies (anti-ECGF, anti-ApoB-100, anti-MMP-10), with autoantibody positivity significantly higher than in healthy controls or non-Lyme RA/PsA/SpA patients, and anti-ECGF levels correlated with synovial microvascular lesions.

PTLDS patients showed substantially higher prevalence of anti-neural antibodies (49%) compared to recovered Lyme disease patients (18.5%) and healthy controls (15%), suggesting an autoimmune contribution to neurological/cognitive symptoms.

In mouse xenodiagnosis studies, B. burgdorferi spirochetes remained detectable up to three months after antibiotic treatment (ceftriaxone or doxycycline), though recovered organisms lacked infectivity-associated plasmid genes (lp25, lp28-1).

In chronically infected mice, antibiotic treatment resulted in persistence of low numbers of spirochetes in tissue, with ticks able to acquire and transmit low levels of infectious spirochetes, and qPCR showed very low spirochetal DNA copy numbers relative to acute infection.
A case report documented persistence of B. burgdorferi in flexor retinaculum tendon tissue of an antibiotic-treated patient, associated with musculoskeletal deformities and tendinous pain.

In four patients with treatment-resistant Lyme arthritis, synovial membrane tissue PCR was positive for B. burgdorferi even when synovial fluid PCR was negative, indicating the membrane as a possible persistence reservoir.
A case series of 10 patients with severe neurological limb paralysis identified mixed infections of Borrelia, Babesia divergens, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and Bartonella.
Long-term combined antibiotic and anti-parasitic treatment for tick-borne co-infections resulted in complete motor recovery in 7 of 10 patients with neurological limb paralysis.

Serologic and lymphocyte transformation test evaluation of co-infections found Bartonella henselae seropositivity in 78% of cases, while Chlamydia trachomatis had only 5% seropositivity but 100% LTT positivity, showing discordance between serology and cellular immune assays.
Mutant OspC-deficient B. burgdorferi showed reduced survival compared to wild-type strain 30 minutes after inoculation in mice, indicating a role for OspC in early immune/complement evasion.
Changes in miRNA expression in response to B. burgdorferi infection can decrease tight junction integrity, compromising the blood-brain barrier and contributing to CNS immune activation.

ME/CFS shares PTLDS's hallmark symptoms of debilitating fatigue, cognitive difficulties, and sleep disturbances, but typically lacks a clear infectious trigger and features additional post-exertional malaise.
Post-viral fatigue syndrome, including that following COVID-19, produces persistent fatigue and cognitive impairment resembling PTLDS but typically resolves within six months, unlike PTLDS.
Preexisting comorbidities such as diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular disease, or chronic pain at the time of initial Lyme disease infection were predictive of long-term post-treatment symptoms.

In vitro studies show that B. burgdorferi can form antibiotic-tolerant persister organisms under antibiotic pressure or stationary-phase growth, offering a candidate mechanism for bacterial persistence in PTLDS.
Disease severity in mouse models of B. burgdorferi infection varied by mouse strain, suggesting host genetic factors may influence susceptibility to persistent disease.

Spirochetes recovered from antibiotic-treated mice up to three months post-treatment via xenodiagnosis lacked infectivity-associated plasmid genes lp25 and lp28-1, suggesting attenuation of surviving organisms.

Rare spirochete-like forms were detected by immunohistochemistry in connective tissue of the heart and tibiotarsal joints of antibiotic-treated mice, though these organisms could not be directly cultured.

Bockenstedt et al. proposed that B. burgdorferi may persist by transforming into cyst-like forms under nutrient deprivation, though true cyst/endospore formation requires structural changes over hours-to-days that were not demonstrated at clinically relevant (six-month+) timeframes.

Hodzic et al. found that antibiotic-treated mice retained low numbers of infectious spirochetes detectable by xenodiagnosis and quantitative PCR, with very low DNA copy numbers compared to the typical post-infection 'spirochetal burst,' indicating altered replication capacity while retaining some infectivity.

Collagen-rich tissues, including ligaments, tendons, and vessels at the base of the heart, were identified as preferential niches for B. burgdorferi survival and possible immune evasion during persistent infection in mice.

A single human case documented persistence of B. burgdorferi in tendon tissue (flexor retinaculum), with spirochetes identified between collagen fibers and along fibroblasts, associated with musculoskeletal deformities and tendinous pain.

In four human subjects with treatment-resistant Lyme arthritis, synovial membrane tissue PCR was positive for B. burgdorferi even when synovial fluid PCR was negative, supporting synovial membrane as a reservoir for persistent infection.

A case series of 10 patients with severe neurological limb paralysis identified mixed tick-borne co-infections involving Borrelia, Babesia divergens, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and Bartonella species.
A study combining long-term antibiotics with anti-parasitic treatment for tick-borne co-infections resulted in complete motor recovery in seven of 10 patients with neurological limb paralysis.

Berghoff described that overlapping symptoms between Lyme borreliosis and tick-borne/non-tick-borne co-infections (e.g., bartonellosis, tularemia, Mycoplasma infections) create diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.

Among tested tick-borne/non-tick-borne co-infections, Bartonella henselae showed the highest seropositivity rate at 78%, though lymphocyte transformation test data were not completed for this pathogen.

Chlamydia trachomatis showed low seroprevalence (5%) but a much higher lymphocyte transformation test positivity rate (100%) among tested patients, indicating discordance between serology and cellular immune testing for co-infection detection.

ME/CFS shares core symptoms with PTLDS such as debilitating fatigue, cognitive difficulties, and sleep disturbances, but unlike PTLDS it typically lacks a clear infectious trigger and features additional post-exertional malaise.

Post-viral fatigue syndrome (PVFS), which can follow viral infections including COVID-19, produces persistent fatigue and cognitive impairment resembling PTLDS but typically resolves within six months, unlike the more prolonged course of PTLDS.

Chronic active Epstein-Barr virus (CAEBV) infection can present with overlapping fatigue, pain, and cognitive symptoms similar to PTLDS, but is distinguished by detectable persistent EBV reactivation (EBV-DNA or specific antibodies) and characteristic clinical features not typically seen in PTLDS.
The majority of patients with hEDS/HSDs and pain showed evidence of central sensitization based on Central Sensitization Inventory scores.
Central Sensitization Inventory scores varied widely among hEDS/HSD patients, ranging from 12 to 94 with a median of 56.
Patients with hEDS/HSDs reported moderate to severe pain on the numerical rating scale, ranging from 2 to 10 with a mean and median of 6.
On initial echocardiogram, 15 of 225 pediatric hEDS subjects had aortic root Z-scores greater than 2.0, with none exceeding 3.0.
In subsequent echocardiographic studies (n=68), aortic root Z-scores showed a statistically significant decline over time compared to earlier measurements.
Among 10 patients with an initial aortic root Z-score >2.0 who underwent repeat echocardiography, seven showed a decline in Z-score to below 2.0.
On final examination, only 9 of 225 (4.0%) hEDS patients had an aortic root Z-score >2.0, a rate not statistically different from that expected in the general population.
No aortic dissection occurred among first- or second-degree relatives of the hEDS cohort.

The authors conclude that aortic root dilation risk in hEDS is likely not different from the general population and propose that routine echocardiography is not required in hEDS absent other cardiac findings or suspicion of another disorder.

Fibroblasts from the vEDS patient carrying the COL3A1 c.766delA frameshift mutation showed reduced COL3A1 transcript levels compared to healthy control cells, with only the normal allele sequence detectable, consistent with nonsense-mediated decay of the mutant transcript.
Fibroblasts carrying the COL3A1 IVS14-2A>G splice-site mutation showed in-frame skipping of exon 15 (54 bp) in the mature transcript, implying a dominant-negative disease mechanism.
Both c.766delA and IVS14-2A>G patient-derived fibroblast lines expressed lower intracellular collagen III and secreted less collagen III than healthy control cells, as measured by western blot.
Intracellular collagen III staining intensity was slightly stronger in c.766delA fibroblasts than in healthy control cells by immunofluorescence.
IVS14-2A>G fibroblasts showed patchy intracellular collagen III staining suggestive of accumulation or aggregation compared to healthy control cells.

Both patient fibroblast lines showed abnormal extracellular matrix collagen III deposition patterns compared to healthy control fibroblasts under macromolecular crowding conditions, with c.766delA cells showing isolated foci and IVS14-2A>G cells showing patchy staining instead of normal fibrils.
A cocktail of two PMO antisense oligonucleotides achieved highly efficient skipping of COL3A1 exon 10 (~96%) at 50 µM in c.766delA patient fibroblasts, compared to only 39.5% skipping at 10 µM.

Despite efficient exon 10 skipping, no detectable changes in intracellular collagen III expression or secretion were observed in COL3A1 PMO-treated c.766delA fibroblasts compared to sham PMO-treated cells.
A single PMO, COL3A1_H15A(+20+44), induced efficient skipping of exon 15 (92.8%) from the normal COL3A1 allele transcript at 50 µM in IVS14-2A>G patient fibroblasts.

Despite efficient exon 15 skipping, intracellular collagen III and secretion remained unchanged, and immunofluorescence showed no change in collagen III deposition in transfected IVS14-2A>G patient cells.

Cycloheximide treatment (a nonsense-mediated decay inhibitor) restored COL3A1 transcript levels in c.766delA patient fibroblasts, confirming haploinsufficiency via nonsense-mediated decay as the underlying mechanism.
Cycloheximide treatment did not increase COL3A1 transcript levels in IVS14-2A>G patient fibroblasts, indicating that the reduced transcript in this line is not due to nonsense-mediated decay.

Despite achieving approximately 90% exon skipping efficiency with no reduction in RNA expression for both exon 10 and exon 15 targets, no phenotypic rescue of collagen III expression or assembly was observed, indicating ASO-mediated exon skipping is not a viable therapeutic approach for these COL3A1 mutations.

Whole-genome sequencing identified 6 distinct, likely causal COL5A1 variants in 7 dogs with clinical signs of classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, none of which were found in 142 whole-genome sequences from unaffected control dogs.
A C>T transition at chromosomal position 9:50091843 shared by half-sibling Dogs 4 and 5 is predicted to create a premature termination codon in COL5A1.
Frameshift-causing 1 bp deletions in Dogs 1 and 2 and a 1 bp insertion in Dog 3 are each predicted to produce premature termination codons in COL5A1.

Dog 6 harbored an in-frame deletion of a highly conserved glutamic acid in the C-terminal propeptide region of COL5A1, predicted to disrupt signal peptide stability and impair trimeric alpha chain assembly.

Dog 7 had a glycine-to-arginine substitution in the triple helix region of COL5A1, resembling a previously reported substitution in two other dogs and predicted to disrupt collagen helix formation and stability.

Despite multiple dogs carrying premature-termination-codon variants predicted to cause haploinsufficiency, the resulting collagen ultrastructural abnormalities and clinical signs differed among them, indicating haploinsufficiency alone does not explain the phenotypic heterogeneity.

Electron microscopy of skin biopsies from 3 affected dogs (Dogs 1, 5, 6) with different COL5A1 variants showed collagen fibrils that were less tightly packed, more variable in diameter, and more irregular in cross-sectional shape than fibrils from an unaffected control dog, though the specific pattern of abnormality differed by dog.

The most common clinical features across the 7-dog cohort with classical EDS were multifocal wounds, atrophic scars, joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and chronic orthopedic abnormalities.

Five of the 7 dogs had clinically relevant orthopedic disease (patellar luxation, joint luxation/subluxation, angular limb deformities, suspected intervertebral disc herniation) that may have been exacerbated by underlying EDS-related joint laxity.
No dog in the series was euthanized directly because of EDS, and most lived to older ages, suggesting long-term survival is possible for dogs with classical EDS given proper care.
In Dog 1, use of a full-body compression suit successfully resolved recurrent seromas over one month, but seromas were not addressed further after the owner discontinued the suit.
Restricting Dog 1 to indoor living with supervised, limited outdoor activity reduced wound occurrence from 1-2 per week to once every 3-4 months.
Unlike some human classical EDS patients who experience delayed wound healing, this was uncommon among the dogs in this cohort, most of which healed normally even after major surgical procedures.

In a large study of human classical EDS patients, musculoskeletal abnormalities were frequent, including sprains (45%), articular pain (40%), subdislocation (29%), walking difficulties (23%), and dislocation (21%), cited for comparison with the canine cohort's orthopedic findings.
Genetic testing identified a heterozygous autosomal dominant COL3A1 mutation confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the patient.

Angiographic maneuvers (neck rotation, swallowing) demonstrated that mechanical compression of the right internal carotid artery by an elongated hyoid bone caused its dissection, leading to a transient ischaemic attack.

Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel was used post-procedure instead of endovascular therapy, given familial dissection history and lack of supporting evidence for intervention, and the patient remained asymptomatic on continued therapy.
Cervical surgical exploration confirmed external compression of the ICA by the posterior horn of the hyoid bone, and resection of the bone fragment resulted in full symptom recovery.

Physical examination of the vEDS patient revealed characteristic phenotypic features including thin skin, joint hyperextensibility, large eyes, thin nose and lips, a small chin, and lobeless ears, along with a lifelong history of spontaneous bruising.

The patient reported a family history of early deaths in young relatives due to postpartum uterine haemorrhage and arterial rupture, and the patient's father died of aortic dissection, consistent with vEDS vascular fragility.
At 3-month follow-up, imaging showed resolution of the right ICA dissection but a new pseudoaneurysm on the right proximal brachiocephalic trunk, which was managed conservatively without surgery.
H&E-stained skin sections showed thick, well-organized collagen bundles in the healthy control compared to disordered, thin collagen bundles in the cEDS, hEDS, and hEDS-scleroderma sections.

In the hEDS-scleroderma sample, H&E staining revealed three distinct dermal regions with heterogeneous collagen density, including a highly dense collagen network and an adjacent collagen-depleted, loosely organized region.

Polarized picrosirius red staining showed localized yellow-stained (disorganized) collagen islets in cEDS and hEDS sections, whereas hEDS-scleroderma showed widespread yellow staining throughout the dermis, suggesting systemic rather than localized collagen matrix alterations.
Quantification of polarized picrosirius red staining showed increasing proportions of disrupted (yellow) collagen across EDS subtypes: 28% in cEDS, 65% in hEDS, and 92% in hEDS-scleroderma.

AFM imaging of yellow-stained (disrupted) dermal regions revealed collagen fibrils lacking preferential orientation, bent or twisted morphology, and loss of D-banding periodicity, in contrast to the well-aligned, D-banded fibrils observed in red-stained (healthy) regions across all four cases.

A distinct amorphous, swollen non-fibrillar collagen matrix adjacent to healthier fibrils was observed specifically in hEDS and hEDS-scleroderma samples but not in cEDS, resembling collagen denaturation by hydrolysis.

Nine untrained raters classified 32 randomized AFM images of dermal collagen as healthy or disrupted with excellent inter-rater agreement (Fleiss' kappa=0.96) and good intra-rater repeatability (Cohen's kappa=0.79±0.1), supporting nanoscale collagen structure as a recognizable disease fingerprint.

Young's modulus distributions of individual collagen fibrils were unimodal in the healthy control (both healthy and disrupted regions) but bimodal in cEDS, hEDS, and hEDS-scleroderma, with a main peak shifted to lower modulus values than control, indicating mechanically weaker collagen fibrils in EDS.

A distinct subpopulation of collagen fibrils with markedly lower Young's modulus than found in cEDS or control was uniquely identified in disrupted regions of the hEDS patient, suggesting increased dermal matrix fragility specific to hEDS.
Genetic testing identified a COL1A1 mutation (c.1053delG in exon 7) in the 24-year-old patient, confirming a diagnosis of classical EDS (cEDS).

Next-generation sequencing panels of more than 30 EDS-associated genes detected no pathogenic sequence or copy number variants in either hEDS patient, consistent with the lack of identified genetic markers for hEDS.
On average, hEDS diagnosis takes ten to sixteen years from symptom onset, reflecting the lack of objective diagnostic markers for this EDS subtype.
Individuals with hEDS have an increased risk of developing fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome, in addition to prominent joint hypermobility and chronic pain.

The two hEDS case-report patients presented with multisystem comorbidities including orthostatic intolerance, migraines, irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, and (in one case) endometriosis, alongside generalized joint hypermobility and skin hyperextensibility.
The patient was genetically confirmed to carry a COL3A1 gene mutation, establishing a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Immunostaining showed no positive type III collagen fibers in the mammary tissue surrounding the tumor in this vascular EDS patient, in contrast to positive staining in an age-matched control woman's mammary tissue.

The invasive lesion in the left lower inner breast was diagnosed as invasive ductal carcinoma (pT1b, pN0, Stage IA), ER-positive (95%), PR-positive (<1%), HER2 score 2 equivocal but FISH-positive, with Ki-67 labeling index of 18%.
The second lesion in the left lower outer breast was diagnosed as non-invasive ductal carcinoma (DCIS, pTis, pStage 0), ER-positive (70%), PR-positive (25%), HER2-positive (score 3), Ki-67 18%.

Despite intraoperative tissue fragility characteristic of vascular EDS, partial left mastectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy were completed safely with minimal blood loss (~75 g) and no abnormal bleeding.
Postoperative radiotherapy (42.4 Gy in 16 fractions) to the preserved left breast was completed without post-irradiation complications in this vascular EDS patient.

Prior literature on radiotherapy in EDS breast cancer patients is mixed: one series reported no significant acute/late toxicity beyond grade 1 dermatitis in four patients, whereas another case report described grade 3 dermatitis after radiotherapy with additional boost irradiation in a vascular EDS patient.

Two months after surgery, the patient developed a sudden spontaneous hematoma in the contralateral axilla/lateral thorax (unrelated surgical site), requiring 4 days hospitalization and resolving with conservative treatment.

Vascular EDS is reported to carry high risk of serious complications, with 77% of patients experiencing arterial rupture, dissection, or aneurysm, 25% developing such complications by age 20 and 80% by age 40, and a median age of death of 48 years.

Vascular EDS is estimated to occur in approximately 5% of all EDS patients (approximately 1 in 50,000-200,000), caused by COL3A1 mutations affecting organs requiring stretch such as heart, vessels, GI tract, and uterus.

Using the Predict prognostic tool, the patient's estimated 10-year breast cancer mortality risk with surgery alone was 5%, reduced by 1 percentage point with addition of endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, and anti-HER2 therapy.
During phacoemulsification in a patient with EDS type VI and brittle cornea syndrome, the cornea underwent spontaneous radial and tangential rupture shortly after phaco-tip insertion and irrigation.

Following intraoperative corneal rupture, phacoemulsification was abandoned and the surgeon converted to extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) to complete cataract removal, leaving the patient aphakic.

At 24-month follow-up after complicated cataract surgery, the patient's best-corrected visual acuity had improved from Hand Motion to 6/60 with a quiescent anterior chamber, though the eye remained aphakic with myopic atrophic fundus changes.

Due to unreliable keratometry from corneal ectasia, the surgical team selected a +7.0 D intraocular lens using a standard keratometry value of 43.25 D (per Watson et al.) to achieve a myopic target refraction of -1.8 D, facilitating predictable outcomes and easier contact lens fitting.

EDS type VI is characterized by severe muscular hypotonia at birth, progressive kyphoscoliosis from early infancy, skin fragility with abnormal scarring, severe joint hypermobility and luxations, Marfanoid habitus, osteopenia, arterial rupture, and early mortality from cardiopulmonary insufficiency.
Blue sclera, seen in connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Marfan syndrome, is associated with significantly reduced central corneal thickness.
The authors recommend maintaining intraocular pressure below 20 mmHg during phacoemulsification in patients with EDS VI/brittle cornea to reduce the risk of spontaneous corneal rupture.
Whole exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous missense variant in TGFBR2 (c.1561T>C, p.Trp521Arg) confirming a diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 2.
The patient developed acute transverse myelitis at the T9-10 spinal level concurrently with previously unrecognized features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 2, a rare co-occurrence.

MRI imaging showed a dolichocephalic skull with decreased cephalic index and atlanto-axial subluxation with mild retroflexion of the dens indenting the anterior subarachnoid space at the craniovertebral junction.

Treatment with intravenous pulse methylprednisolone followed by an oral prednisolone taper over three months resulted in improvement of bilateral lower limb power from MRC grade 0/5 to grade 4/5 with independent ambulation after four months.
Although aortic root aneurysms are reported in up to 98% of LDS patients in the literature, this patient's CT angiography and spinal angiography showed no aneurysms, dissection, or dural ectasia.

Craniofacial anomalies are typically more common in Type 1 LDS and largely absent in Type 2 LDS, yet this genetically confirmed Type 2 LDS patient presented with craniofacial anomalies including hypertelorism and bifid uvula.
The average life expectancy of LDS patients ranges from 26 to 37 years according to prior reports, with fatal outcomes typically related to aortic/arterial dissection or intracranial hemorrhage.

Physical examination showed connective tissue disorder features including joint laxity (positive wrist and thumb signs), marfanoid habitus, arachnodactyly and camptodactyly of the toes, and fixed ankle joint contractures.
Prominent buccal maxillary exostoses were found associated with a hypermobile upper lip, vertical maxillary excess, and altered passive eruption in two patients with excessive gingival display.
Following esthetic crown lengthening with osteoplasty to remove buccal maxillary exostoses, gingival display was reduced by 8 mm and 6 mm in the two patients evaluated 3 to 6 months postoperatively.
Removal of the buccal maxillary exostoses alone accounted for 75% and 67% of the observed excessive gingival display reduction in the two patients, respectively.
Reductions in excessive gingival display following exostoses removal corresponded to observed reductions in upper lip mobility during smile.
De novo urethral hypermobility present at 6 months postpartum was not significantly associated with stress urinary incontinence symptoms at 6 months postpartum.

De novo urethral hypermobility at 6 months postpartum was associated with a higher risk of stress urinary incontinence 12 years after first delivery, with the authors concluding it constitutes a risk factor.

A homozygous COL12A1 missense variant, c.8903C>T (p.Pro2968Leu), was identified in a young girl presenting with joint hyperlaxity, frequent falls, and skin lesions consistent with a myopathic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome/UCMD-like phenotype.
The authors note that COL12A1 dominant pathogenic variants have rarely been reported and that the phenotypic spectrum of COL12A1-related disease has not yet been fully defined.
Children and adolescents with Joint Hypermobility Syndrome showed more severe PTSD symptoms than those without JHS following the 2015 Nepal earthquake.
The severity of PTSD symptoms was strongly predicted by the distance to the earthquake epicentre.
Females showed more severe PTSD symptomatology but lower perturbation in daily functioning compared to males.
Younger children reported greater functional impairment following the earthquake than older children/adolescents.

The editorial states that female patients undergoing hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement syndrome improve to a similar degree as male patients, particularly when capsular closure is routinely performed.
The editorial notes that female patients have a greater incidence of generalized joint hypermobility compared with male patients.
The editorial suggests that capsular plication is used to treat joint hypermobility-related laxity during hip arthroscopy, potentially contributing to equal outcomes between sexes.
A de novo pathogenic RET M918T variant is usually identified in children with MEN2B.
Joint hypermobility is described as a nonspecific extra-endocrine clinical feature of MEN2B syndrome that could aid early recognition.
Persistent constipation is described as a nonspecific extra-endocrine clinical feature of MEN2B syndrome.
All five children ultimately diagnosed with MEN2B had intestinal ganglioneuromatosis, which the authors suggest could have prompted earlier diagnosis.

The authors propose that MEN2B genomic screening should be included in newborn screening programs, alongside careful exclusion of intestinal ganglioneuromatosis, to enable earlier diagnosis and improved outcomes.
Fascia is estimated to contain over 250 million nerve endings, with sensory neurons outnumbering motor neurons 9:1 in some regions, and houses more nerve endings than skin or muscle combined.
Multimorbidity is common in collagen dysregulation disorders, with hEDS patients averaging more than 10 diagnosed conditions.
hEDS/collagen dysregulation is commonly co-reported with dysautonomia, POTS, IBS, reflux and diverticulosis, among other GI and autonomic conditions.
Collagen dysregulation/hEDS is associated with cardiovascular manifestations including mitral valve prolapse and aortic wall hyperelasticity.
Collagen dysregulation/hEDS is commonly co-reported with fibromyalgia, ME/CFS, chronic pain, anesthetic resistance, and central sensitization.
MCAS, joint hypermobility, and dysautonomia form a recognized clinical triad.
Hypermobility/MCAS/dysautonomia triad patients have higher odds of autism, ADHD, panic disorder, anxiety diagnoses, and neurodivergence.
Immobility causes pathological over-accumulation and super-aggregation of hyaluronan in tissue, impairing blood and lymphatic circulation.
Excessive exercise can overstimulate hyaluronan production, causing it to act as a glue rather than lubricant, a phenomenon linked to delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS).
Hyaluronan affects local anesthetic efficacy and release rate, potentially explaining anesthesia resistance reported by patients with collagen dysregulation conditions such as hEDS.
Myofascial expansions, in which about 30% of muscle fibers insert into fascia rather than tendon, account for roughly 30% of mechanical force transmission from muscle.
Noradrenaline upregulates TGF-β1, driving fibroblast-to-myofibroblast differentiation that, under chronic stress or inflammation, initiates fibrosis and contractures.
Chronic adrenaline upregulation can elicit contracture and inhibit effective wound healing, provoking structural fascial adaptation, imbalance, pain, and palpable tension.
MRGPRX2, a mast cell receptor that binds opioids and naltrexone, has been associated with fibrosis, hypertrophic scarring, and Long COVID.

Low dose naltrexone (LDN) is hypothesized to bind mast cell receptors and is being investigated as a treatment for MCAS, anxiety, depression, and neuropathic pain, and to reduce immunosuppressive therapy side effects and pro-inflammatory mediators.
Mast cell stabilizers such as olopatadine and sodium cromoglycate, applied topically or nasally, have been reported to rapidly reduce mast cell activation cascades.
NSAIDs, anesthetics, neuromuscular blocking agents, opioids, and radiologic contrast agents can trigger mast cell activation, with approximately half of all perioperative drugs implicated.

IV saline and IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) have been hypothesized as treatments for underlying fascia-immune dysregulation, following reported therapeutic responses in back pain, plantar fasciitis, and Long COVID.
Fascia contains an abundance of estrogen and relaxin receptors, concentrated on fibroblasts of muscular fascia, implicating hormonal regulation of fascial properties.
People experiencing perimenopause and menopause may be more susceptible to fibromyalgia due to the absence of premenopausal hormone concentrations.
Basal heart rate variability is reported to be lower in fibromyalgia/functional somatic disorder patients than in healthy subjects, suggesting reduced autonomic flexibility.
A positive history of childhood trauma more than doubles the odds of developing fibromyalgia in adulthood.
The likelihood of developing functional somatic disorders is tripled when both childhood and adult trauma are considered together, per meta-analysis.
Post-traumatic stress disorder prevalence in fibromyalgia patients is reported to reach up to 56%, prompting recommendations that all FM patients be screened for PTSD.

Hair cortisol concentration in response to intense pain is higher in early-stage fibromyalgia and decreases as the disease progresses, suggesting a shift from HPA hyperactivity to hypoactivity over time.

Small-fiber pathology, indicated by reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density, is present in nearly half of fibromyalgia patients, supporting a peripheral contribution to FM pathophysiology in a subset of patients.

In a rat pain model, bilateral increase in glutamatergic activity in the insular cortex was responsible for both multimodal pain behavior and loss of peripheral small fibers, suggesting insular overactivity as a driver of small-fiber pathology in FM.

IgG from fibromyalgia patients binds human dorsal root ganglia and, when injected into mice, produces painful sensory hypersensitivity and reduces intraepidermal nerve fiber density, supporting an autoimmune peripheral sensitization mechanism in FMS.
An alteration of the opioid system was found in fibromyalgia patients, linking it for the first time to abnormal function of C-tactile afferents.

Neuroimaging in fibromyalgia showed reduced posterior insular activity during pleasant touch rating and increased anterior insular activity during pain assessment, linked to anhedonia to pleasant touch and abnormal evaluative pain processing.
In a chronic pain sample, an 11-minute C-tactile fiber stimulation paradigm (3 cm/s, 2.5 mN) produced a rapid 23% reduction in pain intensity.

Patients with low-back pain showed reduced pleasantness perception to CT-fiber stimulation, more so in subacute/chronic phases, proposed as a marker of transition from acute pain to chronic pain syndrome.

Patients with complex regional pain syndrome showed reduced pleasantness to CT-fiber stimulation and reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density bilaterally, even in unilateral CRPS, indicating systemic CT-fiber and small-fiber involvement.

Mean salivary and plasma oxytocin levels are higher in patients with chronic migraine than in healthy subjects, opposite to the direction reported in other chronic pain conditions where oxytocin is lower than controls.

In a general-population cross-sectional study, subjects with chronic widespread pain had insecure attachment (preoccupied, dismissing, fearful) more frequently than pain-free subjects, and were estimated to be twice as likely to have chronic widespread pain.

A group-based, eight-session 'brain reprogramming' multimodal non-pharmacological program (n=198) in patients with fibromyalgia and central sensitivity syndromes reduced symptom interference, anxiety and depression, and improved quality of life, with benefits maintained at 3-month follow-up.
The only published clinical trial of intranasal oxytocin for pain reduction in fibromyalgia patients showed negative results, though the authors noted substantial study limitations.
A high prevalence of insecure attachment, particularly the anxious type, is reported in irritable bowel syndrome patients, even higher than that seen in inflammatory bowel disease.

Insecure attachment has been linked to higher disability in migraine patients, even those with episodic migraine, and is more frequent in patients with more severe disease and less perceived social support.

Activation of C-tactile afferents reduces temporal summation of second pain, a neurophysiological marker of central sensitization, in a proposed bottom-up inhibition mechanism relevant to fibromyalgia-type chronic pain.

In patients with small-fiber neuropathy, CT-afferent activation failed to modulate heat pain (unlike in healthy subjects where modulation occurred regardless of stimulus intensity), indirectly confirming that intact CT fibers/IENFD are required for this analgesic mechanism.

In patients with complex regional pain syndrome, repetitive CT-fiber stimulation reduced the heat sensation threshold but did not significantly reduce overall pain intensity, suggesting the analgesic power of the tactile affective system is present but too weak in this chronic pain condition.
The EXOPULSE Mollii suit produced cumulatively larger increases in cortical arousal across sessions, becoming statistically significant by the 8th and 16th sessions with large effect sizes.
Structured exercise (strength/HIIT) produced significant increases in cortical arousal after the 1st and 8th sessions, but the magnitude of effect diminished over the course of training.
In the Suit intervention, distal index finger temperature significantly decreased after the 16th session, suggesting increased parasympathetic modulation with a large effect size.
Exercise sessions produced significant increases in peripheral skin temperature across the 1st, 8th, and 16th sessions, reflecting immediate sympathetic activation from physical exertion.

In the Suit intervention, mean heart rate significantly decreased after the 1st session, and minimum heart rate significantly decreased while SD2 significantly increased after the 8th session, both indicating enhanced parasympathetic activation.
After the full 16-session course, the EXOPULSE Mollii suit significantly improved HRV, suggesting restored autonomic balance and enhanced parasympathetic activity in fibromyalgia patients.

The structured exercise intervention did not produce significant overall improvements in HRV, indicating a potential limitation of exercise alone for correcting autonomic dysregulation in fibromyalgia.

Exercise sessions produced significant shifts in multiple HRV parameters (HF, LF at 1st session; mean/max/min HR, RMSSD, PNN50, SD1 at 8th session; mean/max/min HR, RMSSD at 16th session) with very large effect sizes, suggesting an immediate increase in sympathetic tone following exertion.

Over 38% of All of Us participants self-reported a first-degree family history of any of arthritis (fibromyalgia, gout, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE), osteoporosis, or carpal tunnel syndrome.

Individuals with a first-degree family history of a given condition (among arthritis subtypes, osteoporosis, and carpal tunnel syndrome) had 3.68 to 7.59 times the odds (average 4.90) of having that same condition themselves.

Family history of one of the seven studied conditions was also associated with modestly increased odds (0.70 to 2.10, average 1.24) of having a different one of the studied conditions, suggesting cross-condition shared risk.
The strongest association identified was between family history of osteoarthritis and prevalence of osteoarthritis.
Family history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) was strongly associated with SLE prevalence.
The study found disparities by race/ethnicity and sex in the strength of family history associations with arthritis, osteoporosis, and carpal tunnel syndrome prevalence.
More than 38% of All of Us participants reported a first-degree family history of at least one of arthritis (including fibromyalgia), osteoporosis, or carpal tunnel syndrome.

Low-affinity IgE antibodies against Fel d 1 (affinity ~10^-6 M) can still bind multivalently to FcεRI-bound IgE on basophils and mast cells due to lateral membrane diffusion, triggering degranulation.
Cooling membranes below the Krafft point (e.g., 4°C) blocks lateral diffusion of FcεRI-bound IgE and prevents the multivalent binding needed for mast cell/basophil degranulation.
The naturally dimeric structure of the cat allergen Fel d 1 is proposed to contribute to particularly strong allergic reactions via enhanced multivalent IgE binding.
Low-affinity allergen-specific IgG antibodies fail to neutralize Fel d 1 directly but efficiently block mast cell/basophil activation entirely through engagement of the inhibitory receptor FcγRIIb.

Low-affinity IgG antibodies failed to neutralize allergens and did not block basophil/mast cell activation in either in vitro or in vivo settings when acting through direct competitive neutralization.
High-affinity monoclonal antibodies against Fel d 1 and Bet v 1 efficiently protect against allergic disease in clinical studies.

Anti-Fel d 1 monoclonal antibodies expressed as IgG1 or IgG4 with identical epitope specificity showed the same quantitative ability to block primary human basophil activation via neutralization or FcγRIIb engagement, and similar FcγRIIb binding affinities.

In mouse models, immunization against single peanut allergens Ara h 1 or Ara h 2 blocked systemic and local allergic responses to whole peanut extract, and this protection was strictly dependent on functional FcγRIIb.

A mixed grass-SCIT allergoid formulated with microcrystalline tyrosine and monophosphoryl lipid A adjuvants reduced the combined symptom and medication score by approximately 40% during peak grass pollen season compared to placebo, using only six pre-seasonal injections.
Grass-specific serum IgG4 significantly increased after the MCT/MPL-adjuvanted allergoid treatment, remaining elevated through the pollen season.

Grass-specific total serum IgG significantly increased after the MCT/MPL-adjuvanted allergoid treatment, remaining elevated through the pollen season, and likely mainly reflects IgG1 given its dominance among IgG subclasses.

Reducing the RNA content packaged in Ara h 2-displaying VLPs (VLP Peanut) by approximately half significantly reduced Ara h 2-specific IgG titers and the number of high-avidity antibodies in both wild-type and TLR7 knockout mice.

Under conditions of similar or higher allergen loading on IgE, allergens displayed on virus-like particles failed to significantly activate FcεRI-mediated mast cell signaling, whereas free allergen induced strong cellular activation.
Both the amount and the affinity of allergen-specific IgG antibodies correlate with clinical protection after sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT).
Correlation between clinical AIT outcome and allergen-specific IgG4 levels has been inconsistent across studies, so IgG4 is not considered a validated surrogate biomarker of clinical efficacy.

Patients with Hymenoptera venom allergy, particularly those with severe anaphylaxis, commonly have an underlying clonal mast cell disease such as systemic mastocytosis or monoclonal mast cell activation syndrome.
A baseline serum tryptase level above 11 ng/mL is used as a threshold to trigger tryptase genotyping in the stepwise screening algorithm for clonal mast cell disease.

The Red Española de Mastocitosis (REMA) score, calculated from anaphylaxis clinical features, baseline serum tryptase, and patient sex, is used to estimate pretest probability of clonal mast cell disease, with a score of 2 or greater warranting bone marrow biopsy.

Patients with Hymenoptera venom allergy and clonal mast cell disease are recommended to receive venom immunotherapy for more than 5 years or indefinitely and to carry at least three epinephrine autoinjectors due to their high-risk status.

The authors propose future studies to determine whether KIT D816V-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitors can prevent or reduce the severity of Hymenoptera venom-triggered anaphylaxis in patients with clonal mast cell disease.
Ruxolitinib caused a concentration-dependent inhibition of histamine release from human basophils activated by anti-IgE, with an IC50 of 13.60 ± 3.93 μM.
Ruxolitinib produced a concentration-dependent inhibition of de novo synthesized LTC4 release from anti-IgE-activated basophils, with an IC50 of 21.70 ± 6.73 μM.
