Ruxolitinib caused a concentration-dependent inhibition of IL-4 release from anti-IgE-activated basophils, with an IC50 of 13.20 ± 2.58 μM.
Ruxolitinib caused a concentration-dependent inhibition of IL-13 release from anti-IgE-activated basophils, with an IC50 of 21.60 ± 4.47 μM.
Ruxolitinib caused a concentration-dependent inhibition of IL-4 release from IL-3-activated basophils, with an IC50 of 21.03 ± 5.55 μM.
Ruxolitinib caused a concentration-dependent inhibition of IL-13 release from IL-3-activated basophils, with an IC50 of 18.60 ± 8.86 μM.
Substance P induced concentration-dependent release of histamine, tryptase, and chymase from human skin mast cells (HSMCs) via MRGPRX2 engagement.
Substance P-induced histamine and tryptase release from HSMCs were linearly correlated.
Substance P-induced histamine and chymase release from HSMCs were linearly correlated.
No significant correlation was found between substance P-induced tryptase and chymase release from HSMCs.

Ruxolitinib inhibited tryptase release from substance P-activated human skin mast cells, with an IC50 of 17.7 ± 6.82 μM, not significantly different from the IC50 for histamine or chymase.
Ruxolitinib inhibited chymase release from substance P-activated human skin mast cells, with an IC50 of 13.87 ± 2.60 μM.
Mrgprb2 mRNA is prominently expressed in the mouse colon, in addition to the expected high expression in skin, while it is absent in dorsal root ganglia.
Mrgprb2 expression in the colon is selectively restricted to Mcpt6+ connective tissue mast cells (CTMCs) and is not expressed in Mcpt1+ mucosal mast cells (MMCs).
Acute exposure of colonic explants to Substance P (SP) markedly increased the proportion of degranulating Mrgprb2+ mast cells compared with vehicle.
SP-induced mast cell degranulation and tryptase (Mcpt6) release were abolished in Mrgprb2-/- colon, confirming Mrgprb2 specificity of SP-induced degranulation.
DSS-induced colitis significantly upregulated Mrgprb2 mRNA expression and increased the number of Mrgprb2+ mast cells in the colon, with a morphological shift from round to ramified.
Acute DSS colitis induced marked sprouting of SP+ nerve fibers in the colon and significantly increased spontaneous SP release from colonic explant cultures compared with healthy colon.

After 4 weeks of co-housing, there were no significant differences in fecal microbial OTU abundance, Shannon diversity, or phylum/genus-level composition between WT and Mrgprb2-/- mice prior to DSS treatment, ruling out microbiome confounds.
Mrgprb2-/- mice showed significantly more pronounced weight loss, shorter colon lengths, and increased microscopic damage scores compared with WT mice during acute DSS-induced colitis.
Pro-inflammatory cytokines Il1β, Tnf-α, and Il6 were significantly upregulated in the colon of DSS-treated Mrgprb2-/- mice compared with DSS-treated WT mice.
MPO activity, a marker of neutrophil infiltration, was significantly reduced in DSS-treated Mrgprb2-/- mice compared with DSS-treated WT mice.
Flow cytometry showed significantly reduced total and proportional neutrophil counts in the colon of DSS-treated Mrgprb2-/- mice compared with WT mice.
Intraperitoneal injection of the synthetic Mrgprb2 ligand PAMP9-20 induced a robust increase in peritoneal neutrophils in WT mice, an effect abolished in Mrgprb2-/- mice.
SP stimulation of peritoneal mast cell cultures markedly upregulated neutrophil-recruiting chemokines Cxcl1 and Cxcl2 in an Mrgprb2-dependent manner, an effect absent in Mrgprb2-/- cultures.
During active DSS exposure (days 5 and 7), upregulation of neutrophil-attracting chemokines Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl5, Cxcl1, and Cxcl2 seen in WT colon was markedly attenuated in Mrgprb2-/- colon.

Bulk RNA sequencing of DSS-treated colon revealed profound transcriptional changes in Mrgprb2-/- mice compared with WT, with GO analysis highlighting tissue remodeling (angiogenesis, collagen metabolism) and inflammation as the two major signature changes.

CD31 immunohistochemistry showed markedly increased blood vessel staining in the colon of DSS-treated Mrgprb2-/- mice, particularly in ulcerated mucosal regions, confirming abnormal angiogenic remodeling.
Trichrome-Masson staining showed strongly increased collagen deposition in the mucosa/submucosa and distortion of the muscularis layer in DSS-treated Mrgprb2-/- mice compared with WT.

DSS-treated Mrgprb2-/- mice showed significantly increased Iba-1 and CD68 macrophage immunostaining and upregulated macrophage-associated genes (pan-macrophage, M1, and M2 markers) compared with WT, with no differences seen between healthy WT and healthy KO mice.

Antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion (anti-Ly6G) during DSS colitis caused a significant increase in MHCII+ macrophages in the colon compared with isotype-treated controls, supporting that impaired neutrophil influx drives excess macrophage accumulation.

A common loss-of-function MRGPRX2 SNP (rs10833049, N62S) that impairs SP-induced MRGPRX2 activation and mast cell degranulation was reported to be significantly enriched (4-fold increased prevalence) in a Jewish population with ulcerative colitis, per a cited human genetics study.
IgE-mediated mast cell activation increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) by 60%, indicating enhanced mitochondrial respiration during degranulation.
Oligomycin (complex V inhibitor) decreased IgE- and non-IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in two studies, but this was not confirmed by another study.
Pharmacological inhibition of mitochondrial complex I and III reduced IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation.
In some studies, inhibition of complex III did not decrease IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation, contradicting other complex-inhibition findings.
Collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential via the uncoupler FCCP reduced mast cell degranulation after both IgE and non-IgE stimulation.
Mitochondrial ATP levels increased by nearly 40% within 5 minutes of non-IgE stimulation of mast cells, supplying energy for degranulation.
Inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) reduced ATP production and mast cell degranulation, and reduced anaphylaxis and histamine release in a mouse model.

In an experimental anaphylactic shock model, cardiac mitochondrial dysfunction included a 40% decrease in maximal OXPHOS state and a 30% increase in cardiac lipid peroxidation, with a trend toward increased peroxynitrite (+25%).
Cardiac superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity increased by 40% during anaphylactic shock, suggesting compensatory antioxidant activation.
Bellou et al. reported increased plasma SOD levels in an anaphylactic shock rat model, with no change in catalase activity or TBARs.
In an IgG-mediated anaphylactic shock model in guinea pigs, lipid peroxidation (TBARs) increased in the respiratory tract.
In a peanut allergy mouse model, hepatic H2O2 increased by 52% due to oxidative inactivation of aconitase despite increased SOD activity (+26%), reflecting hepatic mitochondrial dysfunction.
Hepatic OXPHOS through complexes I and II decreased in a peanut allergy anaphylaxis mouse model.

In an ex vivo cardiac anaphylaxis model, lipid peroxidation decreased within 2 minutes of shock onset with no change in superoxide anion, and the iNOS/NO pathway did not appear to be the sole mediator, contradicting other studies showing increased oxidative stress.
Rosic et al. observed increased cardiac ROS (superoxide and H2O2) release during anaphylaxis in ovalbumin-sensitized guinea pigs, with no change in NO concentration.
Ultrastructural cardiac mitochondrial changes (shrunken/disrupted mitochondria, close cristae, dense matrix) were observed immediately during an IgE-mediated anaphylactic shock model in 1972.
Hepatocyte mitochondrial granules significantly decreased in rats after compound 48/80-induced anaphylactic shock, possibly due to intramitochondrial calcium loss.

No change in cardiac mitochondrial ultrastructure was observed within 15 minutes of anaphylactic shock onset despite severe hemodynamic and mitochondrial functional impairment, indicating functional impairment precedes structural damage.
Inhibiting mitochondrial STAT3 reduced histamine release by 43% in a mouse model of passive systemic IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.
Mitochondria-targeted inhibitors Mitocur-1 and Mitocur-3 reduced mitochondrial ATP levels, oxygen consumption rate, and degranulation dose-dependently after IgE mast cell stimulation.
Resveratrol inhibited mast cell degranulation by blocking ERK1/2 activation and downstream mitochondrial STAT3 activation.
Knockdown of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) reduced mitochondrial calcium uptake and degranulation in both IgE- and non-IgE-stimulated mast cells.
A whey-based diet that enhanced hepatic glutathione levels in pigs reduced allergen-induced anaphylactic bronchoconstriction by 45% compared to a control diet.
Ebselen inhibited IgE-mediated ROS production dose-dependently but failed to reduce histamine and β-hexosaminidase release, showing dissociation between ROS suppression and degranulation.

Synthetic antioxidant Didox decreased oxidative stress, enhanced catalase and SOD1 expression, suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines in stimulated mast cells, and reduced temperature drop during anaphylaxis in vivo.
The mitochondria-targeted antioxidant SkQ1 reduced mast cell degranulation in vitro and histamine release in vivo, but did not change allergen-induced ROS production.
Rosmarinic acid inhibited IgE-induced ROS production and mast cell degranulation in vitro, confirmed in a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis mouse model.
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) reduced ROS generation and degranulation from non-IgE mast cell stimulation, but did not significantly reduce degranulation following IgE stimulation.
A whey-based diet increased hepatic glutathione levels and reduced allergen-induced anaphylactic bronchoconstriction by 45% in sensitized pigs compared with control-diet animals.
Ebselen inhibited IgE-mediated ROS production dose-dependently but failed to reduce histamine and β-hexosaminidase release from mast cells.

Didox decreased oxidative stress, enhanced catalase/SOD1 expression, suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL6, IL13, TNF, MIP1a) in stimulated mast cells, and reduced the temperature drop during anaphylaxis in vivo.

SkQ1 reduced mast cell degranulation and tissue histamine release in vivo, but did not change allergen-induced ROS production, indicating a dissociation between its antioxidant and degranulation effects.
Rosmarinic acid inhibited IgE-induced ROS production and mast cell degranulation in vitro, an effect confirmed in a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis mouse model.
Tetramethylthiourea and NAC reduced ROS generation and degranulation after non-IgE mast cell stimulation, but NAC did not significantly reduce degranulation following IgE stimulation.

In an experimental anaphylactic shock model, pretreatment with NButGT combined with epinephrine and vascular filling restored OXPHOS through complexes I and II and improved cardiac contractility and output.

Exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5) enhanced IgE mast cell activation by increasing ROS production, upregulating Mn-SOD activity, β-hexosaminidase release and cytokine production, with enhanced Evans blue extravasation in a mouse passive cutaneous anaphylaxis model.
Acrolein, a component of urban air pollution and tobacco smoke, induced dose-dependent intracellular ROS generation and mast cell degranulation.

Hydrogen treatment of mast cells downregulated NADPH oxidase activity, reduced ROS production and β-hexosaminidase release, and hydrogen-rich water pretreatment decreased Evans blue dye leakage and serum histamine release in vivo.

Overexpression of uncoupling protein 2 (UCP2) reduced mast cell degranulation, whereas UCP2 inhibition enhanced histamine release and vascular permeability in mice after allergic and non-allergic stimulation.

Mitochondrial dysfunction was associated with increased intraluminal pH of secretory vesicles in mast cells, and inhibition of vacuolar H+-ATPase led to increased histamine release, suggesting mtROS may inhibit this pump to promote mediator release.
Mitochondrial calcium efflux during mast cell activation appeared to be mediated by the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) rather than the mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (mtNCX).
Triclosan disrupted mitochondrial calcium buffering by abolishing calcium oscillations, inhibiting subsequent mast cell degranulation.
Forsythiae fructus, an antioxidant traditional Chinese medicine extract, reduced IgE and non-IgE mast cell degranulation and in vivo mouse anaphylaxis through decreasing cytosolic calcium.
Cetylpyridinium chloride decreased IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation by decreasing calcium efflux from the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondrial calcium uptake.
STAT inhibitors Mitocur 1 and 3, as well as EGCG, increased cardiolipin peroxidation in mast cells.
Mitochondrial translocation to the mast cell surface during degranulation depends on Drp1 activity, and Drp1 inhibition blocked both mitochondrial translocation and subsequent degranulation.

Knockdown of myosin 1f (MYOF1) in mast cells downregulated Drp1 activation, reduced mitochondrial fission and translocation to exocytosis sites, and decreased degranulation after IgE and MRGPRX2 activation.
SkQ1 decreased IgE-induced mast cell degranulation by inhibiting ERK1/2-dependent mitochondrial fragmentation.
Mitochondrial translocation to the cell surface during mast cell activation was reversible, with mitochondria returning to the perinuclear region 24 hours after non-IgE stimulation.

IgE and non-IgE mast cell stimulation in vitro and in vivo triggered rapid secretion of extracellular small mitochondrial particles near the mast cell surface that appear to act as autocrine triggers of degranulation and paracrine triggers of cytokine release.

Mast cell activation caused dephosphorylation of PDH and phosphorylation of MITF, detaching MITF from the PDH E1 subunit, enhancing PDH activity, OXPHOS, ATP production, degranulation, and cytokine production.
Drugs activating MRGPRX2 (vancomycin, atracurium, morphine, meglumine amidotrizoate) increased MITF activity in mast cells.

Rotenone (complex I inhibitor) did not inhibit the oxidative burst in mast cells, suggesting IgE-induced ROS production is mostly mediated by NADPH oxidase activity rather than mitochondrial complex I.

Inhibition of NADPH oxidase suppressed antigen-induced phosphorylation of Lyn kinase and its downstream targets, indicating a feed-forward loop between NADPH oxidase-derived ROS and FcεRI signal transduction.
22% of adolescent athletes screened positive for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) via eucapnic voluntary hyperpnoea (EVH) testing.

EIB-positive athletes had significantly lower FEV1/FVC ratio compared with EIB-negative athletes.
EIB-positive athletes showed significantly increased bronchodilator reversibility after EVH testing (post-salbutamol) compared with EIB-negative athletes.
EIB was significantly associated with a previous asthma diagnosis and with atopy in this athlete cohort.
An AQUA questionnaire score of ≥6 was the best predictor for a positive EVH test with 78% sensitivity.
Wheezing during exercise was the best specific predictor for a positive EVH test, with 82% specificity.
FeNO negatively correlated with the maximal fall in FEV1 post-EVH test among atopic athletes.
An AQUA© questionnaire score of ≥6 was one of the best predictors of a positive EVH test, with a sensitivity of 78%.
Self-reported wheezing during exercise was highly specific (82%) for a positive EVH test result.

Loss-of-function mutations in the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.7 (SCN9A) result in a congenital inability to experience pain.
Gain-of-function mutations in NaV1.7 (SCN9A) cause distinct neuropathic pain disorders including erythromelalgia, paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, and small-fiber neuropathy.
Variants in the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.8 (SCN10A) have been linked to human pain disorders.
Variants in the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.9 (SCN11A) have been linked to human pain disorders.
A mutation in the ligand-gated ion channel TRPA1, which responds to environmental irritants, causes a familial episodic pain disorder.

There is a correlation between the impact of ion channel mutations on biophysical channel properties and the severity of the resulting clinical pain phenotype.
Across all three surgical-history subgroups, GES implantation led to significant improvement in upper gastrointestinal symptoms.

An intergenic variant near IRX1 was genome-wide significantly associated with reduced Raynaud's syndrome risk in the meta-analysis.
A lead variant in the HLA region (chromosome 6) was genome-wide significantly associated with increased Raynaud's syndrome risk, previously linked to peripheral vascular disease.
An intronic variant in the NOS3 5' regulatory region was genome-wide significantly associated with increased Raynaud's syndrome risk.
An intronic ACVR2A variant was genome-wide significantly associated with reduced Raynaud's syndrome risk, and has previously been linked to lymphocyte counts.
A rare variant upstream of PCDH10 reached genome-wide significance for increased Raynaud's syndrome risk in the meta-analysis.
An intronic TMEM51 variant reached genome-wide significance and was associated with reduced Raynaud's syndrome risk.
A variant upstream of RAB6C reached genome-wide significance and was associated with increased Raynaud's syndrome risk.
Survival analysis in FinnGen showed that carriers of the ADRA2A risk allele had a higher incidence/earlier onset of Raynaud's syndrome over time in a dose-dependent manner.
The frequency of the ADRA2A risk allele (A) was higher in colder, northern regions of Finland compared to southern regions, consistent with a role in cold-triggered vasoconstriction.
Fine-mapping identified rs7090046 as the most likely causal variant at the ADRA2A locus within a four-variant credible set.
Fine-mapping of the IRX1 locus produced a 19-variant credible set without a single clearly dominant causal variant.
A separate GWAS restricted to secondary Raynaud's syndrome cases found no genome-wide significant loci, in either individual cohorts or meta-analysis, contrasting with primary RS findings.

The RS risk allele at rs7090046 was associated with increased ADRA2A expression specifically in tibial arteries, but not in coronary arteries or aorta, and co-localization confirmed a shared genetic signal between RS risk and ADRA2A expression in tibial arteries.

Mast cells were identified as the primary postoperative source of the rate-limiting BH4-synthesis enzyme, which serves as an obligate cofactor for Tph1-mediated serotonin production.
Mice lacking mast cells, or lacking mast cell-specific BH4-pathway enzyme, showed drastically decreased postoperative pain.
Skin injury induced the nociceptive neuropeptide substance P along with mast cell degranulation and colocalization of mast cell granules with nerves.
Substance P triggered serotonin release in both mouse and human mast cells.
Blockade of the substance P receptor substantially reduced pain hypersensitivity after injury.
Placement of the EndoFLIP catheter in the pyloric region was achieved successfully in all six patients undergoing esophagectomy, with no complications.
Surgical resection of the esophagus, which transects the vagus nerve branches controlling the pylorus, increased the pyloric incremental elastic modulus (Ep) from a preoperative baseline.
Prophylactic balloon dilatation of the pylorus following esophageal resection reduced the elevated pyloric elastic modulus (Ep) back close to preoperative levels.
Pyloric compliance showed a pattern similar to that of the elastic modulus, decreasing after esophageal resection and improving after balloon dilatation.
A meta-analysis reported that NPSLE prevalence among SLE patients reaches up to 56%.

NPSLE and other SLE manifestations occur more commonly among African American, Hispanic, and Asian patients, but White patients show a higher incidence of neuropsychiatric manifestations specifically.
About 90% of NPSLE patients present with pure CNS manifestations, most commonly headache, mood disorders, cognitive dysfunction, seizures, and cerebrovascular disease.
Lupus nephritis affects approximately 40% of SLE patients.
Pericarditis prevalence in SLE is 39%, with incidence ranging between 11% and 54%.
The case patient had low complement C3 (31 mg/dL vs normal 87-200 mg/dL), consistent with active SLE.
The case patient had low complement C4 (less than 8 mg/dL vs normal 19-52 mg/dL), consistent with active SLE.
The case patient had low CH50 (36 mg/dL vs normal 42-91 mg/dL).
The case patient had a high-titer positive ANA (1:1280), supporting active SLE.

In the case patient, pulse methylprednisolone followed by cyclophosphamide infusion for suspected active lupus cerebritis led to improved mentation within three days, with dramatic improvement after the first cyclophosphamide dose.
Systemic glucocorticosteroids produce a positive response in 60% to 75% of NPSLE patients.
Azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil can serve as second-line/maintenance therapy to reduce steroid exposure or replace cyclophosphamide in NPSLE.
Anti-CD20 rituximab, belimumab, plasma exchange, and IVIG can be considered for NPSLE with poor response or failure of standard treatment.
Plasmapheresis is beneficial as additional therapy for chorea or myelitis in NPSLE patients.

Anti-phospholipid antibodies including anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and beta-2-glycoprotein antibodies provide the most diagnostic information in NPSLE, particularly for focal events like cerebrovascular illness and seizures.
Serum anti-ribosomal P antibodies have been proposed to be linked to lupus psychosis.
CSF from NPSLE patients has been found to contain anti-DNA antibodies, oligoclonal banding, immune complexes, interleukin-6, and B-cell activation indicators.
Approximately 10% to 15% of NPSLE cases involve peripheral nervous system symptoms, most commonly peripheral neuropathy.
An eight-week psychoeducational group intervention improved SLE patients' coping skills and produced a significant, sustained improvement in quality of life.
In aPL-seropositive SLE patients, antiaggregant therapy is recommended as the main prevention strategy, with anticoagulants as secondary prevention.
On follow-up, the case patient developed severe proteinuria (515 mg/dL) and CKD stage 2 (GFR 76), raising concern for lupus nephritis, though she declined renal biopsy.

In a prospective UK Biobank cohort, CMV serostatus was not significantly associated with the risk of developing disorders of the autonomic nervous system (ICD-10 G90) after adjusting for demographic and clinical covariates.
The mean EQ-5D VAS score in people with ME/CFS was markedly lower than the UK general population norm.
The mean EQ-5D index value in ME/CFS patients was substantially lower than the UK population norm.
Usual activities was the most severely affected EQ-5D dimension, with nearly all participants reporting some or complete inability to perform usual activities.
Pain and discomfort was the second most affected EQ-5D dimension, with over a quarter of participants reporting extreme pain.
Mobility problems were prevalent, with more than 10% of participants confined to bed.
A majority of participants reported problems with self-care, including some who were unable to wash or dress independently.
Anxiety/depression was the least affected EQ-5D dimension, although still impacting more than 60% of participants.
A statistically significant moderate positive correlation was found between EQ-5D VAS score and EQ-5D index value.
ME/CFS patients who lived alone had significantly lower EQ-5D VAS scores (poorer QoL) than those who did not live alone.
Spearman's rank correlation showed a weak but significant negative correlation between living alone and QoL score.
No statistically significant difference in EQ-5D index values was found between ME/CFS patients living alone versus not living alone.
The most frequently observed EQ-5D health state profile indicated mobility, self-care, usual activity, pain and anxiety/depression problems across multiple domains simultaneously.
About a quarter of participants reported having another chronic condition in addition to ME/CFS.
All ME/CFS and healthy control participants completed the full one-hour multimodal MRI protocol (SV-MRS, task-fMRI, T1/T2WI) without any interrupted or incomplete sequences.
ME/CFS patients reported significantly worse scores than healthy controls across all clinical symptom measures assessed.
Mean handgrip strength did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and HC groups, and did not change from pre- to post-MRI scan within either group.
Considering measurements at both pre- and post-MRI time points, ME/CFS patients were significantly weaker and showed greater variability in handgrip strength than healthy controls.
NAA concentration in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex was higher in ME/CFS patients than healthy controls, a difference that did not survive Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.

No statistically significant differences were found between ME/CFS and HC groups for any other measured metabolites (Cr, PCr, PCh, Ins, GSH, GABA, Gln, Glu, NAAG) across the ACC, brainstem, and DLPFC voxels.

During both 1-back and 2-back working memory task conditions, ME/CFS patients showed greater fMRI brain activation than healthy controls, particularly in the frontal pole, anterior cingulate gyrus, and brainstem.
There was no significant difference between ME/CFS and HC groups in n-back task accuracy or reaction time, nor a group-by-task-difficulty interaction.
NAA levels in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex positively correlated with symptom severity scores for sleep quality, fatigue severity, and pain.
Overall handgrip strength was associated with worsened pain and poorer sleep quality across participants.
The total number of activated fMRI voxels and the maximum Z-value of activation intensity were highly correlated with each other and were examined against pain severity scores.
Correlations between L-DLPFC NAA levels and sleep quality/pain severity were significant only within the ME/CFS subgroup, suggesting a disease-relevant relationship.
A meta-analysis of 31 studies found that 43% of people report lingering or newly appearing symptoms one month after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Population-based studies from the United States estimate that roughly 6.9% of the population suffers from Post-COVID Condition.
At least 68% of individuals with PCC experience post-exertional malaise (PEM).
More than one year after infection, 19–58% of PCC patients meet diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, suggesting a common etiology.
In two-day cardiopulmonary exercise testing, ME/CFS patients showed significant declines in aerobic capacity and workload on the second day, while healthy controls improved.
ME/CFS patients showed greater declines in hand grip strength than healthy controls upon repeated testing, and this decline correlated with higher PEM scores.
A meta-analysis of nine studies (464 subjects) found peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) was on average 4.9 mL/kg/min lower in PCC patients than in fully recovered individuals.
At peak exercise, PCC subjects showed significantly lower levels of fatty acid β-oxidation and higher blood lactate compared with controls, suggesting a premature switch to anaerobic glycolysis.

80% of studies attributing diminished exercise capacity to muscular deconditioning had included subjects previously hospitalized for acute COVID-19, calling the deconditioning explanation into question.

Invasive hemodynamic assessment combined with CPET showed decreased systemic and peripheral oxygen extraction at peak exercise in PCC, attributed to reduced oxygen diffusion in the peripheral microcirculation.

Histological analysis of vastus lateralis biopsies showed a significantly lower percentage of SDH-positive fibers and higher percentage of SDH-negative fibers in PCC patients compared to recovered controls, indicating a shift from oxidative to glycolytic muscle fiber content.

Key TCA cycle metabolites (glutamate, α-ketoglutarate, citrate) and the citrate:lactate ratio were lower in skeletal muscle samples of PCC patients compared to healthy subjects, and further decreased one day after PEM induction.
Citrate synthase protein and mRNA levels were lower, and genetic pathways related to oxidative phosphorylation and cell respiration were downregulated in patients with persistent COVID-19 symptoms.

High-resolution respirometry revealed a significantly reduced oxygen flux for mitochondrial complex II, and complex I and II together, and a loss of cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) activity in PCC patients.

WASF3 protein is significantly increased in muscle cells of ME/CFS patients; ER-stress-induced WASF3 overexpression impaired complex IV and supercomplex III2+IV assembly in mouse muscle, reducing oxidative metabolism and running capacity, while WASF3 knockdown in myoblasts improved respiration.

Higher levels of plasma carnitine-conjugated and free fatty acids at rest were found in PCC compared to control subjects, while decreased plasma acetylcarnitine may be associated with neurocognitive symptoms.

PCC patients exhibit elevated levels of circulating endothelial cells and endothelial colony-forming cells alongside a reduced ADAMTS-13:von Willebrand factor ratio, implying ongoing endothelial cell damage.
Lower flow-mediated dilation in PCC patients suggests maladaptive endothelial vascular tone regulation and has been directly related to symptom persistence and lower exercise capacity.
MRI imaging showed PCC patients exhibit widespread decreased brain oxygen levels in grey and white matter, indicating increased cerebral metabolism.
Endothelial cells cultured in the plasma of ME/CFS patients produce less nitric oxide upon exposure to activating substances than in the presence of healthy control serum.
Supplementation of L-arginine improved flow-mediated dilation, physical performance, and perception of effort and fatigue, supporting endothelial function as a central disease pathway.
Fibrinolysis-resistant microclots have been documented in PCC patients, potentially related to increased levels of antiplasmin, contributing to a thromboinflammatory state.

The increase in clotting proteins fibrinogen chains FGA and FGB 15 minutes after CPET until volitional exhaustion positively correlated with PEM severity experienced by ME/CFS subjects 24 hours post-exercise.

Reduced mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), along with structural membrane damage limiting erythrocyte deformability, have been demonstrated in COVID-19 convalescents and ME/CFS patients.
Autoantibodies binding to adrenergic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors were shown to correlate with symptoms of impaired peripheral microcirculation and cognitive impairment.
PCC patients demonstrate higher antibody responses against viruses such as Epstein-Barr virus, suggesting dysfunctional immune activity may facilitate reactivation of latent viruses.

Immortalized ME/CFS patient-derived lymphoblasts showed mitochondrial deficiency of ATP synthesis due to an isolated complex V inefficiency compared to healthy controls, and PBMCs showed lower ATP-linked respiration rates.

SARS-CoV-2 spike protein induces vWF, adhesion molecule and pro-inflammatory cytokine production in endothelial cells via NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome pathways, promoting endotheliopathy and clotting pathology, and interacts with fibrin(ogen) and prothrombin to cause thrombogenicity.

A report of three PCC cases experienced rapid remission of symptoms after treatment with the monoclonal antibody cocktail casirivimab/imdevimab directed against the spike receptor binding domain, implying a pathomechanistic role of spike persistence.

High systemic levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α relate to coagulation pathway activation and metabolic disruptions in PCC/ME-CFS.

Spike-mediated thrombogenicity is also caused by its direct interaction with fibrin(ogen) and prothrombin.

A case report of three PCC patients experienced rapid remission of symptoms after treatment with the monoclonal antibody cocktail casirivimab/imdevimab targeting the spike receptor binding domain, implicating spike persistence in disease.
ME/CFS patients with elevated resting lactate levels (≥2 mmol/L) were more likely to experience severe PEM than those with normal levels.
In ME/CFS, the severity of symptom flare after moderate exercise is linked to cytokine activity.

Exosome-associated mitochondrial DNA significantly increases after exercise in ME/CFS patients and, upon reaching the CNS through a disrupted blood-brain barrier, stimulates cultured human microglia to secrete IL-1β.

Vasodilators and nitric oxide substrate/cofactor supplementation such as L-arginine are proposed as treatment targets for flow-mediated dilation and eNOS dysfunction in PEM.
Anticoagulation is proposed as a treatment option targeting fibrin amyloid microclots and platelet pathology in PEM.
Immunoadsorption (apheresis) is proposed to deplete vasoactive autoantibodies as a treatment for microvascular alterations in PEM.
Parasympathetic activation techniques such as meditation and breathing exercises are proposed to counter sympathetic overactivity contributing to PEM.
Antiviral therapies (e.g., Paxlovid, Ritonavir, Temelimab) are proposed to target persistent viral antigen components and latent viral infections underlying dysregulated immune activation in PEM.

Anti-inflammatory drugs (corticosteroids, antihistamines) and immunomodulators (kinase inhibitors, rintatolimod) are proposed to target pro-inflammatory pathways and T cell exhaustion in dysregulated immune activation underlying PEM.

Redox balancers (vitamin E, glutathione, ubiquinol, NADH, selenium) and magnesium supplementation are proposed as treatments targeting respiratory complex function and oxidative/inflammatory stress in mitochondrial dysfunction underlying PEM.

Wang et al. demonstrated that alleviating endoplasmic reticulum stress decreased WASF3 expression and thereby improved mitochondrial respiration, though clinical symptom correlation was not investigated.

Pacing, which involves avoiding overexertion, allowing adequate recovery, dividing activities into smaller tasks, and resting before symptoms arise, is promoted as a management strategy to prevent aggravation of bioenergetic capacity in ME/CFS and PCC.

The authors note that case studies and case series on treatment candidates have yielded contradictory results and that more randomized controlled trials with clinically relevant endpoints are needed before individual use outside of studies can be supported.
Approximately 43% of non-hospitalized COVID-19 cases and over half of hospitalized cases reported symptoms consistent with long COVID during the first two years of the pandemic.

Post-exertional malaise/post-exertional neuroimmune exhaustion is common in long COVID and drives its persistent, severe, progressive disablement, suggesting an ME/CFS-like subtype of long COVID is prevalent.
Autonomic dysfunction affects nearly 70% of patients with long COVID, contributing to symptoms such as abnormal blood pressure, heart rate, and blood volume regulation.

In a UK biobank cohort imaged before and after infection, SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals showed significant gray matter thickness reduction and reduced global brain size compared to uninfected controls.

Diffusion microstructure MRI showed widespread white/gray matter microstructural changes in long COVID patients with ongoing symptoms compared to recovered patients, correlating with cognitive dysfunction.
DTI-based perivascular space analysis showed reduced glymphatic function indices in people with long COVID, even following mild acute infection.

Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI showed significant whole-brain leakage indicating increased blood-brain barrier permeability specifically in the 'brain fog' subgroup of long COVID patients, but not in recovered or brain-fog-negative patients.

In a longitudinal study of 14 patients with long COVID-related cognitive impairment, combined DCE-MRI, DTI, and MR spectroscopy revealed BBB and white matter microstructural impairments alongside reduced glutamate/glutamine, suggesting white matter injury via glutamatergic excitotoxicity secondary to BBB breakdown from neuroinflammation.
PET imaging with the [11C]PBR28 tracer for activated microglia showed significantly increased neuroinflammation across many brain regions in long COVID patients.

PET imaging with the [18F]F-AraG tracer showed activated T cells trafficking into CNS sites (brainstem, spinal cord) where they should normally be absent following SARS-CoV-2 infection, with a more exaggerated pattern in patients with long COVID symptoms; residual viral components were found in colon biopsy tissue.
Functional neurologic disorder is a rare condition, estimated to affect around 4-12 per 100,000 people, despite perceptions that it is commonly diagnosed in neurology clinics.

A long COVID patient with acrocyanosis and non-epileptic spells was initially misdiagnosed with FND; the spells were later determined to be presyncopal episodes caused by post-COVID-19 POTS, with the acrocyanosis resolving immediately upon leg elevation.

A tilt table test can differentiate true syncope from pseudo-syncope with adequate sensitivity and specificity, helping to distinguish long COVID/dysautonomia spells from FND-related non-epileptic seizures.
Traditional cognitive screening tests designed to detect Alzheimer's disease are not useful for evaluating cognitive impairment secondary to long COVID.
Multiple studies identified objective neuropsychological deficits via cognitive testing in patients with long COVID, providing evidence against a purely functional origin for brain fog.

Sensory disturbance in long COVID due to post-COVID-19 small fiber neuropathy usually follows a length-dependent neuropathic pattern with reduced pinprick and temperature sensation in the distal extremities, distinguishing it from the non-anatomic sensory loss patterns seen in FND, though non-length-dependent patchy SFN also occurs, especially with comorbid autoimmune disease.
hEDS and HSD patients share a common plasma fragment signature of fibronectin and type I collagen, supporting the idea that hEDS and HSD are a single disorder rather than distinct entities.

Prior work by the same group showed ECM disorganization involving fibronectin, type I collagen, and tenascin in hEDS and HSD dermal fibroblasts, with MMP-generated fragments detected in conditioned media.

Distinctive plasma ECM fragment patterns were also observed in rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and osteoarthritis cohorts, suggesting these fragments could serve as biomarkers for these joint diseases as well.

The authors propose that plasma FN and COLLI fragment patterns could form the basis of the first blood test for diagnosing hEDS/HSD and could guide future therapeutic trials targeting ECM homeostasis.
This case report documents an 18-year-old woman with EDS who also presented with multiple dermatofibromas, an association not previously reported in the literature.

The patient met clinical diagnostic criteria for classical EDS, satisfying two major criteria (skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring, generalized joint hypermobility) and two minor criteria (easy bruising, skin fragility).
The patient exhibited piezogenic papules, Swan-neck deformities of the digits, striae alba, and atrophic scarring, physical signs considered consistent with EDS.
Biopsy of the nodular skin lesions demonstrated fibrohistiocytic proliferation, acanthotic epidermis, and elongated rete ridges, confirming a diagnosis of dermatofibroma.
Prior literature suggests immunosuppression as a possible underlying mechanism for multiple dermatofibromas, based on cases reported in HIV-infected patients.

Literature cited indicates corticosteroid therapy may influence dermatofibroma development, with new lesions appearing during increased corticosteroid dosage in SLE patients and lesion reduction upon discontinuation.

The authors judged that inhaled corticosteroid use was unlikely to have caused this patient's multiple dermatofibromas because of the lack of systemic effects and a one-year gap between discontinuation and lesion onset.

Despite initial suspicion that trauma triggered the lesions, the authors concluded the left elbow trauma/fracture was an unlikely cause of the multiple dermatofibromas given differing anatomical locations and lesion multiplicity.
Genetic analysis on day 60 revealed a COL3A1 abnormality confirming the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The patient presented with intra-abdominal hemorrhage caused by rupture of a hepatic artery aneurysm arising from the celiac artery, requiring emergency angioembolization.

Angiography revealed multiple aneurysms including stenosis at the celiac trunk origin, aneurysms in the celiac, common hepatic, and right hepatic arteries, bilateral renal artery aneurysms, and a left internal carotid artery aneurysm found on brain MRA.
The patient had a prior history of sigmoid colon perforation 12 years earlier, a complication commonly reported in vascular EDS.

Most arterial lesions in vascular EDS occur in branch arteries of the abdominal aorta rather than the aorta itself, as branch arteries are more susceptible to hypertension-related injury and are richer in elastic fibers.

Celiprolol was prescribed after diagnosis and is reported in the literature to prevent aneurysm development in vascular EDS; the aneurysms remained stable under this treatment during outpatient follow-up.
For ruptured aneurysms in vascular EDS, endovascular repair (transarterial coil embolization) has a lower mortality rate than open surgical repair.
The patient exhibited characteristic physical findings of vascular EDS including increased skin permeability/translucency, small jaw, keloid scarring, and joint hypermobility.
Conditional deletion of Col5a1 in fibroblasts at the time of skin wounding resulted in significantly larger, delayed-healing wounds compared to WT mice, with ~25% of wound area still open by day 19.
At 62 days post-injury, scar area was significantly greater in Col5a1CKO mice than in WT littermates.
Transmission electron microscopy revealed grossly disorganized, orthogonally arranged collagen fibrils in wounded skin of Col5a1CKO mice versus parallel fibril arrangement in WT.
Genes related to epidermis development, epithelial differentiation, and filament organization were upregulated after injury in WT but not significantly upregulated in Col5a1CKO wounds.
Expression of inflammatory genes was significantly upregulated in injured tissue of Col5a1CKO mice compared to WT littermates.
ECM organization pathway genes, including matrix metalloproteinases that degrade ECM, were upregulated in Col5a1CKO wounds.
Immunostaining showed increased accumulation of CD45+ and CD11b+ inflammatory cells in Col5a1CKO wound tissue at day 19 post-injury.
Total collagen content, measured biochemically, was significantly decreased in wounds of Col5a1CKO mice compared to WT littermates.
Atomic force microscopy revealed significantly lower Young's modulus (tissue stiffness) in the wound bed of Col5a1CKO mice compared to WT at day 14.
Flow cytometry showed significantly increased αvβ3 integrin expression in cells from injured skin of Col5a1CKO mice compared to WT controls at day 7.
Systemic cilengitide (20 mg/kg i.p.) significantly enhanced wound closure in Col5a1CKO mice compared to vehicle-treated Col5a1CKO mice at day 14/10.
Intradermal injection of WT fibroblasts into Col5a1CKO wounds produced a 50% improvement in wound size by day 14 compared to vehicle-injected Col5a1CKO wounds.
Injection of Col5a1CKO-derived fibroblasts (deficient in Col5a1) into Col5a1CKO wounds did not improve wound healing, unlike WT fibroblasts.
WT fibroblast injection into Col5a1CKO wounds significantly increased expression of epidermal keratin genes Krt6a, Krt6b, Krt16, and Krt17 compared to vehicle-treated Col5a1CKO wounds.

The glenoid concavity angle (GCA) was significantly lower (shallower glenoid) in patients with clinical shoulder hyperlaxity compared to controls, for both readers.
The critical shoulder angle (CSA), which reflects deltoid force vector on the glenoid, did not differ significantly between hyperlax and control patients.
Glenoid dysplasia (posteroinferior glenoid rim deficiency with labral hypertrophy) was more frequent in patients with shoulder hyperlaxity than in controls.
Flat or convex glenoid articular surfaces (as opposed to concave) were significantly more frequent among patients with shoulder hyperlaxity compared to controls.
GCA measurements showed good diagnostic performance for identifying clinical shoulder hyperlaxity, with a cutoff of 4° yielding the best-balanced sensitivity/specificity.

GCA values showed a progressive decrease across subgroups from non-hyperlax non-dysplastic patients, to hyperlax non-dysplastic, to non-hyperlax dysplastic, to hyperlax with dysplasia, suggesting a cumulative severity gradient of glenoid morphologic change.
GCA values were significantly lower in patients with glenoid dysplasia compared to those without, independent of hyperlaxity status.

The patient was diagnosed with musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (mcEDS) caused by mutation in CHST14, confirmed by genetic testing.
Minor trauma (a fall bruising the left thigh) progressed to a massive subcutaneous and intermuscular hematoma causing hemorrhagic shock in this mcEDS patient.
The patient's hemoglobin decreased from 8.1 g/dL at presentation to 6.9 g/dL as bleeding progressed.
Tranexamic acid was administered to halt progression of bleeding after hemoglobin dropped to 6.9 g/dL.
Elevation of the affected area combined with compression achieved hemostasis without compromising lower leg perfusion.

Desmopressin (DDAVP) nasal drops have been reported effective in preventing subcutaneous hematomas in mcEDS by improving platelet-collagen interactions and enhancing von Willebrand factor-mediated platelet adhesion.
Connective tissue fragility in mcEDS is attributed to failures in collagen fibril assembly linked to systemic deficiency in dermatan sulfate.
mcEDS-CHST14 tends to present more frequently with symptom crises compared to mcEDS-DSE.
Approximately 80% of mcEDS patients with large subcutaneous hematomas experience their first episode by age 12.
mcEDS is an exceedingly rare EDS subtype with an estimated prevalence of approximately 1 in 1 million, compared to overall EDS prevalence of 1 in 5,000.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is described as complicating orthodontic treatment due to collagen fragility, causing rapid tooth movement and increased risk of relapse.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 gene, leading to spontaneous arterial dissection and organ rupture.
Left ventricular ejection fraction was significantly lower in vEDS patients compared with matched healthy controls.
Right ventricular ejection fraction was significantly lower in vEDS patients compared with matched healthy controls.
Higher LV end-diastolic volume indexed to body surface area (LVEDVi) independently predicted arterial dissection in vEDS patients.
Higher LVEDVi also independently predicted aneurysm occurrence in vEDS patients.
Higher indexed LV end-systolic volume (LVESVi) independently predicted aneurysm occurrence in vEDS patients.
Lower LVEF independently predicted the presence of any vEDS-related complication (dissection, aneurysm, or pneumothorax).
Individuals with vEDS and LVEF below the cohort mean of 58% had a higher frequency of dissection and/or aneurysm than those with higher LVEF.

Of 34 patients evaluated at the vCTD outpatient clinic, genetic testing confirmed vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in 13, Loeys-Dietz syndrome in 3, and Marfan syndrome in 3, while 15 had no confirmed vCTD and served as controls.
Two of 19 vCTD patients (10.5%) died during follow-up from vascular complications: one from renal artery dissection with bleeding and one from splenic artery rupture.
In vEDS patients, seven remained stable with an arterial progression score of 0, while two patients with the largest score increases (21 to 33 and 0 to 12) died from arterial complications.

Using combined imaging modalities, most arterial segments in vCTD patients showed a tendency toward diameter increase (>10%), with the common femoral artery and abdominal aorta showing growth in 50.0% and 40.0% of cases, respectively.
Diverging vessel diameter measurements with apparent decreases over time when combining imaging modalities were more frequent in non-vCTD controls than in patients with vCTDs.

In ultrasound-only analysis of confirmed vCTD patients (n=12), the abdominal aorta was the most frequently affected segment showing diameter growth, followed by the common femoral and popliteal arteries, with diverging results in the common iliac artery.
Two patients with vEDS developed bilateral internal carotid artery aneurysms during surveillance periods of 1317 and 2537 days, beginning at ages 28 and 49 respectively.
One patient with Loeys-Dietz syndrome developed bilateral popliteal artery aneurysms over a 2286-day surveillance period starting at age 29.
Aggregated trendline analysis by age showed that arterial diameters in almost all territories peaked between ages 30 and 40, with decreasing growth rates and vessel diameters after age 40.
When aggregated by surveillance time rather than age, all arterial territories except the popliteal artery showed continuously increasing diameters over the surveillance period.

Arterial complications clustered in a subset of patients: six patients (mean age 32.8±9.9 years) had multiple events (surgery, dissection, or rupture) while nine patients (mean age 26.8±9.6 years) had no arterial complications during follow-up.

Among 19 confirmed vCTD patients, six had medically treated hypertension, nine had a history of cardiovascular surgery, three had a history of aneurysm rupture, and five had a history of arterial dissection, with dissections and ruptures occurring across intracranial, aortic, visceral, and peripheral arterial territories.
Children with JIA and joint hypermobility had higher disease activity at baseline compared to those with JIA alone.
Patients with JIA and joint hypermobility had more active arthritis joints than JIA-only patients.
Physician global assessment of disease activity scores were higher in JIA+JH patients compared to JIA-only patients.
JIA+JH patients reported worse patient-reported well-being compared to JIA-only patients.
The differences in disease activity and well-being between JIA+JH and JIA-only groups persisted over time despite treatment.
Patients with JIA and joint hypermobility had a 19-20% greater likelihood of maintaining high disease activity scores and worsening over subsequent visits compared to JIA-only patients.

A 7-year-old girl with skeletal dysostosis, dysmorphic features, hypermobility, laryngo-tracheo-bronchomalacia, and atrioventricular septal defect was found to carry compound heterozygous loss-of-function variants in BMP5.
The paternally inherited BMP5 variant c.88_89del causes a frameshift predicted to introduce a premature stop codon and trigger nonsense-mediated decay.

The maternally inherited BMP5 splice donor variant c.1104+2del was predicted by SpliceAI and Pangolin to abolish the exon 5 donor splice site, and RNA sequencing of maternal fibroblasts confirmed skipping of exon 5, producing an aberrant transcript.
The patient exhibited severe hypermobility of the shoulders (100° rotation), elbows (20° hyperextension), knees (30° hyperextension), and ankles.
Skeletal imaging revealed absent ossification of the inferior pubic rami and ischial rami, bilateral patellar aplasia, four sacral segments, and anterior angulation of the coccyx.

The patient had an atrioventricular septal defect surgically repaired at 6 weeks of age, complicated by third-degree AV block requiring pacemaker implantation, and later required surgery for severe left AV valve insufficiency.
Trachea-bronchoscopy revealed moderate laryngo-tracheo-bronchomalacia, a stalked omega-shaped epiglottis, and a short right main bronchus.
STRING bioinformatic analysis showed that BMP5 interacts with BMPER, TBX4, PITX1, and LMX1B, genes associated with human skeletal dysplasias featuring similar pelvic and patellar abnormalities.
Exon 5, which is deleted in the maternal allele, encodes the evolutionarily conserved cysteine 353 within the TGF-beta-like domain, important for proper protein folding required for receptor binding.

Monozygotic twins with unilateral ear hypoplasia were previously reported to carry heterozygous variants in BMP2 (p.Ser111Ile) and BMP5 (c.833-4C>G), but segregation or cDNA studies were not performed, leaving the pathogenicity of those variants unclear.

Prior studies of chicken embryonic heart development showed BMP5 expression in the endoderm underlying precardiac mesoderm and in the myocardium of the atrioventricular canal and outflow tract, sites of endocardial cushion and valve/septa formation, suggesting BMP5 is essential for myocardial and endocardial cushion tissue development.

The patient's two healthy siblings were heterozygous carriers of only the maternal c.1104+2del variant, consistent with a recessive compound heterozygous inheritance pattern underlying the disease phenotype.
Women with fibromyalgia reached a lower absolute and relative peak heart rate than control women during a maximal graded exercise test.
The on-transient heart rate response parameters (time constant τ, amplitude Aon, baseline HR0) at the onset of submaximal exercise did not differ between women with fibromyalgia and control women.

During the steady-state phase of submaximal cycling exercise, mean HR and HRV indices (Ln-SDNN, Ln-RMSSD, Ln-SD1, Ln-SD2, SD1/SD2) showed no significant group, time, or group-by-time interaction effects between FM and control women.

Mean heart rate during submaximal exercise expressed relative to peak HR or to maximum predicted HR did not differ significantly between FM and control women, indicating similar relative internal training load.
FMS patients had significantly higher VAS pain scores compared to healthy controls.
FMS patients had significantly higher anxiety scores (HADS-A) compared to healthy controls.
FMS patients had significantly higher depression scores (HADS-D) compared to healthy controls.
FMS patients showed significantly higher scores than healthy controls on FIQ-R, Fibromyalgia Severity scale, Widespread Pain Index, and Symptom Severity scale.
FMS patients showed a trend towards higher IL-6 levels compared to healthy controls, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Within the FMS group, IL-6 levels were slightly higher among patients with greater FIQ-R-defined severity.
Serum serotonin levels were lower in FMS patients compared to healthy controls.
Within FMS patients stratified by FIQ-R severity, serotonin levels were higher with greater severity, with moderate patients having lower levels than severe and very severe patients.
A one-compartment pharmacokinetic model with double extravascular (first-order plus zero-order) absorption and linear elimination best characterized reserpine plasma concentrations in rats.
Reserpine was rapidly eliminated from plasma (half-life 2.25 h), yet FMS-like behavioral alterations persisted or emerged weeks later, suggesting mechanisms beyond acute monoamine depletion.

The final PK–PD model used a precursor-pool structure in which reserpine stimulates transit of a precursor pool into a monoamine response compartment, with quantified production, transit and elimination rate constants.

Brain region was identified as a statistically significant covariate on the precursor production rate constant (kin), consistent with different baseline monoamine levels across prefrontal cortex, spinal cord, and amygdala.
Inter-animal variability was low-to-moderate for most PK–PD parameters but very high for absorption-related parameters (ka1, F1) and the reserpine drug-effect slope on precursor transit (SLP1).
Residual unexplained variability was moderate for both PK and PD observations, attributed to the destructive/sparse longitudinal sampling design.
After repeated reserpine dosing, brain monoamine levels showed an initial rapid rise, then depletion to a minimum around 72 hours, followed by partial recovery toward baseline by 96 hours.

Simulation of higher, untested reserpine doses (2 and 4 mg/kg QD x3) predicted progressively greater monoamine depletion (lower Cmax, Cmin, and AUC) relative to the reference 1 mg/kg dose across amygdala, prefrontal cortex, and spinal cord.

The amygdala showed the greatest monoamine precursor-pool synthesis among the analyzed brain regions, whereas prefrontal cortex and especially spinal cord showed precursor-pool depletion at higher simulated doses (2 and 4 mg/kg).

The reserpine-monoamine PK–PD relationship was best described by a linear drug-effect model across the 0.1–1 mg/kg dose range, indicating a proportional relationship between reserpine exposure and monoamine response.

FMS-like sleep disturbances in the reserpine model develop from the third week after administration, long after monoamine levels have returned near baseline, suggesting other pathophysiological mechanisms are triggered.
Prior literature cited in this paper reports decreased monoamines and their main metabolites in the cerebrospinal fluid of people with fibromyalgia.
Prior literature cited in this paper indicates antidepressant drugs that increase monoamine levels have shown effectiveness in relieving fibromyalgia symptoms.
Prior literature cited proposes aberrant amygdala activation in pain-related fear as a candidate biomarker of fibromyalgia, given its role in the affective component of pain.
Recent literature cited notes that mammalian astrocytes express VMAT-2 receptors, raising the possibility that reserpine directly affects glial function and contributes to FMS-like symptoms.
The patient carries two heterozygous pathogenic ALPL (TNSALP) variants in exons 5 and 12, genetically confirming childhood-onset hypophosphatasia.
At baseline the patient showed the characteristic HPP biochemical profile: low serum ALP, low FGF-23, moderate vitamin D deficiency, and elevated PLP.
Circulating hsa-let-7i-5p, a non-tissue-specific miRNA, increased from 20 000 to 30 000 rpm (50%) over the course of asfotase alfa treatment.
Muscle-specific hsa-miR-1-3p decreased from 60 to 20 rpm (66.66% reduction) over 400 days of asfotase alfa treatment, paralleling functional improvement.
hsa-miR-1294, a non-bone/muscle-specific miRNA mainly expressed in small airway epithelial cells, increased from 55 to 90 rpm (63.63%) during treatment.
Muscle/bone-specific hsa-miR-206 decreased from 187 to 27 rpm (85.57% reduction) over the treatment course, corresponding to increased ALP enzyme activity.
hsa-miR-375-3p, involved in osteogenesis regulation via LRP5/Wnt/β-catenin signaling, decreased from 70 to 20 rpm (71.43%) during asfotase alfa therapy.
hsa-miR-624-5p, a non-bone/muscle-specific miRNA, increased from 36 to 61 rpm (69.44%) over the treatment course.

The authors propose that downregulation of muscle-specific hsa-miR-1-3p and hsa-miR-206 during asfotase alfa therapy could serve as a novel biomarker of treatment response in HPP, since it coincided with improved chair-raise time, walk distance, and pain/quality-of-life scores.
Pain severity and pain interference (Brief Pain Inventory) improved substantially over 16 months of asfotase alfa treatment.
Fatigue Severity Scale score improved from 4.7 at baseline to 3.1 at 16 months (33.33% reduction) under asfotase alfa treatment.
The Patient Global Impression of Improvement score improved from 4 at baseline to 1 at 16 months (75% improvement) under asfotase alfa.
WOMAC score improved from 42 points at baseline to 15.4 points at end of the 16-month observation period (63.29% reduction) under asfotase alfa treatment.

Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) score, used here as a general musculoskeletal symptom/function measure, decreased from 29.3 to 16.7 (43.02% reduction) under asfotase alfa treatment in this HPP patient.
Chair Raise Test time improved from 15.3 seconds at baseline to 8.5 seconds at 10 months (44.46% reduction), indicating improved leg power under asfotase alfa treatment.
Six-minute walk test distance increased from 358 m at baseline to 479 m at 10 months (33.89% increase) under asfotase alfa treatment.
Hand grip strength increased in both hands (right 24 to 27 kg, +12.5%; left 17 to 21 kg, +23.53%) from baseline to 27 months under asfotase alfa treatment.
Non-IgE-sensitized LAD2 cells (ai-NS-MAT) stimulated with 25 µL of CSU patient sera showed significantly higher CD63+ activation than with control sera, with AUC 0.78 by ROC analysis.
ai-NS-MAT stimulated with a lower serum volume (10 µL) showed the strongest discrimination between CSU patients and controls, with the highest AUC (0.82) among all tested conditions.

IgE-sensitized LAD2 cells (ai-S-MAT) stimulated with 25 µL of CSU sera showed significantly higher CD63 activation than with control sera, though with weaker discrimination (AUC 0.66) than the non-sensitized assay.
IgE-sensitized LAD2 cells (ai-S-MAT) stimulated with a lower serum volume (10 µL) did not significantly differentiate CSU patients from healthy controls.
CD63 responses on non-sensitized LAD2 cells at 25 µL and 10 µL serum stimulation were significantly correlated across the cohort.
CD63 responses on IgE-sensitized LAD2 cells at 25 µL and 10 µL serum stimulation were strongly correlated across the cohort.
The majority of CSU patients tested positive for aiMAT, with 81% positive for ai-NS-MAT, 63% for ai-S-MAT, 60% positive for both, and 84% positive for either test.
Patients positive for ai-NS-MAT had a significantly lower proportion of females compared to ai-NS-MAT-negative patients.
Patients positive for ai-S-MAT were older, had higher baseline urticaria activity, and had lower total serum IgE and basophil counts than ai-S-MAT-negative patients.
aiMAT results (ai-NS-MAT and ai-S-MAT) did not differ significantly between omalizumab responders and nonresponders, indicating aiMAT is not predictive of omalizumab treatment response.
Both omalizumab responders (OMA-R) and nonresponders (OMA-NR) showed significantly elevated ai-NS-MAT CD63 responses compared to healthy controls.

CSU patient and control sera did not alter surface IgE expression on LAD2 cells during stimulation, indicating that patient IgE itself is not responsible for LAD2 mast cell activation and supporting an IgG autoantibody-driven mechanism instead.

Basophil activation test (BAT) results with donor basophils did not differ between patients who tested positive versus negative for aiMAT, suggesting aiMAT and BAT may reflect different or complementary aspects of autoimmune activity.
Mast cells are the predominant source of histamine in the CNS, accounting for more than half of total brain histamine content upon degranulation.
Mast cells are the only brain cells that preform and store TNF-α, releasing it to promote neuroinflammation.
Mast cell tryptase activates PAR-2 receptors, increasing VCAM-1, TLR4 and TNF-α expression while reducing occludin and claudin-5, thereby increasing blood-brain barrier permeability.
Mast cell-derived IL-1β disrupts the BBB by inducing HIF-1/VEGF-A expression in astrocytes and by promoting IL-6/TNF-α secretion that increases paracellular permeability.
In ischemic stroke rats, mast cell activators significantly increased brain edema, whereas mast cell stabilizers or mast cell-deficient rats showed reduced brain edema.

Elevated cerebrospinal fluid IL-6 levels in stroke patients were positively correlated with infarction size, consistent with meningeal mast cell IL-6 release exacerbating cerebral edema in animal models.
High expression of the PTGS2 gene is linked to mast cell activation specifically in ischemic stroke, and inhibiting PTGS2 decreased infarction volume and neurological deficits.
PEA-OXA significantly attenuated mast cell activation/detachment and NF-κB pathway activation in ischemic stroke rats, reducing lesion size, cytokine expression, and histological damage.

Mast cells release endogenous anticoagulant heparin after intracerebral hemorrhage, impairing coagulation and contributing to hematoma expansion; stabilizing or depleting mast cells reduced hematoma size in ICH rats.
Hydrogen inhalation exerted neuroprotective effects after ICH by reducing Lyn kinase phosphorylation, thereby inhibiting mast cell activation and degranulation.
IVIG inhibited mast cell activation after ICH via the FcγRIIB/SHIP1/PIP3 pathway, reducing neuroinflammation and improving BBB permeability.
Human intracranial aneurysm tissue analysis showed significantly higher mast cell infiltration in ruptured aneurysms compared to unruptured aneurysms.
Intravenous MSC injection activated the COX-2-dependent pathway, suppressed mast cell activation, and effectively prevented intracranial aneurysm rupture in an animal model.

Extensive mast cell infiltration was observed in the brains of Alzheimer's disease patients, particularly in regions of amyloid-beta accumulation, with mast cells increasing prior to visible Aβ deposition in animal models.
Among Aβ1-42, Aβ1-40, and Aβ-35, Aβ1-42 exhibited the most potent effect in stimulating mast cells to secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines.

Mast cell depletion in 5XFAD mice upregulated neuroprotective disease-associated microglia (DAM) transcriptomic features, downregulated reactive astrocyte markers, and improved hippocampal-dependent cognitive function.

The tyrosine kinase inhibitor and mast cell stabilizer masitinib exerted neuroprotective effects by inhibiting mast cell-mediated increases in BBB permeability and suppressing neuroinflammation at the onset of Alzheimer's disease in preclinical models.

Elevated histamine levels and increased presence in the substantia nigra have been observed in Parkinson's disease patients and animal models, contributing to dopaminergic neuron death via H2R/H4R receptor activation.
Activated mast cells were observed in degenerative regions of the CNS (prefrontal cortex, pyramidal tract) and spinal cord of ALS patients, as well as in skeletal muscle motor axons of ALS rats.

The mast cell inhibitor masitinib decreased mast cell population in extensor digitorum longus muscle, reduced neuromuscular junction denervation and motor deficits in ALS rats, and a phase III clinical trial of masitinib in ALS patients showed positive outcomes.
Mast cells promote neuron growth and enhance microglial phagocytic capacity for β-amyloid via secretion of NGF, which binds tyrosine kinase A receptors on microglia.

Mast cell-derived histamine can mitigate NMDA- and glutamate-induced neuronal excitotoxicity via the cAMP/PKA pathway or by upregulating glutamate transporter currents and glutamine synthetase expression.
MCETs, marked by extracellular tryptase and c-Kit interspersed around nerve fibers and wrapped around blood vessels, were present in the skin of HbSS sickle mice but absent in HbAA control mice.

TNF-α and hemin each increased MCET length in cultured mast cells, with a greater synergistic effect when combined, and HbSS mast cells showed significantly longer MCETs than HbAA mast cells under TNF-α/hemin stimulation.
Pharmacologic TLR4 inhibition (TAK242) and siRNA silencing of TLR4 or FcεR1 both prevented TNF-α/hemin-induced MCET formation in HbSS mast cells.

The PAD4 inhibitor GSK484 completely blocked TNF-α/hemin-induced MCET formation in HbSS mast cells, more effectively than TLR4 or FcεR1 inhibition, indicating a necessary and sufficient role for PAD4.
Daily subcutaneous GSK484 treatment reduced MCET formation in vivo, with minimal tryptase release and c-Kit expression near nerve fibers and vessels in sickle mouse skin.
Chronic daily GSK484 treatment significantly reduced mechanical and thermal (heat) hyperalgesia in HbSS mice, with effects sustained over a 4-week treatment period, while HbAA mice showed no change.
Cold hyperalgesia showed the most robust improvement with GSK484 treatment, reaching levels comparable to HbAA control mice that do not display cold hyperalgesia.
GSK484 treatment did not affect spontaneous, non-evoked musculoskeletal hyperalgesia, likely because this pain arises from avascular necrosis unrelated to MCET formation.

Both GSK484 (PAD4 inhibitor) and imatinib (mast cell/c-Kit inhibitor) pretreatment prevented hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R)-induced acute mechanical, thermal, and musculoskeletal hyperalgesia compared with vehicle, modeling vaso-occlusive crisis pain.
Pretreatment with GSK484 or imatinib significantly reduced hemin-induced vascular stasis in a dorsal skin-fold chamber model, indicating amelioration of vaso-occlusion-like processes.
Four weeks of GSK484 treatment significantly reduced circulating white blood cell counts, serum GM-CSF, and numbers of degranulating cutaneous mast cells in HbSS mice compared with vehicle.
GSK484 treatment significantly reduced skin release of MCP-1, TNF-α, and RANTES, cytokines constitutively elevated in HbSS mice, compared with vehicle.
HbSS mast cells express significantly higher Tlr4 and Fcer1a transcripts than HbAA mast cells, potentially priming downstream PAD4 activation and histone citrullination.
Plasma PAD4 activity and expression are reported to be higher in SCD patients experiencing acute vaso-occlusive crisis compared with healthy individuals without SCD.
The proportion and number of mast cells were increased in testicular tissue from cryptorchidism patients compared with controls, consistent with prior animal models.
Genes involved in mast cell activation and degranulation (FCER1G, FCER1A, SYN, FYN, LYN) were highly expressed specifically in mast cells from cryptorchidism patients.
Degranulation-associated components LTC4S, CTSG, TGFB1, and TNF were upregulated in mast cells from the cryptorchidism group.

Immunofluorescence confirmed significantly more abundant chymase-positive (CC1+) mast cells with more granules and scattered extracellular granules in cryptorchidism tissue compared to obstructive azoospermia controls, indicating degranulation.
Mast cells were found to contribute to interstitial fibrosis in cryptorchidism through secretion of TGF-β1 and cathepsin G (CTSG).

Cell-cell communication analysis identified the CTSG-PARD3 ligand-receptor pair of the PAR signaling pathway as a key differential interaction sent from mast cells to other testicular cells in cryptorchidism.
PARD3 receptor expression was high in nearly all germ cells and somatic cells in the cryptorchidism group compared with lower expression in controls, validated by immunofluorescence.

Signaling analysis identified a KIT pathway (KIT ligand/stem cell factor) from endothelial cells, Leydig/interstitial cells, Sertoli cells, and smooth muscle cells to mast cells that was largely undetectable in controls, suggesting a mechanism for mast cell recruitment/proliferation in cryptorchidism.

Seminal plasma levels of chymase (mast cell degranulation marker), CXCL8/IL-8 (leukocyte migration marker), and PINP (fibrosis marker) were significantly elevated in cryptorchidism patients compared to healthy controls.
Chymase levels positively correlated with both PINP and CXCL8 in seminal plasma, suggesting a mechanistic link between mast cell activation and testicular fibrosis.
Western blot analysis showed increased TGF-β1 protein levels in testicular tissue from cryptorchidism patients compared to controls.

Gene set scoring showed the TGF-β pathway was more active in Leydig/interstitial and myoid cells of the cryptorchidism group, and CCN1 (a matricellular protein influencing matrix production) was more highly expressed than in controls.
Immunofluorescence staining confirmed increased collagen I and collagen III deposition in testicular interstitium of cryptorchidism patients, consistent with interstitial fibrosis.

Germ cell numbers progressively declined starting from spermatogonial stem cells in the cryptorchidism group, with significantly reduced PRM1+ (spermatid) and FGFR3+ (undifferentiated spermatogonia) cell counts confirmed by immunofluorescence.
KEGG apoptosis pathway scoring was higher across nearly all germ cell types in the cryptorchidism group, potentially explaining the decreased germ cell numbers.

GO enrichment of genes specifically expressed in the cryptorchidism vs. control group showed downregulation of cell cycle-related functions (DNA repair, chromosome organization, chromosome segregation, nuclear division) in both spermatogonial stem cells and differentiating spermatogonia.

Cell cycle progression genes CCND1 and CDC25A were highly expressed in control spermatogonia, whereas cell cycle arrest genes TP53, CDKN1A, and RB1 were elevated in cryptorchidism spermatogonia across all states.

Cell cycle scoring showed a significant increase in the proportion of spermatogonia in G1 phase and a significant reduction in S and G2/M phase scores in the cryptorchidism group compared to controls.

Principal-component and signature score analyses showed that spermatogonia from cryptorchidism patients transcriptionally resemble seminoma, the predominant testicular germ cell tumor type, more closely than control spermatogonia.

Sertoli cells in cryptorchidism showed upregulated mitochondrial ATP synthesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) pathway genes (including SOS1 and NFE2L2), indicating an abnormal oxidative stress state.

Despite a much higher number of Sertoli cells captured by scRNA-seq in the cryptorchidism group, immunofluorescence quantification of SOX9+ cells per tubule showed no significant difference in true Sertoli cell number between cryptorchidism and control groups, suggesting the scRNA-seq discrepancy reflected capture bias rather than proliferation.

Both Leydig-like cells (LICs) and myoid cells were more abundant (by cell count) in the cryptorchidism group compared to controls, with similarity in fibrosis-related upregulated genes between the two cell types.

Cross-dataset comparison with idiopathic nonobstructive azoospermia (iNOA) and Klinefelter syndrome datasets showed that significant mast cell activation and degranulation gene expression occurred specifically in cryptorchidism mast cells, not in iNOA mast cells, which instead showed enrichment for myeloid differentiation pathways.

CellChat analysis showed an overall increase in the number and strength of cell-cell interactions in the cryptorchidism group compared to controls, except for late-stage germ cells with limited cell numbers.
Melatonin was moderately resistant to simulated gastrointestinal digestion, showing 36% duodenal bioaccessibility relative to the undigested nutraceutical formulation.
PEA was highly sensitive to gastrointestinal digestion, retaining only 1.59% bioaccessibility in the duodenal phase.

NF, PEA, and MEL pretreatment significantly reduced IL-6 mRNA expression in stimulated HMC-1.2 cells, with a greater effect for NF than the individual compounds.
NF, PEA, and MEL reduced secreted TNF-α protein levels in HMC-1.2 culture supernatants, with a greater reduction observed with NF than the single components.
NF, PEA, and MEL reduced secreted IL-6 protein levels in HMC-1.2 culture supernatants, with NF producing the largest reduction.
NF significantly reduced COX-2 (PTGS2) mRNA expression by 30% versus stimulated cells, while single-compound treatments with PEA or MEL did not reach statistical significance.
PEA directly inhibited COX-2 enzymatic activity with an IC50 of 0.152 μg/mL, showing greater potency than MEL.
Melatonin directly inhibited COX-2 enzymatic activity with an IC50 of 47.47 μg/mL (204.3 nM), a concentration higher than its calculated intestinal bioaccessibility, limiting physiological relevance.
The combined nutraceutical formulation (NF) inhibited COX-2 enzymatic activity with an IC50 of 0.135 μg/mL, comparable to PEA alone, and largely below its intestinal bioaccessibility.
ATP12A mRNA expression was higher in PPI-Nonresponsive EoE compared to PPI-Responsive EoE and controls.
ATP4A mRNA expression was higher in PPI-Nonresponsive EoE compared to PPI-Responsive EoE and controls.
Tryptase-beta 2 (TPSB2), a mast cell marker gene, was more highly expressed in PPI-Nonresponsive EoE than PPI-Responsive EoE or controls.
CLC (eosinophil marker gene) expression was higher in PPI-Nonresponsive EoE compared to PPI-Responsive EoE or controls.
IL13 gene expression was higher in PPI-Nonresponsive EoE compared to PPI-Responsive EoE or controls.
Immunohistochemical staining of ATP12A protein was higher in both PPI-Responsive and PPI-Nonresponsive EoE compared to non-EoE controls.
Among the pediatric EoE cohort, only 32% (8 of 25) achieved histologic remission with PPI therapy, classifying them as PPI-Responsive EoE.

The authors propose a mechanistic cascade in which PPIs may trigger mast cell activation leading to IL-13 release, which upregulates the proton pump genes ATP12A and ATP4A, ultimately promoting eosinophil recruitment and PPI treatment failure.
C3-deficient mice showed significantly reduced perfusion recovery and diminished collateral artery caliber growth after femoral artery ligation compared to wildtype mice.
C3-deficient mice showed a significantly smaller increase in the inner luminal diameter of growing collateral arteries after femoral artery ligation than wildtype mice.
C3-deficient mice showed a significantly lower percentage of proliferating (BrdU+) vascular cells in growing collaterals compared to wildtype mice 7 days after arterial ligation.
At day 3 after ligation, the number of perivascular M1-like macrophages was significantly lower in C3-deficient mice than in wildtype mice, despite similar total macrophage numbers.
At day 3 after ligation, C3-deficient mice showed a significantly increased number of perivascular M2-like macrophages compared to wildtype mice.
By day 7, C3-deficient mice had significantly fewer total perivascular macrophages and M1-like macrophages than wildtype mice, with M2-like macrophages also reduced but to a lesser extent.

No differences were found between C3-deficient and wildtype mice in platelet-neutrophil aggregate or monocyte-platelet aggregate formation, or in peripheral blood platelet, neutrophil, and monocyte counts 24 hours after ligation.

Mast cell recruitment and degranulation in the perivascular space were not different between C3-deficient and wildtype mice, though ligation increased degranulated mast cells versus sham in both strains equally.

The shear stress-induced increase in MCP-1 mRNA expression in growing collaterals after arterial ligation was seen only in wildtype mice, not in C3-deficient mice, which showed generally low MCP-1 expression.

Pharmacological mast cell activation with Compound 48/80 rescued MCP-1 mRNA expression in C3-deficient collaterals to the level seen in untreated wildtype mice, and also significantly increased MCP-1 expression in C48/80-treated wildtype mice.

Treatment with mast cell activator Compound 48/80 or with recombinant MCP-1 restored M1-like macrophage numbers in C3-deficient mice to wildtype levels at day 3 after ligation, without affecting total macrophage counts or M2-like macrophage numbers.
