By day 7, Compound 48/80 treatment drastically increased both M1-like and M2-like macrophage numbers in C3-deficient mice, even exceeding wildtype levels, whereas MCP-1 treatment mainly restored M1-like macrophages and total macrophage numbers to the wildtype level.
Treatment with Compound 48/80 or MCP-1 significantly increased vascular cell proliferation and rescued perfusion recovery in C3-deficient mice to wildtype levels 7 days after femoral artery ligation.
Memory B cell antibody repertoires from patients with suspected rocuronium hypersensitivity showed high V(D)J gene diversity with no evidence of clonal expansion.
Recombinantly expressed patient-derived antibodies were specific and had low affinity for rocuronium with no cross-reactivity to other neuromuscular blocking agents.
When expressed as IgE, patient-derived rocuronium-specific antibodies triggered activation of human mast cells.
Rocuronium-specific IgE antibodies induced passive systemic anaphylaxis when tested in transgenic mice.
The low affinities of patient-derived rocuronium antibodies were insufficient for them to function as neuromuscular blockade reversal agents.
High-affinity rocuronium-specific antibodies were isolated from mice immunized with rocuronium.
The highest-affinity mouse-derived antibody reversed rocuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade in nonhuman primates with reversal kinetics comparable to the standard reversal agent sugammadex.

The human-derived rocuronium-specific antibodies expressed as IgE, despite triggering mast cell activation and anaphylaxis, had affinities too low to function as neuromuscular blockade reversal agents.
High-affinity rocuronium-specific antibodies were successfully isolated from mice immunized with rocuronium, in contrast to the low-affinity antibodies found in human patients.

The highest-affinity mouse-derived rocuronium-specific antibody reversed rocuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade in nonhuman primates with reversal kinetics comparable to the standard agent sugammadex.
Formononetin significantly and dose-dependently reduced IgE production in IgE-producing human myeloma (U266) cells with no cytotoxicity.
Formononetin significantly decreased IgE production from human PBMCs collected from food-allergic patients at 20 and 10 µg/mL without cytotoxicity.
Formononetin at 10 and 20 µg/mL significantly reduced beta-hexosaminidase release (a marker of mast cell degranulation) in RBL-2H3 basophilic/mast cell line at 24 and 48 hours without cytotoxicity.

Formononetin at 10 and 20 µg/mL significantly decreased beta-hexosaminidase release in KU812 human basophil cells sensitized with peanut-allergic patient serum and challenged with peanut extract, without cytotoxicity.

Computational target mining identified 25 formononetin targets overlapping with food allergy genes, 51 with IgE disease genes, and 19 with mast cell disease genes, with 12 targets shared across all three disease categories.

KEGG pathway enrichment of formononetin's shared targets highlighted JAK-STAT signaling, PI3K-Akt signaling, Epstein-Barr virus infection, measles pathway, Th1/Th2/Th17 differentiation, and AGE-RAGE pathways as linked to food allergy.
Gene ontology analysis identified CD27 as a formononetin target recurring across multiple B-cell-related GO pathways, suggesting it as a candidate mechanistic node for future study.
In U266 plasma B cells, formononetin (10 µg/mL, 72h) significantly increased mRNA expression of NFKBIA, TP53, and BCL-2 relative to vehicle control.
In U266 plasma B cells, formononetin significantly decreased mRNA expression of BTK, TYK2, CASP8, STAT3, CCND1, STAT1, NFKB1, and IL7R relative to vehicle control.
In KU812 human basophil cells, formononetin (10 µg/mL, 24h) significantly increased mRNA expression of NFKBIA, TP53, and BCL-2 relative to vehicle control.
In KU812 human basophil cells, formononetin significantly decreased mRNA expression of BTK, TYK2, CASP8, STAT3, CCND1, STAT1, NFKB1, and IL7R relative to vehicle control.
At the protein level, formononetin significantly increased IκBα expression and decreased NF-κB expression in U266 cells, consistent with the mRNA changes observed for NFKBIA and NFKB1.
Molecular docking analysis showed that formononetin has strong predicted binding affinity and interaction with TYK2, BTK, TP53, BCL2, NFKBIA, and CASP8 protein structures.
SFN+ patients had reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENF/mm) at skin biopsy compared with SFN- patients, independent of age and sex.
Electromyography (EMG) abnormalities of Motor Unit Action Potentials (short duration, small amplitude, polyphasic) were significantly more common in SFN+ than SFN- patients.

Optical coherence tomography showed retinal nerve fiber layer thinning and retinal pigment epithelium abnormalities more frequently in SFN+ patients, a finding not previously described in post-COVID SFN.
ANA positivity was frequent in SFN+ patients but did not differ significantly from SFN- patients.
Prevalence of studied HLA haplotypes did not differ between SFN+ and SFN- patients, suggesting no clear genetic predisposition identified in this cohort.
Clinical, serological, pulmonary (HRCT/DLCO), and joint ultrasound biomarkers did not differ between SFN+ and SFN- patients.
Treatment with steroids, pregabalin, DMARDs and multi-nutrient supplementation significantly reduced motor impairment, fatigue, and burning pain between T3 (9 months) and T4 (12 months).

Brain fog and sensitivity disorders (thermal disarray, numbness, stocking-glove sensation) improved significantly only by the 12-month follow-up (T4) compared to baseline, later than motor/fatigue/pain symptoms.
Arthritis disease activity (DAS28/ESR) significantly improved between 6 and 9 months, and remained improved at 12 months of follow-up.
Visual fog symptoms and OCT-detected retinal abnormalities did not improve despite immunomodulatory and neuropathic pain treatment over 12 months.
Joint ultrasound pattern shifted from symmetric to asymmetric involvement in most SFN+ patients by 6 months of follow-up, coinciding with treatment.

This study is the first to describe small fiber neuropathy co-occurring with undifferentiated arthritis following COVID-19 infection or vaccination, a combination not previously reported except as a rare anti-TNF-α treatment complication in rheumatoid arthritis.
IENF/mm reduction in SFN+ patients was length-dependent, occurring at the distal leg but not the proximal thigh.

One patient developed SFN after COVID-19 vaccination with a generalized, non-length-dependent pattern, resembling the atypical pattern reported after HPV vaccination rather than typical post-viral length-dependent SFN.

The authors hypothesize that genes encoding voltage-gated sodium ion channels may confer susceptibility to SFN triggered by viral infection-induced immune overactivation, though this was not directly tested in the present study.
A minority of SFN+ patients showed low-titer myositis-associated autoantibodies (anti-Ro52, anti-HMGCR) and elevated CPK levels.

Loeys-Dietz Syndrome results from a mutation in the transforming growth factor beta receptor (TGFBR) family of genes and is associated with aortic aneurysms and dissections in this affected father-daughter pair.

Both father and daughter with Loeys-Dietz Syndrome underwent successful open surgical repair of thoracoabdominal aneurysms after prior endovascular repair had failed, with the daughter requiring stent graft explantation while the father's stent graft remained in place.

The authors emphasize the importance of early genetic testing of patients and first-degree relatives with a strong family history of aortic disease, even in the absence of typical connective tissue disorder physical exam findings.
Genotype frequencies of the COL1A1 rs1800012 polymorphism differed significantly between cervical insufficiency patients and healthy controls.
Genotype frequencies of the TGFB1 rs1800471 polymorphism differed significantly between cervical insufficiency patients and healthy controls.
The C allele of the TGFB1 rs1800471 polymorphism was significantly more frequent in cervical insufficiency patients than in controls, suggesting it predisposes to the disease.
The COL1A1 rs1800012 polymorphism was found to be associated with a clinical history of cervical cerclage among patients.
The TT/GG composite genotype across COL1A1 rs1800012 and TGFB1 rs1800471 was significantly less frequent in cervical insufficiency patients than controls, indicating a protective combined genotype.
The TT genotype of the COL1A1 rs1800012 polymorphism appeared protective against cervical insufficiency.
The high stress reactivity (SR) group showed greater CREB gene expression in whole blood compared to the low SR group, consistent with tonic sympathetic nervous system activation.
The high SR group exhibited proinflammatory changes in whole blood compared to the low SR group.
Brain imaging revealed neuroplastic changes in the high SR group consistent with upregulation of ascending arousal systems and sensory processing and integration regions.
Functional connectivity within the central autonomic network was altered in the high SR group compared to the low SR group.
Stress reactivity moderated the sex difference observed in extraintestinal symptoms among participants.

Tonically increased sympathetic nervous system activity is proposed as a plausible risk factor for increased autonomic reactivity to psychosocial stressors and low-grade immune activation, occurring in both IBS and healthy controls but with greater prevalence in IBS.
Chemoradiotherapy did not alter the number of myenteric ganglia, total neurons, or ChAT- or nNOS-expressing neuron subclasses per mm of myenteric plexus.
No differences in mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory (IL6, TNFα) or anti-inflammatory (IL13) cytokines were detected between rectal muscle unexposed or exposed to chemoradiotherapy.
Numbers of CD45-positive lymphocytes in circular and longitudinal muscle regions were similar between chemoradiotherapy-exposed and unexposed rectal tissue, indicating no persistent inflammation.

In chemoradiotherapy-naive human rectum circular muscle, electrical field stimulation (EFS) most commonly evoked cholinergic (atropine-sensitive) contraction and, less often, nitrergic (L-NAME-sensitive) relaxation, both abolished by tetrodotoxin.
Chemoradiotherapy increased the incidence of nitrergic relaxation relative to cholinergic contraction during EFS across muscle strips compared with chemoradiotherapy-naive tissue.
In chemoradiotherapy-naive rectum, the 5-HT4 agonist prucalopride caused a small but significant increase in EFS-evoked contractile activity.
In chemoradiotherapy-naive rectum, the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor donepezil caused a large increase in EFS-evoked contraction amplitude, both with and without L-NAME.
After chemoradiotherapy, prucalopride lost its ability to consistently alter EFS-evoked contractile responses, with or without L-NAME, indicating reduced prokinetic drug efficacy.
After chemoradiotherapy, the excitatory (prokinetic) activity of donepezil on EFS-evoked contractions was markedly reduced, particularly in the presence of L-NAME.
Chemoradiotherapy did not alter direct muscle contractile responses to the muscarinic agonist carbachol, suggesting the neuromuscular changes were neuronal rather than muscular in origin.

Chemoradiotherapy did not change direct muscle relaxation responses to the NO donor sodium nitroprusside, indicating the increased nitrergic EFS response reflects altered neuronal rather than smooth muscle NO-sensitivity.

Unlike a prior pilot study, this study found no nuclear translocation of HuC/D protein and no change in nNOS-immunoreactive neuron soma size after chemoradiotherapy, indicating absence of the neuronal stress/hyperexcitability changes reported previously.
TGF-β1 stimulation of human dermal fibroblasts increased Col1, fibronectin, and αSMA expression at both protein and mRNA levels.
PIK-III at 5 μM significantly inhibited TGF-β1-induced Col1, fibronectin, and αSMA expression (protein and mRNA) in human dermal fibroblasts without affecting cell viability.
PIK-III (5 μM) reduced TGF-β1-induced collagen gel contraction in dermal fibroblasts, indicating reduced contractile/myofibroblast activity.
The PIK3C3 inhibitors SAR405 and autophinib did not significantly attenuate TGF-β1-induced profibrotic responses in dermal fibroblasts, unlike PIK-III.

Genetic silencing of PIK3C3 via shRNA did not regulate ECM (Col1, FN) or αSMA protein expression in dermal fibroblasts with or without TGF-β1, indicating fibroblasts do not require PIK3C3 for profibrotic gene expression.
A MAPK phosphorylation antibody array showed that TGF-β1 stimulated activation (phosphorylation) of GSK3, JNK, p38, and p53 in dermal fibroblasts.
PIK-III treatment reduced p38 phosphorylation in TGF-β1-induced dermal fibroblasts, identified via phosphorylation array and confirmed by western blot as a novel target of PIK-III.
The p38 inhibitor SB203580 attenuated TGF-β1-induced fibronectin, Col1, and αSMA expression in dermal fibroblasts, mimicking the effect of PIK-III.
Overexpression of p38 (via lentiviral p38-DDK construct) reversed the inhibitory effect of PIK-III on αSMA and ECM expression in TGF-β1-stimulated dermal fibroblasts.

In a bleomycin-induced mouse model of dermal fibrosis, PIK-III (5 mg/kg IP) significantly reduced dermal thickening and collagen deposition (measured by hydroxyproline assay and trichrome staining) compared to bleomycin alone.
PIK-III treatment reduced p38 activation in the skin of bleomycin-treated mice compared to bleomycin alone.
In TGF-β1-stimulated human lung fibroblasts, PIK-III exposure produced significantly lower levels of fibronectin, collagen, and αSMA.
In an intratracheal bleomycin mouse model of lung fibrosis, PIK-III (5 mg/kg) attenuated lung fibrosis (assessed by trichrome staining and hydroxyproline assay) and reduced p38 activation at day 21.

PIK-III, SAR405, and autophinib all reduced autophagy in PIK3C3-overexpressing cells (confirming target engagement), yet only PIK-III exerted anti-fibrotic effects, indicating PIK-III's anti-fibrotic mechanism is independent of PIK3C3/autophagy inhibition.

In skin biopsies from children with Marfan syndrome, the relative number of tryptase-high and CD117-expressing mast cells nearly doubled compared to normal skin, reaching up to one-fifth of all dermal cells.
The relative area of elastic fibers compared to collagen fibers was not significantly reduced in most MFS patients, with a noticeable decrease detected in only two of seven patients.
Mast cells in children with Marfan syndrome showed significantly more frequent close contact and targeted secretory activity toward elastic fibers than in normal skin.
Mast cells in MFS skin more intensively expressed CD117 (KIT), suggesting greater potential for differentiation, survival, and functional activity of the mast cell population.
Mast cells in Marfan syndrome skin exhibited increased biogenesis of TGF-β, with more mast cells showing moderate-to-high TGF-β content located among fibrous components of the dermis.

In MFS skin dermis, more than half of mast cells were colocalized with fibroblasts, either through direct contact or within a 20–30 µm paracrine distance, often accompanied by active secretion of tryptase, chymase, and CPA3 toward fibroblasts.
Mast cells in MFS skin showed increased frequency of contact with α-SMA-positive cells (smooth muscle/vascular), often near postcapillary venules and smooth muscle islands in the dermis.

Mast cells formed functional chains connecting multiple fibroblasts and other dermal cells over considerable distances, sometimes tracking along elastic fibers, and this pattern was much more common in MFS patients than in controls.

Active targeted secretion of tryptase, chymase, carboxypeptidase A3, and heparin directly onto elastic fibers was observed in MFS skin, supporting a direct role for mast cells in remodeling the fibrous ECM component, potentially including degradation via elastase and cathepsin G.

Across the study cohort, tryptase-high and CPA3-high mast cells comprised about 10% of dermal cells, while chymase-high and CD117+ mast cells were less frequent, with nearly all skin mast cells exhibiting a Tryptase+Chymase+CPA3+ phenotype typical of connective-tissue-type mast cells.
Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene (15q21.1), encoding fibrillin-1, which is essential for microfibril formation, elastic fiber assembly, and regulation of TGF-β bioavailability.
Dysfunctional fibrillin-1 fails to properly sequester latent TGF-β-binding protein (LTBP), leading to increased release of TGF-β into the extracellular matrix in Marfan syndrome.
SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with a higher overall risk of incident gastrointestinal disease in the post-acute period, consistently across the discovery, Japanese, and UK Biobank cohorts.
GERD incidence was significantly increased in the post-acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection in the discovery cohort.
Functional intestinal disorder incidence was significantly increased in the post-acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection in the discovery cohort.
The increased risk of GERD and functional intestinal disorders after SARS-CoV-2 infection was replicated in the Japanese validation cohort A.
SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with a higher risk of developing hepatobiliary disease after 30 days post-infection, consistent across all three cohorts.
Inflammatory liver disease risk was substantially increased during the post-acute phase of COVID-19 in the discovery cohort.
The association between COVID-19 and inflammatory liver disease was replicated with an even larger effect size in the Japanese validation cohort A.
Other digestive abnormalities were more common after SARS-CoV-2 infection than in non-infected individuals in the discovery cohort.
Other digestive abnormalities showed a much larger increase in risk after SARS-CoV-2 infection in the Japanese validation cohort A than in the discovery cohort.
In the UK Biobank replication cohort, other digestive abnormalities were slightly more common after SARS-CoV-2 infection than in non-infected individuals.
Risk of developing nausea, vomiting, and dysphagia symptoms was significantly higher after SARS-CoV-2 infection in the discovery cohort.
The increased risk of nausea, vomiting, and dysphagia after SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed in the Japanese validation cohort A with a substantially larger effect size.
Receiving two or more SARS-CoV-2 vaccine doses was associated with a 43% lower risk of developing gastrointestinal disease after COVID-19 compared with fewer/no doses.
Vaccination dose number was not significantly associated with the risk of post-acute hepatobiliary disease.
Patients who received two or more vaccine doses had a slightly increased risk of developing other digestive abnormalities.
Patients with moderate-to-severe COVID-19 had a 66% higher risk of developing gastrointestinal disease compared to non-infected individuals.
Patients with moderate-to-severe COVID-19 had more than double the risk of developing hepatobiliary disease compared to non-infected individuals.
Moderate-to-severe COVID-19 was associated with a higher risk of other digestive abnormalities compared to non-infection.
The elevated risk of gastrointestinal disease persisted even beyond 6 months after initial SARS-CoV-2 infection.
The elevated risk of hepatobiliary disease after SARS-CoV-2 infection was significant only within the first 3 months, attenuating thereafter.
Other digestive abnormalities showed a modest but significant elevated risk in the early post-acute time window following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
NfL levels in both CSF and plasma were significantly elevated in MSA patients compared to PD patients and healthy controls, with no difference between PD and HC.
CSF GFAP was significantly elevated in MSA compared to healthy controls, but did not differ between MSA and PD or between PD and HC.
Plasma GFAP levels did not differ significantly between MSA, PD, and healthy control groups.
Neither GFAP nor NfL levels (CSF or plasma) differed significantly between MSA-cerebellar and MSA-parkinsonian motor subtypes.
CSF NfL showed high diagnostic accuracy for discriminating MSA from PD, with an AUC of 0.97.
Plasma NfL also showed high diagnostic accuracy for discriminating MSA from PD, with an AUC of 0.90.
CSF GFAP levels significantly predicted baseline UMSARS I+II disease severity scores in MSA patients after adjusting for age.
Plasma GFAP levels also significantly predicted baseline UMSARS I+II disease severity scores in MSA patients after adjusting for age.
Neither CSF nor plasma NfL levels significantly predicted baseline UMSARS disease severity scores in MSA in multiple regression analysis.
Baseline CSF NfL levels positively correlated with 1-year longitudinal progression of UMSARS scores in MSA patients.
Baseline plasma NfL levels also positively correlated with 1-year longitudinal progression of UMSARS scores in MSA patients.
Baseline GFAP levels (CSF or plasma) did not correlate with 1-year longitudinal progression of UMSARS scores in MSA patients.
Danilenko et al. found significantly increased autoantibodies against β2-glycoprotein-I, various neural antigens, and voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
De Bellis et al. reported higher titres of anti-pituitary (APA) and anti-hypothalamic (AHA) antibodies in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls, associated with HPA axis dysfunction.
De Bellis et al. found reduced growth hormone, basal cortisol, cortisol peak, and ACTH levels in ME/CFS patients compared to controls, with large effect sizes.

Ryabkova et al. found significantly increased anti-GABA-receptor autoantibodies specifically in ME/CFS patients with comorbid fibromyalgia, but not in ME/CFS patients without fibromyalgia versus healthy controls.
Skowera et al. found no association between ME/CFS and antinuclear antibodies, including those targeting the nuclear envelope, compared to healthy controls.

Maes et al. (2012) found elevated serum IgM levels against anchorage molecules (palmitic acid, myristic acid, S-farnesyl-L-cysteine) and acetylcholine self-epitopes in ME/CFS patients, associated with perceived symptomology, while nitrosative self-epitopes showed no change.

Fonseca et al. developed a 26-antibody classifier able to discriminate ME/CFS patients from healthy controls, but it could not distinguish ME/CFS patients with infection-triggered onset from those without or of unknown origin.

Fonseca et al. found no significant difference in IgG-EBV peptide sequence homology with human proteins between ME/CFS patients and controls, suggesting infection-triggered onset relates to broader ME/CFS pathogenesis rather than an autoimmune B-cell mechanism via molecular mimicry.
Maes et al. (2013) reported significantly increased proinflammatory cytokines specific to the 5-HT receptor in ME/CFS patients, with 5-HT-positive patients showing exacerbated symptoms.
Lande et al. found significantly increased frequencies of HLA class I and II risk alleles (notably HLA-C and HLA-DQB1) in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls in a large cohort.

Upon stratification and linkage disequilibrium analysis, the elevated HLA risk allele frequency in ME/CFS was significantly correlated with comorbidity with other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, psoriasis, and rheumatoid arthritis, complicating attribution of HLA association to ME/CFS specifically.
Wang et al. reported significant enrichment of immunomodulatory genes IKZF2, IKZF3, ABCE1, BACH2, CD3D, and HSPA8 in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Wang et al. found that female ME/CFS patients showed significant enrichment of interferon-stimulated genes IFIT1, ISG15, and IF16 compared to controls.
Wang et al. found further upregulation of the enriched immunomodulatory genes in bedridden ME/CFS patients who had a previously known autoimmune disease (30% of cohort).

Steiner et al. found significantly decreased CD19+ B-cell counts in ME/CFS patients with infection-triggered onset compared to controls, while CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell populations showed no change across the whole cohort.

Steiner et al. found ME/CFS patients with infection-triggered onset had increased frequency of immunoregulatory alleles PTPN22 and CTLA4 compared to those without infection-triggered onset and healthy controls.

Steiner et al. reported small, near-zero Cohen's d effect sizes for IRF5 and TNF-related SNPs (rs1800629, rs1799724) across whole, ITO, and w/ITO ME/CFS subgroups, in contrast to the more robust PTPN22/CTLA4 associations.
A pooled meta-analysis of 13 studies (1973 long COVID patients) found that 51% satisfied ME/CFS diagnostic criteria.
Long COVID patients commonly experienced post-exertional malaise, the hallmark symptom of ME/CFS.
Across all three groups (healthy controls, PASC, ME/CFS), 8 weeks of inspiratory muscle training significantly improved inspiratory muscle pressure.
Exercise capacity, measured by 6-minute walk distance, improved after IMT across all groups.
Resting heart rate improved (decreased) after 8 weeks of IMT across all groups.
Heart rate variability, a marker of autonomic function, improved after 8 weeks of IMT across all groups.
Sleep-related symptoms improved after 8 weeks of IMT across all groups.
In the ME/CFS group specifically, IMT was associated with improved vascular function as measured by the COMPASS-31 questionnaire.
In the ME/CFS group specifically, 8 weeks of inspiratory muscle training led to additional improvement in vascular autonomic function.
In the ME/CFS group specifically, IMT led to additional improvement in secretomotor autonomic function.
The ME/CFS group showed additional improvement in the total weighted COMPASS 31 autonomic dysfunction score after IMT, beyond what was seen in other groups.
The ME/CFS group experienced an additional improvement in pain-related symptoms after IMT that was not observed in the PASC or healthy control groups.
PwPCC were significantly older than pwME/CFS.
PwME/CFS had a significantly longer illness duration than pwPCC.
PwME/CFS reported significantly more symptoms in total than pwPCC, including among only those meeting ME/CFS case criteria.
60.0% of pwPCC fulfilled formal ME/CFS case criteria (Fukuda, CCC, or ICC).
Dyspnoea was associated with poorer scores in most SF-36v2 quality-of-life domains, including Physical Functioning, Role Physical, Bodily Pain, Vitality and Social Functioning.
Light-headedness or dizziness was associated with worsened Physical Functioning, Role Physical and Social Functioning scores.
Nausea had negative associations with Physical Functioning, General Health, Social Functioning and Mental Health scores.
Muscle weakness unexpectedly returned positive associations with several SF-36v2 quality-of-life domains (Physical Functioning, Role Physical, Vitality, Social Functioning).
Dyspnoea was associated with poorer (higher disability) scores in all six WHODAS 2.0 domains examined.
Among pwPCC, cold extremities returned the most negative associations with SF-36v2 domains, including Role Physical, Vitality and Social Functioning.
Hierarchical cluster analysis of symptom presence identified four symptom clusters, none of which were specific to ME/CFS or PCC.
Cluster 2 had significantly lower General Health scores than Cluster 3.
Cluster 2 had significantly higher (worse) Cognition disability scores on the WHODAS 2.0 than Cluster 3.
The Vitality domain of the SF-36v2 had insufficient internal consistency reliability (McDonald's ω = 0.556, below the 0.7 threshold).
Thermostatic intolerance symptoms were associated with poorer scores across several PROM subscales in pwPCC, whereas among pwME/CFS only sweating showed an association (with Role Emotional).
Memory loss was burdensome in both illness cohorts but showed more numerous negative associations with patient-reported outcomes among pwPCC than pwME/CFS.

Pain (notably myalgia), muscle weakness and sleep disturbances were associated with increased QoL/functional capacity scores among pwME/CFS but with poorer patient-reported outcomes among pwPCC, a divergence the authors suggest may reflect illness-stage differences.
Negative associations between gastrointestinal symptoms (namely nausea) and QoL were more pronounced among pwME/CFS than pwPCC.

Cluster 2, characterised by the longest illness duration, had the highest total symptom count and highest proportion meeting the International Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS, significantly more than Cluster 3.
Muscle weakness was the only symptom that differed significantly in severity across the four symptom clusters.
Comorbid Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is reported to affect up to 60% of pwME/CFS, and new-onset IBS has been disproportionately observed among COVID-19 survivors, according to cited literature.
A plasma Gal-9 concentration above 1725 pg/ml distinguished LC patients from healthy controls with high diagnostic accuracy.
A plasma Gal-9 cutoff above 2779 pg/ml differentiated LC patients from recovered SARS-CoV-2 individuals in the discovery cohort.
The Gal-9 diagnostic cutoff distinguishing LC from recovered individuals was reproduced in an independent validating cohort infected with Delta/Omicron variants.
Plasma Gal-9 levels positively correlated with serum amyloid A (SAA) levels in LC patients in both discovery and validating cohorts.
Plasma Gal-9 levels positively correlated with IP-10 (CXCL10) levels in LC patients in both discovery and validating cohorts.
Plasma Gal-9 showed a moderate positive correlation with soluble CD14 (sCD14) levels in LC patients across both cohorts, suggesting Gal-9 shedding by activated innate immune cells.
Plasma Gal-9 positively correlated with intestinal fatty acid binding protein (I-FABP) levels in LC patients in both cohorts, consistent with compromised gut epithelial integrity.
Plasma LPS-binding protein was significantly increased in LC patients compared to recovered individuals, indicating microbial translocation and gut barrier compromise.
Plasma Gal-9 levels positively correlated with impaired cognitive function (cognitive failure) scores in LC patients with ME/CFS in both cohorts.
No association was found between Gal-9 levels and pain severity or widespread pain scores in LC patients.
A plasma ARTN cutoff above 2813 pg/ml distinguished LC patients from healthy controls in the discovery cohort.
A plasma ARTN cutoff above 2780 pg/ml differentiated LC patients from recovered individuals in the discovery cohort.
ARTN's ability to differentiate LC from recovered individuals was validated in an independent second cohort with a slightly different cutoff.
Plasma Gal-9 and ARTN concentrations showed a moderate positive correlation with each other in LC patients in both cohorts.
Plasma ARTN levels were significantly reduced in people living with HIV (PLWH) compared to healthy controls, despite Gal-9 being elevated in HIV.
Plasma TGF-β levels were sharply elevated in PLWH compared to healthy controls, in contrast to reduced TGF-β previously reported in LC patients.
ARTN levels were substantially lower in PLWH compared to LC patients, despite shared chronic immune activation between the two conditions.
Consistent with prior work, plasma Gal-9 was previously reported to positively correlate with CRP, MIP-1β, IL-10, and VCAM-1 in LC patients.
The proportion of T cells among PBMCs was significantly increased in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
NK cell proportion among PBMCs was significantly decreased in ME/CFS relative to healthy controls.
Monocyte proportion among PBMCs was significantly decreased in ME/CFS.
No significant difference in overall B cell proportion was observed between ME/CFS and healthy controls.
cDC proportion among PBMCs was significantly decreased in ME/CFS.
pDC proportion among PBMCs was significantly decreased in ME/CFS.
CD4+ naive T cell numbers were significantly increased (2.18-fold) as a proportion of total CD4+ T cells in ME/CFS.
CD4+ TEM proportion of total CD4+ T cells was significantly decreased (2.23-fold) in ME/CFS.

CD8+ naive T cell numbers were significantly increased (2.27-fold) among total CD8+ T cells in ME/CFS, while CD8 TCM, TEM and γδT proportions showed no consistent significant change in the text description.
NKT cell frequency was significantly increased (3.15-fold) in ME/CFS compared to healthy controls.
Granzyme B expression in NK cells from ME/CFS patients was at the lower limit of the normal range, while CTL levels remained unaffected relative to normal thresholds.
CD107a surface expression on NK cells from ME/CFS patients was reported as significantly impaired upon PMA/Ionomycin stimulation.
Perforin expression was significantly diminished in NK cells from ME/CFS patients relative to normal values.
NK cells from ME/CFS patients showed significantly reduced cytotoxicity against CD4+ T target cells compared to normal reference values.

A distinct set of transcription factor regulons (KLF2, JUND, ZBTB7A, USF2, RELA, KDM5A) showed disorganized/altered activity specifically in CD4+ T cells of ME/CFS patients, with several regulons enriched in IL-18 and IL-17 signaling and cell differentiation pathways.

Increased activity of transcription factor regulons (ZBTB7A, JUND, ESRRA, SP3, KDM5A) was observed in CD8+ T cells of ME/CFS, enriched in cellular senescence, infectious disease and neurodegenerative disease pathways.

CD4+ T cells in ME/CFS showed upregulation of T cell activation and T cell receptor signaling genes along with upregulation of neurodegenerative disease pathways (ALS, prion disease, Parkinson's, Huntington's) by GO/KEGG enrichment.
B cell subsets in ME/CFS showed KEGG pathway upregulation linked to Parkinson's disease, prion disease, ALS, and Epstein-Barr virus infection.
Monocytes in ME/CFS showed upregulation of genes involved in phagocytosis, endocytosis, and Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis pathways.

Cell-cell communication network analysis showed monocyte clusters had markedly enhanced communication with other immune cell types in ME/CFS, identifying monocytes as a central hub of altered cellular interactions.

The APP-CD74 ligand-receptor pathway was significantly upregulated and was the predominant, distinctive signaling pathway mediating monocyte communication with other immune cells specifically in ME/CFS, not observed in healthy controls.
APP protein expression was significantly increased in PBMCs of ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, confirmed by both immunohistochemistry and Western blot.
ESRRA expression was higher in ME/CFS monocytes than healthy controls by scRNA-seq, and this was independently corroborated using an external public dataset (GSE214284) of male patients.

Regulon analysis identified ESRRA as a candidate transcriptional regulator of APP expression in monocytes, with a significant ESRRA-APP correlation unique to ME/CFS, suggesting ESRRA may drive amyloid-beta precursor production in this disease.
662 genes upregulated in CD8+ naive T cells of ME/CFS were enriched in 290 KEGG pathways, predominantly related to neurological and infectious diseases.
CCR7, CD28, LCK, and SMAD3 were among genes upregulated in CD8+ naive T cells, implicated in immune activation, signaling, viral processes, and cytokine synthesis.
EZR, CSK, ACTB, and ITGB7 were upregulated in CD8+ naive T cells, encoding proteins involved in cytoskeleton dynamics, cell adhesion, and motility.
GATA3, ZFPM1, MYC, LEF1, and XBP1 were upregulated in CD8+ naive T cells, playing roles in gene regulation and transcription factor function.
Plasma cell proportion among total B cells trended higher in ME/CFS but did not reach statistical significance, likely due to small sample size.

Memory B cells from ME/CFS patients occupied early pseudotime positions versus mid-to-late pseudotime in healthy controls, and a distinct branch appeared in memory and plasma B cell trajectories unique to ME/CFS.
Regulon analysis identified KLF2, TFDP1, and MBD4 as putative regulons controlling B-cell growth that were differentially active in ME/CFS.
CD81, PTPN6, INPP5D, PTPRC, IGHG4, and IGHA2 were common genes shared across B cell subsets contributing to B cell activation and antibody synthesis pathways upregulated in ME/CFS.
B cell KEGG pathway analysis showed increased signaling related to Parkinson's disease, Prion disease, ALS, and EBV infection in ME/CFS.
BAX, ADRM1, PSMC5, and PSMD1 were identified as specific genes playing critical roles in B cell regulatory biological processes and homeostasis in ME/CFS.
CD56bright NK cell proportion showed a discernible decreasing trend in ME/CFS relative to total NK cells but did not reach statistical significance.
NKT cell frequency was significantly increased 3.15-fold in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
NK-CD56bright and NKT cell clusters were positioned along early pseudotime trajectories in ME/CFS versus mid-to-late in healthy controls, suggesting suppressed differentiation.
Transcription factors ZBTB7A, KLF2, KLF13, RELA, CEBPB, and CEBPD were highly activated in NK cells of ME/CFS patients.

ME/CFS-specific activated NK cell TFs including ZBTB7A/7B, RELA, KLF2, NFKB1, ASCL2, and POLE3 were enriched in proliferation, differentiation, stress response, and IL-17/IL-18/IL-6 signaling pathways.

In healthy controls, NK cell regulon activity was dominated by FOS, JUN, JUNB, IRF1, and BCLAF1, associated with integrated stress response and cytokine signaling, contrasting with the ME/CFS-specific regulon profile.

603 genes were upregulated and 213 downregulated in NK cells of ME/CFS, enriched in response to external stimuli, immunoglobulin-mediated immune response, antigen processing/presentation, and adaptive immune response via somatic recombination.

NK cell KEGG analysis showed upregulated genes linked to infectious disease (HIV, EBV, COVID-19), amyloidotic neurodegenerative disease (ALS, PD), and autoimmunity, while downregulated genes were involved in IL-17 signaling and NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity.
Granzyme B expression in NK cells from ME/CFS patients was at the lower limit of the normal range, while unaffected in cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
CD107a surface expression on NK cells from ME/CFS patients was significantly impaired following PMA/Ionomycin stimulation compared to normal reference values.
Perforin expression was significantly diminished in NK cells of ME/CFS patients compared to normal reference range.
NK cells from ME/CFS patients showed significantly lower cytotoxicity against CD4+ T cell targets compared to normal, confirming impaired NK function.
A distinct group of highly activated transcription factors (KLF2, JUND, ZBTB7A, USF2, RELA, KDM5A) became disorganized/hyperactive in CD4+ T cells of ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS-specific CD4+ T cell regulons IRF1, KLF2, FOS, ZBTB7A, FLT1 and RELA showed significant enrichment in cell differentiation, IL-18 and IL-17 signaling pathways.

GO Biological Process analysis of CD4+ T cell subsets revealed significant upregulation in T cell activation pathways, including the T cell receptor signaling pathway and positive regulation of T cell activation, in ME/CFS.

KEGG analysis showed significant upregulation of cellular senescence and neurodegenerative signaling pathways (ALS, prion disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease) in CD4+ T cell subsets of ME/CFS patients.
Genes CCR7, CD81, PTPRC, LCK, TESPA1, CSK, FYN, ZAP70 and CD28 were identified as upregulated in pathways governing T cell activation and TCR signaling in ME/CFS CD4+ T cells.
Genes ATXN2L, FUS, OPTN, PSMC5, MAP2K2, SDHA, SIGMAR1 and VCP, implicated in neurodegeneration signaling pathways, were found among coregulated genes in ME/CFS CD4+ T cells.
Mitochondrial respiratory chain genes SDHD, NDUFB2 and ATP5PO, involved in electron transfer and ATP synthesis, were among the coregulated genes identified in ME/CFS CD4+ T cells.

The proportion of γδT cells among CD8+ T cell subsets showed a statistically significant difference between ME/CFS and healthy controls per figure legend (p=0.042), though the main text described it as non-significant.

In CD8+ T cells, transcription factors ZBTB7A, JUND, ESRRA, SP3 and KDM5A were more highly activated in ME/CFS compared to healthy controls, whose CD8+ T cell TFs were mainly involved in integrated stress response and cytokine signaling.

Highly activated TFs in ME/CFS CD8+ T cells (PSMD8, NFKBIA, PSMD7, NFKB1, REST, TAF7, MYC) showed significant enrichment in cell proliferation, differentiation, cellular senescence, infectious diseases, and neurodegenerative diseases (AD, HD).

In CD8+ naïve cells, 662 elevated genes were linked to 290 KEGG pathways, with significant enrichment in pathways relevant to neurological diseases and infectious diseases caused by viral and bacterial pathogens.
DEGs CCR7, CD28, LCK, and SMAD3 in CD8+ naïve cells play roles in immune cell activation, signaling, viral processes, and cytokine synthesis in ME/CFS.

In CD8+ naïve cells, genes EZR, CSK, ACTB and ITGB7 (cytoskeleton/adhesion) and GATA3, ZFPM1, MYC, LEF1, and XBP1 (transcription factor function) were among the elevated DEGs contributing to enriched GO BP pathways in ME/CFS.

Pseudotime analysis showed memory B cells from ME/CFS patients positioned in early pseudotime while HC memory B cells were in mid-to-late pseudotime, with a distinct branch appearing in both the memory B and plasma B clusters unique to ME/CFS.
Regulon analysis identified KLF2, TFDP1, and MBD4 as putative important regulons controlling B-cell growth that differ in ME/CFS.
Common regulated genes CD81, PTPN6, INPP5D, PTPRC, IGHG4, and IGHA2 were identified across B cell subsets, contributing to B cell signaling, immune response control, and antibody synthesis in ME/CFS.
KEGG pathway analysis of B cell subsets revealed increased signaling pathways linked to Parkinson's disease, Prion disease, ALS, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection in ME/CFS.
Specific genes BAX, ADRM1, PSMC5, and PSMD1, linked to proteasome-related processes, were identified as critical regulators of B cell function and homeostasis in ME/CFS.
In NK cells, transcription factors ZBTB7A, KLF2, KLF13, RELA, CEBPB, and CEBPD were highly activated in ME/CFS, whereas FOS, JUN, JUNB, IRF1, and BCLAF1 were most associated with HC NK cells.

ME/CFS-specific highly activated NK cell TFs (ZBTB7A/7B, RELA, KLF2, NFKB1, ASCL2, POLE3) showed notable enrichment in population proliferation, cell differentiation, nucleic acid metabolism, cellular stress response, and IL-17/IL-18/IL-6 signaling.

603 upregulated and 213 downregulated DEGs in NK cells of ME/CFS patients were enriched in biological processes related to response to external stimuli, immunoglobulin-mediated immune response, antigen processing/presentation, and adaptive immune response regulation.

KEGG enrichment of upregulated NK cell genes in ME/CFS revealed associations with infectious diseases (HIV, EBV, COVID-19), amyloidotic neurodegenerative diseases (ALS, PD), and autoimmunity, while downregulated genes were involved in IL-17 signaling and NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity.
Monocle3 trajectory analysis showed reduced branching/differentiation diversity of CD14 monocytes in the ME/CFS group compared to healthy controls.
Monocyte transcription factors ZBTB7A, KLF13, RXRA, IRF2, and SPI1 showed increased activity in ME/CFS, while HC monocyte regulons were primarily EGR1, EGR2, FOSB, EGR3, and DDIT3.
Clinical trials from Norway reported that B-cell depletion therapy with rituximab produced clinical benefit in a subset of ME/CFS patients.
In a subset of ME/CFS patients, antiviral drug treatment was reported to reduce fatigue and increase natural CD4+ T cell and NK cell counts.

Autoantibodies against various antigens, including neurotransmitter receptors, have been identified in some ME/CFS patients and may be sufficient to drive a chronic immune response underlying neurological symptoms.
Prior coronavirus infection has been reported to trigger ME/CFS onset in approximately 11% of patients.
Approximately 80% of ME/CFS cases were reported to begin following a viral infection.
Both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from ME/CFS patients exhibited reduced glycolysis at rest, consistent with a previous study.
CD8+ T cells from ME/CFS patients also showed diminished glycolysis following activation.
ME/CFS patients often exhibit an abundance of exhausted T cells, a reversible state associated with chronic viral infection that impairs T cell proliferation, survival, and cytotoxicity.

KEGG Human Disease pathway enrichment in ME/CFS peripheral immune cells fell into two unexpected classes: virus infection-related pathways (e.g., HSV, HPV, CMV, EBV, COVID-19) and amyloid neurodegenerative disease pathways (AD, ALS, PD, HD, prion disease), despite active infection being excluded by screening.
ADRM1 and PSMD2, genes implicated in the amyloid neurodegenerative pathway enrichment, are both components of the 26S proteasome complex responsible for degrading ubiquitinated proteins.

IVIG is proposed to work by supplying pooled antibodies that modulate immune responses via cytokine and autoantibody neutralization, FcRn saturation, complement inhibition, and regulation of T and B cell inflammation.

In severe acute COVID-19, early administration of IVIG together with plasmapheresis has been reported to reduce the need for mechanical ventilation, shorten ICU and hospital stays, and lower mortality.
In small patient cohorts, IVIG has been shown to alleviate persistent symptoms of post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC/long COVID), though this research is still in early stages.
IVIG has shown benefits in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), a condition with symptomatic overlap with PASC, though studies to date have yielded mixed results.
IVIG treatment carries potential adverse effects including anaphylaxis, headaches, thrombosis, liver enzyme elevations, and renal complications, and its high cost can deter payers and patients.

Using a novel semiparametric bivariate hierarchical state space model, the circadian relationship between ACTH and cortisol was found to be erratic in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia, in contrast to a normal day-night circadian pattern observed in controls.

The bivariate hormone modeling approach revealed altered ACTH-cortisol coupling (nonparametric population-average and subject-specific circadian components) distinguishing chronic fatigue syndrome/fibromyalgia patients from controls.
After 8 weeks, the CAA herbal extract group showed a significantly greater reduction in total Fatigue Severity Scale score compared to placebo.
CAA significantly reduced FSS item 6 ("my fatigue prevents sustained physical functioning") compared to placebo at week 8.
CAA significantly reduced FSS item 7 ("fatigue interferes with duties/responsibilities") compared to placebo at both weeks 4 and 8.
CAA reduced FSS item 8 (fatigue as a top-3 disabling symptom) significantly at week 4 but only as a trend at week 8.
Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory total score decreased significantly more in the CAA group than placebo after 8 weeks.
The MFI 'general and physical fatigue' subscale showed only a non-significant decreasing trend in the CAA group at week 8.
CAA significantly reduced the MFI 'reduced activity' subscale score at week 8 compared to placebo.
CAA significantly improved the MFI 'motivation' subscale score at week 8 compared to placebo.
24-hour post-exercise VAS fatigue score significantly decreased in the CAA group after 8 weeks.
The 30-minute post-exercise VAS fatigue score showed only a non-significant decreasing trend in the CAA group.
Time to exhaustion during maximal cycle ergometer testing increased significantly more in the CAA group than placebo after 8 weeks.
Distance covered until exhaustion increased significantly more in the CAA group than placebo after 8 weeks.
Maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) was significantly enhanced in the CAA group compared to placebo after 8 weeks.
No significant difference in anaerobic threshold level was found between the CAA and placebo groups.
Within the CAA group, significant within-group changes occurred over 8 weeks in maximum heart rate and maximum respiratory quotient during exercise testing.
Baseline (pre-exercise) creatine kinase levels decreased significantly over time in the placebo group but not in the CAA group.
Myoglobin decreased significantly in the placebo group but not the CAA group at 30 minutes post-exercise recovery at week 8, producing a significant between-group difference.

Aside from myoglobin at one timepoint, no other blood biochemical markers (lactate, LDH, CK, BUN, creatinine, inorganic phosphate, ammonia, glucose) showed significant between-group differences between CAA and placebo.
In prior in vitro work cited by the authors, CAA extract reduced intracellular reactive oxygen species approximately 20-fold in cell culture.
In a prior exercised mouse model cited by the authors, CAA increased maximum running time, decreased serum LDH by ~40%, and increased PGC-1alpha protein expression compared to exercise controls.

In a prior mouse study cited by the authors, CAA-treated mice showed reduced fatigue-related biomarkers including lactate dehydrogenase (~30%), creatine kinase (~20%), IL-1beta (~10%), and IL-6 (~10%) compared to controls.
The vast majority of women with hEDS or HSD reported TMD pain symptoms.
Most participants also reported temporomandibular joint clicking.
Over half of participants reported temporomandibular joint crepitation.
Women with hEDS or HSD and TMD symptoms had a considerably impaired oral health-related quality of life as measured by the OHIP-14.
Among OHIP-14 subdomains, oral function had the lowest impact on quality of life.
Orofacial pain was the OHIP-14 subdomain with the greatest impact on quality of life.
Self-reported bruxism was significantly associated with worse oral health-related quality of life.
Poorer self-reported general health was significantly associated with worse oral health-related quality of life.
Comorbid symptoms were significantly associated with worse (higher/impaired) OHIP-14 scores among women with hEDS or HSD and TMD symptoms.
Women with confirmed hEDS or HSD and TMD symptoms overall experienced considerably impaired oral health-related quality of life, indicating a need for targeted management strategies.
POTS was self-reported as one of the most common comorbidities among individuals with HSD/hEDS in this Delphi cohort.
Fibromyalgia was self-reported as one of the most common comorbidities among individuals with HSD/hEDS.
MCAS was self-reported as one of the most common comorbidities among individuals with HSD/hEDS.
Migraine was self-reported as one of the most common comorbidities among individuals with HSD/hEDS.
IBS was self-reported as one of the most common comorbidities among individuals with HSD/hEDS.
ASD was self-reported as one of the most common comorbidities among individuals with HSD/hEDS.
Asthma, anxiety, depression, ADHD and osteoarthritis were also among the most commonly self-reported comorbidities in this HSD/hEDS cohort.
Individuals with HSD/hEDS experienced a substantial delay between symptom onset (mean age 11 years) and clinical diagnosis (mean age 29 years), an average gap of approximately 18 years.

Following three Delphi rounds and a consensus meeting with patients, family/carers and healthcare professionals, 30 symptoms across eight specialties (MSK/orthopaedics, social aspects, pain, gynaecology/urology, negative affect, neurological, sleep/fatigue, and gastrointestinal) reached ≥70% consensus as critically important and were included in the core outcome set for HSD/hEDS.
In Round 1 of the Delphi, only 17 of 74 rated symptoms (23.0%) reached the ≥70% consensus threshold for critical importance across all stakeholder groups.
Healthcare professionals rated psychological/negative-affect symptoms such as 'feeling depressed' and 'feeling distressed' as more critically important than individuals with HSD/hEDS themselves did.
Only 55% of the professional participants had previously received hypermobility-specific training, highlighting a knowledge gap among healthcare professionals.
The family, friends or carers stakeholder group rated symptoms as more critically important overall than the individuals-with-HSD/hEDS and professional groups.

Dermatological symptoms failed to reach consensus as critically important, being rated below 35% by individuals with HSD/hEDS, in contrast to MSK/orthopaedic and pain-related symptoms which exceeded the consensus threshold.

Psychosocial factors including negative healthcare experiences, medical gaslighting, and being made to feel fraudulent/stigmatised/misunderstood reached consensus as critically important symptoms across all three stakeholder groups.
Both high-load and low-load strengthening exercise programs produced large effect sizes on the Western Ontario Shoulder Instability Index in two studies.
Kinesiology taping across the glenohumeral joint line showed a large effect size on WOSI in both intervention groups in one study.
Pain outcomes improved with large effect sizes for both interventions in the Liaghat exercise trial, while kinesiology tape showed small-to-medium effect sizes for pain reduction.
Kinesiophobia showed negligible effect sizes in both groups of a home-based exercise program, while a small effect size was seen in one group of a supervised strength training program.
Functional outcomes measured by Patient Specific Functional Scale and Upper Extremity Functional Index showed positive (small to medium) effect sizes across the exercise and kinesiology tape studies.

Strength measurements (isometric and isokinetic) showed mostly negligible effect sizes, with only small effect sizes for isometric external rotation strength in the high-load exercise group and isokinetic power at 180°/s in the compression orthoses group.
Compression orthoses (elasticized short-sleeve jacket) wear reduced pain on the visual analog scale from 3.5/10 to 2.5/10 after 4 weeks, although this did not reach statistical significance.
Wearing the compression jacket significantly decreased the occurrence of joint instability episodes compared to not wearing it after 4 weeks.

At 24-week follow-up, both home-based exercise interventions demonstrated large effect sizes for WOSI, and function (PSFS) improved from small to large effect size in one group, while kinesiophobia improved from negligible to small effect size in both groups.

One-year follow-up of the high-load vs low-load strength trial showed continued maintenance of improved WOSI scores in both groups, with a favorable effect on emotional wellbeing attributed to the high-load strength program.
The shoulder is highly symptomatic in hEDS/HSD, with a prior report cited that 84% of individuals report shoulder pain.
hEDS/HSD is associated with comorbidities including fatigue and dysautonomia, which may hinder ability to attend in-person appointments and support the rationale for home-based exercise delivery.
Genetic testing identified a COL3A1 mutation (c.2337G>A) causing single base skipping at the last nucleotide of exon 33, confirming the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
A patient with vascular EDS developed pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection, diagnosed by two positive sputum cultures with nodular-bronchiectasis type disease.

Decreased collagen III, the main pathology of vEDS, is thought to reduce extracellular matrix (ECM) function in the lungs, predisposing to pulmonary complications including pneumothorax, hemothorax, hemoptysis, and cystic pulmonary lesions.

The authors propose that ECM abnormality from collagen III deficiency in vEDS may facilitate M. avium binding to damaged non-ciliated epithelium and reduced mucus clearance, increasing susceptibility to MAC infection.
The patient's very low BMI (12.4) and associated malnutrition, likely related to prior intestinal surgery/stoma, are proposed as a contributing risk factor for developing pulmonary MAC infection.

Three-drug therapy (rifampicin 300mg/day, ethambutol 500mg/day, clarithromycin 400-600mg/day) for approximately 2 years (804 days) resulted in sputum culture conversion to negative by day 92 and partial radiographic improvement, with sustained negative sputum after treatment completion.
The patient's bilateral external iliac artery dissection and left pneumothorax, complications of vascular fragility in vEDS, spontaneously resolved with conservative management alone.

The patient experienced recurrent vascular/pulmonary complications during MAC treatment, including a right spontaneous pneumothorax on day 92 and a right intercostal artery rupture (hemopneumothorax) on day 406, both managed conservatively.
Vascular EDS has an estimated frequency of 1/50,000 to 1/250,000 and a median survival age as young as 48 years, based on prior cohort studies.

Genetic abnormalities in the CHP2 region have been implicated in host susceptibility to nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, but this gene is distinct from COL3A1 and located on a different chromosome, indicating no established genetic link between EDS and MAC susceptibility.
Among 94 EDS patients with gastrointestinal involvement, gastrointestinal perforation was the most common manifestation overall.
Functional gastrointestinal symptoms were the second most common gastrointestinal manifestation among EDS patients.
Digestive arterial disorders were reported in a subset of EDS patients with gastrointestinal involvement.
Vascular-type EDS (vEDS) was the most frequent clinical subtype among patients with gastrointestinal involvement.
Hypermobile-type EDS (hEDS) was the second most frequent clinical subtype among patients with gastrointestinal involvement.
COL3A1 was the most frequently mutated gene among EDS patients with gastrointestinal involvement.
Among vEDS patients, gastrointestinal perforation was the most frequent gastrointestinal manifestation.
Arterial lesions were seen in a subset of vEDS patients with gastrointestinal involvement.
Among vEDS patients, 18.0% had digestive arterial lesions as a gastrointestinal manifestation.
Among vEDS patients, 14.0% presented with functional gastrointestinal symptoms.
Among hEDS patients, 90.0% presented with functional gastrointestinal symptoms, the dominant GI manifestation in this subtype.
Among hEDS patients, 15.0% presented with visceral prolapse as a gastrointestinal manifestation.
Among hEDS patients, 5.0% presented with intestinal volvulus as a gastrointestinal manifestation.
Despite correct intrathecal placement and adequate dosing of hyperbaric bupivacaine spinal anesthesia, the patient developed no motor blockade and reacted to surgical incision.

A saphenous nerve (adductor canal) block with 20 mL 0.5% ropivacaine followed 90 minutes later by 10 mL 2% lidocaine perineurally produced no change in pain intensity despite ultrasound-confirmed catheter placement directly under the nerve.

Subcutaneous infiltration of 1% lidocaine at the nerve block access site and combined ropivacaine/ketorolac injected into the knee soft tissue/periosteum failed to produce expected local anesthesia or postoperative pain control.
The patient reported a history of intense, refractory pain during dental procedures even when given additional numbing medications, suggesting a longstanding pattern of local anesthetic resistance.

The authors hypothesize that a common voltage-gated sodium channel genetic variant could underlie both the patient's epilepsy and her resistance to local anesthetics, since her antiepileptic drugs lamotrigine and lacosamide act via the same channel class targeted by LAs.

In vivo models show that specific mutations near the sodium channel intracellular pore region can decrease the inactivated channel's affinity for local anesthetic by up to 21-fold, a proposed mechanism of hereditary LA resistance.

In a prior human family study, three family members with local anesthetic resistance carried a genetic variant in the voltage-gated sodium channel that was absent in the unaffected family member, following failure of an ultrasound-guided brachial plexus block.
An IV ketamine infusion at 10 mg/h for 24 hours produced pain improvement sufficient for the patient to be discharged home after failure of multiple local anesthetic routes.
Connective tissue disorders are cited in the literature as a risk factor for local anesthetic resistance, but this patient explicitly denied any history of connective tissue disorder.

Children with generalized joint hypermobility (GJH) showed no significant difference in elbow joint position reproduction (JPR) errors compared to normal mobile children across all task conditions (unilateral, bilateral, four target angles, preferred/non-preferred arm).
No significant main effect of arm side (preferred vs non-preferred) was found on joint position reproduction error, though non-preferred arm error was slightly lower.
Elbow target angle strongly influenced joint position reproduction error, with the smallest error at 90° (1.84°) and larger errors at 70° (7.34°) and 50° (8.22°) across all children.
Bilateral elbow position matching produced significantly larger errors than unilateral matching, indicating unilateral repositioning is more accurate.
A significant interaction between task type (unilateral/bilateral) and angle showed that the disadvantage of bilateral matching was greater at more difficult, flexed angles (70° and 50°).
Height discrimination (wedges/heel-height detection) penalty scores did not differ significantly between hypermobile and normal mobile children.
Loading (standing, weight-bearing) improved ankle-height discrimination accuracy compared to the unloaded (seated) condition, indicated by lower penalty scores.
Penalty scores in the loaded and unloaded wedges tasks were weakly but significantly correlated.
Unilateral and bilateral elbow position matching errors were moderately correlated with each other.
Elbow range of motion was not significantly related to elbow joint position sense task performance.
Knee and ankle range of motion showed no significant relationship with loaded or unloaded wedges (ankle-height discrimination) task performance.

Correlations between upper-extremity (elbow JPR) and lower-extremity (wedges) proprioception measures were not significant, suggesting proprioceptive performance does not generalize across body parts.

The authors cite a prior study (Clayton et al. 2021) in which, unlike joint angle matching, a hand position test showed hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome subjects to be less accurate than controls, highlighting that some proprioceptive test types may reveal deficits not captured by joint angle matching.

A 45-year-old male with classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome sustained bilateral spontaneous patellar tendon ruptures during eccentric quadriceps contraction while attempting to stabilize a falling trolley.
EDS patellar tendons have been reported to demonstrate lower biomechanical properties compared with tendons from controls, attributable to altered fibrillar collagen metabolism.
Healthy patellar tendons require a force of approximately 17.5 times body weight to rupture, whereas EDS patients may require substantially less force due to connective tissue weakness.
At 12-month follow-up after bilateral primary patellar tendon repair, the patient scored 'fair' knee function on the Lysholm Knee Scoring Scale.
The patient scored 66.7% (right) and 67.8% (left) on the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) Knee Score at 12-month follow-up following bilateral tendon repair.
At 12 months post-operatively, the patient achieved a full active range of motion without extensor lag and returned to pre-injury activities of daily living.
A literature review identified three prior case reports of patellar tendon rupture in EDS patients; all patients were male, with an average age of 21 years (range 13-27 years).
Knee instability is described as the most commonly involved joint manifestation in EDS, possibly contributed to by quadriceps and hamstring weakness.

Diagnosis of patellar tendon rupture is confirmed radiologically by ultrasound and plain radiograph demonstrating patella alta, indicated by an Insall-Salvati ratio greater than 1.2, and this was used to confirm the diagnosis in the present patient.

The paper reports that Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has become an increasingly prevalent topic in occipitocervical fusion literature, reflecting growing scrutiny of its association with craniocervical instability.
Dysphagia has remained a consistently and commonly cited topic in the occipitocervical fusion literature over time.
Rheumatoid arthritis has decreased in publication frequency as a topic within occipitocervical fusion literature, possibly reflecting advances in medical management and surgical techniques.
Joint hypermobility spectrum disorder was present in more than 75% of FND patients compared with only 15% of healthy control participants.
FND patients showed higher sensory sensitivity than healthy controls.
FND patients had a greater number of both psychiatric and physical comorbidities compared with healthy controls.
FND patients exhibited a greater frequency of polarized behaviors than healthy controls.
FND patients showed an increase in characteristics and sensations typical of anxiety compared with healthy controls.
FND patients scored higher than controls across all five dimensions of the neuroconnective endophenotype, supporting its use as a candidate FND subtyping tool.
Patients with lifetime exercise exposure scores above the median reported significantly higher total quality of life scores than those below the median.
Current frequency of exercise was positively correlated with psychosocial quality of life scores.
Current frequency of exercise was positively correlated with physical quality of life scores.
Current frequency of exercise was positively correlated with total quality of life score.

No significant difference in aortic size or need for surgical intervention was found between patients above versus below the median exercise exposure score, or between those who did versus did not participate in competitive sports.
Despite 88% of patients being restricted from exercise by their medical provider, 65% reported competitive sports participation and 93% reported recreational exercise.
A patient with five arterial aneurysms carried a heterozygous variant in TNXB, the gene encoding Tenascin-X, whose biallelic pathogenic variants cause classical-like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

A patient with eight arterial aneurysms carried a heterozygous SMAD3 variant, a gene in which pathogenic variants cause Loeys-Dietz syndrome 3 (aneurysms-osteoarthritis syndrome), and this patient had onset of aneurysm disease at age 40.

A patient with six arterial aneurysms carried two heterozygous TET2 variants (one frameshift, one nonsense), genes associated with clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), with aneurysm diagnosis at age 78.
The same patient with TET2 variants also carried a heterozygous PPM1D variant; PPM1D is part of the DNA damage response pathway and is associated with CHIP.

Whole exome sequencing of nine patients with multiple arterial aneurysms identified 24 variants across 23 different genes associated with vascular disease, comprising 14 missense, seven frameshift and three nonsense variants.
Copy number variant (CNV) analysis performed in all nine patients did not reveal any relevant pathogenic findings.

The patient carrying the SMAD3 variant, who underwent endovascular aortic repair (EVAR) with iliac side branches, developed Type 1a and 1b endoleaks with aneurysm sac expansion after 2.5 years, requiring reintervention to prevent secondary rupture.
The patient carrying the TNXB variant, who also underwent EVAR with iliac side branches, presented no complications within two years of follow-up.
Among the other seven patients, four received EVAR for AAA, and only the patient with TET2 and PPM1D variants developed a relevant endoleak (1b) requiring reintervention five years after EVAR.

The most frequently mutated CHIP driver genes (DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1) are reported in the literature to increase risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, with TET2 mutation carrying a hazard ratio of 1.9.

A cited multicenter retrospective study of endovascular aortic interventions in patients with connective tissue disease reported high early technical success (98.2%), low perioperative mortality (2.9%), and 5-year survival comparable to open surgery (80.6% Marfan, 85.2% Loeys-Dietz, 43.8% vascular EDS), with most patients treated for dissections rather than degenerative aneurysms.

Genetic testing and counselling is recommended for patients with thoracic aortic disease younger than 60 years, with a positive family history, or with coexisting intracranial or peripheral aneurysms.

In prior work by the same group, a high ratio of positive genetic variants in fibrillin (FBN) and actin alpha 2 (ACTA2) genes was found in preselected patients with Stanford type B aortic dissections, contrasting with the genes (e.g., TNXB) implicated in the current cohort with multiple arterial aneurysms.
Two affected brothers were found to carry compound heterozygous likely pathogenic EFEMP1 variants, one splice-site variant and one missense variant.

An unrelated man carried a monoallelic (heterozygous) EFEMP1 splice-site variant causing exon skipping and start-loss, with no second variant identified despite targeted reanalysis and RNA-sequencing.
The two affected brothers presented with marfanoid habitus, recurrent inguinal and umbilical hernias, generalized joint hypermobility, and scoliosis.
Parents and halfsiblings of the affected brothers, presumed heterozygous carriers, reported milder joint hypermobility and umbilical hernias.
The elder affected brother died at age 16 from incarcerated gastrointestinal herniation complicated by gastric and bowel necrosis with perforation.
Autopsy of the deceased brother revealed widespread intestinal diverticula.
The unrelated 58-year-old proband and his dizygotic twin brother and mother had high myopia associated with EFEMP1 variant carriage.

Family members (parents, half-siblings, twin brother, mother) of the probands also reported joint hypermobility, umbilical hernias, or recurrent hernias, suggesting a heritable phenotype pattern consistent with EFEMP1-related disease.
Autopsy of the elder sibling revealed widespread intestinal diverticula despite normal skin and fascia immunohistochemistry, including normal elastic fiber staining.
Autopsy of the 59-year-old man showed extensive diaphragmatic herniation, bowel diverticula, and pulmonary emphysema, and he died at age 59.

Despite identifying a heterozygous EFEMP1 splice variant causing exon skipping and start-loss, targeted genome reanalysis and RNA-sequencing failed to identify a second pathogenic variant on the other allele in the unrelated proband.

The authors conclude that EFEMP1-related disease represents a distinct entity within the heritable connective tissue disorder spectrum, with severe recurrent hernias, gastrointestinal dilatation, and diverticulosis conferring increased risk of life-threatening complications requiring early recognition and close monitoring.

A 44-year-old woman presented with acute severe abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting for 3 days, ultimately diagnosed with torsion of a wandering (ectopic) spleen with 720-degree rotation of its vascular pedicle causing splenic infarction, confirmed by CT and surgery.

Ligamentous laxity leading to wandering spleen can be congenital, due to malformation of splenic suspensory ligaments, or acquired due to factors such as pregnancy-related increased estrogen levels, splenomegaly, or trauma, which weaken the ligaments.

Wandering spleen predominantly affects reproductive-age women, especially multiparous women, believed to be due to abdominal wall laxity, with age distribution showing two peaks (infancy and third decade of life).

CT imaging is diagnostic for wandering spleen torsion, showing absence of the spleen in the left upper quadrant, an ovoid or comma-shaped abdominal mass with a classic 'whorled' appearance, a long twisted vascular pedicle, and possible lack of contrast opacification indicating infarction.

Splenopexy is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic wandering spleen, while splenectomy is indicated when torsion has led to splenic infarction; in this case, splenectomy was performed and the patient recovered well, being discharged on day 5.

In individuals with generalized joint hypermobility, quadriceps peak torque was significantly higher during both external and internal attentional focus instructions compared to a neutral attention condition.
Postural stability performance was significantly better during external attentional focus compared to internal focus and neutral conditions in subjects with generalized joint hypermobility.
Y Balance Test composite score increased during the external attentional focus condition compared to internal focus and neutral conditions in subjects with generalized joint hypermobility.
The patient developed splenic torsion due to a wandering spleen, resulting in splenic vein occlusion, venous thrombosis, and infarctive changes confirmed on pathology.

Failure of development or trauma to the four splenic ligaments (gastrosplenic, splenorenal, splenocolic, splenophrenic) creates ligamentous laxity that elongates the vascular splenic pedicle, predisposing to torsion and vascular compromise.
The acquired form of wandering spleen often results from ligament weakening associated with elevated hormone levels during pregnancy, trauma, or surgical manipulation.
Among CT findings for wandering spleen and splenic torsion, the whorled appearance of the splenic vessels around the hilum is the most specific diagnostic sign.

Management of wandering spleen and splenic torsion depends on vascular viability: splenectomy is indicated when infarction has occurred, whereas splenopexy may be considered to preserve splenic immunologic function when vasculature is intact.
The patient's presenting complete blood count showed an unquantifiable platelet count due to massive platelet clumping, which resolved with improved platelet count after splenectomy.

This case represents the first reported association between wandering spleen and a history of duodenal atresia, though the authors attribute the ligament laxity more likely to the patient's prior surgical intervention than to a failure of intestinal recanalization from the atresia itself.
Endogenous and GFP-tagged VPS13B preferentially colocalizes with the cis-/medial Golgi marker GM130 rather than trans-Golgi markers.
The purified PH domain of VPS13B binds phosphoinositides PI3P, PI4P, and PI5P in vitro.
Pharmacological reduction of PI4P (via PI4K inhibitor PAO or high-dose PI3K/PI4P-reducing inhibitor LY294002) strongly reduces the association of endogenous VPS13B with the Golgi.
Double siRNA depletion of PI4KA and PI4KB, but not either alone, moderately reduces Golgi-associated VPS13B, indicating redundant kinase control of Golgi PI4P for VPS13B recruitment.
siRNA depletion of Rab6A or Rab2A, or expression of dominant-negative Rab6A-T27N, does not block the Golgi association of VPS13B or its PH domain.
The N-terminus of VPS13B, containing a phospho-FFAT motif, interacts with VAPB (but not VAPA or MOSPD3), with the phosphomimetic S560D mutation moderately increasing this interaction.
Mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation identified Sec23IP (p125) as a novel VPS13B-interacting protein.
CRISPR-Cas9 knockout of Sec23IP causes Golgi fragmentation that phenocopies VPS13B knockout.
Coexpression of VPS13B strongly recruits Sec23IP-positive ER exit sites (ERES) to the Golgi, forming an extensive ERES-Golgi interface, an effect also observed at endogenous protein levels.
VPS13B knockout significantly reduces ERES-Golgi association, and additional Sec23IP knockdown in VPS13B KO cells further reduces this association.
The VAB domain of VPS13B directly and specifically binds Sec23IP (but not Sec16A or Sec23A), primarily via repeats R2-R5, with R1 required for cellular recruitment.
The N-terminal region of Sec23IP, containing PxP motifs (including residues 176-178 and 213-215), is necessary and sufficient for direct binding to VPS13B-VAB.
Multiple Cohen syndrome-associated missense mutations in the VPS13B VAB domain impair its interaction with Sec23IP, with G2729R, N2993S, S3142R, and S3328R almost completely abolishing binding.
VPS13B knockout dramatically impairs the formation of Rab1B-induced tubular ERGIC (tERGIC), reducing both its length and number compared to control.
Sec23IP knockout, like VPS13B knockout, also significantly impairs the formation of tubular ERGIC.
A lipid transfer-deficient VPS13B mutant fails to rescue the tERGIC formation defect in VPS13B knockout cells, indicating lipid transfer activity is required for tERGIC biogenesis.
Sec23IP-binding-deficient VPS13B mutants (ΔR1-6) and disease-associated missense mutants (N2993S, S3142R, S3328R) fail to rescue the tERGIC formation defect in VPS13B knockout cells.

siRNA depletion of VPS13B or Sec23IP in primary mouse embryonic fibroblasts does not block but significantly delays ER export of procollagen, causing its accumulation in the ER, providing a candidate mechanistic link between VPS13B dysfunction and joint laxity in Cohen syndrome.

Quantitative mass spectrometry of secreted proteins showed that levels of several collagen species, including collagen IA, were significantly reduced in the medium of VPS13B-depleted primary MEFs compared with control.
Primary MEFs from VPS13B-/- mice show substantially delayed procollagen trafficking compared with MEFs from WT littermates, confirming the trafficking defect in vivo.

Tango1 depletion inhibits procollagen secretion to a much greater extent than VPS13B or Sec23IP depletion, suggesting VPS13B/Sec23IP are more general regulators of ER-to-Golgi trafficking rather than procollagen-specific factors.
Decreased SICI (reduced cortical inhibition) was associated with gabapentinoid use in FMS patients.
Decreased SICI was associated with a history of nicotine use in FMS patients.
Decreased SICI was associated with increased fatigue levels in FMS patients, suggesting a link to compensatory mechanisms for non-painful FMS features.
Increased motor intracortical facilitation (ICF) was linked with greater pain severity in FMS patients.
Increased ICF was linked with shorter FMS duration.

Higher resting motor threshold (rMT) was associated with less effective pain modulation, indicated by lower conditioned pain modulation (CPM), suggesting disruption of the pain compensatory mechanism.
Ursolic acid reduced degranulation and chemokine production induced by the MRGPRX2 agonists compound 48/80 and substance P in LAD2 mast cells in vitro.
Ursolic acid alleviated compound 48/80- and substance P-induced systemic anaphylaxis and passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in vivo.
Ursolic acid showed strong binding affinity to the MRGPRX2 protein and decreased calcium influx in LAD2 cells and MRGPRX2-transfected HEK293 cells stimulated with compound 48/80 and substance P.
Ursolic acid suppressed phosphorylation of proteins in the PLCγ signaling pathway downstream of MRGPRX2.
Ursolic acid suppressed phosphorylation of proteins in the NF-κB signaling pathway downstream of MRGPRX2.
