Octapeptin C4 induced potent, concentration-dependent calcium mobilization, degranulation, and CCL-2 (MCP-1) release in LAD2 human mast cells.
Polymyxin B produced concentration-dependent calcium mobilization, degranulation, and CCL-2 release in LAD2 mast cells.
Colistin produced concentration-dependent calcium mobilization, degranulation, and CCL-2 release in LAD2 mast cells.
CRISPR-Cas9 knockdown of MRGPRX2 in LAD2 mast cells significantly reduced calcium mobilization, degranulation, and CCL-2 release induced by polymyxins, confirming MRGPRX2 dependency.
Pharmacological inhibition of MRGPRX2 using an inverse agonist significantly reduced polymyxin-induced calcium mobilization, degranulation, and CCL-2 release in LAD2 mast cells.

Polymyxin nonapeptides were far less potent calcium mobilisers than octapeptin C4, polymyxin B, and colistin, and failed to induce functional degranulation in LAD2 mast cells, suggesting lower liability to trigger hypersensitivity reactions.
Conditioned media from compound 48/80-activated peritoneal mast cells markedly increased sprouting in ex vivo choroidal explants compared to controls.
Conditioned media from activated peritoneal mast cells accelerated choroidal endothelial cell migration in a scratch wound assay.
Conditioned media from activated peritoneal mast cells enhanced tubulogenesis of choroidal endothelial cells in Matrigel.
After laser-induced injury, degranulating mast cells accumulated at the choroidal neovascularization site, peaking around day 1-3 and subsiding by day 7.
Mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice showed markedly smaller choroidal neovascularization lesions than wild-type mice 7 days after laser injury.
Systemic reconstitution of mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice with bone marrow-derived mast cells restored (prevented the reduction of) choroidal neovascularization size.
Pretreatment with the mast cell stabilizer ketotifen fumarate markedly decreased choroidal neovascularization lesion size 7 days after laser burn.
Ketotifen fumarate treatment reduced vascular leakage measured by fundus fluorescein angiography 7 days after laser burn.
Recombinant mouse tryptase (mMCPT6) promoted choroidal endothelial cell migration in a dose-dependent scratch assay.
Recombinant mouse tryptase (mMCPT6) enhanced tubulogenesis of choroidal endothelial cells.
mMCPT6 tryptase increased sprouting in ex vivo choroidal explants compared to control.
Avidin D and tryptase double-positive mast cells were substantially increased at the CNV lesion site 3 days post-laser burn, consistent with clinical AMD observations.
The selective mast cell tryptase inhibitor APC 366 significantly reduced choroidal neovascularization lesion size by day 7 post-laser burn.
Transcriptomic GSEA of RPE/choroid complex 3 days post-laser burn showed significant enrichment of the mast cell activation gene set compared to control.
GSEA showed significant enrichment of the collagen catabolism gene set in laser-induced CNV choroid/RPE tissue compared to control.
GSEA showed significant enrichment of the extracellular matrix (ECM) organization gene set in laser-induced CNV choroid/RPE tissue compared to control.
Gene ontology enrichment analysis of the top upregulated genes in laser-induced CNV tissue relative to control identified ECM remodeling and innate immune response as top pathways.

Collagen turnover, assessed by CHP binding, was decreased in mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice compared to wild-type at day 7 post-laser burn and was restored by mast cell reconstitution, indicating mast cells drive collagen remodeling in CNV.

Among 42 veterans diagnosed with Gulf War Illness who underwent skin biopsy at the New Jersey War Related Illness and Injury Study Center, 24 (57%) were also diagnosed with biopsy-confirmed small fiber neuropathy.
Veterans with GWI and SFN did not report significantly more autonomic nervous system symptoms than veterans with GWI who did not have SFN.
A potential known etiology for SFN was identified in 16 of 24 (67%) veterans with GWI and SFN, rising to 19 of 24 (79%) when hyperlipidemia was included as a contributing cause.
No explanatory condition was identified in 5 of 24 (21%) veterans with GWI and SFN, and the authors suggest deployment-related toxic exposures could plausibly contribute to this idiopathic SFN.
IENFD of the distal leg had the highest diagnostic accuracy for DSP among all tested measures, with an AUC of 0.78.
The IENFD leg/thigh ratio had similar diagnostic capability for DSP as IENFD of the distal leg alone, while IENFD of the proximal thigh performed significantly worse, as did all CCM parameters.
The MNSIq had the third-highest diagnostic AUC for DSP, comparable to IENFD of the distal leg.
IENFD of the distal leg had improved diagnostic accuracy for definite DSP compared to probable DSP.
IENFD of the distal leg had the best diagnostic accuracy for small fiber neuropathy, with a higher AUC than for DSP overall.
The IENFD leg/thigh ratio performed similarly to IENFD of the distal leg for diagnosing SFN.
IENFD of the distal leg significantly outperformed IENFD of the proximal thigh and all CCM parameters for diagnosing SFN, with CCM AUCs ranging from 0.45 to 0.62.
IENFD of the proximal thigh had diagnostic accuracy for SFN similar to that of CCM parameters, both being inferior to IENFD of the distal leg.
The MNSIq had the third-highest AUC for diagnosing SFN, not significantly different from IENFD of the distal leg.
Among participants with DSP, manual CCM parameters were strongly intercorrelated with each other.
Manual CCM parameters did not correlate with IENFD or other clinical DSP scales.
Among participants with DSP, lower IENFD of the distal leg was significantly correlated with worse (higher) scores on the UENS and mTCNS clinical neuropathy scales.
The IENFD leg/thigh ratio was also significantly and negatively correlated with UENS total score and mTCNS sensory score among DSP participants.
Among participants with SFN, manual CCM parameters were also strongly intercorrelated with each other.
Corneal nerve tortuosity coefficient correlated with the IENFD leg/thigh ratio among SFN participants; other manual CCM parameters did not correlate with IENFD or clinical SFN scales.
Among participants with SFN, lower IENFD of the distal leg correlated with worse UENS pinprick scores.
The IENFD leg/thigh ratio was negatively correlated with mTCNS pinprick/temperature score among SFN participants, but not with UENS pinprick score.
Patient preference between skin biopsy and CCM was roughly evenly split, with a slight majority preferring skin biopsy.
In this cohort of adults with obesity, 22.9% had probable DSP, 14.3% had definite DSP, and 14.3% had SFN.
Penk mRNA, encoding the opioid precursor proenkephalin, was significantly (albeit moderately) upregulated in DRGs of NaV1.8/NaV1.9 double knockout mice compared with wild-type.
Ano2 (Tmem16b), a calcium-activated chloride channel gene normally barely detectable in DRG neurons, was significantly upregulated in DKO DRGs, though absolute expression remained low.
A total of 47 genes were significantly downregulated in DKO DRGs, enriched by gene ontology analysis for gene networks associated with ion transport and cellular excitability.

The NaV1.5-encoding gene Scn5a was significantly downregulated (to a lesser extent than Scn10a/Scn11a) in DKO DRGs, confirmed by independent qPCR, consistent with the absence of a residual TTX-resistant current in DKO neurons.
Among downregulated genes, only two other ion channel genes were identified: Cacna1i (encoding the CaV3.3 T-type calcium channel α-subunit) and Chrna4 (nicotinic acetylcholine receptor α4 subunit).
Canonical marker genes of C-low-threshold mechanoreceptors (C-LTMRs) were collectively downregulated in DKO DRGs, suggesting a loss or functional alteration of this sensory neuron subtype.
Immunostaining showed strongly decreased TH immunoreactivity in DKO DRG sections compared with wild-type, corroborating loss or functional impairment of C-LTMR neurons at the protein level.

Whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings confirmed functional double knockout: DKO DRG neurons produced exclusively fast-activating, fast-inactivating (TTX-sensitive) Na+ currents, with complete loss of the slow-gating TTX-resistant currents mediated by NaV1.8/NaV1.9 seen in wild-type neurons.

DKO DRG neurons showed significantly reduced action potential peak amplitude (by 15 mV) and hyperpolarized voltage threshold and after-hyperpolarization minimum, while resting membrane potential and spike width were unchanged.
Despite altered action potential waveform, repetitive firing frequency of evoked action potentials (using -20 mV detection threshold) was indistinguishable between DKO and wild-type DRG neurons.
Among spontaneously active neurons, DKO DRG neurons had a lower frequency of spontaneous action potential firing than wild-type neurons.

Electron microscopy revealed moderate chronic axonal degeneration and Schwann cell abnormalities in unmyelinated fibers of DKO sciatic nerve, while DRG somata and glabrous skin nerve fascicles appeared largely normal, consistent with a mild peripheral neuropathy.
NaV1.8/NaV1.9 DKO mice showed significantly higher noxious mechanical pressure thresholds (Randall-Selitto test) than wild-type mice, indicating reduced sensitivity to noxious mechanical stimuli.
Innocuous mechanical sensitivity, measured with the von Frey test on the hind paw, was not significantly different between DKO and wild-type mice.
Heat pain thresholds, assessed with the 55°C hot plate test and the Hargreaves test, were similar between DKO and wild-type mice.
Cold sensitivity, measured by cold plate (5°C, 10°C), acetone application, and dry ice application, showed no significant differences between DKO and wild-type mice.

Thermal place preference testing across three temperature pairings showed no significant differences between DKO and wild-type mice, though DKO mice showed a nonsignificant trend toward the coldest plate in the 30°C-vs-5°C paradigm.

Formalin-induced nocifensive behavior (licking/biting/flinching) during the 60-minute observation period, including phase I and phase II, was not significantly different between DKO and wild-type mice.

Heterologous expression of the human congenital-analgesia-associated NaV1.9-L811P mutant in DKO DRG neurons caused a -20 mV hyperpolarizing shift in half-maximal voltage of channel activation compared with wild-type NaV1.9, without change in activation slope factor, and increased the inactivation slope factor.

NaV1.8/NaV1.9 DKO DRG neurons enabled robust heterologous expression and functional electrophysiological characterization of human NaV1.8 and NaV1.9 channels without interference from endogenous TTX-resistant currents, providing a new tool for studying channelopathy variants including notoriously difficult NaV1.9.
The L811P mutation increased the inactivation slope factor (kh) of human NaV1.9 channels without significantly altering the half-maximal inactivation voltage when expressed in DKO DRG neurons.
In a thermal place preference test comparing 30°C and 5°C plates, DKO mice showed a nonsignificant tendency to spend more time on the cold 5°C plate compared with WT.
Heterozygous breeding of NaV1.8/NaV1.9 DKO mice produced offspring at expected Mendelian ratios and normal sex distribution, and body weights were unaffected in both sexes.
Off-target sequencing analysis of the top 5 predicted off-target sites per sgRNA (23 sites total) found no indel mutations in founder and F1 DKO mice, confirming CRISPR editing specificity.

Number and distribution of unmyelinated nonpeptidergic (IB4+/PlxnC1+) and peptidergic (CGRP+) C-nociceptors were unchanged in NaV1.8/NaV1.9 DKO DRGs by immunostaining and flow cytometry, and their relative proportions remained stable with age despite an age-related decline in total neuron number.
Spontaneously firing DKO DRG neurons had a lower firing frequency than WT spontaneously firing neurons, although the fraction of neurons showing spontaneous activity was similar between genotypes.

Evoked action potential firing frequency as a function of injected current was indistinguishable between WT and DKO DRG neurons when using a −20 mV spike-detection threshold, indicating the double knockout impairs action potential shape but not overall evoked firing frequency.
Passive membrane properties (cell capacitance, input resistance) and outward (KV-mediated) current densities were unchanged between WT and DKO DRG neurons, while inward current density was reduced.

Resting membrane potential and action potential width at threshold were unchanged between WT and DKO DRG neurons, whereas after-hyperpolarization minimum voltage and voltage threshold were decreased in DKO neurons.
TTX block onset and recovery kinetics of Na+ currents were identical between WT and DKO DRG neurons, confirming that TTX-sensitive channel pharmacology was unaffected by the double knockout.

The formalin test showed no significant difference in nocifensive licking/biting/flinching behavior between DKO and WT mice across the 60-minute observation period or in pooled phase I/II analysis, contrasting with NaV1.7 knockout which shows reduced nocifensive behavior and with NaV1.8Cre-DTA neuronal ablation which dramatically reduces phase II responses.
Canonical C-low-threshold mechanoreceptor (C-LTMR) marker genes and associated genes were collectively downregulated in DKO DRGs, suggesting loss or dysfunction of this sensory neuron subtype.

Electron microscopy revealed moderate chronic axonal degeneration and Schwann cell abnormalities (swollen axons, collagen pockets, degenerating axons, enlarged ER, autophagic deposits, basal lamina onion bulbs) in unmyelinated Remak bundles of DKO sciatic nerve, while DRGs and glabrous skin nerve fascicles appeared largely normal, consistent with mild peripheral neuropathy.
CRISPLD2 expression/reactivity was increased in TGF-β-induced fibroblasts compared to untreated fibroblasts.
ACTA2 (α-SMA) expression decreased significantly in TGF-β-mediated fibroblasts when CRISPLD2 was upregulated, suggesting a negative regulatory relationship.
CRISPLD2 was confirmed to participate in TGF-β-induced fibroblast fibrosis through a negative feedback regulatory mechanism, acting at multiple levels.
Rectal barostat studies show that visceral hypersensitivity is present in over 60% of IBS patients and correlates with severity of GI symptoms.
IBS biopsy supernatant contains higher levels of histamine, proteases, and serotonin compared with healthy supernatant.
Increased serine proteases, including mast cell-derived tryptase and epithelial-derived trypsin-3, have been consistently observed in the gut of IBS patients.
Increased serotonin levels were observed in colonic biopsies of IBS-D patients, possibly due to increased enteroendocrine cell numbers or mast cell activation.

IBS biopsy supernatant induces greater neuronal activation of murine gut nociceptors and human submucosal neurons than healthy supernatant, an effect reversed by blocking histamine or protease signaling.
TRPV1 expression is elevated in biopsies of IBS patients and correlates with abdominal pain intensity.

Despite increased pain perception to rectal capsaicin in hypersensitive IBS patients, rectal TRPV1 mRNA and protein expression was similar between IBS patients and healthy individuals, indicating channel sensitization rather than overexpression.
Histamine sensitizes TRPV1, TRPV4, and TRPA1 channels in murine DRG neurons via the histamine 1 receptor (H1R), an effect reversed by H1R antagonism or receptor knockout.
Proteases such as trypsin-3 and tryptase signal through PAR2 on gut nociceptors, promoting DRG neuron hyperexcitability in vitro and visceral hypersensitivity in vivo.
Mas-related G protein-coupled receptors Mrgpra3 and Mrgprc11 were found to sensitize gut afferents in mice via TRPA1, although their role in human IBS remains unstudied.
Increased levels of nerve growth factor and brain-derived neurotrophic factor have been found in IBS patients, but their exact role in visceral hypersensitivity remains elusive.

A long-lasting increase in T cell and mononuclear cell numbers was observed in the mucosa of patients who developed IBS after acute infectious gastroenteritis, a finding confirmed by a recent meta-analysis.

An unbiased gene expression array revealed a subset of IBS patients (33%) with upregulation of IL-1β (3-fold), PTGS2 (2.1-fold), and mast cell-specific MRGPRX2 (10.7-fold), though these changes were unrelated to clinical symptoms.
Weston et al. reported increased mucosal mast cell numbers in the terminal ileum of IBS patients, and Barbara et al. found increased mast cell numbers in rectal biopsies of IBS patients.

Some studies failed to detect differences in mast cell numbers between healthy and IBS patients, or even reported lower mast cell counts in IBS biopsies, indicating mast cell number is a poorly reliable biomarker.
Degranulated mast cells found in close proximity to mucosal nerves in IBS patients correlate with the frequency and severity of abdominal pain.

In vivo, mast cell stabilizers, histamine antagonists, or protease inhibitors effectively reduce visceral hypersensitivity in murine models, confirming a causal role for mast cells in visceral hypersensitivity.

Injection of food extracts into the cecal mucosa elicited a local weal-and-flare reaction associated with mast cell activation (but not increased serum IgE) in up to 77% of patients with chronic abdominal symptoms, versus none of the healthy controls.

Confocal laser endoscopy showed food extract application to duodenal mucosa elicited positive reactions with intraepithelial lymphocyte increases, interepithelial gap formation, and cell shedding in two-thirds of IBS patients, with positive reactions associated with eosinophil-cationic protein release.

Injection of food antigens into the rectosigmoid colonic mucosa of 12 IBS patients versus 8 healthy controls elicited a mucosal reaction in IBS patients but not controls, and reactive antigens matched patient-reported food triggers.

Despite showing mucosal responses to food antigens, IBS patients do not respond via skin prick testing and do not exhibit increased food-specific IgE antibody titers in serum, distinguishing this response from classic food allergy.

In a mouse model, dietary ovalbumin exposure during Citrobacter rodentium infection led to local IgE-dependent mast cell activation and histamine-mediated TRPV1 sensitization upon re-exposure, causing visceral hypersensitivity; this was prevented by IgE-blocking antibodies or IgE deficiency, with OVA-specific IgE detectable only in colonic tissue, not serum.
The mucosa of IBS patients exhibited increased numbers of IgE-sensitized mast cells near nerve endings, correlating with abdominal pain severity.

In a small pilot study, IBS-D patients treated with the mast cell stabilizer cromolyn sodium reported significantly reduced abdominal pain and improved stool consistency, associated with reduced signs of mast cell activation.
Ketotifen, another mast cell-stabilizing drug, decreased visceral hypersensitivity and improved symptoms in IBS patients.
Case reports describe clinical improvement of IBS symptoms in severe asthma patients treated with the anti-IgE antibody omalizumab.
The 5-HT3 receptor antagonist alosetron provided adequate pain relief, decreased urgency and stool frequency, and increased stool firmness, but its use is restricted due to risk of ischemic colitis.
Ramosetron, a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, showed significantly more global improvement, increased stool consistency, and reduced abdominal pain and discomfort in IBS-D patients in Japanese studies.

In a pilot study, 46% of IBS patients receiving the H1R antagonist ebastine reported significantly improved symptom relief and reduced abdominal pain after 12 weeks, compared to 13% on placebo, with barostat studies confirming reduced visceral hypersensitivity.
A randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial confirmed the efficacy of ebastine in improving global symptom relief and abdominal pain intensity in IBS-D patients.
Women with IBS showed a significantly higher percentage of NREM sleep during the first four NREM-REM sleep cycles compared to healthy controls.
Normalized high frequency HRV power was significantly higher in women with IBS during the first four NREM-REM sleep cycles compared to healthy controls, indicating increased parasympathetic activity.
Normalized low frequency HRV power was significantly lower in women with IBS during the first four NREM-REM sleep cycles compared to healthy controls.
The LF/HF ratio of HRV was significantly decreased in women with IBS during the first four NREM-REM sleep cycles compared to healthy controls, suggesting a shift toward parasympathetic dominance.
Normalized EEG delta band power was significantly lower in women with IBS during the first four NREM-REM sleep cycles and over the whole night compared to healthy controls.

The phase shift (lag time) between normalized HF HRV and normalized EEG delta band power was significantly longer in the IBS group than in healthy controls, indicating dysregulated autonomic-central nervous system interaction.
The coherence between normalized HF HRV and normalized EEG delta band power was lower in the IBS group compared to controls, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.

Dominant-negative loss-of-function STAT3 variants causing autosomal dominant Hyper-IgE Syndrome are associated with connective tissue pathology including joint hypermobility, arterial tortuosity, and coronary/cerebral aneurysms alongside immunodeficiency and elevated IgE.

Gain-of-function PLCG2 variants cause elevated basal PLCγ2 activity with increased IP3/DAG production, leading to temperature-sensitive spontaneous mast cell activation below 37°C and the cold urticaria/immunodeficiency syndrome PLAID.
DNCB-induced AD model mice showed significantly higher dermatitis severity scores than control mice, confirming successful model establishment.
LLT treatment significantly lowered dermatitis scores compared to the AD model group, particularly for erythema, scaling, and epidermal desquamation.
AD model mice showed a 5.1-fold increase in ear epidermal thickness and a 10.8-fold increase in back skin thickness compared to control mice.
AD model mice exhibited a 4.0-fold increase in mast cell infiltration in ears and a 5.3-fold increase in back skin compared to control mice.
LLT treatment significantly reduced epidermal thickening in ears (67.7%) and back skin (70.4%) compared to the AD model group.
LLT treatment halved the number of infiltrated mast cells in both ear (50.0%) and back skin (50.4%) compared to the AD model group.
DNCB sensitization caused a 2.5-fold increase in serum IgE levels compared to control mice, which was significantly attenuated by LLT treatment.
Serum IL-4 levels were significantly increased in DNCB-sensitized AD model mice and were reduced by LLT treatment.
Serum IL-6 levels were significantly increased in DNCB-sensitized AD model mice and were reduced by LLT treatment.
TMT-proteomic analysis identified 213 upregulated and 186 downregulated differentially expressed proteins between LLT-treated and AD model skin tissue.

Proteins downregulated by LLT treatment relative to the AD model were enriched for immune/defense biological processes including complement activation, phagocytosis, inflammatory response, regulation of cell adhesion, and cell migration.
Proteins upregulated by LLT treatment were involved in skin development and intermediate filament cytoskeleton organization.

KEGG pathway analysis of differentially expressed proteins showed significant enrichment in S. aureus infection, complement and coagulation cascades, neutrophil extracellular trap formation, estrogen signaling, and Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis pathways.
KRT10 (Keratin 10), linked to skin development and the S. aureus infection pathway, was significantly reduced in the AD model group and restored following LLT treatment.
FGG (Fibrinogen gamma chain), associated with regulation of cell adhesion, was significantly increased in the AD model group and normalized following LLT treatment.

Complement activation-associated proteins (C1QA, C1QB, C1S, C4B, C5, BF, MASP2) were upregulated in the AD model group compared to control, and their expression was restored toward normal following LLT treatment.
Phagocytosis and cell migration-related proteins FCGR3 (Fc-gamma RIII) and ITGB2 (Integrin beta) showed increased expression in the AD model group, which was reversed by LLT treatment.
ELISA validation confirmed serum C1QA, C4B, and C5 were significantly upregulated in AD model mice and reduced to near-control levels following LLT treatment.
Serum FCGR3 protein, associated with phagocytosis and cell migration, was significantly elevated in the AD group and reduced to near-control levels by LLT treatment.

UPLC-MS/MS analysis of serum after LLT administration identified 125 compounds, including amino acids, alkaloids, lipids, nucleotides, phenolic acids, organic acids, flavonoids, and terpenes, representing candidate bioactive components of LLT.

Unsupervised clustering of EHR diagnosis, procedure, and medication codes identified six clinically distinct Long COVID subphenotypes in pediatric patients, with cardiorespiratory presentations being the most common.

The respiratory/cardiac subphenotype was characterized by a significantly greater proportion of respiratory diagnoses (56.7%) than any other subphenotype and was further stratified into six cluster-specific presentations differing by severity, age, and upper vs. lower respiratory predominance.
A musculoskeletal pain subphenotype comprising 13.9% of the Long COVID cohort was distinguished by pain-related diagnoses, with "other chronic pain" as the most common code.

A neuropsychiatric conditions subphenotype (10.9% of patients) showed a significantly greater proportion of neuropsychiatric diagnoses than other subphenotypes, with anxiety disorder the most common specific diagnosis.
A gastrointestinal symptoms subphenotype (9.3% of patients) showed a significantly greater proportion of GI diagnoses than other subphenotypes.
A headache subphenotype (7.1% of patients) had significantly greater headache diagnoses and the highest volume of post-acute healthcare utilization aside from a more severe lower respiratory cluster.

The fatigue subphenotype (5.0% of patients) had significantly greater fatigue/malaise (41.7%) and Long COVID (63.5%) diagnoses, plus common chest pain, arrhythmias, respiratory signs, headaches, musculoskeletal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and POTS-like symptoms (dizziness, giddiness), a constellation the authors suggest is consistent with ME/CFS.

Children younger than 4 years were almost exclusively assigned to the respiratory/cardiac subphenotype, split between a more severe lower respiratory cluster (with arrhythmias, fluid/electrolyte disturbance, hospitalizations, ICU admissions) and a less severe upper respiratory cluster (cough, fever, nasal congestion).

Female patients were relatively underrepresented in the respiratory/cardiac and musculoskeletal pain subphenotypes and overrepresented in the fatigue, headache, gastrointestinal, and neuropsychiatric subphenotypes.

Racial/ethnic subphenotype distributions differed: Hispanic patients were overrepresented in respiratory/cardiac and neuropsychiatric subphenotypes; non-Hispanic Black patients overrepresented in neuropsychiatric, musculoskeletal pain, and respiratory/cardiac subphenotypes; non-Hispanic Asian/Pacific-Islander patients overrepresented in respiratory/cardiac; non-Hispanic White patients overrepresented in fatigue, headache, and musculoskeletal pain subphenotypes.

Neuropsychiatric and gastrointestinal Long COVID subphenotypes appeared relatively close in embedding space to clusters from a matched non-COVID control cohort, whereas headache, fatigue, and respiratory/cardiac subphenotypes were further from control clusters, suggesting the former are harder to distinguish from a general care-seeking population.
Patients with an existing non-complex chronic condition were overrepresented in the gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric conditions subphenotypes.
Patients with more severe acute COVID-19 infection were classified almost entirely within the respiratory/cardiac subphenotype, specifically the lower respiratory, severe cluster.

Subphenotypes identified in the validation cohort (Cohort B) closely resembled those in the training cohort (Cohort A), with all six subphenotypes present in similar proportions, supporting the validity/reproducibility of the clustering approach.

A distinctly cardiac subphenotype and neurocognitive difficulties ("brain fog") commonly reported in Long COVID literature were not clearly identified in this EHR-based clustering, likely due to exclusion of MIS-C patients and under-ascertainment of brain fog in structured EHR codes.
The review proposes that salubrinal, which modulates endoplasmic reticulum/cellular stress responses, may have therapeutic potential to improve symptoms in ME/CFS and long-COVID.
The paper states that ME/CFS shares commonality with long-COVID, suggesting a shared clinical/pathophysiological relationship between the two conditions.

Six weeks of 16 g/day oral creatine monohydrate supplementation significantly increased total brain creatine concentration in the pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC) by 8.3% in ME/CFS patients.
Six weeks of creatine supplementation significantly increased brain creatine concentration in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) by 2.9%.
NAA levels did not change significantly after creatine supplementation in either the pgACC or DLPFC, indicating the observed effect was specific to creatine rather than a global metabolite shift.
Chalder Fatigue Scale (ChFS) scores significantly decreased after six weeks of creatine supplementation, indicating reduced fatigue.
Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) scores significantly decreased after six weeks of creatine supplementation.
Depression, pain, and sleep quality scores decreased numerically after creatine supplementation but did not reach statistical significance.
Reaction time on congruent trials of the Stroop test significantly decreased after six weeks of creatine supplementation.
Reaction time on incongruent trials of the Stroop test significantly decreased after six weeks of creatine supplementation.
Reaction time on 1-back trials of the N-back working memory task significantly decreased after creatine supplementation.
There was no significant change in inhibitory control (the RT difference between incongruent and congruent Stroop trials) after creatine supplementation.
Hand-grip strength significantly increased after six weeks of creatine supplementation in ME/CFS patients, the first reported ergogenic effect of creatine in this condition.
Change in pgACC creatine concentration significantly negatively correlated with change in reaction time on the congruent Stroop trial.
Change in pgACC creatine concentration significantly negatively correlated with change in reaction time on the incongruent Stroop trial.
Change in DLPFC creatine concentration significantly positively correlated with change in accuracy on 3-back trials of the N-back task.
No other significant correlations were found between change in brain creatine concentration and other cognitive measures, clinical symptom scores, or hand-grip strength.

Creatine monohydrate supplementation was generally well tolerated in ME/CFS patients, with no dropouts due to adverse events, though isolated cases of weight gain, nausea/vomiting, and sleep disturbance occurred.
A previously published 7T MRS study found lower creatine concentrations in the pgACC of ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, motivating the current supplementation study.
A prior MRSI study by Mueller et al. found decreased brain creatine in only 1 of 47 regions tested (parietal cortex) when comparing ME/CFS patients to healthy controls.

In a small placebo-controlled long COVID trial, 4 g/day creatine monohydrate for up to 6 months reduced fatigue and increased creatine levels in frontal and parietal white matter at 3 months, with effects plateauing by 6 months.
The increase in pgACC creatine concentration following supplementation was significantly correlated with a reduction in reaction time on the Stroop incongruent trials.
The increase in DLPFC creatine concentration was significantly correlated with improved accuracy on the 3-back trials of the N-back working memory task.

Apart from the two Stroop and one N-back correlations, changes in brain creatine concentration did not significantly correlate with changes in other cognitive measures, clinical symptom scores, or hand-grip strength.

Creatine monohydrate supplementation at 16 g/day was generally well tolerated over six weeks, with no participant discontinuing treatment, though isolated adverse effects (weight gain, nausea/vomiting, sleep disturbance) occurred.

A prior MRSI study by Mueller et al. found decreased brain creatine in ME/CFS patients relative to healthy controls in only 1 of 47 regions tested (the parietal cortex), in a cross-sectional design without any intervention.

In a placebo-controlled 16-week fibromyalgia trial, creatine monohydrate supplementation increased muscle phosphocreatine content and improved upper- and lower-body muscle strength, but did not change cognitive function including Stroop performance.

A randomised controlled trial in women with CFS found that 12 weeks of guanidinoacetic acid (a creatine precursor) supplementation increased muscle creatine concentration, improved functional performance, and improved specific fatigue subdomains.
A study of a low-dose creatine-containing polynutrient supplement in CFS patients failed to show benefits on fatigue severity or functional impairment.
Structural connectivity degree (number of connections) from the left anterior-inferior hypothalamus was increased in adolescents with ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
Structural connectivity degree from the right anterior-inferior hypothalamus was increased in adolescents with ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
Structural connectivity degree from the left anterior-superior hypothalamus was increased in adolescents with ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
Total structural connectivity degree of the left hypothalamus was increased in adolescents with ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
In contrast to degree, the strength (weight) of hypothalamus connections did not show significant evidence of difference between adolescents with ME/CFS and healthy controls.
A weak relationship between right intermediate hypothalamus connectivity strength and fatigue severity was found in the ME/CFS group, a relationship that was not present in healthy controls.
76.1% of ME/CFS participants had at least one of six chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPCs), compared to only 17.4% of healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia prevalence was 45.0% in ME/CFS participants, with a prevalence ratio of 147.74 compared to healthy controls, the highest among all COPCs studied.
Chronic low back pain prevalence was 33.1% in ME/CFS participants with a prevalence ratio of 39.45 versus healthy controls.
Interstitial cystitis/irritable bladder prevalence was significantly higher in ME/CFS with a prevalence ratio of 13.78 versus healthy controls.
Chronic migraine/headache was the most prevalent COPC among ME/CFS participants at 48.1%.
Irritable bowel syndrome prevalence was 31.6% among ME/CFS participants, significantly higher than healthy controls.
Endometriosis prevalence was not significantly different between female ME/CFS participants and female healthy controls.
Vulvodynia prevalence did not significantly differ between female ME/CFS participants and female healthy controls.

Chronic low back pain and fibromyalgia were each associated with a large impact on pain-related interference in ME/CFS, with BPI-Interference of Pain differences of 3.77 (Cohen's d=1.6) for cLBP and 2.39 (d=0.9) for FM.
cLBP and FM comorbidities were associated with significantly higher BPI Severity of Pain scores in ME/CFS participants (cLBP Δ=2.81, d=1.3; FM Δ=2.04, d=0.9).
Chronic migraine/headache comorbidity was associated with higher CDC-SI Headache severity scores in ME/CFS participants (Δ=4.04, d=0.9).
IBS comorbidity was associated with higher CDC-SI gastrointestinal symptom scores (stomach/abdominal pain Δ=3.14, d=0.8; diarrhea Δ=1.83, d=0.6) in ME/CFS participants.
IC/IB comorbidity was largely not significantly associated with pain measure differences in ME/CFS, except for CDC-SI Joint Pain.
FM, cLBP, and IC/IB comorbidities were associated with significantly worse SF-36 Physical Functioning scores in ME/CFS participants with moderate effect sizes.
FM and cLBP comorbidities were associated with increased post-exertional malaise (CDC-SI Fatigue After Exertion) in ME/CFS participants.
cMHA, FM, cLBP, and IBS comorbidities were each associated with worse PROMIS Sleep-Related Impairment scores in ME/CFS participants.

Combinations of multiple COPCs commonly co-occurred in ME/CFS participants: cMHA+FM was most common in those with two conditions, FM+cMHA+IBS in those with three, and cMHA+FM+IBS+cLBP in those with four; only two participants had all six COPCs.
Participants with long COVID had significantly higher BMI than healthy controls.
Monocyte counts differed nominally between groups (higher in HC and long COVID vs ME/CFS) but significance was lost after Bonferroni correction.
Basophil counts were nominally higher in HC compared with ME/CFS but did not remain significant after correction.
Both ME/CFS and long COVID participants reported significantly lower quality of life across all SF-36 domains compared with healthy controls.
Both ME/CFS and long COVID participants reported significantly higher disability levels across all WHODAS domains compared with healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients reported more difficulty in the WHODAS Self-Care domain than long COVID patients.
Comorbid fibromyalgia (n=2) and POTS (n=3) were reported among ME/CFS participants.
IBS was co-reported by 2 long COVID and 2 ME/CFS participants.
HLA-DQA1 was among the most strongly downregulated genes in long COVID compared with healthy controls.
HLA-DQB1 was significantly downregulated in long COVID compared with healthy controls.
KIR2DL5A/B was the most highly upregulated gene in long COVID compared with healthy controls.
A cluster of type I interferon alpha genes (IFNA4/7/10/17/21) was significantly downregulated in ME/CFS compared with healthy controls, contradicting prior reports of elevated IFNA in ME/CFS.
IGHG1 immunoglobulin gene was significantly downregulated in ME/CFS compared with healthy controls, suggesting possible immunodeficiency.
IFNA6 was significantly downregulated in ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
CEACAM3 was the most highly upregulated gene in ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
TNFAIP3 gene expression was significantly upregulated in both ME/CFS and long COVID compared with healthy controls, a shared overlapping gene.
Gene set analysis identified enrichment of PD-1, IL-6, TGF-β, antigen presentation, MAPK, and mTOR signaling pathways in long COVID compared with healthy controls.
Gene set analysis in ME/CFS identified enrichment of PPAR signaling, fatty acid metabolism, NK receptors, glycolysis/glucose import, anergy, B cell exhaustion, and epigenetic modification pathways.

Overlapping enriched gene sets between ME/CFS and long COVID included chemokine signaling, type I and II IFN signaling, TNF signaling, CTLA4 signaling, DAP12 signaling, JAK/STAT signaling, and other IL signaling.
The gene-expression-derived abundance of exhausted CD8 T cells was significantly lower in ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
The gene-expression-derived abundance of Tregs was significantly lower in ME/CFS compared with long COVID.

Top biological functions associated with differentially expressed genes in long COVID included abnormal lymphocyte morphology, leukocyte activation, immediate hypersensitivity, antigen-presenting cell activation, and lack of lymphocytes.

Top biological functions in ME/CFS included rosette formation, immune cell response, and myeloid cell activation, overlapping with long COVID only in leukocyte activation and antigen-presenting cell activation.

Canonical pathway analysis identified distinct top pathways for long COVID (antigen presentation, autoimmune thyroid disease signaling, allograft rejection signaling, B cell development) and ME/CFS (IL-12 signaling in macrophages, primary immunodeficiency signaling, rheumatoid arthritis-related signaling, neutrophil extracellular trap signaling), with macrophage alternative activation signaling shared between both.
HLA-DQA1, HLA-DQB1, and IGHG1 were identified as pivotal genes in top biological pathways/diseases in long COVID, overlapping with ME/CFS with the addition of IGHG3, CCL2, CEACAM3, and IFNA6.
PI3KR1 gene expression was significantly altered in both ME/CFS and long COVID participants, consistent with prior NanoString-based reports of altered protein kinase gene expression in severe ME/CFS.
RA patients recognized significantly fewer S. pneumoniae protein antigens on average (18) than the combined ME/CFS and healthy control group (40), indicating impaired antibody breadth in RA.

ME/CFS patients showed no significant difference from healthy volunteers in total or S. pneumoniae antigen-specific IgG levels, indicating that ME/CFS itself does not impair naturally acquired antibody responses to S. pneumoniae.
RA sera showed significantly weaker IgG responses to multiple individual pneumococcal antigens compared to controls, including the immunodominant antigens PspA, PsaA, Ply, PiuA and PiaA.

IgG responses to a panel of human respiratory viral protein antigens showed no significant differences between RA, ME/CFS, and healthy control cohorts, indicating the reduced pneumococcal antibody response in RA is pathogen-specific rather than a generalized antibody deficiency.

Aggregate IgG binding to S. pneumoniae protein antigens measured by array correlated with functional whole-cell ELISA and flow cytometry IgG opsonization of live S. pneumoniae in both RA and ME/CFS subjects, supporting the functional relevance of the array-measured antibody deficits.

IgG opsonization of S. pneumoniae correlated with array-measured IgG levels to six specific antigens (PsaA, PspA, Ply, PiaA, PiuA and PspC), most of which showed significantly reduced responses in RA sera, supporting a functional consequence of the RA antibody deficit for pathogen clearance.
Rituximab (B-cell depletion) therapy caused a small but statistically significant decrease in total serum IgG in RA patients.
Rituximab treatment had no detectable effect on whole-cell ELISA IgG recognition of S. pneumoniae serotype 4 or 35B strains in RA patients.
Flow cytometry assays showed a fall in IgG opsonization of S. pneumoniae serotype 4 (TIGR4), but not serotype 35B, following rituximab treatment in RA patients.

Array analysis of the top 170 ranked pneumococcal antigens identified four proteins (SP_0283, SP_0908, SP_1034 and SP_1890) with significantly reduced IgG in post-rituximab RA sera, while overall antigen breadth and aggregate IgG were unchanged.

Individual-level analysis showed that 24 of 31 RA subjects had significant changes (increases, decreases, or mixed) in IgG recognition of five or more pneumococcal antigens after rituximab, contrasting with the stable antibody repertoire observed in ME/CFS control sera collected 6 months apart.

Aggregate anti-pneumococcal IgG levels did not correlate with total serum IgG levels or with anti-CCP autoantibody levels in RA patients, indicating the pneumococcal antibody deficit is not simply due to global hypogammaglobulinemia or overall autoimmune disease severity.
Aggregate anti-S. pneumoniae IgG levels correlated weakly with age, being lower in both RA and control subjects aged 56 years and older.
Mongelli and colleagues found evidence of DNA methylation-based biological age acceleration (DeltaAge) in PACS patients, particularly pronounced in younger individuals, compared to controls.
PACS patients showed significant telomere shortening in peripheral blood compared to controls.
ACE2 expression in peripheral blood was reduced in PACS patients compared to controls.

Huoman et al. used a genome-wide DNA methylation approach and found overrepresentation of differentially methylated genes in the Wnt signalling, muscarinic/acetylcholine receptor, and gonadotropin-releasing hormone pathways in PACS/long-COVID patients.

Yin and colleagues found differentially methylated regions in transposable elements and immune/stress response genes, indicating mild activation of transposable elements and incomplete recovery of immune-related genes in long-COVID patients.
Lee and colleagues found significant CpG hypomethylation at the IFI44L gene, involved in innate immune activation, in PACS patients (8-12 weeks post-infection) compared to controls.
Lee and colleagues found significant CpG hypomethylation at the ANKRD9 gene, involved in Class I MHC-mediated antigen processing and presentation, in PACS patients compared to controls.
Contrary to Mongelli et al., Lee and colleagues found no evidence of epigenetic age acceleration in PACS patients compared to controls.
Lee et al. found no significant genome-wide DNA methylation differences between patients with long-COVID (symptomatic ≥3 months) and infected-but-recovered participants.

Nikesjö et al. found significant differential DNA methylation in the SNORD3B, CETP and DLGAP1 genes in long-COVID patients, implicating angiotensin II/G-protein signalling, histamine H1 receptor signalling, PI3 kinase pathway and muscarinic acetylcholine receptor (CHRM1/3) signalling.
Balnis and colleagues identified 71 differentially methylated regions in immune and inflammation-related pathways in long-COVID patients one year after infection compared to controls.
Circulating miR-21 and profibrotic transcripts (TGF-β, Col1A2, Col3A1, α-SMA) were significantly increased in long-COVID patients with ARDS-related lung abnormalities compared to controls.
miR-21 showed high diagnostic value, differentiating long-COVID patients with ARDS-related lung abnormalities from controls with over 72% sensitivity and over 80% specificity.

Garcia-Hidalgo and colleagues found distinct circulating miRNA profiles associated with radiologic abnormalities (miR-9, miR-24, miR-221, miR-21) and with reduced carbon monoxide diffusion capacity (miR-17, miR-27a, miR-126, miR-495, miR-146a) in ARDS-related long-COVID patients.
Risk factors for developing long-COVID include female sex and younger age, contrasting with acute COVID-19 severity/mortality risk factors of older age and male sex.

The authors highlight that long-COVID symptoms closely resemble those of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), including profound fatigue, sleep and cognitive disturbances, and post-exertional symptom exacerbation, with ME/CFS frequently reported to begin after a viral infection.
Participants with a CFS diagnosis showed significantly reduced overall physical movement compared to controls using UK Biobank actigraphy data.
CFS participants exhibited lower activity amplitude (a measure of circadian activity rhythm strength) compared to controls.
CFS participants had lower wrist temperature amplitude compared to controls, indicating altered daily temperature rhythms.
One of 30 SNVs previously reported as associated with CFS was also significantly associated with subjective fatigue symptoms in the general (control) population.
One of 30 SNVs previously reported as associated with CFS was also significantly associated with actigraphic measurements in the general (control) population.

At long-term follow-up (average 3 years post-infection), 90.2% of discharged patients continued to experience long COVID symptoms and had not returned to their pre-COVID-19 health state, while only 9.8% reported full recovery.
Despite most patients not fully recovering, 64.2% of those still symptomatic reported their symptoms were the same or had improved since discharge from the service.
EQ-5D-5L index scores significantly improved from a mean of 0.52 at service entry to 0.65 at discharge, exceeding the minimal clinically important difference.
C19-YRSm Symptom Severity scores improved significantly from a mean of 18.4 at initial assessment to 13 at discharge, exceeding the minimal clinically important difference of 4.
Functional Disability scores decreased from a mean of 6.7 to 5.9 during service engagement, but this change did not reach clinical significance.
Overall Health scores improved from a mean of 4.9 to 6 at discharge but did not return to the pre-COVID-19 average of 7.3.
EQ-5D-5L VAS scores improved by a clinically significant mean of 13.1 points between initial assessment and discharge from the service.
Despite improvement during service engagement, the mean EQ-5D-5L index value of 0.65 at discharge remained well below that of the healthy population (0.92).
After discharge from the service, symptom severity worsened significantly, with average C19-YRSm symptom severity increasing from 13 at discharge to 15.1 at follow-up.
Average EQ-5D-5L index scores dropped below discharge levels by 0.12 after discharge from the service, representing a significant deterioration in functional levels.
EQ-5D-5L VAS scores deteriorated between discharge and follow-up by 7.3 points (from 65 to 57.7), narrowly missing the clinical significance threshold of 7.5.
Employment status was adversely affected in 43% of the cohort at follow-up, with 20% having retired or changed jobs due to long COVID.
43% of the sample (48 of 112 patients) met NICE diagnostic criteria for suspected ME/CFS at long-term follow-up after long COVID.
40% of participants reported more than three other significant health problems at follow-up, indicating new-onset comorbidities attributed to ongoing long COVID.

The mean EQ-5D-5L index value at post-discharge follow-up (0.53) was comparable to the mean EQ-5D-5L index scores reported for other long-term conditions such as COPD, heart failure and multiple sclerosis.
Participants reported a total of 52 new referrals to NHS services (excluding GP visits) after discharge from the long COVID service, reflecting ongoing healthcare need and flare-ups.
The 43% prevalence of suspected ME/CFS found in this long COVID cohort is broadly consistent with prior literature reporting 45.2-58% of long COVID patients meeting ME/CFS criteria.
Patients who had COVID-19 had a significantly higher risk of developing chronic fatigue syndrome compared to matched patients without COVID-19.

Subgroup analyses showed increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome after COVID-19 across different age groups, sexes, races, and comorbid conditions, with the increase being particularly significant in adults aged 18 years and older.

Latent Class Growth Analysis identified four distinct fatigue trajectory subgroups among CFS patients undergoing CBT: no improvement (23%), weak improvement (45%), moderate improvement (23%), and strong improvement (9%).
Higher pre-treatment levels of depressive symptoms predicted membership in the 'no improvement' fatigue trajectory subgroup during CBT.
Higher pre-treatment levels of anxiety symptoms predicted membership in the 'no improvement' fatigue trajectory subgroup during CBT.
Higher pre-treatment levels of somatic symptoms predicted membership in the 'no improvement' fatigue trajectory subgroup during CBT.
Higher pre-treatment levels of perceived stress predicted membership in the 'no improvement' fatigue trajectory subgroup during CBT.
Lower pre-treatment levels of positive affect predicted membership in the 'no improvement' fatigue trajectory subgroup during CBT.
Cross-lagged structural equation modelling showed that reductions in anxiety symptoms preceded reductions in fatigue during CBT.
The relationship between depressive symptoms and fatigue during CBT was found to be bidirectional in cross-lagged modelling.
At the group level, participants showed a statistically significant reduction in fatigue over the course of 15 sessions of CBT, despite substantial individual variability in response.
Cross-lagged modeling suggested that reductions in perceived stress preceded improvements in fatigue during CBT.
Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) was found to be common among patients with Parkinson's disease, present in 66.7% of the PD cohort.
Non-motor symptoms of PD, including emotional-affective, cognitive, autonomic disorders and pain, were more common in patients with concurrent CFS.
Serum CCL5 concentration showed a strong correlation with the severity of chronic fatigue syndrome as measured by FSS in PD patients.
Serum soluble VCAM-1 concentration correlated strongly with CFS severity in PD patients.
Serum NCAM concentration correlated strongly with CFS severity in PD patients.
Serum soluble ICAM-1 concentration correlated strongly with CFS severity in PD patients.
In newly diagnosed, treatment-naive PD patients with CFS, correlations between serum inflammatory markers and CFS severity were stronger than seen overall.
Genotype and allele frequencies of the CCL5 rs2107538 polymorphism differed significantly between PD patients and controls.
Genotype and allele frequencies of the PAI-1 rs2227631 polymorphism differed significantly between PD patients and controls.
The CCL5 rs2107538 polymorphism did not influence the variability of serum CCL5 protein levels in patients with PD.
The PAI-1 rs2227631 polymorphism did not influence the variability of serum PAI-1 protein levels in patients with PD.
Neither the CCL5 nor PAI-1 gene polymorphisms studied were associated with the development of chronic fatigue syndrome in patients with Parkinson's disease.
Genotype and allele distributions of CCL5 rs2107538 and PAI-1 rs2227631 differed between PD patients and controls.
A meta-analysis of six RCTs found that qigong, tai chi, or yoga significantly reduced physical fatigue severity compared with control interventions in adults with CFS or PCS.
The same six-RCT meta-analysis found a significant reduction in mental fatigue with mindful exercises compared with control interventions.

A meta-analysis of six RCTs (including one PCS trial) showed a significant reduction in overall fatigue with mindful exercises compared with control interventions, with moderate heterogeneity attributed to the single PCS trial using aerobic training as control.
A meta-analysis of four RCTs using qigong or yoga in adults with CFS found significantly reduced anxiety symptoms compared with control interventions.
A meta-analysis of four RCTs using qigong or yoga in adults with CFS found significantly decreased depressive symptoms compared with control interventions.
A meta-analysis of three RCTs using qigong in adults with CFS found qigong significantly improved sleep quality compared with control interventions.
Four of the included RCTs reported minor and transient adverse events associated with the mindful exercise interventions, such as dizziness, fatigue, pain, or diarrhea.

The review cites prior evidence that graded exercise therapy (GET), unlike the low-intensity mindful exercises studied here, has been reported to elicit large negative symptom responses in more than half of CFS patients, underscoring safety concerns distinct from the mindful exercise interventions evaluated.
Females were far more likely than males to be diagnosed with hEDS or HMS compared to the sex distribution in the general population.
Patients diagnosed with hEDS or HMS were significantly older on average than the general population comparator group.
Over half of hEDS patients and over 40% of HMS patients were diagnosed with a gastrointestinal-related condition, making digestive disorders the most prevalent comorbidity in both groups.
A substantial proportion of hEDS and HMS patients had at least one cardiac condition, most commonly tachycardia, palpitations, and orthostatic hypotension.
Respiratory disorders (including asthma) were substantially more common in hEDS and HMS patients than in the general population.
Anxiety and neurodevelopmental disorders (autism, ADHD) were highly prevalent among hEDS patients.
Neurodevelopmental disorders including autism and ADHD were present in nearly a quarter of hEDS patients.
A quarter of HMS patients had a diagnosis of anxiety, and about a fifth had a developmental disorder.

Although each individually affected under 5% of all populations, eating disorders, addiction, and obsessive compulsive disorder all showed increased prevalence in hEDS and HMS relative to the general population.
Depression rates were equivalent across hEDS, HMS, and general population groups, with no statistically significant difference.
Multisystem diagnoses (co-occurring systemic disorders) were far more common among hEDS and HMS patients than the general population.
Fewer hEDS and HMS patients had no additional systemic diagnosis compared to the general population, indicating higher comorbidity burden.
Over a quarter of hEDS patients had more than three systemic diagnoses, representing a substantial cumulative disease burden.
In the youngest age bracket (10-14 years), digestive disorders, neurodevelopmental disorders, and eating disorders did not differ significantly between the hEDS group and the general population.
The prevalence of a POTS-like phenotype observed in this hEDS/HMS cohort is consistent with prior literature estimates ranging from 5% to 41%.

Excessive connective tissue elasticity is proposed to cause enlargement of the gastrointestinal wall, activating mechanoreceptors responsible for bloating sensation and altering motility/gas transit in hEDS/HMS.

Connective tissue laxity impairing vasoconstriction is proposed to cause orthostatic blood pooling and intolerance, which combined with peripheral neuropathy may drive autonomic impairment in hEDS/HMS.
Asthma symptoms in hEDS/HMS may be attributable to aberrant mast cell activation, which may contribute to dysfunction across multiple organ systems.
A prior study cited by the authors found that 66% of hEDS patients also met diagnostic criteria for MCAS.
In an allergy/immunology clinic cohort of 974 patients, 10% had both MCAS and hEDS/HSD, and 19% had MCAS, hEDS/HSD, and immunoglobulin deficiency together.
Immunohistochemistry from a cited prior study found increased chymase, a mast cell mediator, in undamaged skin of patients with connective tissue disorder features.
A cited prior study reported a higher incidence of recurrent infections, particularly urinary tract infections, in hEDS patients versus the general population.
A cited functional analysis of fibroblasts from JHS/hEDS patients found altered immune responses including decreased cytokine production, possibly contributing to increased infection risk.
A National Inpatient Sample analysis cited by the authors found that nearly one in three patients diagnosed with MCAS have a comorbid diagnosis of hEDS.
In this study's cohort, 61.1% of hEDS participants reported a history of recurrent infections compared to 28.5% of first-degree relative controls.
72.2% of hEDS participants had a documented medical history of mast cell hypersensitivity compared to 14.2% of controls.

A protein-protein interaction network of hEDS-specific gene variants showed significantly more interactions than expected by chance, clustering into six functional groups including antigen presentation, mucosal genes, collagen genes, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial OXPHOS, and triplet repeat expansion genes.
The first PPI cluster of hEDS-specific variant genes involved antigen processing and presentation via MHC complex genes including HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C, HLA-DRB1, and HLA-DRB5.
A second PPI cluster related to defective GALNT3/HFTC included mucosal barrier genes MUC3A, MUC16, MUC19, and ZNF717, suggesting a possible mechanism for infection susceptibility in hEDS.
A third PPI cluster of hEDS-specific variants was associated with collagen chain trimerization and extracellular matrix structural constituents, including COL4A2, COL6A2, and MMP16.
A fifth PPI cluster was associated with the mitochondrial complex I assembly/OXPHOS system, including MT-CYB, MT-ND1, EMC1, and ACAD9.

Expanding the PPI network with known EDS-related genes revealed additional hEDS-specific variant genes (COL6A2, COL6A6, COL4A2, COL12A1, COL24A1, KMT2E, FNDC1, ZNF521, PHACTR1, MMP16) interconnected with established collagen-metabolism EDS genes.

Expanding the PPI network with known MCAS genes revealed additional hEDS-specific variant genes interconnected with MCAS-related genes, with yellow-node genes implicated in inflammatory responses and positive regulation of IL-10 production.
88% (16 of 18) of hEDS subjects carried at least one variant in genes linked to mast cell activation syndrome.
Five key genes (MT-CYB, HTT, MUC3A, HLA-B, HLA-DRB1) were identified, with 94% of hEDS subjects carrying at least one variation among them.

A novel missense variant, HLA-B p.(Leu119Trp), was the most common variant identified among hEDS participants, present in over half of them and absent in controls, proposed as a potential hEDS biomarker.
The authors propose that MT-CYB variants may contribute to mast cell dysregulation in hEDS via impaired mitochondrial ATP production needed for FcεRI-dependent mast cell activation.
The authors propose that HTT variants may contribute to immune dysregulation in hEDS given HTT's role in cytokine production processes in mast cells.
Variants in ZNF521, ZNF717, RUNX2, and MMP16, genes implicated in bone mineralization and osteoblast differentiation, may explain higher fracture rates observed in hEDS patients.
The authors cite prior literature linking HLA-B and HLA-DRB1 variants to osteoporosis and reduced bone mineral density via immune-mediated pathways, suggesting relevance to hEDS bone health.
A cited prior study found that mitochondrial DNA variants influence bone mineral density and osteoporosis risk, supporting a possible mitochondrial contribution to bone health impairment in hEDS.
The patient was diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome based on a COL3A1 gene mutation identified 8 years prior, following a spontaneous right common iliac artery dissection.

The patient developed a spontaneous coronary artery dissection (type 2, distal right coronary artery) causing a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, 24 hours after presenting with multiple peripheral arterial dissections.

CT angiography identified multiple concurrent extra-coronary arterial dissections and haematomas (right subclavian artery, chronic right external iliac dissection, new left external iliac dissection) along with bilateral renal and splenic infarcts, in this EDS patient.
A sirolimus-eluting stent was successfully implanted in the dissected right coronary artery, restoring distal coronary flow.

Optical coherence tomography and subsequent coronary CT revealed an intramural haematoma extending through the stented and proximal RCA and an additional haematoma in the mid-distal left anterior descending artery that was not visible on the initial coronary angiogram, demonstrating the added diagnostic value of multimodal imaging.

Total hip arthroplasty performed in patients with Ehlers Danlos Syndrome was associated with satisfactory clinical and radiological outcomes and no significant complications at a median 3-year follow-up.
One EDS patient undergoing THA developed post-operative surgical wound erythema that resolved within 48 hours, representing the only notable wound complication in the series.
The majority of EDS patients undergoing THA had a chronic history of low back pain and were smokers.
Vascular EDS is estimated to occur in about 1 in 50,000 people and Classical EDS in about 1 in 20,000-40,000.
A Welsh population study reported a combined prevalence of hEDS and Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder of 1 in 500.
Hypermobile EDS accounts for roughly 90% of all EDS cases but still lacks an identified genetic marker.
In a 2,491-patient genetic study cohort, most participants self-reported joint subluxations (90%), a majority reported dislocations (60%), and the large majority reported chronic pain (89%).
Morlino et al. found that 70% of 189 EDS/hypermobility clinic patients had dislocated a joint at least once (most often shoulders, TMJ, hips) and 83% had spine problems.
Patients with significant hypermobility (37% with EDS) had more surgeries, at more joint sites, and at a younger age compared to a chronic pain group without hypermobility.
A retrospective review of 150 EDS orthopedic surgery patients found a 91% complication rate and an infection rate more than 18 times the institution's baseline.

In patients undergoing open shoulder capsular reconstruction, EDS patients had significantly lower postoperative ASES functional scores than a non-EDS hyperlaxity syndrome group, despite similar preoperative scores.
Open inferior capsular shift surgery for multidirectional shoulder instability in adolescents with EDS or hyperlaxity produced good satisfaction and functional scores at long-term follow-up.
Shoulder arthroplasty in EDS patients with osteoarthritis or rotator cuff arthropathy improved mean VAS pain scores from 6.5 to 1.7 with comparable range-of-motion gains to matched controls.
Achilles allograft-augmented capsulorraphy for shoulder instability in EDS achieved stability in 4 of 5 shoulders with improved ASES and VAS pain scores.
Total knee arthroplasty in EDS patients improved Knee Society Functional Score from pre-surgery to post-surgery and follow-up, though scores remained lower than typical TKA outcomes.
In a matched cohort study, EDS patients undergoing TKA were not at increased risk of revision compared to osteoarthritis controls, although the EDS cohort had more prior knee surgeries.

Medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction in EDS restored patellar stability but had a 19.1% failure rate at midterm follow-up, with worse failure predictors and inferior patient-reported outcomes than non-EDS populations.

EDS patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty had higher rates of perioperative dislocation and lower implant survival than matched controls, with significantly increased odds of revision at 5 years.
In a matched case-control study, EDS patients had a higher post-op dislocation rate after THA than controls, though reoperation, revision rates and Harris Hip Scores did not differ significantly.

EDS patients undergoing anterior cervical discectomy and fusion had significantly higher 90-day complication rates and a 15-fold increase in anterior revision rates at 2 years compared to matched controls.

In a propensity-matched study of transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion, EDS patients had a higher risk of adjacent segment disease at 36 months compared to matched controls, with no difference in overall complications or pseudoarthrosis.
In a pediatric NSQIP database analysis, EDS patients undergoing spine surgery did not differ from non-EDS patients in 30-day reoperations, wound infection, or overall complications.
A large genetic study of 2,491 EDS participants found high self-reported rates of joint subluxations, dislocations, and chronic pain.
Morlino et al. found that 70% of 189 patients seen at an EDS/hypermobility clinic had dislocated a joint at least once, most commonly shoulders, TMJ, and hips, and 83% had spine problems.
Wright et al. found that patients with significant hypermobility had more surgeries at multiple joint sites and at a younger age compared to patients with chronic pain syndrome without hypermobility.
Yonko et al. reported a 91% complication rate for musculoskeletal surgery in an EDS cohort, with an infection rate more than 18 times the institution's baseline.
Across five elbow surgery reports totaling 16 patients, all reported good outcomes including functional improvement, no recurrent subluxations, and excellent range of motion.
Across hand surgery reports of 16 EDS patients, outcomes were generally favorable including improved pain and grip strength, though 2 patients had resolved complications.
Hevesi et al. found that operative thumbs showed a trend toward improved pain and grip strength, while non-operative patients had decreasing thumb range of motion over time.
Dermatis et al. reported that minimally invasive ankle/rearfoot stabilization surgery in hEDS patients improved pain, function, and reduced ankle sprains at greater than 6 months follow-up.
Erickson and Wolman noted that soft tissue ankle ligament repair and joint stabilization procedures have relatively high failure rates and recurrent instability in EDS patients.
Beijk et al. reported that sacroiliac joint fusion using a proprietary device was satisfactory in 8 of 10 EDS patients, though 2 required revision surgery.

The scoping review identified 71 manuscripts from 1990-2023 on orthopaedic surgery outcomes in EDS, finding no randomized controlled trials or systematic reviews and mostly non-standardized outcome measures.

The Beighton Score, though standard for diagnosing generalized joint hypermobility in EDS, has limitations for surgical decision-making and outcome measurement because it does not address functional joint stability.

The Pediatric Spine Study Group's multicenter prospective registry found that non-operative casting and bracing postponed surgical intervention in a small sample of EDS/connective tissue disorder patients with moderate early onset scoliosis.

The review's authors state that the rate of surgical failure is clearly higher in persons with EDS, particularly for procedures involving ligament repair, due to inferior biomechanical properties of collagen-containing structures.
Five studies using magnetic resonance arthrography found statistically significant increases in capsular cross-sectional area in patients with atraumatic shoulder hypermobility/instability.
Two studies reported significant superior capsular elongation on MRA in patients with multidirectional instability.

Labrocapsular distance, glenocapsular ratio, and the combined sail and triangle sign on MRA were reported as highly sensitive and specific imaging parameters for identifying multidirectional instability.
Findings regarding alterations of glenohumeral anatomy were inconsistent across included studies.
Ultrasound-measured acromiohumeral distance was significantly increased in patients with multidirectional instability, but not in those with hypermobility alone.
Muscle activity measured by electromyography and glenohumeral translations differed significantly in patients with multidirectional instability but not in those with hypermobility alone.

The review concludes there are no definitive imaging markers for diagnosing atraumatic shoulder hypermobility in the absence of multidirectional instability, despite useful markers existing for MDI itself.
Glenohumeral translation measurements differed significantly in patients with multidirectional instability but not in shoulders with hypermobility alone.
Studies examining glenohumeral bony anatomy in atraumatic shoulder hypermobility yielded inconsistent findings across the included studies.
The review concludes that no definitive imaging markers currently exist for diagnosing atraumatic shoulder hypermobility in the absence of multidirectional instability.

In healthy subjects, six of seven cervical spine radiographic measurements (clivo-axial angle, basion-dens interval, Grabb-Oakes/perpendicular basion measurement, hard palate to C1, hard palate to C2, and one other) differed significantly between flexion and extension x-ray positions.
Basion-axial interval and atlanto-dental interval measurements did not differ significantly between flexion and extension x-ray positions in healthy patients.
Clivo-axial angle, hard palate to C1, and hard palate to C2 showed the lowest coefficients of variance across imaging modalities, suggesting greater measurement reliability.

The study establishes normative reference ranges and variability for seven cervical spine radiographic measurements in a healthy population, intended to aid diagnosis of craniocervical instability, a condition common in connective tissue disease such as Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome.

A pathogenic homozygous autosomal recessive nonsense mutation in the P3H1 gene was identified by clinical exome analysis as the cause of a non-lethal form of osteogenesis imperfecta type VIII in a female toddler presenting with short stature, limb hypermobility, and recurrent fractures.
The patient was started on cyclical pamidronate infusion therapy for management of her osteogenesis imperfecta, though treatment outcomes were not reported.

In a Danish population survey, 13% of adults reported generalised joint hypermobility including knee joint hypermobility, and half of these reported knee pain greater than those without hypermobility.
Individuals with knee joint hypermobility often experience decreased physical function, reduced quality of life, and increased risk of developing osteoarthritis in addition to chronic knee pain.
Reduced stiffness of passive tissues (tendons and ligaments) and impaired neuromuscular function are hypothesised to underlie symptoms and joint instability in people with knee joint hypermobility.

High-load strength training produces similar benefits to low-intensity training for reducing knee pain and improving proprioception and function, while additionally increasing muscle cross-sectional area, neural drive, and tendon stiffness.

In a pilot feasibility study of 16 young women with symptomatic knee joint hypermobility, high-load strength training was well tolerated and led to substantial reductions in knee pain, improved muscle strength, functional performance, and knee proprioception, plus increased patellar tendon stiffness.

In a survey of 13 Danish primary care physiotherapists external to the study, 11 (85%) agreed or strongly agreed that the study's standard care exercise programme was suitable for training patients with hypermobile joints and knee pain.
GJH subjects showed significantly greater postural sway (SWAY) than healthy controls during eyes-open static balance testing.
GJH subjects had significantly higher center-of-pressure displacement amplitude (RMS) than healthy controls in the eyes-open condition.
GJH subjects showed significantly greater postural sway (SWAY) than healthy controls in the eyes-closed condition, indicating reliance on visual input for balance.
GJH subjects had significantly higher center-of-pressure displacement amplitude (RMS) than healthy controls in the eyes-closed condition.
GJH subjects walked significantly slower than healthy controls during the 15 m walk test.
GJH subjects had significantly shorter stride length than healthy controls.
The percentage of the gait cycle spent in the loading response phase did not differ significantly between GJH and healthy subjects.
GJH subjects spent a significantly greater percentage of the gait cycle in the flat-foot phase compared to healthy controls.
The percentage of the gait cycle spent in the push-off phase did not differ significantly between GJH and healthy subjects.
GJH subjects spent a significantly smaller percentage of the gait cycle in the swing phase compared to healthy controls, a finding contrasting with most prior studies.

Across the included rare genetic syndromes, the incidence of hip problems (dysplasia, subluxation, dislocation) ranged from 12% to 35%, far exceeding general population rates of 1-1.5% (5/1000 male, 13/1000 female infants).

In Kabuki syndrome, hip health problems were found in 10-12% of infants and in 18-40% of studies including older children and adults, with risk factors including ligamentous laxity, joint hypermobility, and hypotonia.
In 49,XXXXY (Fraccaro) syndrome, hip dysplasia was found in 14% of a pooled cohort, increasing with age from 3.2% under 5 years to 17.1% in individuals over 10 years.
Hip dysplasia occurred in 8-30% of individuals with Prader-Willi syndrome, with 1.4-11.25% requiring surgical intervention.
In the most recent Prader-Willi syndrome cohort with the youngest participants, hip dysplasia improved with age in those treated with growth hormone, and only 1 of 72 required acetabuloplasty.
Incidence of hip dysplasia/subluxation in PURA syndrome ranged from 11% to 28%, and hypotonia was identified beyond infancy in 79.9% of individuals.

In cohorts including children with Koolen de Vries syndrome, hip dislocation or dysplasia was reported in 7.4% to 12.5%, hypotonia was present in 96% in infancy and 83-88% at older ages, and joint hypermobility was reported in 85% of children.
Hip subluxation or dislocation was reported in 47% of cases of Emanuel (4p-) syndrome, with significant centrally based hypotonia present in all individuals.
Hip dysplasia or subluxation were reported in 25-26% of cases with TRPM3-related disorders, and hypotonia was present in 75% of the reported cases.

Two of ten children with Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome had bilateral hip dislocation, and poor bone quality led to non-union or fracture following hip surgeries including varus derotation osteotomies and acetabuloplasty.

In a retrospective cohort of 63 children with mostly undiagnosed developmental central hypotonia, a hip migration percentage above 33% was more common in children older than 8 years and was associated with higher GMFCS levels, with four children requiring surgery.

Across 15 of 79 included studies discussing risk factors, joint or ligamentous laxity was the most highly reported risk factor for hip problems (8 studies), followed by hypermobility and hypotonia (5 studies each).
In children with Kabuki syndrome, 2 years of growth hormone treatment was associated with decreased hypermobility (from 60% to 6%) and improved motor control.

Conservative treatment (splinting, casting, traction, open/closed reduction, soft-tissue releases) was successful in 13 children while 13 others required additional pelvic and/or femoral osteotomies; osteotomies were successful in 21 children while 10 required surgical revision due to re-dislocation or fracture.

The review explicitly excluded diagnoses where joint hypermobility, ligamentous laxity, and hip issues relate to a connective tissue disorder such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, distinguishing these from developmental central hypotonia-related hip pathology.

The authors recommend hip ultrasound screening between 6 weeks and 6 months of age for all infants with significant hypotonia regardless of diagnosis, plus annual orthopaedic review with radiographs starting at 12 months.

A migration percentage greater than 33% was most common in children with developmental central hypotonia older than 8 years, in contrast to children with cerebral palsy and spasticity where this threshold is more commonly reached between 3 and 5 years of age.
Mean electrochemical skin conductance (mESC) of hands and feet, measured by SUDOSCAN, was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Moderate-to-severe small fiber neuropathy, defined by SUDOSCAN mESC cut-offs, was more prevalent in fibromyalgia patients (68.2%) than in healthy controls (50%, with no severe cases).
CAN-RS (cardiac autonomic neuropathy risk score) tended to be higher in fibromyalgia patients than controls, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Serum serotonin levels were non-significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls.
