Serum tryptophan levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum substance P levels were non-significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls.
Health-related quality of life, measured by EQ5D and EQ5D visual analogue scale, was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.

Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score (total and symptom, reflex, sensory subscores) was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls, indicating greater neuropathy symptom burden.
Vibration perception threshold and deep pressure pain perception threshold did not significantly differ between fibromyalgia and control groups.
SNAP amplitudes of the right sural and right superficial peroneal sensory nerves were significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients than controls.
EMG parameters (onset latency, CMAP amplitude, conduction velocity, F-waves) of right tibial and median motor nerves were comparable between fibromyalgia and control groups.

SNAP amplitudes of bilateral distal sensory nerves (medial plantar, dorsal sural, medial dorsal cutaneous) were significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls, indicating distal sensory neuropathy even without proximal nerve abnormality.
Onset latencies of right medial plantar, left medial dorsal cutaneous, and left dorsal sural nerves were significantly higher (prolonged) in the fibromyalgia group compared with controls.
In fibromyalgia patients, hands and feet mESC values were negatively correlated with fibromyalgia disease duration, suggesting worsening small fiber damage with disease progression.
Hands and feet mESC were negatively correlated with the serum tryptophan-to-serotonin ratio in fibromyalgia patients.
Serum serotonin levels were positively correlated with hands and feet mESC in fibromyalgia patients, linking lower serotonin to greater small fiber dysfunction.
Total fibromyalgia impact questionnaire (FIQ) score, widespread pain index, and pain VAS score were not significantly correlated with hand or foot mESC values.

Fibromyalgia patients who responded to tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) therapy had significantly higher (more preserved) baseline mESC values than non-responders, and non-responders had a much higher prevalence of moderate-to-severe SFN.
Only the waking component of the FIQ and the symptom severity score showed a significant correlation with hand mESC values, unlike other FIQ subscores.
Pioneering studies by Staud and Vierck demonstrated central sensitization in fibromyalgia patients, showing enhanced sensitivity to pain and exaggerated responses to normally non-painful stimuli.

An fMRI study by Gracely et al. (2002) found that fibromyalgia patients showed heightened activity in pain-processing brain regions (insula, anterior cingulate cortex) in response to stimuli perceived as non-painful by healthy controls.

Increased resting-state functional connectivity within the default mode network (posterior cingulate cortex and medial prefrontal cortex) has been associated with widespread pain and cognitive dysfunction in fibromyalgia.

The insula and salience network are often hyperactive in nociplastic pain (including fibromyalgia), producing exaggerated responses to both painful and non-painful sensory stimuli such as light and sound.

Hyperconnectivity between the amygdala and pain-processing regions (insula, anterior cingulate cortex) is associated with amplified emotional/affective dimensions of pain and distress in fibromyalgia, making the amygdala a proposed neurofeedback target.
Some studies have found reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density in a subset of fibromyalgia patients, suggesting a possible small fiber neuropathy component underlying widespread pain.

The role of small fiber neuropathy in nociplastic pain (including fibromyalgia) remains controversial, as nerve fiber density findings are inconsistent across studies and may reflect secondary neuroplastic changes rather than a primary cause.
Autonomic dysfunction, including orthostatic intolerance, gastrointestinal disturbances, and excessive sweating, is commonly reported in fibromyalgia and other nociplastic pain conditions.

Some studies suggest dysregulated autonomic responses such as abnormal heart rate variability or blood pressure changes may contribute to heightened pain sensitivity and fatigue in nociplastic pain patients, though causality remains unclear.

SNRIs (duloxetine, milnacipran) and tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline) are recommended as first-line centrally acting pharmacologic options for nociplastic pain/fibromyalgia, though efficacy varies among patients.

Gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin) may be considered for patients with a prominent neuropathic component, but their utility in purely nociplastic pain remains unclear, with inconsistent results across clinical trials.

Cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBTi) is more effective than sleep hygiene alone at improving sleep quality and reducing pain sensitivity in chronic pain conditions like fibromyalgia, and is associated with reductions in pain severity, fatigue, cognitive difficulties, and changes in brain connectivity.

Some studies suggest hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) may reduce central sensitization and improve symptoms in fibromyalgia patients, but overall evidence is weak and it is not widely endorsed, with BACPAP recommending it be considered experimental.
The amygdala has been identified as a potential therapeutic target for neuromodulation via neurofeedback for treating fibromyalgia symptoms.

Pressure pain threshold (PPT) measurement via algometry is a widely used, objective method for assessing central sensitization and detecting allodynia in fibromyalgia and chronic low back pain patients.
Fibromyalgia patients show substantially reduced muscle oxygen saturation compared to healthy norms, with decreases of up to 20% from an expected average of about 75%.
Fibromyalgia patients exhibit diminished oxygen levels and suboptimal oxygen extraction in muscles during both rest and physical exertion.
Mitochondrial dysfunction is hypothesized to underlie reduced muscle oxygen saturation in fibromyalgia via impaired aerobic energy production.
Fibromyalgia patients show reduced heart rate variability, a non-invasive marker of autonomic nervous system activity, indicating autonomic dysregulation.
A propensity for sympathetic predominance in fibromyalgia is proposed to cause vasoconstriction, further limiting oxygen supply to muscles and intensifying symptoms.
Research indicates diminished levels of coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) in fibromyalgia patients, positioning it as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target.
Accumulation of metabolic byproducts including lactate and hydrogen ions in oxygen-deprived fibromyalgia muscle tissue is proposed to trigger pain receptors and elevate pain sensitivity.
Mitochondrial dysfunction may lead to increased production of reactive oxygen species, driving oxidative stress, cellular damage, and inflammation in fibromyalgia.
Microcirculatory dysfunction, including vasoconstriction and impaired endothelial function, is hypothesized to hinder oxygen delivery to muscle tissues in fibromyalgia.
NIRS is highlighted as a non-invasive optical technique enabling real-time, continuous measurement of muscle oxygenation changes at rest and during activity in fibromyalgia patients.

Graded, individualized exercise programs with adequate rest intervals and low-impact modalities (e.g., swimming, walking, yoga, tai chi) are recommended to improve oxygen supply during exertion without aggravating fibromyalgia symptoms.
CoQ10 supplementation is proposed to bolster mitochondrial function and improve muscle oxygen saturation and energy production in fibromyalgia patients.
Vasodilator medications are proposed as a means to relax vascular smooth muscle, dilate blood vessels, and improve microcirculatory blood flow to muscles in fibromyalgia.
Mindfulness-based stress reduction and biofeedback are proposed to modulate autonomic nervous system responses and may positively affect blood flow and oxygen delivery to muscle in fibromyalgia.

Beta-blockers and centrally acting agents are discussed as pharmacological options to recalibrate sympathetic-parasympathetic balance and potentially improve oxygen delivery to muscles in fibromyalgia, requiring careful individualized use.
Fibromyalgia predominantly affects women at approximately a 3:1 ratio compared to men, with prevalence increasing with age and peaking between 50 and 60 years.

Impaired aerobic metabolism and limited ATP availability in fibromyalgia are linked to cognitive impairments known as 'fibro fog,' characterized by difficulties in concentration, memory, and mental sharpness.
IL-6 levels showed a significant positive correlation with FIQ scores (functional disability) in fibromyalgia patients.
Fibromyalgia patients with IL-6 levels above 2 pg/mL had significantly higher FIQ (disability) scores than those with lower IL-6 levels.
IL-8 levels correlated positively with pain intensity (NRS) over the past 24 hours and past week, but these correlations did not reach statistical significance.
IL-1 levels tended to correlate with higher pain and disability scores but high inter-individual variability limited statistical significance, showing only a trend (p<0.1).
Multiple regression analysis showed IL-6 was the strongest predictor of FIQ (disability) scores among the interleukins studied.
Multiple regression analysis showed IL-8 was the most significant predictor of pain severity (NRS) over the past week among the interleukins studied.
Higher IL-8 levels (>20 pg/mL) were associated with greater pain intensity than lower levels, though the difference was not statistically significant.
Mrgprb2 receptor signaling on mast cells was identified as an IgE-independent pathway mediating colonic mast cell activation and inflammation in a mouse model of acute colitis.

Using Mrgprb2-knockout mice, the study showed that Mrgprb2-dependent mast cell signaling improves colonic mucosal integrity during acute colitis by enhancing neutrophil recruitment and other immune processes.
The study identified a neuro-immune axis between substance P-positive nerve fibers and Mrgprb2-expressing mast cells in the distal colon during colitis.

The human paralog gene MRGPRX2 is proposed as a potential therapeutic target for modulating gut inflammation without affecting IgE-mediated immune responses, though its presence and function in human colonic mast cells requires confirmation.

Prior comprehensive mast cell distribution analysis (Tauber et al) showed Mrgprb2-positive connective tissue mast cells reside in the muscularis propria, whereas Mrgprb2-negative mucosal mast cells are restricted to the lamina propria.
GC-MS analysis identified cannabidiolic acid (CBDA) and cannabichromenic acid (CBCA) as the major cannabinoid components of the Cannabis sativa L. extract (CSL).
HS-GC/MS analysis identified myrcene and α-pinene as the major terpenes in the Cannabis sativa L. extract.
LPS-treated mice showed markedly decreased sucrose preference (anhedonia) compared to control mice.
CSL administration dose-dependently increased sucrose preference in LPS-treated mice, reaching significance at all doses tested.
LPS-treated mice showed significantly increased immobility time in the tail suspension test compared to controls.
CSL administration reduced TST immobility time in LPS-treated mice, with a significant reduction only at the 20 mg/kg dose.
LPS-treated mice showed significantly increased immobility time in the forced swimming test compared to controls.
CSL reduced FST immobility time dose-dependently, with the greatest and only significant reduction at 30 mg/kg, which also outperformed the 10 and 20 mg/kg doses.
LPS administration substantially elevated the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), indicating increased systemic inflammation.
CSL dose-dependently reduced NLR in LPS-treated mice, with significant reductions at 20 and 30 mg/kg.
LPS administration increased monocyte counts compared to controls, but CSL did not significantly change monocyte values.
No significant differences in eosinophil or basophil counts were observed between any of the experimental groups.
LPS administration did not significantly alter lymph node area or mast cell numbers in deep cervical or submandibular lymph nodes, and CSL treatment likewise did not affect these parameters.
LPS administration significantly increased mast cell degranulation rate in the submandibular lymph nodes compared to controls.
CSL significantly reduced mast cell degranulation rate in submandibular lymph nodes only at the 30 mg/kg dose.
LPS administration significantly increased mast cell degranulation rate in deep cervical lymph nodes (dcLNs) compared to controls.
CSL reduced dcLN mast cell degranulation rate dose-dependently, with significant reductions at 20 and 30 mg/kg, consistent with a prior study using another Cannabis sativa strain.
Neither LPS nor CSL administration significantly altered mast cell numbers in the parietal or superior sagittal sinus (SSS) regions of the dura mater.
LPS administration increased mast cell degranulation rate in the parietal region of the dura mater compared to controls, and CSL reduced this only at 30 mg/kg.
LPS administration increased mast cell degranulation rate in the superior sagittal sinus (SSS) region of the dura mater, a region closely tied to meningeal lymphatic drainage.
CSL dose-dependently suppressed degranulation of mast cells in the SSS region of the dura mater, with significant reductions at 20 and 30 mg/kg, and 30 mg/kg outperforming 10 mg/kg.
LPS administration significantly increased TNF-α mRNA expression in the prefrontal cortex compared to controls.
CSL administration dose-dependently reduced TNF-α mRNA levels in the prefrontal cortex, with significant reductions at 20 and 30 mg/kg.
LPS administration significantly increased IL-1β mRNA expression in the prefrontal cortex compared to controls.
CSL administration reduced IL-1β mRNA levels in the prefrontal cortex in a dose-dependent manner, with significance reached only at 30 mg/kg.
The NOD2 IVS8+158 (c.2798+158C>T) variant was the most common variant, present in 14 of 22 (63.6%) patients with Yao syndrome.
The R702W NOD2 variant was present in 8 of 22 (36.4%) patients and was more prevalent in this cohort than in the original Yao et al. YAOS cohort.
The 1007fs NOD2 variant was identified in 4 of 22 (18.2%) patients with Yao syndrome.
A previously unreported NOD2 variant, R311W (c.931C>T, p.Arg311Trp), was identified in one patient with Yao syndrome, representing a novel genotype.
The recently described NOD2 V955I susceptibility variant for Yao syndrome was identified in one patient in this cohort.
Eight patients (36.4%) had compound NOD2 variants, most commonly IVS8+158 plus either R702W or 1007fs, a higher rate of compound genotypes than in the original YAOS cohort.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), diagnosed by tilt table testing, was found in 4 of 15 patients with dizziness (26.7%), a previously undescribed association in Yao syndrome.
Orthostatic intolerance was present in 10 of 22 patients (two-thirds of those with dizziness), described as a novel feature of Yao syndrome.
Orthostatic hypotension was noted in 2 patients (13.3% of those with dizziness) in this Yao syndrome cohort.
Non-vertiginous dizziness occurred in 15 of 22 patients (68.2%) with Yao syndrome, a novel symptom not previously detailed in this condition, though no patient showed frank autonomic failure.

One patient with Yao syndrome was diagnosed with small fiber neuropathy, confirmed by abnormal autonomic testing and skin biopsy showing reduced epidermal nerve fiber density, and also had a comorbid myoclonic movement disorder.
One patient was diagnosed with mast cell activation disorder concurrent with Yao syndrome based on elevated serum tryptase and elevated urinary N-methylhistamine levels.
Twelve patients (54.5%) experienced episodic facial flushing resembling mast cell activation disorder, but ten of these had normal blood tryptase levels.
Glucocorticoids were used in 20 of 22 patients (90.9%) with YAOS, with clinical benefit noted in 15 (75%).

Sulfasalazine was trialed in 14 patients (63.6%); five had allergic reaction/intolerable side effects and only one experienced symptomatic improvement, contrasting with prior reports of sulfasalazine efficacy in YAOS.
Thirteen patients (59.1%) achieved adequate disease control on therapy, including eleven maintained on IL-1 inhibitor therapy alone or combined with conventional synthetic DMARDs.
One patient was treated long-term with an IL-6 receptor inhibitor with adequate disease control.
Colchicine was trialed in 8 patients with generally insufficient benefit, consistent with prior reports of general inefficacy in YAOS.
Seven patients (31.8%) were diagnosed with gastrointestinal dysmotility (gastric, small intestine, or colonic), a feature not previously described in Yao syndrome.
No association was clearly observed between specific NOD2 genotypes and disease severity or treatment refractoriness in this cohort.
Variants in SCN9A, encoding the Nav1.7 sodium channel subunit, have been identified in patients with small fiber neuropathy.
Variants in SCN10A, encoding the Nav1.8 sodium channel subunit, have been identified in patients with small fiber neuropathy.
Variants in SCN11A, encoding the Nav1.9 sodium channel subunit, have been identified in patients with small fiber neuropathy.
Variants in the TRPA1 gene have also been found in small fiber neuropathy patients.

Small fiber neuropathy can be associated with systemic conditions including diabetes, autoimmune diseases, drug and toxin exposure, and infection, with the list of associated diseases continuing to expand.
There is growing interest in immune-mediated forms of small fiber neuropathy, which may help identify potentially treatable subgroups.

Diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy is established through clinical examination, intraepidermal nerve fiber density assessment, and/or quantitative sensory testing according to international criteria.
Autonomic functional tests allow better characterization of dysautonomia in small fiber neuropathy, which may be subclinical.

Management of small fiber neuropathy prioritizes treating the underlying condition when identified, using a multidisciplinary approach combining symptomatic pain therapy, lifestyle changes, and biopsychological interventions.

58.8% of IBS patients (30/51) achieved a long-term response to the adapted low-FODMAP diet (AdLFD), defined as an improvement of ≥50 points on the total IBS-SSS score after a mean follow-up of 62.5 months.
Comorbid fibromyalgia did not significantly influence the long-term response rate to AdLFD, with similar improvement in IBS-SSS between IBSF and IBSWF groups.
Mean IBS-SSS total score significantly decreased from 313.5 ± 95 at baseline to 220 ± 112 after AdLFD, across all patients and both IBSF and IBSWF subgroups.
At baseline, IBS patients with comorbid fibromyalgia (IBSF) showed significantly higher anxiety (HAD-A) and depression (HAD-D) scores compared to IBS-only patients (IBSWF).
IBSF patients showed a significant decrease in both HAD-A (3.7 points, p = 0.002) and HAD-D (2.1 points, p < 0.001) scores after AdLFD, whereas IBSWF patients' improvement did not reach significance.
86.3% of patients (44/51) demonstrated good long-term adherence to the AdLFD (FARS ≥ 20), with no difference in adherence between IBSF and IBSWF groups or between IBS subtypes.
Length of follow-up time was not correlated with long-term adherence to AdLFD in either IBSF or IBSWF patients.
IBSF patients showed a significant reduction in the frequency of watery stools after AdLFD, while IBSWF patients showed no change, despite similar baseline frequency of watery stools between groups.
On multivariate analysis, higher baseline frequency of watery stools was independently associated with a greater probability of long-term response to AdLFD.
Severity of baseline abdominal pain was the only clinical feature independently associated with long-term adherence to AdLFD (assessed by FARS).
Patients with severe IBS at baseline showed a higher long-term response rate to AdLFD compared to those with moderate or mild IBS.

Considering all IBS patients, the bowel habits questionnaire showed significant reductions after AdLFD in abdominal pain (2.6/4 to 1.5/4, p<0.001), abdominal bloating (2.9/4 to 2.3/4, p=0.025), and watery stools (1.9/4 to 1.5/4, p=0.049).
In the IBS-D subgroup, AdLFD was associated with a significant increase in frequency of hard stools, a decrease in liquid/watery stools, and improved abdominal bloating.

Of the initial 105 IBS patients started on the strict low-FODMAP diet, 41 (39%) discontinued due to lack of efficacy in the first 8 weeks, with no differences in fibromyalgia frequency, IBS subtype, age, or gender between responders and non-responders to the strict phase.
Over a five-year follow-up, 11.2% of the population-based cohort developed bodily distress syndrome (BDS).
Multi-organ BDS had a markedly lower five-year incidence (0.6%) than single-organ BDS, which drove most of the overall BDS incidence.
Female sex was associated with the highest incidence of BDS, while the trend toward higher incidence in younger age was not statistically significant.
The five-year incidence of any of the four functional somatic syndromes (CWP, CF, IB, MCS) was 10.5%, with a preponderance of women and younger persons.
Five-year incidence of irritable bowel (IB) allowing for comorbid FSS was 2.7%, corresponding to 50.4 cases per 10,000 person-years, with a female preponderance.
Without comorbid FSS, five-year incidence of IB was 1.6%, corresponding to 29.8 cases per 10,000 person-years, lower than when comorbid FSS were allowed.
Five-year incidence of chronic widespread pain (CWP) allowing for comorbid FSS was 4.8%, corresponding to roughly 9 cases per 1,000 person-years, and was highest in older age-groups.

Five-year incidence of chronic fatigue (CF) allowing for comorbid FSS was 5.7%, corresponding to about 106 cases per 10,000 person-years, and was highest in the youngest age group with a female preponderance.
Five-year incidence of multiple chemical sensitivity (MCS) allowing for comorbid FSS was 0.8%, the lowest among the four FSS delimitations, with a female preponderance.
Remission of total BDS was observed in 44% of cases at 5-year follow-up, while only 10.8% of multi-organ BDS cases remitted.
Remission was observed in 46% of FSS cases and was associated with male predominance for both BDS and FSS.
Remission of CWP and CF was higher in males than females, whereas no sex difference in remission was seen for IB or MCS.
Persistence of BDS at follow-up was observed in more than half of baseline cases, with a female predominance.
5.8% of single-organ BDS cases at baseline converted to multi-organ BDS at follow-up, while more than half of multi-organ BDS cases converted to single-organ BDS.
More than half of FSS cases (CWP, CF, IB, MCS) persisted at 5-year follow-up, with a female predominance, and MCS persistence was higher in females than males.

Substantial interchangeability was observed among the four FSS delimitations over 5 years, with the highest interchange seen for MCS, where nearly a quarter of cases converted to one of the other three delimitations; change from CF to another delimitation was more frequent in older age-groups.
Non-participation in the 5-year follow-up study was associated with younger age, female sex, and having FSD at baseline, raising concern for selection bias.

The patient's Loeys-Dietz syndrome type V, caused by TGFB3 gene mutation, presented with extensive vascular disease including a giant common iliac artery aneurysm, internal iliac artery aneurysm, arterial tortuosity, and a true deep femoral artery aneurysm.

The patient underwent open surgical repair of a true deep femoral artery aneurysm and a two-staged repair of a giant common iliac artery aneurysm involving coiling of the ipsilateral internal iliac artery aneurysm followed by endovascular aortic repair (EVAR).
Monocrotaline (MCT) exposure increased intrapulmonary mast cell numbers by 143% compared to the vehicle control group.
Inhalation of 4% molecular hydrogen (H2) reduced the size of the mast cell population in lung acini and other structures compared to the MCT-only group.
After H2 inhalation, tryptase content per mast cell remained lower than in the control (untreated healthy) group, indicating persistent reduction of tryptase expression.
MCT exposure increased TGF-β expression, which became detectable in all mast cells, compared to the low-level expression seen in most MCs of control lungs.
H2 inhalation reduced the number of TGF-β-positive cells in the lungs and decreased TGF-β expression within mast cells, compared to the MCT-only group.
MCT exposure increased elastic fiber content in the lung stroma of large airways/vessels and interalveolar septa compared to control.
MCT exposure increased the collagen fibrous component of the lung, largely driven by a significant increase in reticular fibers.
H2 inhalation significantly decreased the integral area of collagen fibers in the lung stroma compared to the MCT-only group, though not down to control levels.
H2 exposure reduced reticular fiber content compared to the MCT group, reaching a level comparable to the control group.
MCT exposure produced α-SMA-expressing cells outside normal airway/vascular smooth muscle structures, suggesting increased fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transformation.
The number of metachromatic mast cells lacking tryptase was significantly reduced after MCT exposure compared to the control group.
H2 exposure was associated with increased heparin excretion by mast cells (evidenced by metachromasia of secreted granules), alongside blockade of tryptase release, compared to the MCT group.

The authors cite prior literature indicating that mast cell tryptase is known to stimulate type I collagen synthesis in human lung fibroblasts, supporting a mechanistic link between mast cell tryptase and pulmonary fibrosis.
Despite the antifibrotic benefits of H2, the toxic effects of MCT were not completely eliminated, as regions with active collagen fibrillogenesis involving mast cells persisted in the lungs.
H2 exposure was associated with reduced infiltration of immunocompetent cells in the lungs compared to animals exposed only to MCT, and mast cell-neutrophil contacts were largely absent.
A study reported IBS prevalence of approximately 4.4%-4.8% in Canada, the UK, and the US, with higher incidence in women and individuals under fifty.
A 2012 systematic review across 81 countries with 260,960 individuals estimated global IBS prevalence at approximately 11%, prior to Rome IV criteria.
A Rome Foundation global survey of 73,000 individuals across 33 countries found IBS prevalence of 4.1% using Rome IV criteria versus 10.1% using Rome III criteria.
Female IBS patients showed increased gray matter volume and cortical thickness in primary/secondary somatosensory cortices and some subcortical regions compared to healthy women.
The same study found reductions in cortical thickness, surface area, and gray matter volume in the posterior insula and superior frontal gyrus of IBS patients.
IBS patients show higher activation of the anterior cingulate cortex, insula, prefrontal cortex, cerebellum, and thalamus in response to rectal stimulation compared to non-IBS individuals.
IBS patients commonly show reduced parasympathetic activity and increased sympathetic nervous system activity, modulated by vagal tone.
BDNF-TrkB-PKMζ signaling from the thoracolumbar spinal cord to enteric glial cells in the lamina propria is a key communication pathway affecting visceral hypersensitivity.
An experimental study showed BDNF administration to enteric glial cells reduced enteric inflammation, restored gut function, supported intestinal barrier maintenance, and promoted neuroplasticity.
BDNF interacts with Toll-like receptors, particularly TLR4, on enteric nervous cells.
CRF-TLR4 proinflammatory cytokine signaling mediates gut barrier disruption and visceral hypersensitivity in IBS.
Nosu et al. found that apelin activates CRF-TLR4 signaling, creating a proinflammatory cytokine cycle central to IBS pathology in an IBS rat model.
CRF-TLR4 signaling leads to elevated LPS levels and intestinal permeability, contributing to abdominal pain in IBS.
Serotonin (5-HT) levels differ by IBS subtype: IBS-D patients typically show increased serotonin levels while IBS-C patients show decreased levels, influencing GI motility.
Abnormal colonic transit times occur in 10-20% of IBS-C/IBS-M patients and 25-45% of IBS-D patients.
DuPont et al. found delayed gastric emptying in 76% of IBS patients using a wireless pH/pressure recording capsule.
Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which are involved in serotonin production, are found at higher levels in IBS patients.

Muller et al. found reduced activity in ileal myenteric plexus neurons of germ-free mice compared to specific pathogen-free mice, indicating enteric neuronal under-stimulation without normal gut microbiota.
Anitha et al. found that mice lacking TLR4 and germ-free mice exhibited delayed intestinal transit and destruction of enteric neurons.
In a study of 142 IBS patients and 120 controls, IBS patients had significantly lower gut microbial diversity than controls.
IBS patients showed increases in Enterobacteria, anaerobes, E. coli, Ruminococcus gnavus, and Bacteroides, and decreases in Lactobacilli, Collinsella, and Bifidobacteria compared to controls.
Bacteroides and Allisonella were more prevalent specifically in IBS-M patients.

In fecal samples from IBS-D patients versus controls, Clostridiaceae, Leuconostocaceae, Enterococcaceae, Peptostreptococcaceae, and Lachnospiraceae were decreased while Sutterellaceae, Acidaminococcaceae, and Desulfovibrionaceae were increased.

Acute gastrointestinal infections are among the strongest risk factors for IBS (post-infection IBS/PI-IBS), with parasitic infections conferring the greatest risk, followed by bacterial and then viral infections.
A meta-analysis assessing genes associated with inflammatory mediators found no clear association with most of these genes and IBS.

In a study comparing fecal samples from IBS-D patients and controls, several bacterial families (Clostridiaceae, Leuconostocaceae, Enterococcaceae, Peptostreptococcaceae, Lachnospiraceae) were decreased while others (Sutterellaceae, Acidaminococcaceae, Desulfovibrionaceae) were increased.
Acute gastrointestinal infections are among the strongest risk factors for post-infection IBS, with parasitic infections carrying the greatest risk, followed by bacterial and then viral infections.

In a mouse model, bacterial infection increased intestinal permeability, allowing previously tolerated food antigens to trigger a localized gut immune response with histamine release, altered motility, and visceral hypersensitivity.

Genetic background, including numerous SNPs affecting symptom phenotype, barrier function, inflammatory mediators, neurotransmission regulation, ion channels, and bile acid metabolism, appears to contribute to IBS, though evidence remains preliminary.
A meta-analysis of genes related to inflammatory mediators found no clear association between most of these genes and IBS.
Downregulation of miR-199 is associated with upregulation of TRPV1, contributing to visceral hypersensitivity and heightened visceral pain in IBS.

Using NanoString mRNA measurements of colonic neuroimmune gene expression, TRPV1 expression was higher in gnotobiotic mice colonized with microbiota from IBS patients, correlating with both visceral hypersensitivity and anxiety-like behavior.

A low FODMAP diet is highly recommended as first-line dietary treatment for IBS, supported by randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses per British Gastroenterological Society (2021) and ACG (2022) guidelines.

Gut-directed hypnotherapy improves gastrointestinal motility and visceral sensitivity, enhancing symptoms and quality of life, likely through regulation of the autonomic nervous system and vagus nerve.
Stress-modifying therapies such as SSRIs have shown limited effectiveness for IBS despite their potential action on the enteric nervous system.
For IBS with diarrhea, rifaximin, eluxadoline, and alosetron are generally recommended pharmacologic treatments, despite potential adverse effects.
For IBS with constipation, the ACG (2022) guidelines strongly recommend linaclotide and conditionally recommend tenapanor, plecanatide, tegaserod, and lubiprostone.
The role of probiotics (Lactobacillus rhamnosus, Lactobacillus plantarum, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Bifidobacteria) in IBS treatment remains controversial.
Prebiotics and synbiotics have shown beneficial effects on intestinal microbiota diversity and activity, and fecal microbiota transplantation is emerging as a promising future treatment for IBS.
Co-occurrence of two or more chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPCs) affects 48% to 62% of individuals who have at least one COPC.
Having multiple co-occurring COPCs is associated with increased pain, disability, emotional distress, and reduced quality of life compared with having a single COPC.
The OPPERA-2 study found a significant positive association between the number of COPCs an individual has and the degree of pain amplification.
Individuals with a COPC show heightened depression, anxiety, and stress levels compared with healthy controls.
Psychological distress experienced before the onset of a COPC is a robust predictor of subsequent COPC development.
The authors' recent study found that psychological distress profiles increase incrementally as the number of co-occurring COPCs increases.
A review of longitudinal studies indicates that sleep disturbances have a stronger effect on subsequent pain than pain has on subsequent sleep disturbances.
Laboratory studies support a causal role of sleep deprivation in increasing pain severity and pain amplification.
Insomnia is an important risk factor for the onset and recurrence of depressive and anxiety disorders.
A laboratory study found that partial sleep deprivation led to a significant increase in psychological distress among patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
Experimental circadian disruptions in animal studies lead to increased nociceptive sensitivity.
Human studies show increased pain sensitivity among night-shift workers.
Synthesis of preclinical and clinical studies suggests a strong connection between circadian disturbances and anxiety and depression.
RBD was present in 95% of probable MSA patients in this cohort.
Poor sleep quality was reported in 80% of the probable MSA cohort.
Secondary insomnia and intermittent awakenings were universally observed (100%) in the cohort.
Excessive daytime sleepiness was present in 26% of the cohort.
Risk for obstructive sleep apnea was identified in 51.7% of patients.
Snoring was reported in 85% of probable MSA patients.
MSA patients reported a mean improvement of 38.2±22.9% in sleep with medications.
No significant difference was found between MSA-parkinsonian and MSA-cerebellar phenotypes in any sleep parameter measured.
Sleep quality was poorer in MSA patients with pre-motor onset RBD compared to those with post-motor onset RBD.
Poor sleep quality showed a moderate positive correlation with RBD duration in MSA patients.
Disease severity in MSA positively correlated with both RBD duration and poor sleep quality.
The review states that nearly half of long COVID patients meet diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, highlighting substantial symptomatic overlap between the two conditions.
The review notes that despite various viral infections being proposed as triggers of ME/CFS onset, no single specific pathogen has been identified across all cases of postinfectious ME/CFS.
ME/CFS participants had significantly higher Test of Premorbid Functioning (TOPF) standard scores than healthy controls.
No significant difference was found between ME/CFS and healthy controls on age-corrected WAIS-IV Digit Span Forward and Backward scores at T0 and T1.
Traditional attention/working memory tasks (Digit Span Forward/Backward) showed only weak convergence with the CogState computerized battery tasks.

ME/CFS participants did not differ from healthy controls in psychomotor speed/reaction time (Detection task) at baseline, but showed progressively slower reaction times over the following days, reaching clinically meaningful effect sizes by 48 hours after the clinic visit.

ME/CFS participants showed no difference from healthy controls in attention-task response latency at baseline, but demonstrated variable and increased response times over subsequent timepoints while controls remained steady.
ME/CFS participants took significantly longer than healthy controls to respond on the One Card Learning task across all timepoints.
ME/CFS participants took significantly longer than healthy controls to respond on the 1-Back working memory task across all timepoints.

There were no significant group-by-time interaction effects for reaction-time latency measures (DET-LMN, IDN-LMN, OCL-LMN, ONB-LMN), indicating both groups improved similarly with repetition despite overall group differences.
ME/CFS participants took significantly longer than healthy controls on the complex working memory (2-Back) task at both in-clinic timepoints, with a small clinically meaningful effect.
ME/CFS participants showed moderately reduced executive function/learning efficiency (Groton Maze Learning, moves per second) compared to healthy controls at both in-clinic timepoints.

Performance accuracy on the CBSB tasks did not differ between ME/CFS and healthy controls across timepoints, except for a small effect on Detection task accuracy at 48 hours, attributable to slowed reaction time.

Among ME/CFS participants, those who underwent exercise testing showed better (higher) Groton Maze Learning moves-per-second scores than those without exercise testing at both in-clinic timepoints, a difference that persisted after adjustment for age, race, education, TOPF, and psychomotor speed.
Addition of a maximal cardiopulmonary exercise test to the study visit did not result in further cognitive dysfunction beyond that provoked by the clinical visit itself.
ME/CFS participants had significantly worse illness symptoms and functional status than healthy controls, as expected.
Individuals with current ME/CFS had a much higher rate of clinically significant anxiety symptoms (37.6%) compared to those with no history of ME/CFS (6.1%).
Individuals with current ME/CFS had a much higher rate of clinically significant depressive symptoms (49.0%) compared to those with no history of ME/CFS (6.7%).
Individuals with previous ME/CFS had a higher rate of clinically significant anxiety symptoms (26.5%) compared to those with no history of ME/CFS (6.1%).

Individuals with previous ME/CFS had a higher rate of clinically significant depressive symptoms (33.4%) compared to those with no history of ME/CFS (6.7%), indicating persistence of psychological symptom burden even after recovery.

The protocol describes development of a modular online patient education program (BAYNET FOR ME/CFS) based on the ModuS concept for children/adolescents with ME/CFS, their parents, siblings, and school staff, delivered in short (45-90 minute) online sessions.

Recruitment fell short of the goal of 30 patients, as some previously participated in in-hospital training and declined the online program, and sibling recruitment was unexpectedly low despite advertising through multiple channels.

The study design assumed, based on a prior diabetes staff-training study (EduKids), a comparable 87% high-acceptance rate, and calculated that 30 participants would provide sufficient precision (12% half-width of 95% CI) to estimate this proportion.

The training program is designed to mitigate postexertional malaise (PEM) risk by structuring sessions with energy check-ins at the start, midpoint, and end, a mid-session break, and the option for participants to leave early.

The study identifies limitations including small, self-selected voluntary participant numbers likely biased toward less severely affected patients, single-center recruitment, and short-term-only evaluation with no long-term outcome data in phases I-III.
The paper's title indicates it examines how common ME/CFS is following SARS-CoV-2 infection, but no abstract or results text was provided to extract specific quantitative findings.
Both the synbiotic and placebo groups showed a significant reduction in general fatigue after 3 months compared to baseline, with no clear synbiotic-specific advantage reported for this outcome.
The synbiotic showed a significant time-by-treatment interaction for post-exercise malaise, with the synbiotic group showing greater attenuation of post-exercise malaise than placebo.
The synbiotic significantly increased choline levels in the thalamus compared to placebo.
The synbiotic significantly increased creatine levels in the left frontal white matter compared to placebo.
The synbiotic significantly increased creatine levels in the left frontal grey matter compared to placebo.

Participants reported that the PaceMe adaptive pacing app helped them identify personal PEM triggers and understand appropriate rest, reducing frequency and severity of post-exertional malaise episodes.

Real-time heart rate and activity monitoring via the app allowed participants to discover previously unrecognized PEM triggers, such as singing or playing an instrument, that raised heart rate and preceded symptom flares.
Participants described the app as providing an important source of emotional and practical support that they had not received from medical professionals, likening it to a 'crutch' or 'lifeline.'

Use of the app's objective data provided participants with validation of their symptom experience, countering feelings that their illness was 'all in their head' and helping them justify rest needs to others.

The app supported participants in regaining a sense of control and agency over their health and daily lives, which had been lost due to long COVID, including improved ability to set boundaries with work and family.
All participants reported the PaceMe app was helpful in some way, though the degree of perceived benefit ranged from profound to modest.

In a randomized trial of 28 moderate-to-severe COVID-19 patients, five HBOT sessions were associated with no deaths versus three deaths in the control group, and HBOT patients required lower supplemental oxygen delivery.
HBOT reduced CRP, ferritin and LDH and increased CD3+ T-cell counts compared to controls in COVID-19 patients, indicating alleviation of inflammation and partial restoration of T-cell responses.

In vitro, one hour of HBO treatment increased eNOS expression and decreased ICAM expression and reactive oxygen species production in TNF-alpha-pretreated bone-marrow-derived endothelial progenitor cells, without altering wound closure or cell proliferation.

In a retrospective analysis of patients undergoing coronary stent implantation, HBOT was associated with significantly higher flow-mediated dilation, nitric oxide and CGRP, and significantly lower hs-CRP and endothelin-1 compared to non-HBOT controls.

In healthy volunteers, HBOT decreased neutrophilic ROS production and phagocytic activity after the second and third sessions, but did not alter plasma malondialdehyde or cytokine (TNF, IL-6, IL-10) concentrations.
In patients with necrotising fasciitis, three days of HBO therapy significantly reduced the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α while increasing the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10.

In 10 consecutive Long-COVID patients given 10 HBOT sessions at 2.4 ATA over 12 days, statistically significant improvements were seen in the Chalder fatigue scale, global cognition, executive function, attention, information processing and verbal function.

A small observational study of 6 Long-COVID patients found that five returned to pre-infection symptom levels and one showed significant improvement after HBO2, along with reduced symptom duration and improved quality of life.

In the only randomized, sham-controlled trial to date (73 Israeli patients, 40 HBOT sessions at 2 ATA over two months), HBOT induced structural and functional brain repair, improved white matter connectivity, and improved cognitive, behavioral and emotional function in Long-COVID patients.

In the same sham-controlled Israeli trial, fMRI showed a correlation between clinical improvements following HBOT and a significant increase in blood flow in several brain regions, with microstructural changes detected in the supramarginal gyrus, supplementary motor area, insula and frontal gyri.

In the same trial population, HBOT significantly improved global longitudinal strain (subclinical left ventricular systolic dysfunction) compared to sham, from -17.8±1.1 to -20.2±1.0, despite normal ejection fraction at baseline.

Long-term follow-up (486±73 days post-HBOT) of the Israeli trial population showed sustained improvements in SF-36 quality of life domains, sleep quality (effect sizes 0.47-0.79), neuropsychiatric symptoms (BSI-18), and pain severity/interference persisting at least one year after treatment.

A small observational study (n=10) reported that HBO decreased fatigue and improved processing speed (SDMT) in Long-COVID patients, attributed to improved energy metabolism, mitochondrial function and cerebral blood flow.

An Austrian study of 59 Long-COVID patients (33 female, 26 male; mean age 43.9) found statistically significant improvements after HBO in physical functioning, physical role, energy, emotional well-being, social functioning, pain, and reduced activity limitation at three-month follow-up.

A Swedish randomized placebo-controlled trial using only 10 HBOT sessions (fewer than the usual 15-30) reported an unexpectedly high frequency of adverse events in its interim safety report, and efficacy results remain pending.

In a 2022 study of 31 Long-COVID patients (90% overweight/obese) given 15 HBOT sessions, significant improvements were found in anxiety, depression, perceived pain, physical fitness (Fullerton test), working memory and concentration, with benefits persisting after treatment completion.

A 2023 pretest-posttest study of five post-COVID patients receiving 15-50 HBOT sessions found attenuated ROS production, lipid peroxidation, DNA damage, NO metabolites and inflammation biomarker levels after treatment.

Long-COVID patients show dysregulated T cell activation, increased activated CD14+/CD16+ monocytes and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and significantly increased IFN-β and IFN-λ1 interferon levels compared to healthy controls, with a distinct combination of IFN-β, pentraxin 3, IFN-γ, IFN-λ2/3 and IL-6 detectable 8 months post-infection.

Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), with several clinical subtypes, is described as a symptom occurring as part of Long-COVID, alongside chronic dyspnoea, cough, chest pain and palpitations.

HIF-1α is proposed to act as an antiviral defense mechanism by suppressing expression of ACE2 receptor and TMPRSS2, thereby limiting SARS-CoV-2 cell entry, while prolonged hypoxia triggers a 'HIF-shift' toward HIF-2/HIF-3 that attenuates this protective HIF-1 response.

SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in the brain tissue of 30-40% of deceased COVID-19 patients in some post-mortem series, while other post-mortem examinations found no corresponding histological changes or detectable virus, and RNA/spike protein were found in 50%/40% of brainstem samples respectively in another study.

Elevated IL-6 levels observed in severe and moderate COVID-19 infection contribute to inflammation and oxidative stress via excessive ROS production and depleted antioxidant systems, creating a mutually reinforcing cycle of hyperinflammation in Long-COVID patients.

Patients with ME/CFS and/or long/post-COVID syndrome generate patient-generated data (PGD) from wearables as evidence to validate their subjective symptoms and to substantiate the legitimacy ('doctorability') of their illness, given these conditions are difficult-to-grasp and often not fully credited by physicians.

A patient with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, discussed in the context of chronic-fatigue-type illness, described relying on a smartwatch to confirm his subjective sense of exhaustion, illustrating how wearable data is used to validate embodied fatigue experience.

A patient with long/post-COVID syndrome reported that her heart rate behaves abnormally during physical exertion (failing to decrease at rest or increase appropriately during exertion), a fluctuating symptom not reliably captured by a standard in-clinic ECG, for which she used smartwatch data as evidence.

For both the ME/CFS and long/post-COVID cases described, physicians tolerated the patient-generated wearable data (did not dismiss it as useless) but did not incorporate it into medical files or actively work with it, and did not encourage further self-tracking.

In the discussion, the authors state that PGD often represents the only means for ME/CFS and long/post-COVID patients to 'prove' they are truly chronically ill, yet this data is frequently dismissed by physicians as insufficiently meaningful or ignored altogether.

In cardiology, physicians actively welcome patient-generated wearable ECG recordings to establish a 'symptom-rhythm correlation' for objectifying suspected cardiac arrhythmias, transforming initially uninvited data collection into encouraged, invited participation.

A somnologist described consumer smartwatch-measured oxygen desaturation events as a useful 'mini-screener' indication warranting further clinical investigation for sleep apnoea, though not treated as definitive diagnostic evidence.

Sleep specialists in the sample uniformly responded negatively to consumer-device-generated sleep data, fundamentally questioning its quality and asserting the superiority of in-lab polysomnography, tolerating PGD only as a rough indicator rather than diagnostic evidence.

Patients with lipoedema use wearable-derived activity/calorie data as 'proof' that they adhere to exercise recommendations, countering stereotypes that they are lazy or unathletic, and this documentation is also required by health insurers (MDK) to approve treatments such as bariatric surgery.

Individuals with type 1 diabetes in the sample proactively tracked physical activity using additional consumer devices (beyond the blood glucose meter) to manage glucose levels and prevent comorbidities, and diabetologists were generally positive about this additional data but limited by lack of interoperable interfaces.

Across the five health domains studied, the more researched a condition and the more established patient self-management, the more positively physicians responded to patients' initially uninvited PGD; conversely, conditions that are more complex to diagnose (such as ME/CFS and long/post-COVID) tended to provoke defensive reactions or reluctance from physicians.
A patient with hypermobile EDS who had experienced rapid functional decline underwent 30 hours of hippotherapy and showed substantial improvements in fatigue, chronic pain, and walking ability.
Hippotherapy improved postural balance, motor skills, proprioception, muscle function, and endurance in the patient with hypermobile EDS.
Hippotherapy positively affected the patient's cognitive and emotional regulation by stimulating sensory inputs that activate neural pathways, providing relief from pain and fatigue.
The patient transitioned from wheelchair reliance to walking with crutches and then greatly enhanced both gait quality and speed following hippotherapy.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS had significantly lower pressure pain thresholds (indicating greater pressure hyperalgesia) at the trapezius muscle compared to healthy controls.
Deltoid muscle pressure pain thresholds were significantly lower in adolescents with HSD/hEDS than controls.
Tibialis anterior pressure pain thresholds were significantly lower in adolescents with HSD/hEDS than controls.
Paraspinal lower back pressure pain thresholds were significantly lower in adolescents with HSD/hEDS than controls, indicating widespread/generalized hyperalgesia.
Pain intensity was significantly higher over the previous week and at the time of assessment in the HSD/hEDS group compared to controls.
A majority of adolescents with HSD/hEDS reported widespread pain (60%) or multi-quadrant pain (22%) on a pain drawing, whereas most controls reported no pain (75%) or only local pain (25%).

Exercise-induced hypoalgesia (EIH) at the tibialis anterior muscle differed significantly between groups, with a smaller pain-inhibitory effect after exercise in adolescents with HSD/hEDS compared to controls.
There was no significant between-group difference in exercise-induced hypoalgesia at the trapezius (remote, non-exercising) muscle.
Within the HSD/hEDS group, PPT at the trapezius muscle did not significantly change after exercise, unlike controls who showed a significant increase.
Within the HSD/hEDS group, PPT at the tibialis anterior (exercising) muscle significantly increased after the cycling exercise, indicating a local hypoalgesic effect.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS cycled for a significantly shorter duration during the exercise test than controls, despite no significant differences in end-exercise heart rate or perceived exertion.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS reported significantly worse general fatigue than controls.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS reported significantly worse sleep/rest fatigue than controls.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS reported significantly worse cognitive fatigue than controls.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS scored significantly higher on pain catastrophizing than controls.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS scored significantly higher on depression symptoms (HADS) than controls.
Adolescents with HSD/hEDS scored significantly higher on anxiety symptoms (HADS) than controls.
Whole-genome sequencing identified a heterozygous missense mutation c.1691G>A (p.Arg564His) in COL1A1 in a teenager clinically diagnosed with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

The COL1A1 variant was previously reported as likely pathogenic in a patient with connective tissue abnormality but is currently classified as of unknown clinical significance in the ClinVar database.

The patient experienced recurrent adnexal (ovarian/fallopian tube) torsion, with an unusually long right utero-ovarian ligament observed at laparoscopy, hypothesized to result from hEDS-associated connective tissue laxity.

A laparoscopic right oophoropexy with shortening of the elongated utero-ovarian ligament, plus salpingostomy for hydrosalpinx drainage, resulted in the patient remaining asymptomatic with no further abdominal pain at one-year follow-up.
The discussion notes that oophoropexy, though the standard preventive procedure for ovarian torsion, may be less effective than previously thought according to recent research.
Cardiac evaluation revealed an atrial septal aneurysm and a highly mobile patent foramen ovale, which were treated with percutaneous closure using a self-expanding double-disc occluder.
The patient additionally suffered from depression, migraines and episodes of vertigo, treated with paroxetine 20 mg daily and riboflavin 300 mg daily.

The patient's mother carried the same COL1A1 variant and had joint hypermobility, scoliosis, and migraines, but did not meet full diagnostic criteria for hEDS, suggesting hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD) with incomplete penetrance and variable expression.
More than half of patients with hEDS experience abdominal pain, often attributed to gastrointestinal causes such as disorders of gut-brain interaction or irritable bowel syndrome.

Postoperative right hip pain was diagnosed via CT/MRI as femoroacetabular impingement syndrome with a focal acetabular labral tear and iliopsoas tendinitis, likely due to perioperative injury related to patient positioning during laparoscopic surgery, and treated conservatively.

A systematic literature search using 'Ehlers Danlos' and 'torsion' as terms found no other reports of adnexal torsion in EDS, but did find reports of appendiceal, testicular, and uterine torsion in patients with known or suspected EDS, with ligamentous laxity hypothesized as a key contributing feature.
Migraine prevalence is markedly higher in hypermobile patients (40-75%) compared to the general population prevalence of 14%.

In a retrospective study of 733 patients from an EDS clinic, migraine was reported in 42.5% of HSD/hEDS patients and chronic migraine in 13.8%; among those with comorbid fibromyalgia, migraine rose to 63.8% and chronic migraine to 34.1%.
Hypermobile patients with migraine experience greater attack frequency, greater associated disability, and younger age at onset compared to the general migraine population.
Prevalence of dysautonomia in EDS has been reported to be as high as 78% in the literature.
71% of an EDS cohort with headaches also had a diagnosis of autonomic dysfunction, suggesting a possible causal association.
In a prospective study of 24 consecutive PoTS patients, 14 had orthostatic headaches during daily activity while 15 developed orthostatic headaches during head-up tilt testing.

Orthostatic headache was found to be a predictive symptom for PoTS in adolescents, present in 33/37 patients with PoTS versus 7/33 without PoTS, giving a sensitivity of 89.2% and specificity of 78.8%.
A systematic review found the reported prevalence of orthostatic headache in PoTS varied widely, ranging between 2.2% and 58.3% across four eligible studies.
In a prospective study of SIH patients, 18% of a cohort of 50 had a heritable connective tissue disorder and another 16% had benign joint hypermobility syndrome or isolated hypermobility features.
Brain MRI can be normal in up to 20% of spontaneous intracranial hypotension cases, meaning a normal MRI does not exclude the diagnosis.

Conservative management of spontaneous intracranial hypotension (bed rest, hydration, caffeine, analgesics, abdominal binders) has a relatively low success rate, estimated at 28% in one meta-analysis.
A meta-analysis found that a first epidural blood patch leads to resolution of symptoms in 64% of spontaneous intracranial hypotension patients, with diminishing returns on repeat procedures.

Schievink and colleagues reported that 10% of patients with orthostatic headaches and normal brain MRI/conventional spinal imaging had an underlying CSF venous fistula detected on digital subtraction myelogram.

Milhorat and colleagues found that 12.7% of 2,813 patients with Chiari malformation type 1 met diagnostic criteria for a heritable connective tissue disorder, with hEDS accounting for over 41% of this overlapping cohort.
Headache is present in up to 81% of Chiari malformation type 1 patients and is often triggered by Valsalva manoeuvres such as coughing.
An Iranian observational-analytical study found no significant difference in the frequency of tension-type headache between patients with benign joint hypermobility syndrome and healthy controls.

Bendik et al. found a comparable prevalence of tension-type headache between hypermobile patients and healthy controls but noted higher TTH attack frequency in the hypermobile cohort (n=28), though the small sample size limits conclusions.
Rozen and colleagues reported cervical hypermobility in 11 patients and widespread hypermobility in 10 patients with new daily persistent headache (NDPH).

Cheema and colleagues found a background of joint hypermobility syndrome in 11.2% of NDPH patients (n=366) and 18.5% of transformed chronic daily headache patients (n=696), the latter group being 99% composed of chronic migraine patients.
An inflammatory aetiology for NDPH has been proposed, supported by associations with EBV and HSV infections and elevated tumour necrosis factor alpha levels in the CSF of patients with NDPH.
Conservative management of temporomandibular joint disorders can improve symptoms in 50-90% of patients, and up to 40% achieve remission without any intervention.
Approximately 50% of patients diagnosed with chronic migraine revert to episodic migraine following withdrawal from overused analgesics (medication overuse headache treatment).

A study found no difference in the incidence of cervical spondylosis on imaging between patients diagnosed with cervicogenic headache and healthy controls, undermining the specificity of radiological features used to diagnose cervicogenic headache.

Even among expert-selected patients meeting strict eligibility criteria, 25% of fusion patients for hypermobility-related upper cervical instability report no improvement in quality of life after surgery.
People with HSD/hEDS incur $11,600–$21,100 more in healthcare costs than similar non-hypermobile individuals.
People with hypermobility have compromised proprioception and motor control, which is further worsened by chronic neck pain.
Motor control training of the lumbar spine has been shown to enhance cervical motor control and decrease neck-related disability, demonstrating a remote (non-local) benefit of motor training.

Beighton scores confirmed generalized joint hypermobility in two of the three patients (Emma 7/9, Kay 9/9), while the third (Jay) had historical but not current hypermobility per the 5-Item Questionnaire.
Chiropractic cervical adjustment (activator technique) provoked a severe UCI flare in Jay, leaving him bed-bound and unable to stand or walk the following day.

A 2-day trial of rigid cervical collar use increased Kay's symptoms, while tilting her head 1 cm to the left temporarily resolved all symptoms, and Jay was worse in a rigid collar but better in a soft collar.

Jay, who had the fewest red flags (0/7 subjective, 2/9 physical), progressed well with conservative neuroplasticity-based PT alone, improving from complete disability to no disability on the NDI and returning to full-time work.

Emma initially improved with conservative PT but flared severely when PT access was interrupted by COVID restrictions; she subsequently underwent O-C3 fusion and improved to mild disability with post-fusion PT, though hardware loosening caused a temporary relapse to severe disability.

Kay, who had the most red flags (7/7 subjective, 7/9 physical), showed minimal and inconsistent improvement despite O-C3 fusion, hardware removal, and prolonged conservative PT, with fluctuating NDI between complete and severe disability and overall functional decline on SF-36.

The number of Red Flags at initial evaluation (Jay 2/9, Emma 4/9, Kay 8/9 physical exam RF) appeared to correspond with clinical severity and outcome, with more RF associated with worse prognosis despite treatment.

Psychosocial Yellow Flags (negative mood, fear avoidance, poor social support) appeared to be associated with poorer physical therapy outcomes, consistent with prior research on Yellow Flags predicting outcomes.

Pressure and laser biofeedback training, which meet requirements for therapeutic neuroplasticity, have previously been shown to benefit chronic neck pain and cervical instability, though not yet studied specifically in hypermobility-related UCI.

Neurological presentation (including autonomic, cranial nerve, and cognitive symptoms) is increasingly recognized as part of hEDS/HSD complicated by upper cervical instability, beyond the joint-related manifestations typically associated with this connective tissue disorder.
One patient (Emma) was diagnosed with Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) alongside Chiari malformation, upper cervical instability, and hypermobility.
Vascular EDS is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in COL3A1 affecting the pro-alpha 1 chain of type III procollagen, leading to defective collagen in skin, blood vessels, and internal organs.

A 21-year-old male with clinical features suggestive of vEDS (aortic insufficiency, joint instability, spontaneous pneumothorax, acquired foot deformity, iliofemoral DVT) presented with spontaneous sigmoid colon perforation requiring emergent sigmoid colectomy.

Nine days after initial bowel surgery, the patient developed ruptured hepatic artery aneurysms with massive hemorrhage requiring REBOA placement and hepatic artery embolization, ultimately dying of multi-organ failure and coagulopathy.
Spontaneous hollow viscus perforation, most commonly of the sigmoid colon (~80% of cases), is a well-known complication of vEDS with reported mortality of 12-20%.

Postoperative complications commonly seen in vEDS patients include reperforation of the GI tract, anastomotic rupture or leaks, fistula formation, hernia formation, and poor wound healing leading to dehiscence and evisceration.

Surgical precautions for vEDS patients include careful minimal tissue handling, use of soft-jawed or shodded vascular clamps, buttressing of suture lines, and leaving skin sutures in place longer than normal, with Hartmann's procedure considered a relatively secure surgical choice for spontaneous colonic perforation.

The authors hypothesize that a relationship exists between spontaneous colon rupture and subsequent arterial pseudoaneurysm or dissection complications in vEDS, possibly mediated by increased collagenase activity after perforation or peritonitis, though only one prior case report has described this vascular catastrophe following colonic perforation.
The patient carried a pathogenic COL3A1 deletion mutation (c.855_872del) confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The patient also carried a pathogenic SMAD3 splice-region mutation (c.401-6G>A) confirming a concurrent diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 3.
The patient's aortic arch demonstrated rapid aneurysmal degeneration, growing 3 cm over 4 years to reach a maximum diameter of 7 cm.

Total aortic arch replacement using the frozen elephant trunk (ThoraFlex) technique with subsequent extension TEVAR to the celiac artery resulted in an intact repair and return to baseline functional status at 8-month follow-up.

Intraoperatively, the patient's aortic and cardiac tissue was extremely thin and friable, evidenced by a purse-string suture in the right atrium cutting completely through tissue and multiple areas of anastomotic tearing and bleeding during rewarming.

vEDS is associated with a median life expectancy of 50 years, driven primarily by vascular rupture/dissection and gastrointestinal perforation, with 66% of arterial emergencies occurring in the thoracic aorta.
In LDS, most patients will either suffer aortic dissection or undergo elective thoracic aortic surgery before age 40.
Survival in vEDS is affected by underlying mutation type and molecular mechanism, with emergency surgery for arterial events having an approximate mortality/survival rate of 70%.

LDS3 (SMAD3-related Loeys-Dietz syndrome) has a strong predisposition for osteoarthritis, with aortic disease severity similar to LDS1 and LDS2, though some described SMAD3 mutations show no radiological evidence of osteoarthritis.

Genetic testing identified a heterozygous COL3A1 variant, c.1331G>A (p.Gly444Glu), classified as likely pathogenic and associated with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, in a man who died of arterial rupture.
The patient died of hemoperitoneum caused by medial dissection and rupture of the superior mesenteric artery and its branches.

Autopsy revealed multivessel arteriopathy including bilateral renal artery dissections causing patchy renal infarcts and pancreaticoduodenal artery medial dissection, consistent with multivisceral arterial involvement typical of vEDS.

The patient's clinical history included easy bruising, joint hypermobility, sigmoid bowel perforation requiring partial colectomy at age 20, and a right popliteal artery pseudoaneurysm rupture with compartment syndrome, all features suggestive of an underlying connective tissue disorder later confirmed as vEDS.

The patient's father had a history of a ruptured right femoral artery in his forties and prior surgery for an aortic aneurysm, suggesting a heritable vascular disorder in the family consistent with autosomal dominant vEDS.

Prior genotype-phenotype studies indicate vEDS is typically a severe early-onset disease with arterial complications (dissections/aneurysms of iliac, renal, and carotid arteries) in 80% of cases involving multiple locations, spontaneous colonic perforation in 85% of cases, and obstetrical events in 12% of affected women.

A cited study of 68 individuals with vEDS found that mutations leading to minimal production of normal type III collagen were associated with multivisceral arterial involvement, whereas haploinsufficiency mutations (producing about half-normal collagen levels) were associated with a higher prevalence of aortic disease, later-onset events, and milder arterial disease.

Among children with connective tissue disorders (CTD, including EDS) undergoing open reduction for dislocated hips, 17% of hips re-dislocated, a rate numerically higher than but not statistically different from a non-syndromic DDH cohort.

Residual acetabular dysplasia (RAD) occurred in 35% of hips with underlying CTD after open reduction, numerically lower than the 55% reported in a non-syndromic DDH multicenter study, though authors caution this likely reflects similar rather than truly reduced risk.

Proximal femoral growth disturbance (PFGD) occurred in 22% of hips with CTD after open reduction, lower than the 44% reported in a non-syndromic DDH cohort, though this is not interpreted as a true protective effect.
Postoperative arthrofibrosis (stiffness) developed in 39% of hips with CTD after open reduction, similar to the 36% rate previously reported at the same center for typical (non-syndromic) DDH.
Despite complications, 96% of hips in the CTD cohort ultimately achieved a stable, concentric reduction (IHDI grade 1) at final follow-up.
In a separate published series, 67% of hips with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome undergoing open reduction for dislocation re-dislocated, a substantially higher rate than found in the current CTD cohort.
In a series of Kabuki syndrome patients, open reduction for hip dislocation resulted in a 29% re-dislocation rate and 29% PFGD rate.
In a Marfan syndrome cohort, DDH incidence was 2% and all affected hips were successfully treated with closed reduction alone, without need for open reduction.

Underlying syndromes associated with joint hypermobility, including EDS, Larsen syndrome, and Marfan syndrome, are associated with markedly increased rates of DDH, reported as high as 4%, compared to the approximately 1% incidence in the general population.
Bivariate analysis found no significant association between patient age at surgery and any of the four adverse outcomes (re-dislocation, RAD, PFGD, stiffness).
Duration of postoperative hip spica cast immobilization was not significantly associated with re-dislocation, RAD, PFGD, or stiffness.
A history of prior attempted closed reduction was not significantly associated with re-dislocation, RAD, PFGD, or stiffness after subsequent open reduction.

Adding a femoral osteotomy to a concurrent pelvic osteotomy did not significantly change rates of re-dislocation, RAD, PFGD, or stiffness compared to isolated pelvic osteotomy in CTD-associated hip dislocations.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was the most common single diagnosis associated with connective tissue disorder in the cohort, accounting for 13% of hips, though diagnosed clinically rather than by genetic testing.
A one-year-old male with EDS and right-sided hip dislocation underwent open reduction with Dega acetabuloplasty and achieved a stable, concentric hip reduction maintained at 5 years postoperatively.
The reported patient with wandering liver had a pre-existing history of Sashi-Pena syndrome, a condition noted only as part of his medical background without further elaboration in the text.
Wandering liver is described as arising from weakening, laxity, or absence of the liver's normal supportive ligaments, allowing abnormal hepatic mobility within the abdominal cavity.
Rates of access site complications after large-bore percutaneous closure did not significantly differ between patients with confirmed genetic aortopathy (0%) and those without (8%).
Rates of unplanned femoral cutdown did not significantly differ between genetic aortopathy patients (0%) and nongenetic aortopathy patients (6%).
Patients with genetic aortopathy undergoing large-bore percutaneous access were significantly younger than those without genetic aortopathy.
Patients with genetic aortopathy had higher rates of prior open femoral access compared to those without genetic aortopathy.
Patients with genetic aortopathy had higher rates of prior ipsilateral percutaneous access compared to those without genetic aortopathy.

Among 33 patients with confirmed genetic aortopathy, 3 (9%) had vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, alongside 7 (21%) Marfan syndrome, 7 (21%) Loeys-Dietz syndrome, and other patients with ACTA2, PRKG1, FOXE3, and LOX mutations.

In a supplementary 10-year analysis of all genetic aortopathy patients (2014-2023), only one patient required an unplanned cutdown, yielding an overall technical success rate of 97% for percutaneous closure.
Beyond Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, and vascular EDS, the genetic aortopathy cohort also included patients with ACTA2, PRKG1, FOXE3, and LOX mutations.

Thoracic endovascular aortic repair was the most common procedure in the genetic aortopathy group (52%), followed by zone II arch replacement with frozen elephant trunk (21%), whereas fenestrated/branched endovascular aortic repair was most common in the nongenetic group (43%) followed by TEVAR (25%).
Median femoral sheath size used for large-bore access was identical (20F) between patients with and without genetic aortopathy.
Patients with genetic aortopathy had significantly higher rates of prior open ipsilateral femoral access than those without (27% vs 12%).
Patients with genetic aortopathy had significantly higher rates of prior percutaneous ipsilateral access than those without (58% vs 39%).
In a supplemental 10-year analysis of all genetic aortopathy patients (2014-2023), only one patient required unplanned cutdown, yielding an overall percutaneous closure technical success rate of 97%.
Mitochondrial miR-145-5p levels were significantly increased in PBMCs of fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Mitochondrial miR-223-3p expression did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and controls.
Mitochondrial miR-23a-3p expression did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and controls.
Pain scores were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.
Fatigue scores were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.
Sleep quality scores were significantly worse in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls.
Mitochondrial miR-223-3p levels in PBMCs did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and controls.
Mitochondrial miR-23a-3p levels in PBMCs did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and controls.
The IASP adopted nociplastic pain in 2017 as a third mechanistic pain descriptor, defined as pain arising from altered nociception not fully explained by nociceptive or neuropathic mechanisms.
Peripheral and/or central sensitization, manifesting as allodynia and hyperalgesia, is typically present in nociplastic pain but is not specific to it.

Criteria for possible nociplastic pain in the musculoskeletal system require at least four features: pain duration over 3 months, regional/multifocal/widespread distribution, pain not entirely explained by nociceptive or neuropathic mechanisms, and clinical signs of pain hypersensitivity in the painful region.
Current pharmacological treatment of nociplastic pain resembles that used for neuropathic pain, but opioids should be avoided.

In fibromyalgia, proposed pathophysiological mechanisms include autoreactive antibodies acting at the dorsal root ganglia and aberrant cerebral pain processing with altered brain network architecture.
Mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice showed markedly reduced heterotopic bone volume and surface area at 8, 12, and 24 weeks after tenotomy compared with WT mice.
Mast cell deletion altered the temporal expression pattern of osteochondral markers, delaying and reducing endochondral ossification maturation in injured tendon tissue.
IL-1β expression was markedly decreased at 4, 8, and 12 weeks and TNFA was decreased at 4 and 8 weeks after injury in mast cell-deficient mice compared with WT mice.
Mast cell deletion markedly decreased overall inflammatory cell infiltration in injured tendon tissue at 4 and 8 weeks post-injury.

Toluidine blue staining revealed mast cell infiltration in traumatized tendon tissue peaking at 8 weeks after injury, coinciding with peak HO activity, and activated mast cells (CAM1+) showed a similar pattern.
LPS treatment of bone marrow-derived mast cells markedly upregulated Ntrk1 (TrkA) expression, while Ngf itself was not detected in mast cells, indicating mast cells respond to but do not produce NGF.
Costimulation of BMMCs with recombinant NGF (≥10 ng/mL) and LPS (100 ng/mL) induced degranulation morphology, whereas either agent alone had no effect.
BMMCs released increasing amounts of histamine and β-hexosaminidase (degranulation markers) with increasing rmNGF concentrations during LPS costimulation.
TrkA colocalized with mast cell markers FCER1A, KIT, and activated marker CAM1 in injured tendon tissue, confirming TrkA is expressed on mast cells in vivo.
In vivo administration of recombinant NGF increased ectopic bone volume, while the TrkA inhibitor GW441756 markedly decreased ectopic bone volume compared with control after tenotomy.
Direct costimulation of tendon-derived stem cells (TDSCs) with rmNGF or GW441756 did not influence their chondrogenic differentiation, indicating NGF does not act directly on stem cells.

Single-cell RNA-seq of traumatized tissue confirmed that mast cells were the exclusive immune cell type expressing TrkA (Ntrk1), while tissue-specific stem cells expressed scarce TrkA but abundant TrkC.
In vivo NGF administration increased IL1B+ and TNFA+ cells and mast cell activation (CAM1+), while TrkA inhibition with GW441756 reduced these effects.
Administration of NGF in mast cell-deficient (KitW-sh/W-sh) mice did not significantly increase HO formation, confirming that NGF's pro-HO effect requires mast cells.
LPS-treated mast cells showed marked upregulation of Ntf3 (encoding NT3), while Ntrk3 (encoding TrkC) was not expressed, indicating mast cells produce but do not respond to NT3.
Serum NT3 was markedly elevated after tenotomy in WT mice compared with sham-operated animals but was not elevated in mast cell-deficient mice.
TrkC expression was markedly increased in damaged tendon and bone cells in HO-modeled tissue compared with sham-operated tissue.
Ntrk3 (TrkC) knockdown reduced chondrogenic differentiation of tendon-derived stem cells, while recombinant human NT3 treatment increased it.
TLR4 inhibition with Resatorvid did not alter NT3 expression in mast cells, and Tlr4 itself was not markedly expressed in mast cells, ruling out TLR4 as the LPS receptor mediating NT3 secretion.
