LPS, via its lipid A moiety, directly binds TrkA (confirmed by competitive binding assay and molecular docking with hydrogen bonding to specific TrkA residues) and cooperates with NGF to enhance TrkA phosphorylation, whereas delipidated LPS (polysaccharide only) failed to induce TrkA phosphorylation.
NGF promoted NT3 secretion from mast cells in a dose-dependent manner in the presence of LPS.
Conditioned medium from mast cells treated with both NGF and LPS enhanced chondrogenic differentiation of tendon-derived stem cells, and this effect was blocked by Ntf3 knockdown in the mast cells.

Adoptive transfer of Ntf3-overexpressing or NGF-supplemented mast cells into mast cell-deficient mice increased ectopic bone volume, whereas transfer of Ntf3-knockdown mast cells decreased it, directly confirming mast cell-derived NT3 drives HO formation in vivo.

scRNA-seq showed Ntf3 was expressed by mast cells, monocytes, T lymphocytes, and macrophages, but only mast cells co-expressed Ntrk1 (TrkA), with peak coexpression of Ntf3 and Ntrk1 in mast cells occurring on day 7 after injury.

In human traumatic ligament tissue, mast cell infiltration and NGF expression increased with time after trauma and in HO tissue, TrkA expression was scarce while TrkC markedly increased by day 7, and activated mast cells (CAM1+) colocalized with TrkA and NT3.

TLR4 inhibition with Resatorvid did not alter NT3 expression in LPS-treated BMMCs, and TLR4 itself was not markedly expressed in the microarray or Western blot data, indicating LPS-induced NT3 secretion is not mediated via TLR4.

A protein competitive binding assay and molecular docking demonstrated direct binding between LPS and TrkA, with lipid A hydrogen bonding to N-terminal TrkA residues Pro115, Arg116, Ser139, and Gln141.

Delipidated LPS (polysaccharide only) could not induce TrkA phosphorylation, whereas costimulation of mast cells with rmNGF and intact LPS markedly increased TrkA Tyr490 phosphorylation, indicating lipid A acts as a costimulatory factor with NGF for TrkA activation.
NGF promoted NT3 secretion from mast cells in a dose-dependent manner in the presence of LPS, and this effect was blocked by the TrkA inhibitor GW441756.
In vivo, rmNGF injection markedly increased CAM1+/NT3+ mast cell numbers in traumatized tendon tissue while GW treatment decreased them relative to saline controls.

Conditioned medium from mast cells treated with rmNGF and LPS markedly enhanced chondrogenic differentiation of tendon-derived stem cells, whereas conditioned medium from Ntf3-knockdown mast cells inhibited it.
Neutralizing NT3 antibody further confirmed the role of NT3 in promoting chondrogenic differentiation of tendon-derived stem cells.

Adoptive transfer of NT3-overexpressing mast cells or mast cells plus rmNGF into mast cell-deficient mice markedly increased ectopic bone volume compared with control mast cell transfer, while Ntf3-knockdown mast cells decreased ectopic bone volume.

Single-cell RNA-seq of the injury site showed Ntf3 expressed by mast cells, monocytes, T lymphocytes, and macrophages, but only mast cells expressed Ntrk1, with peak coexpression of both genes on day 7 after HO induction.
In human Achilles tendon and ligament specimens, mast cell and inflammatory cell infiltration was markedly increased 7 days after trauma and in heterotopic ossification tissue compared with day 0.

IHC staining of human ligament tissue showed NGF expression increased progressively with time after trauma, while TrkA expression was scarce and TrkC expression markedly increased by day 7, suggesting a shift from NGF/TrkA to NT3/TrkC signaling.

Polychromatic immunofluorescence in human ligament tissue 7 days after trauma showed activated mast cells (CAM1+) co-expressing TrkA and secreting NT3, confirming the NGF-mast cell-NT3 axis in human HO pathogenesis.

The authors note that mast cell deletion did not entirely block HO, and cite prior work showing FOP was reduced by ~50% with depletion of mast cells or macrophages alone, and up to 75% when both were depleted, suggesting multiple inflammatory cell types cooperate in HO.
Tanezumab, an NGF-neutralizing antibody effective against arthritis pain, has limited clinical viability for HO due to marked adverse reactions at high doses and limited effectiveness at low doses.
Mast cell inhibitors imatinib and cromolyn decrease HO but their clinical use is limited by lack of specificity and potential unintended effects on other physiological functions.
The study examined both male and female animals and reported similar findings for both sexes regarding mast cell-driven heterotopic ossification.
Melatonin reduced mechanical hyperalgesia induced by nitroglycerin in a rat migraine model.
Melatonin reduced c-fos expression in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis that had been induced by nitroglycerin.
Melatonin reduced CGRP expression in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis that had been induced by nitroglycerin.
Melatonin reduced CGRP expression in the trigeminal ganglia that had been induced by nitroglycerin.
Melatonin reduced CGRP release from meningeal afferents in an ex-vivo meningeal preparation.
Melatonin suppressed nitroglycerin-stimulated meningeal mast cell activation as assessed by toluidine-blue staining and histological examination.
The nonselective MT1/MT2 receptor antagonist luzindole abolished the anti-hyperalgesic and anti-inflammatory effects of melatonin in the NTG-induced migraine model.
The selective MT2 receptor antagonist DH97 abolished the anti-hyperalgesic and anti-inflammatory effects of melatonin, indicating a key role for MT2 receptors in melatonin's antimigraine action.

The potent MT3 antagonist prazosin did not reverse melatonin's effects on CGRP, c-fos, or mast cell activation, but did reverse melatonin's effect on mechanical hyperalgesia, suggesting MT3 receptors are not the primary mediator except for pain behavior.

Combinations of luzindole or DH97 with prazosin also canceled melatonin's effects, except for CGRP expression in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis, indicating complex, partially overlapping receptor involvement.

The overall pattern of receptor antagonist experiments indicates that melatonin's antimigraine effects are mainly mediated through MT2 receptors, without excluding a possible contributory role for MT1 receptors.

Cryo-EM structural studies resolved the high-resolution ligand-bound structure of MRGPRX2, revealing a shallow binding pocket with negatively charged and hydrophobic sub-pockets that accommodate structurally diverse cationic ligands.

MRGPRX2 lacks the canonical TM3-ECL2 disulfide bond found in family A GPCRs and instead relies on a TM4-TM5 inter-helix disulfide bond required to preserve receptor signaling integrity, allowing an unusually open ligand-binding surface.
Patients with cutaneous mastocytosis show increased MRGPRX2 expression in skin lesions.
Patients with chronic urticaria have overall increased skin expression of MRGPRX2.
Non-histaminergic itch has been attributed to MRGPRX2 signaling.
Hymenoptera venom- and drug-induced anaphylaxis in patients with negative skin testing has been attributed to altered or increased mast cell MRGPRX2 expression.
Rhinovirus-induced beta-defensin production in bronchial epithelial cells activates MRGPRX2 and mediates asthma exacerbations.
MRGPRX2 mRNA is detectable in adipose tissue, esophagus, urinary bladder, and lungs, with highest expression in skin, but not detected in kidney, liver, ovary, spleen, or pancreas.
MRGPRX2 was shown to be the exclusive opiate receptor expressed by human skin mast cells, with ligands such as codeine triggering receptor internalization and desensitization to further X2 ligands.
Patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria show increased skin mast cell MRGPRX2 expression and display exacerbated skin reactivity to intradermal injection of X2 agonists such as substance P.
Elevation of MRGPRX2 expression was also observed in patients with allergic contact dermatitis and asthma.

A case report described a patient with systemic mastocytosis who had multiple episodes of anaphylaxis to Hymenoptera venom and ciprofloxacin, both known MRGPRX2 stimulators, suggesting X2-mediated systemic mast cell activation.

Homology modeling, docking simulations, and calcium mobilization assays identified fluoroquinolone-binding residues M109 and F78 on MRGPRX2, and missense mutations at these sites were predicted to exacerbate responsiveness to drugs such as ciprofloxacin.
Silencing of Orai1, Orai2, or Orai3 (CRAC channel components) decreased MRGPRX2/substance P-induced calcium mobilization, degranulation, and cytokine/chemokine production in mast cells.
GRK2 differentially regulates mast cell activation, inhibiting IgE/FceRI-triggered degranulation while enhancing MRGPRX2/Mrgprb2-dependent mast cell activation.
In human skin mast cells, beta-arrestin-1 is required for agonist-induced internalization of MRGPRX2.
MRGPRX2 activation phosphorylates and activates the transcription factor MITF via nuclear translocation of Lysyl t-RNA synthetase, a pathway also shared downstream of FceRI crosslinking.

EP262, a first-in-class once-daily oral selective small molecule MRGPRX2 antagonist, received FDA clearance to initiate a Phase 1 study in January 2023, followed by a randomized placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial for chronic spontaneous urticaria and a Phase 2a trial for atopic dermatitis.

Genistein-derived small molecule MRGPRX2 antagonists dose-dependently inhibited mast cell activation in vitro and ex vivo (b-hexosaminidase release, calcium flux, chemokine/lipid mediator production, b-arrestin recruitment) and showed promising inhibitory effects in vivo in mouse models of acute inflammation and systemic anaphylaxis.
MRGPRX2 may participate in rosacea-like inflammation, highlighting a pro-inflammatory role for beta-arrestin-2 downstream of the receptor.
MRGPRX2 is expressed not only in mast cells but also in sensory neurons and keratinocytes.

A GPCR database identified over 100 missense single-nucleotide polymorphisms in MRGPRX2, which along with epigenetic and post-transcriptional modifications, may contribute to variable ligand responsiveness.
A meta-analysis informing EAACI guidelines found skin prick testing to be highly sensitive for diagnosing cow's milk and cooked egg allergy.
Molecular allergology components-specific IgE showed higher specificity than whole extract sIgE for peanut, hazelnut, and cashew allergy.
Meta-analysis found BAT to be both highly sensitive and specific for diagnosing peanut and sesame allergy, the only allergens with sufficient study numbers for pooled analysis.
With optimal cutoffs, BAT achieved very high sensitivity and specificity for peanut allergy, outperforming SPT and sIgE.
The mast cell activation test showed markedly higher diagnostic performance (AUC) than skin prick testing.
MAT showed lower sensitivity than BAT for peanut allergy diagnosis, attributed to the need for non-autologous IgE transfer.
The bead-based epitope assay demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for peanut allergy epitope detection.
In Ghanaian children, IgE cross-reactivity between peanut and Schistosoma Mansoni was found to be mediated by cross-reactive carbohydrate determinants rather than true peanut sensitization.
IgE against the alpha-Gal glycan has previously been associated with delayed anaphylaxis to meat.
In the LEAP study, peanut-specific IgG4 increased over time in the group that consumed peanut from year one of life, and this group had less peanut allergy.

A cross-sectional egg allergy study found that specific IgG4 to egg, egg white, ovomucoid and ovalbumin was higher in allergic than tolerant children, and higher in those consuming egg than avoiding it.
A cohort study found higher plasma food-specific IgA counts in children with peanut allergy, but no evidence that IgA protects against food allergy development or is useful for diagnosis.

A study of peanut oral immunotherapy patients identified discrete peanut-reactive T cell immunotypes based on Th2A cell proportions that were significantly related to distinct responses to immunotherapy.
Tfh13 cells, a T follicular helper subset, may induce anaphylaxis by promoting high-affinity IgE via sequential class-switching of B cells from IgG1 to IgE.
An artificial neural network study of cow's milk allergy recovery identified higher FoxP3 intensity in cow's milk allergic children linking Treg/Th2 expression to disease persistence.
A unique CD23+IgG1+ memory B cell population has been described in children with long-term persistent peanut allergy, with frequency correlating to serum IgE levels.

A multi-omic oral microbiome study found Prevotella abundance protective against Th2-mediated response in peanut allergy, while Neisseria-dominant milieus were associated with Th2-mediated allergic response, alongside differences in short-chain fatty acids and IL-4.

A fecal metabolome network analysis from infancy to mid-childhood found reduced microbiome diversity and altered histidine, butyrate, and isovalerate pathway metabolites associated with development of peanut allergy.
A prospective multiscale microbiome study found Veillonella and Bacteroides species prevalence significantly associated with high-threshold (less reactive) peanut-allergic patients.
Plasma cytokine profiles in sensitized infants showed higher allergy-defining IL-4, IL-13, IL-12p70 and lower IL-10 as predictors of food allergy diagnosis and resolution.
A prospective study found significantly raised median TNF-α and IL-6 before a therapeutic elimination diet in food-allergic participants, with significant decreases after the diet.
Plasma IL-5 and IL-13 decreased after food allergen immunotherapy, though this immunologic suppression was noted to be transient.
Single-cell profiling of peanut-allergic patients revealed a delayed, IL-2-dependent upregulation of CD154 on Treg marker-expressing cells.
Single-cell analysis of CD3/CD28-stimulated naïve CD4+ T cells in food-allergic adolescents showed significantly greater IL-6 and TNFα production and lower IFN-γ production.
A machine-learning ensemble voting algorithm using cytosine-phosphate-guanine methylation data achieved 100% accuracy identifying food allergy.
A Random Forest machine learning model successfully predicted tolerance to oral food challenge for heated egg with high sensitivity and specificity.
Unsupervised K-Means clustering applied to mast cell activation test data successfully created distinct phenotype clusters among patients with similar MAT responses.

The prevalence of scleritis was significantly higher in patients with idiopathic small fiber neuropathy (0.62%) compared with patients without SFN (0.29%) after adjusting for age, gender, race, and ethnicity.
Episcleritis prevalence was numerically higher in SFN patients (0.48%) than in non-SFN controls (0.28%), but this difference was not statistically significant after adjustment.
Among 2100 patients with idiopathic SFN and a documented eye exam, 23 (1.1%) had episcleritis and/or scleritis without another immune-mediated systemic disease.
A 61-year-old woman with posterior scleritis and biopsy-confirmed length-dependent SFN had both her neuropathy and eye symptoms controlled on IVIg for three years.

A 23-year-old woman with bilateral scleritis and biopsy-confirmed SFN improved on IVIg and later remained stable for four years on subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIg) with low-dose prednisone and no reported side effects.
Compared with non-SFN controls, patients with idiopathic SFN in this study were more likely to be female and White, and less likely to be Hispanic.
Prior confocal microscopy studies (cited) found reduced corneal nerve fiber density, branch density, and fiber length, along with increased nerve fiber tortuosity, in patients with SFN.

A cited study of 55 Chinese patients with neuropathic pain found that a 13-item SFN symptom inventory questionnaire (including dry eyes) had moderate diagnostic value for SFN, with 80% sensitivity and 81.8% specificity among the 20 patients diagnosed with SFN.
A cited case series described three patients with neuropathic corneal pain (NCP) and biopsy-confirmed SFN, suggesting an association between SFN and NCP pathogenesis.
All 7 patients with small-vessel vasculitis or perifolliculitis on skin biopsy were seropositive for TS-HDS, FGFR-3, or Plexin D1 antibodies, a statistically significant association.
Skin biopsy inflammation (small-vessel vasculitis or perifolliculitis) was strongly associated with a non-length-dependent (NLD) inflammation or pathology pattern in small-fiber neuropathy patients.

Inflammation (small-vessel vasculitis or perifolliculitis) was identified on skin biopsy in 7 of 80 patients with pure small-fiber neuropathy, suggesting it may serve as an additional autoimmune biomarker.
Both COVID-19-infected and vaccinated patients showed a significant reduction in somatic (epidermal) small nerve fiber density on skin biopsy compared to healthy controls.
Autonomic skin innervation density did not differ between P-COVID or P-VAC patients and healthy controls, indicating preserved autonomic nerve fibers despite somatic denervation.

Small fiber neuropathy incidence, defined by abnormal epidermal nerve fiber density, was numerically higher in natural COVID-19 patients (94%) than in vaccinated patients (79%), but this difference was not statistically significant.
Autonomic symptom burden measured by COMPASS-31 was significantly higher in patients after natural COVID-19 infection than after vaccination, while other clinical scales did not differ.
The latency between the inciting event and onset of neuropathic symptoms was significantly longer in patients after natural COVID-19 infection than after vaccination.

Autoimmune diseases and newly detected autoimmune abnormalities (mainly Hashimoto thyroiditis) were similarly frequent in both P-VAC (58%) and P-COVID (55%) patient groups, with no significant between-group difference.

Prevalence of autoimmune dysfunction did not significantly differ between patients with and without small fiber neuropathy, suggesting autoimmune disorders do not increase risk of SFN after COVID-19/vaccination.
Small fiber neuropathy was reported to be more frequent among male patients in this cohort.
Epidermal nerve fiber density at the leg and thigh was inversely correlated with neuropathic pain (DN4) and autonomic symptom (COMPASS-31) scores.
The COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom score was positively correlated with pain severity (DN4) and negatively correlated with quality of life (SF-36).
Motor and sensory nerve conduction studies of ulnar, sural, and tibial nerves were normal in all recruited subjects, indicating sparing of large myelinated peripheral nerve fibers.
The proximal-to-distal ratio of skin denervation indicated a length-dependent, predominantly distal small nerve fiber loss in both P-COVID and P-VAC groups.

ROC curve analysis identified optimal epidermal nerve fiber density cutoffs for diagnosing SFN of 9.6 fibers/mm at the lower leg (80% sensitivity, 96% specificity) and 12.8 fibers/mm at the thigh (77% sensitivity, 100% specificity).

All P-COVID patients had chronic pain lasting more than 3 months meeting long COVID criteria, and since most also had SFN, the authors suggest SFN may be part of the long COVID phenotype explaining pain and orthostatic tachycardia symptoms.

The authors propose, citing prior literature, that direct SARS-CoV-2 damage to dorsal root ganglion neurons via ACE2 and neuropilin-1 receptors is a hypothesized mechanism for small fiber neuropathy, although autopsy studies have not confirmed virus presence in peripheral nerves.

The authors propose that a cytokine storm/hyperinflammatory state releasing inflammatory mediators that act on sensory nerve endings (neurogenic inflammation and nociceptor hypersensitivity) is a candidate mechanism for nociceptor damage in post-COVID/post-vaccine SFN.
Genetic sodium channelopathies have been identified in small fiber neuropathy, providing insight into disease mechanisms and revealing overlap with other sodium channelopathies.
SFN diagnosis in clinical practice is frequently based on the Besta Criteria, involving skin biopsy and quantitative sensory testing, while ACTTION criteria are recommended for clinical trials.

SFN involves the thinly myelinated Aδ and unmyelinated C fibers of the peripheral nervous system, causing neuropathic pain (often burning) typically in hands and feet ascending proximally, and can lead to autonomic dysfunction due to involvement of small fibers in the autonomic nervous system.
A wide variety of underlying conditions—metabolic, immune-mediated, infectious, toxic, and hereditary—have been associated with SFN.

The authors hypothesize that primary bladder neck obstruction may arise from neurogenic dysregulation of the sympathetic nervous system, including upper motor neuron lesion or peripheral autonomic neuropathy such as small fiber neuropathy, or from increased sympathetic tone due to anxiety/stress.

Among 17 women with bladder neck obstruction and pelvic pain treated with botulinum toxin A injection to the bladder neck, 14 (77%) reported improvement on the Global Response Assessment, with an average VAS score of 8.3.
All six patients with biopsy-confirmed small fiber neuropathy showed significant improvement after botulinum toxin A injection, with a higher average VAS score (8.7) than the overall cohort.
Postoperative symptom flares occurred in six patients after botulinum toxin A injection, lasting an average of 16 days.
77% of patients indicated they would repeat the botulinum toxin A injection procedure despite the occurrence of symptom flares.
The most commonly improved symptoms after BoNT-A injection included feeling of incomplete emptying, difficulty starting stream, urethral burning, pain with urination, and pelvic pain.

The authors propose that primary bladder neck obstruction may arise from neurogenic dysregulation of the sympathetic nervous system, including upper motor neuron lesion or peripheral autonomic neuropathy such as small fiber neuropathy, or from increased sympathetic tone due to anxiety or stress.

Bladder neck obstruction was diagnosed using Nitti Criteria based on video urodynamics showing high bladder pressure with low flow at the bladder neck, supplemented by additional criteria including high voiding pressure, prolonged voiding attempts, Valsalva effort, and cystoscopic findings.
A normative study of over 1,350 healthy adults found no significant sex differences in electrochemical skin conductance values at the hands or feet.
Normative studies showed race/ethnicity-based variation in ESC values, leading to adjusted diagnostic thresholds (lowered by 10) for Chinese, Indian, and African-American populations.
Precision testing per FDA guidelines found ESC to have a coefficient of variation of 4% in healthy subjects and 7% in diabetic patients across repeated measurements on multiple devices.
Sudoscan's ESC and intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) showed comparable diagnostic accuracy for small fiber neuropathy, with similar areas under the ROC curve.
ESC correlated strongly with intraepidermal nerve fiber density when adjusted for body weight.
Sudoscan showed higher diagnostic accuracy (AUC) than QSART for detecting small fiber and diabetic neuropathy in two separate studies of already characterized patients.
One study found Sudoscan had higher diagnostic performance compared with Neuropad, though the comparison is limited because Neuropad is a qualitative colorimetric test rather than a quantitative one.
In a small cohort of patients with transthyretin familial amyloid polyneuropathy, ESC strongly correlated with corneal nerve fiber length measured by in vivo confocal microscopy.

Compared with four reference small fiber neuropathy diagnostics, Sudoscan was less sensitive than laser evoked potentials, marginally better than quantitative sensory testing for warm detection, and much better than cold detection threshold and sympathetic skin response.
Lower ESC values were associated with a higher frequency of neuropathy signs, correlating significantly with both the Utah Early Neuropathy Scale and the Michigan Neuropathy Screening Instrument.
A manufacturer-sponsored clinical study found strong agreement between Withings' Body Scan/BodyComp scale ESC measurements (feet only) and standalone Sudoscan devices.
Small unmyelinated nerve fibers regenerate at approximately 0.177 fibers/mm/day in healthy controls, with neuropathy associated with a further reduction in this regenerative rate.

In an animal model, electrical field stimulation of eccrine sweat glands from monkey palms induced immediate sweat secretion that was dose-dependently suppressed by the cholinergic antagonist atropine and completely inhibited by lidocaine (but not by the direct cholinergic agonist methacholine), indicating that stimulation activates cholinergic nerve pathways rather than the gland directly.

Adrenergic fibers act on CFTR chloride channels in sweat gland ducts, and defective CFTR channels in cystic fibrosis lead to increased chloride ion concentration in sweat, forming the basis of the diagnostic sweat chloride test.
Sudoscan testing in 100 healthy children showed ESC values aligned with adult normal values, though this sample size was considered small for establishing definitive pediatric norms.

Network analysis of symptoms across 17 functional somatic syndromes identified ten distinct symptom communities, including cognitive problems/fatigue/depression, sensory problems, facial pain, head/neck/upper back pain, dizziness/nausea, throat pain/swallowing problems, chest pain, widespread pain, abdominal pain/digestion problems, and genital pain.

The symptoms "tired", "down, depressed, or hopeless", and "tired after minimal exertion" showed the highest node strength (centrality) in the symptom network, indicating fatigue and depression act as key connecting symptoms across functional somatic syndromes.

Most correlations (edges) between symptoms in the FSS network were small (46.5%) or small-to-medium (47.1%) in magnitude, indicating generally moderate rather than strong interconnections among symptoms.

One of the ten identified symptom communities in the FSS network consisted of abdominal pain and problems with digestion, indicating that IBS-type gastrointestinal symptoms form a distinct but interconnected cluster within the broader network of functional somatic symptoms.

Case 1 carries a likely pathogenic missense TGFB2 variant confirming LDS4, presenting with severe mitral regurgitation from billowing bileaflet prolapse with torn chordae, moderate pulmonary regurgitation, and mild sinus of Valsalva dilation without other vessel tortuosity.

Case 2-1 carries a pathogenic missense TGFB2 variant causing LDS4 with severe aortic regurgitation from a floppy, myxomatous aortic valve and severe mitral regurgitation from billowing bileaflets, without aortic dilation.

Case 2-2 (sister of Case 2-1), carrying the same TGFB2 mutation, presented with bicuspid aortic valve, severe mitral regurgitation from a redundant valve, and moderate tricuspid regurgitation, without aortic arch enlargement or ocular findings.
Case 3-1 carries a likely pathogenic frameshift TGFB2 variant of unknown significance associated with aortic arch enlargement and aortic valve regurgitation, without valve billowing features.

The elder brother of Case 3-1, carrying the same frameshift TGFB2 mutation, presented with aortic dissection requiring a Bentall procedure, plus a history of myocardial infarction and carotid artery dissections, without significant Marfanoid features except talipes planus.

Missense mutations located within the RKKR furin cleavage motif of TGFB2 (Cases 1, 2-1, 2-2) are proposed to impair proper release of mature TGFβ from the latency-associated peptide, and these patients manifested predominantly valvular disease.

Frameshift mutations in the C-terminal cytokine domain of TGFB2 (Cases 3-1, 3-2), outside the RKKR motif, were associated with aortic arch enlargement/dissection and milder valvular involvement, in contrast to RKKR-motif missense mutations (Cases 1, 2-1, 2-2) associated with multivalvular billowing/prolapse without severe aortic dilation.
A prior published report described four LDS4 cases with significant mitral valve prolapse, two of whom required surgical valve replacement.
A review of LDS4 patients reported aortic aneurysm in approximately 60% and mitral valve prolapse in only 22% of cases.
Preventive aortic surgery is recommended when aortic arch enlargement reaches 40 mm in LDS overall or 45 mm specifically in LDS4, due to dissection risk even without further enlargement.

Concomitant congenital heart defects (ventricular septal defect in Case 1, bicuspid aortic valve in Case 2-2) were observed but are common in the general population and may not be directly related to LDS4.

Distinctive billowing/redundant deformities occurring simultaneously in more than two cardiac valves, as seen in Cases 1, 2-1, and 2-2, are uncommon in the general population and may serve as a diagnostic clue for LDS/connective tissue disease.
Preservation of the perigastric vagus nerve (VPG) reduced the incidence of postsurgical gastroparesis compared with vagus nerve resection (VRG).
Preservation of the hepatic branch of the vagus nerve (VPG) eliminated postoperative gallstone formation compared with resection (VRG).

Patients in the vagus nerve resection group (VRG) reported significantly worse appetite loss and nausea/vomiting symptoms at 6 months and worse appetite loss at 12 months compared with the preservation group (VPG).
The VRG group had persistently higher reflux and eating-related symptoms on the gastric-cancer-specific quality-of-life questionnaire at both 6 and 12 months compared with VPG.
No significant differences were observed between VPG and VRG groups in intraoperative blood loss or postoperative surgical complications (bleeding, anastomosis leakage, pancreatic fistula).
Vagus nerve preservation surgery required significantly longer operation time than vagus nerve resection surgery.
Time to recovery from postsurgical gastroparesis was shorter in the vagus nerve preservation group than the resection group.
Males who later developed Long Covid showed increased TGF-beta signaling during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with males who recovered.
Females who later developed Long Covid showed reduced TGF-beta expression during acute infection, opposite to the pattern seen in males.

Females who developed Long Covid showed increased expression of an unnamed RNA gene implicated in autoimmunity during acute infection compared with females who recovered (the gene name was lost/garbled in the provided abstract text).
Alterations in monocyte phenotype and activation state were observed as immune features of Long Covid that were conserved across both sexes.
NF-kB transcription factors were upregulated in many cell types at both acute and convalescent (3- and 12-month) time points in Long Covid.

Individuals with ongoing Long Covid showed reduced expression of an unnamed factor across lymphocyte subsets, alongside elevated intracellular IL-4 in T cell subsets, suggesting a role in driving Th2-like immune responses (the specific gene/protein name was lost/garbled in the provided abstract text).
Individuals with ongoing Long Covid demonstrated elevated intracellular IL-4 in T cell subsets, consistent with a skewed Th2-like immune response.

MiR-10b-5p was significantly downregulated in spinal cord tissue of SCI rats compared to sham controls, consistent with prior GEO dataset (GSE19890) analysis showing downregulation at 3 and 7 days post-SCI.
Intrathecal agomiR-10b-5p overexpression elevated BBB motor function scores and reduced spinal cord water content (edema) in SCI rats compared to negative control agomir.

MiR-10b-5p overexpression upregulated the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 and downregulated pro-apoptotic Bax, cleaved-caspase-3, and cleaved-PARP in spinal cord tissue of SCI rats, indicating promotion of cell survival.
LPS stimulation of PC12 cells reduced miR-10b-5p expression compared to untreated controls, and this reduction was reversed by agomiR-10b-5p transfection.
MiR-10b-5p overexpression reduced LPS-induced proinflammatory cytokine production (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α), apoptosis (TUNEL-positive cells), and ROS production in PC12 cells.

MiR-10b-5p directly binds the 3'UTR of PTBP1 mRNA (predicted by TargetScan, confirmed by FISH colocalization, RNA pull-down, and luciferase reporter assay), resulting in decreased PTBP1 luciferase activity and expression.
PTBP1 was upregulated in spinal cord tissue of SCI rats and in LPS-stimulated PC12 cells relative to controls.
PTBP1 overexpression reversed the protective effects of miR-10b-5p in SCI rats, restoring BBB score, spinal cord water content, lesion severity, and normal motor neuron index to near baseline levels.
PTBP1 overexpression counteracted the inhibitory effects of miR-10b-5p on LPS-induced PC12 cell apoptosis, inflammatory cytokine production, and ROS production.
TGF-β1 and phosphorylated Smad3 protein levels were reduced in spinal cord tissue of SCI rats compared to sham, and this reduction was reversed by miR-10b-5p overexpression.
PTBP1 overexpression accelerated TGF-β1 mRNA degradation (shortened half-life) in LPS-treated PC12 cells, indicating PTBP1 destabilizes TGF-β1 mRNA.

PTBP1 physically binds TGF-β1 mRNA, as shown by RNA pull-down enrichment with TGF-β1 sense (but not anti-sense) probe and RIP enrichment with anti-PTBP1 (but not IgG) antibody in LPS-treated PC12 cells.

Overall, miR-10b-5p alleviates spinal cord injury by repressing PTBP1-mediated TGF-β1 mRNA decay, thereby activating the TGF-β1/Smad3 pathway and reducing neuronal apoptosis, inflammation, and oxidative stress.

In LDS (Tgfbr1M318R/+) vascular smooth muscle cells, transcripts related to ECM-receptor interactions and elastic/contractile integrity of the aortic wall were broadly downregulated relative to control VSMCs.
Pathways related to stress responses (hypoxia, p53-dependent), inflammation, senescence and cell death were enriched among transcripts upregulated in Tgfbr1M318R/+ LDS VSMCs.
Mechanosensitive transcripts Thbs1, Cyr61/CCN1 and Ctgf/CCN2 were upregulated in LDS VSMCs, suggesting defective ECM-integrin interactions induce mechanical stress responses.
Transcription factor target enrichment analysis showed Nrf2 (NFE2L2) target genes were over-represented among transcripts downregulated in LDS VSMCs.
Target genes of GATA transcription factors and CEBPD were enriched among transcripts upregulated in LDS VSMCs, implicating GATA-driven transcription in LDS pathology.
MERFISH spatial transcriptomics showed Gata4 and Agtr1a were more highly detected in the aortic root than the ascending aorta of LDS mice.
Cebpb (proinflammatory mediator) and Meg3 (lncRNA that negatively regulates TGF-beta signaling and promotes VSMC proliferation) transcripts were spatially enriched in the LDS aortic root.
Carmn (positive regulator of VSMC contractile function) and Myh11 (differentiated VSMC marker) expression were enriched in the distal ascending aorta, a region only mildly affected in LDS mice.

A transcriptionally distinct VSMC2 subcluster, defined in part by Gata4 expression, was identified in scRNA-seq with expression highest in the aortic root and progressively diminishing along the proximal-to-distal axis of the ascending aorta in both control and LDS mice.

In a reanalyzed human LDS/donor aortic scRNA-seq dataset, GATA4 expression was highest in the VSMC2 cluster from the aortic root, with no detectable expression in the ascending aorta, mirroring the mouse pattern.

CoGAPS latent pattern analysis identified transcriptional patterns 4 and 5 enriched in VSMC2 and VSMC1 respectively in mouse LDS aorta, with pattern 4 (VSMC2-associated) transcripts enriched for GATA family transcription factor targets; this pattern structure was conserved when projected onto human LDS aortic scRNA-seq data.

VSMC2-defining transcripts were enriched for inflammation, senescence and cellular stress pathways in both mouse and human LDS aortic datasets, while VSMC1 expressed higher ECM-receptor interaction and contractile function transcripts.
GATA4 mRNA and protein were further upregulated in VSMCs of the LDS aortic root compared with control, confirmed by scRNA-seq, RNA in situ hybridization, immunofluorescence, and immunoblot.

Postnatal, VSMC-specific deletion of Gata4 (GATA4SMcKO) in LDS mice significantly reduced progressive aortic root dilation and root growth compared with LDS mice retaining GATA4 (GATA4Ctrl), and improved aortic root medial architecture.
No notable dilation was observed in the ascending aorta of Tgfbr1M318R/+ mice at 16 weeks, and GATA4 deletion had no effect on ascending aorta diameter.
GATA4 deletion in VSMCs did not associate with changes in blood pressure.
VSMC-specific GATA4 deletion in LDS mice reduced expression of Agtr1a (angiotensin II type 1a receptor) in the aortic root, consistent with GATA4 driving AT1R signaling.
VSMC-specific GATA4 deletion reduced expression of the proinflammatory transcription factors Cebpb and Cebpd, which were otherwise upregulated in LDS VSMCs.

Reanalysis of a published SHF- and CNC-lineage-traced VSMC dataset showed that the VSMC1/VSMC2 transcriptional subclusters were not strictly defined by embryological lineage of origin, with cells of both SHF and CNC lineages present in either subcluster.
Plasma ficolin-1 levels were significantly lower in patients with IPF and CTD-ILD compared with healthy controls.
Serum TGF-β1 levels were significantly elevated in IPF and CTD-ILD patients compared with healthy controls.
Ficolin-B protein/mRNA expression was decreased and fibronectin increased in lungs of bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis mice compared with control mice.
Fcnb expression was negatively correlated with fibrosis-related genes Acta2, Fn1 and Tgfb1 in BLM-treated mouse lungs.
Ficolin-B was highly expressed in pro-Spc-positive alveolar epithelial cells but not in Fsp1-positive myofibroblasts in lung sections.
Ficolin-B knockout mice showed greater weight loss and reduced survival after bleomycin treatment compared to wild-type mice.
Ficolin-B knockout mice exhibited markedly worse lung fibrosis histology and significantly higher Ashcroft fibrosis scores than wild-type mice after bleomycin treatment.
Ficolin-B knockout mice had significantly worse lung function (compliance, elastance, inspiratory capacity) than wild-type mice after bleomycin treatment.
Hydroxyproline content (a measure of collagen deposition) was higher in lungs of Fcnb-/- mice compared with wild-type mice after bleomycin treatment.
BLM-treated Fcnb-/- mice had more inflammatory cells (mainly macrophages) in BALF and higher fibronectin and Collagen I protein in lung tissue than wild-type mice.
RNA-seq comparing BLM-treated Fcnb-/- and wild-type mouse lungs identified 1684 differentially expressed genes, with 875 upregulated and 809 downregulated.
Core TGF-β1 signaling genes were significantly altered in Fcnb-/- mice, and this change was reversed by ficolin-B overexpression.
TGF-β1 was markedly increased in BALF of BLM-treated mice and further elevated in Fcnb-/- mice, indicating amplified TGF-β1 signaling with ficolin-B deficiency.
Lung-specific AAV6-mediated overexpression of ficolin-B improved body weight and reduced BLM-induced pulmonary fibrosis histology and Ashcroft scores.
Lung-specific ficolin-B overexpression reduced inflammatory cell infiltration, decreased fibrosis markers (Fn1, Col1a2), and downregulated Tgfb1 transcription in BLM-treated mice.
Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed a direct physical interaction between ficolin-1 and TGF-β1 in human plasma for the first time.
Immunofluorescence showed co-localization of TGF-β1 and ficolin-1 in lung tissue sections from an IPF patient.
In A549 alveolar epithelial cells, ficolin-1 protein expression decreased in a dose-dependent manner following TGF-β1 stimulation.
Noradrenaline treatment increased Ki67 expression (a proliferation marker) in A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells compared to control.
Noradrenaline increased HRAS gene expression in A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells relative to untreated control.
Noradrenaline increased VEGFA gene expression in A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells relative to untreated control.
Noradrenaline decreased TGFBR2 gene expression in A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells relative to untreated control.
Co-treatment with propranolol blocked the noradrenaline-induced increase in cell proliferation and gene expression changes, showing no significant difference from control.
Co-treatment with landiolol blocked the noradrenaline-induced increase in cell proliferation and gene expression changes, showing no significant difference from control.
8.4% of long COVID patients met all three international diagnostic criteria (Fukuda, Canadian Consensus, IOM) for ME/CFS.
The proportion of long COVID patients developing ME/CFS significantly declined across successive viral variant phases (Preceding, Delta, Omicron).
The proportion of patients meeting the Fukuda Criteria for ME/CFS decreased from 23.9% in the Preceding period to 15.1% in the Delta period and 11.9% in the Omicron period.
The proportion of patients meeting the Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS fell sharply from 25.7% in the Preceding period to 4.7% in the Omicron period.
The proportion of patients meeting the IOM Criteria for ME/CFS decreased from 26.1% in the Preceding period to 13.1% in the Omicron period.
Age distribution did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS long COVID patients.
Gender ratio did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and non-ME/CFS groups, though both were slightly female-dominant.
Smoking habit was significantly more common in the ME/CFS group than in the non-ME/CFS group.
Alcohol drinking habit was significantly more common in the ME/CFS group than in the non-ME/CFS group.
Acute-phase COVID-19 severity (moderate to severe) was significantly higher in the ME/CFS group than in the non-ME/CFS group, along with a higher rate of hospital admission.
Overall vaccination rate was significantly lower and the unvaccinated rate significantly higher in the ME/CFS group compared with the non-ME/CFS group.
In the Delta-dominant period, unvaccinated patients showed a non-significant trend toward higher transition rate to ME/CFS.
Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS) scores, including both physical and mental subscales, were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in non-ME/CFS long COVID patients.
Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) scores were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients (median 51) than in non-ME/CFS long COVID patients (median 48), both above the healthy reference range of 20-40.
During the Preceding viral phase, ME/CFS patients had significantly higher frequencies of fatigue, insomnia, and dizziness than non-ME/CFS long COVID patients.
During the Delta-dominant phase, ME/CFS patients had significantly higher frequencies of fatigue, headache, dizziness, and chest pain than non-ME/CFS patients.
During the Omicron-dominant phase, ME/CFS patients had significantly higher frequencies of fatigue, headache, and poor concentration than non-ME/CFS patients.
Serum ferritin levels were significantly higher in female ME/CFS patients than in female non-ME/CFS patients during the Preceding viral phase, but not during the Delta or Omicron phases.

Brain fog prevalence was higher in ME/CFS patients than non-ME/CFS patients overall, with the difference becoming significant and larger during the Delta and especially the Omicron phase, despite the declining overall ME/CFS prevalence.
The TG/PG ratio was the single strongest NMR biomarker association with ME/CFS, with each 1-SD increase associated with 46% higher odds of ME/CFS.
VLDL particle size showed the largest effect size among non-derived biomarkers in ME/CFS.
GlycA, an NMR marker of systemic inflammation, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS.
HDL-CE showed the strongest inverse association with ME/CFS, with higher levels reducing odds of disease.

ME/CFS showed increased VLDL particle concentration and all VLDL lipid components (FC, CE, PL, TG), elevated triglycerides across most lipoprotein subclasses, elevated ApoB and ApoB/ApoA1 ratio, and inverse associations with HDL particle concentration and ApoA1.
Surface phospholipid species (sphingomyelins, phosphatidylcholines, total cholines) were decreased in ME/CFS, consistent with prior metabolomics literature.
A non-gender-specific elevation of glucose was observed in the ME/CFS cohort.
Alanine was significantly elevated in females with ME/CFS, potentially reflecting increased amino acid catabolism for ATP production.
Various fatty acids were positively associated with ME/CFS specifically in females, with implications for inflammatory cell membrane processes.
Ketone bodies were inversely associated with ME/CFS specifically in females, suggesting ketolysis as an alternative energy pathway.
Total branched-chain amino acids were elevated in ME/CFS at the trait-wise significance threshold.
Citrate, acetate and acetone showed inverse (reduced) associations with ME/CFS at the trait-wise threshold.
Seven biomarkers (PUFA, linoleic acid, M-VLDL-C, L-LDL-P, M-LDL-L, M-LDL-PL, L-VLDL-TG%) were significantly associated with ME/CFS only in the female subgroup, not in the whole cohort.

Four biomarkers (IDL-C, IDL-CE, S-HDL-P, S-LDL-C%) were uniquely associated with ME/CFS in males, with inverse cholesteryl ester and total cholesterol associations suggesting an HDL maturation/cholesterol transfer defect.
XXL-VLDL-TG% was the only biomarker association uniquely specific to ME/CFS and not shared with any of the seven comorbid conditions examined.

ME/CFS biomarker associations showed substantial overlap with comorbid conditions: 81% similarity with hypertension, 85% with depression, 73% with asthma, 97% with IBS, 46% with hay fever, 88% with hypothyroidism, and 89% with migraine.
In participants with shorter ME/CFS disease duration (<2 years), six of the 168 significant biomarker associations remained significant and showed greater effect sizes than in the full cohort.
Hand-grip strength, an indicator of muscle fatigue, was significantly lower in ME/CFS compared to all comorbid cohorts except hypothyroidism.
Basal metabolic rate was lower in ME/CFS compared to most comorbid cohorts, except IBS (no difference) and hypothyroidism/migraine (both lower than ME/CFS).
Pulse rate was elevated in the ME/CFS cohort compared to comorbid and control cohorts.
The ME/CFS cohort reported significantly higher rates of tiredness/lethargy (89%) and overall pain (81%) than most comorbid cohorts, with 75% experiencing headaches.

A composite LightGBM-derived ME/CFS score, combining 19 baseline characteristics and 9 NMR biomarkers, was strongly associated with ME/CFS, showing ~2.5-fold greater association than the top individual biomarker.

The final LightGBM model using 19 baseline characteristics and 9 NMR biomarkers achieved AUC 0.83 and recall 0.70 on an independent blind test set, with false positive rate 0.20 and false negative rate 0.30.

Variance decomposition showed that C-reactive protein and neutrophil count explained substantial variance in GlycA, while urate and cystatin C explained variance in creatinine, and testosterone and serum urea explained variance via creatinine and valine respectively, in the ME/CFS cohort.

In the high ME/CFS-score percentile group (most severe), biomarker associations were stronger than in the full cohort, with TG/PG OR increasing from 1.46 to 1.74 and GlycA OR increasing from 1.39 to 1.64.
In male ME/CFS participants, four biomarkers (IDL-C, IDL-CE, S-HDL-P and S-LDL-C%) were significantly associated with ME/CFS that were not seen in the female-only or combined analyses.
Seven biomarkers including PUFA, linoleic acid and several LDL/VLDL measures were significantly associated with ME/CFS only in the female-only subgroup analysis.
C-reactive protein explained 20.5% of the variance in GlycA, an NMR marker of systemic inflammation, in the ME/CFS cohort.
Neutrophil count explained 7.1% of variance in GlycA in the ME/CFS cohort, consistent with an inflammatory mechanism.
Kidney function markers urate and cystatin C explained 22.3% and 21.3% of the variance in plasma creatinine, respectively, in the ME/CFS cohort.
Testosterone explained 16.2% of the variance in plasma creatinine in the ME/CFS cohort.
Serum urea explained 15.3% of the variance in plasma valine levels in the ME/CFS cohort.

WBC leucocyte count and IGF-1 contributed differently to biomarker variance between the general study population and the ME/CFS cohort, explaining PUFA/MUFA ratio (9.3%) and PUFA% (4.9%) variance specifically in ME/CFS.
The final LightGBM machine learning model combining 19 baseline characteristics and nine NMR biomarkers achieved an AUC of 0.83 and recall of 0.70 on an independent blind test set.
The LightGBM ME/CFS score was more strongly associated with ME/CFS (OR 3.61) than any single biomarker, roughly 2.5 times stronger than the top individual biomarker TG/PG.

In the ME/CFS subgroup with the highest disease-score percentiles (96th-100th), the odds ratios for TG/PG and GlycA were higher than in the full cohort, suggesting stronger biomarker signals with greater disease severity.
Among ME/CFS participants in the lowest ME/CFS score percentile group (1st-80th), biomarker associations were negligible, possibly representing less-affected individuals.

Sensitivity analysis using E-values showed that the inverse association between HDL-CE and ME/CFS (OR 0.65) would require an unmeasured confounder with an association strength of OR 2.43 to fully explain away the effect.

In a subset of 181 ME/CFS participants with disease duration under 2 years, six lipoprotein-related biomarkers remained significantly associated with ME/CFS and showed greater effect sizes than the full cohort.

In a 354-person ME/CFS subset with 0-1 defined comorbidities (average 0.6 comorbid conditions vs 3.0 in full cohort), only 31 of the original 168 biomarker associations remained significant, suggesting comorbidity burden amplifies biomarker signal strength.

The authors propose that a previously reported 2-fold overexpression of microRNA-29a in ME/CFS may inhibit LPL translation, reducing LPL activity and impairing VLDL/triglyceride clearance, potentially explaining the observed lipoprotein profile.
Cortisol is described as the most reliable biomarker in ME/CFS research to date, with lower levels reported in ME/CFS at the meta-analysis level, a feature also seen in Long COVID.

The study did not detect any aromatic amino acid anomalies in ME/CFS via NMR, contrasting with a recent Raman spectroscopy study on peripheral blood mononuclear cells that identified such biomarkers, likely due to differences in biofluid and quantification methods.
No ME/CFS participants in this UK Biobank cohort reported comorbid POTS, and only 2.5% reported fibromyalgia, likely reflecting underreporting due to limited clinical recognition of these conditions.
At the trait-wise significance threshold, total BCAAs were positively associated with ME/CFS while citrate, acetate and acetone showed inverse associations.
XXL-VLDL-TG% was the only biomarker found to be uniquely associated with ME/CFS and not shared with any of the seven comorbid conditions tested.

ME/CFS shared 85% biomarker association similarity with the depression cohort, but total cholines, phosphatidylcholines and phosphoglycerides were increased in depression while decreased in ME/CFS, providing a biochemical distinction between the two conditions.

ME/CFS and migraine shared associations with ketone body biomarkers but showed opposite associations with glucose, suggesting a partially shared but distinct metabolic mechanism potentially related to headache symptoms.
In CIRS, the regulatory neuropeptide MSH is typically reduced compared to normal levels.
TGF-ß1 is often elevated in CIRS as one of the three characteristic inflammatory markers.
Complement fragment C4a is often elevated in CIRS as one of the three characteristic inflammatory markers.
MMP-9 is often elevated in CIRS as one of the three characteristic inflammatory markers.
CIRS patients may show dysregulation of the ACTH-cortisol axis.
CIRS patients may show dysregulation of ADH and osmolality regulation.
Abnormalities in gliadin antibodies are noted in CIRS patients.
Abnormalities in anticardiolipin antibodies are noted in CIRS patients.
Abnormalities in VEGF are noted in CIRS patients.
Visual contrast sensitivity (VCS) testing abnormalities are commonly present in CIRS patients and used as a diagnostic screen.

A comprehensive literature review found that 112 of 114 epidemiological articles (98.2%) identified a correlation between water-damaged building/dampness exposure and adverse health effects, with statistically significant OR/RR ≥2.0 in 79 of these articles across multiple organ systems.

The Shoemaker Protocol is reported as the only treatment in the published literature documenting statistically significant biomarker changes and symptom resolution for CIRS, across ten papers reporting eleven clinical studies.

Controlled repetitive re-exposure studies showed that patients who had improved with treatment worsened symptomatically and biochemically upon re-exposure to water-damaged buildings and improved again with retreatment, supporting a causal role for indoor biotoxin exposure.

The authors argue that most individuals diagnosed with ME/CFS are likely to have unrecognized CIRS, since ME/CFS symptoms fall within the CIRS symptom set and CIRS biomarker panels often meet the CIRS case definition in these patients.

Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) and graded exercise therapy (GET) were reported as beneficial in six studies for ME/CFS and were the most widely recommended treatments, but were acknowledged as noncurative.
Nutritional interventions showed improved symptoms in three ME/CFS studies (including one review), while one other study found no beneficial outcome.
A case history documenting 675 days of IV saline infusion showed symptomatic improvement in ME/CFS.
A case history documenting use of EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) showed symptomatic improvement in ME/CFS.
A study with 32 cases and 18 controls found improvement in ME/CFS symptoms with whole-body cryotherapy and static stretching.
Three review studies of acupuncture and/or moxibustion reported efficacy for ME/CFS, though two rated evidence quality as moderate to very low and the third did not report p-values.
The monoaminergic stabilizer OSU6162 showed benefit in an open-label trial of 33 ME/CFS patients, but this was not confirmed in a subsequent randomized controlled trial.
Aripiprazole showed some benefit for ME/CFS in a prospective single-arm study of 101 patients, but carries safety concerns including black box warnings.

A retrospective study of 218 participants treated with low-dose naltrexone showed a high frequency of treatment response for ME/CFS, though psychiatric drugs in general were noted to lack a clear sustainable response.
A study utilizing molecular hydrogen for ME/CFS documented no treatment efficacy.
A randomized single-blind controlled trial with 409 participants found no treatment efficacy for distant healing in ME/CFS.
VIP, a component of the Shoemaker Protocol for CIRS, is the most expensive medication step, is not covered by insurance, and can cause light-headedness as a side effect.
Cholestyramine, used in the Shoemaker Protocol, is associated with constipation as a side effect.
Six studies reported cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and graded exercise therapy (GET) as beneficial and the most widely recommended ME/CFS treatments, though acknowledged as noncurative.

A systematic review by Larun et al. concluded exercise therapy leads to improvement in ME/CFS, but many overlapping CIRS patients have exercise intolerance and reduced VO2 max that preclude participation.
Three studies found various nutritional approaches improved ME/CFS symptoms, while one other study found no beneficial outcome.
A case history documenting 675 days of intravenous saline infusion showed symptom improvement in an ME/CFS patient.
Use of eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) was documented to show symptom improvement in ME/CFS.
A study of 32 cases and 18 controls found improvement in ME/CFS symptoms with whole-body cryotherapy and static stretching.
Three review studies of acupuncture and/or moxibustion reported efficacy for ME/CFS, but the quality of evidence was rated moderate to very low, and one study lacked statistical significance testing.
An open-label trial of the monoaminergic stabilizer OSU6162 in 33 ME/CFS patients suggested clinical benefit.
A subsequent randomized controlled trial failed to confirm the benefit of OSU6162 suggested by the earlier open-label trial in ME/CFS.

A prospective single-arm study of 101 patients showed aripiprazole provided some benefit for ME/CFS, but the drug carries two black box warnings and litigation risk regarding pediatric type 2 diabetes.

A retrospective study of 218 participants treated with low-dose naltrexone showed a high frequency of treatment response for ME/CFS, though psychiatric drugs generally have not shown clear sustained response.
A study using molecular hydrogen documented no treatment efficacy for ME/CFS.
A randomized single-blind controlled trial of distant healing in 409 participants documented no treatment efficacy for ME/CFS.
The CDC states there is no cure or approved treatment for ME/CFS, though some symptoms can be treated or managed, with not all individuals benefiting from symptom management.
Therapeutic apheresis led to a decline in beta-1 adrenergic receptor autoantibody levels in all 20 post-COVID patients.
Therapeutic apheresis led to a decline in beta-2 adrenergic receptor autoantibody levels in all 20 post-COVID patients.
The study reports an association between decline of autoantibodies and clinical improvement in post-COVID patients following therapeutic apheresis.
The majority of patients experienced reductions in fatigue, physical activity restrictions, myalgia, post-exertional malaise, and concentration disorders after therapeutic apheresis.

The authors propose that agonistic autoantibodies targeting beta-1, beta-2 adrenergic and M3, M4 muscarinic receptors may play a crucial role in the pathomechanism of both ME/CFS and post-COVID conditions.

A 71-year-old woman with periodic depression presenting as extreme fatigue, initially diagnosed 30 years earlier as chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis and unable to walk for six years, was successfully treated with electroconvulsive therapy (ECT).

The authors note that while misdiagnosis of CFS/ME as depression is well described in the literature, the reverse scenario of depression being diagnosed as CFS/ME does not appear to have been previously reported.
ME γδT cells show decreased expression of cytotoxic effector genes GZMB, FCGR3A, and KLRF1 compared to controls.
Monocyte-attracting chemokines CCL3 and CCL3L1 are downregulated in ME γδT cells.
The proinflammatory transcription factor FOSB is upregulated in ME γδT cells despite decreased chemokine expression.
GSEA of ME γδT cells shows enrichment for TNFα signaling via NF-κB and IL-6 signaling pathways, with positive trends for TGF-β signaling and IFNγ response.
CellChat analysis of the female-only cohort revealed increased intercellular signaling interactions for IL-2, TGF-β, and IL-16 pathways between γδT cells and other lymphocytes in ME patients.
CCL5, a chemokine involved in lymphocyte localization to inflamed tissue, is elevated in ME γδT cell signaling, consistent with prior findings implicating CCL5 in ME.
Th1 and Th17 CD4+ T cell subsets show modestly elevated single-cell effector indices in ME patients, with no differences in other CD4+ subsets.
Late effector memory CD8+ T cells (cluster 0) in ME show marked downregulation of GNLY, IKZF2 (HELIOS), and IL18R1, genes related to effector function and activation.

KLRB1, an inhibitory receptor with antagonistic roles in cytotoxic programs, and the exhaustion-associated transcription factor TBX21 (T-BET) are upregulated in ME late effector memory CD8+ T cells (cluster 0).
Cluster 6 late effector memory CD8+ T cells in ME show downregulation of GNLY and additional repression of transcription factors related to T cell activation/effector function (ID2, JUNB, FOS, IRF1).
GSEA of TEMlate CD8+ T cell clusters 0 and 6 revealed downregulation of gene sets related to regulation of immune responses in ME, suggesting functional impairment.
PD-1 (PDCD1) was not substantially upregulated overall in TEMlate cluster 0, but a higher proportion of cells within this cluster express PD-1 in ME.

RNA-seq of purified memory CD8+ T cells (TM) shows increased expression of the exhaustion transcription factor EOMES and the inhibitory receptors SLAMF6 and SLAMF7 in ME patients relative to healthy controls.
Naïve CD8+ T cells (TN) from ME patients show higher expression of GNLY and TNFRSF1A, suggesting a partial loss of naive identity and adoption of a more effector-like transcriptional program.

GSEA showed that ME memory CD8+ T cells (TM) are transcriptionally concordant with a chronic infection exhausted T cell (Tex) signature, with negative enrichment for genes normally downregulated in Tex and positive enrichment for genes normally upregulated in Tex.
ME memory CD8+ T cells show lower expression of hexokinase HK1 and higher expression of glucose transporter SLC2A1, indicating impaired glycolytic potential consistent with T cell exhaustion.
The chemokine receptor CCR4 is significantly downregulated in ME memory CD8+ T cells, suggesting impaired responsiveness to tissue homing signals.

ATAC-seq of ME memory CD8+ T cells identified 471 upregulated and 1,477 downregulated chromatin-accessible regions, with decreased accessibility at genes involved in chemokine/cytokine signaling (CCR4, CCL2, CSF2, IL3) and NF-κB/TNFα and KRAS signaling pathways.

ME memory CD8+ T cells show higher chromatin accessibility at the TOX locus without a corresponding significant increase in TOX transcription, suggesting cells are epigenetically primed toward an exhausted state before overt gene expression change.

Chromatin regions with significantly higher accessibility in ME memory CD8+ T cells are enriched for IRF7, EOMES, and T-BET (TBX21) transcription factor binding motifs, suggesting these cells are driven toward late-stage exhaustion.
Chromatin regions with lower accessibility in ME memory CD8+ T cells are enriched for TCF7 (TCF1) and TCF7L2 (TCF4) motifs, transcription factors associated with early exhaustion progression.

ROR family transcription factor motifs (RORA, RORB, RORC) and FOXP3 are enriched in chromatin regions with reduced accessibility in ME memory CD8+ T cells, potentially contributing to functional impairment.
Chromatin regions upregulated in ME naive CD8+ T cells (TN) are strongly enriched for NF-κB family transcription factor motifs, suggesting priming toward increased activation.
Flow cytometry of circulating CD8+ T cells following an exercise challenge showed a significantly higher frequency of SLAMF6hi cells in total CD8+ T cells in ME patients compared to controls.
ME patients in the RNA-seq/ATAC-seq cohort reported significantly lower SF-36 physical component scores and lower Bell Activity Scale scores than controls, indicating greater functional impairment.

In flow cytometry, ME patients showed significantly elevated frequencies of SLAMF6hi cells and higher SLAMF6 expression within PD-1+CD69- subsets of intermediate (EM4) and late (EM3) effector memory CD8+ T cells compared to controls.
Terminally differentiated effector (Eff) CD8+ T cells from ME patients showed significantly higher SLAMF6 abundance than controls.
Terminally differentiated TEMRA subsets (pE1 and pE2) from ME patients showed a trend toward higher TOX expression than controls, though not statistically significant.
Naïve CD8+ T cells (TN) from ME patients unexpectedly showed significantly higher TOX abundance and frequency of TOXhi cells compared to controls, with no corresponding change in SLAMF6.
A subpopulation of SLAMF6hi CD8+ T cells was found at significantly higher frequency in total circulating CD8+ T cells of ME patients compared to controls.
Frequency of PD-1+ total CD8+ T cells did not differ significantly between ME and controls, though a non-significant trend toward increased PD-1 expression (gMFI) was observed in ME.

The paper cites a prior report of disrupted catecholamine biosynthesis in the central nervous system of ME patients, consistent with a broader autonomic/stress-related contribution to T cell exhaustion.
The paper notes prior findings of decreased serum catecholamines and their metabolites in Long COVID patients, drawing a parallel to autonomic dysfunction in ME.
The authors hypothesize that beta-adrenergic signaling linked to autonomic nervous system activity may mediate T cell exhaustion, potentially explaining how exertion drives post-exertional malaise.

Monocytes exhibiting increased tissue-homing hallmarks in ME may upregulate coinhibitory PD-L1/PD-L2 and CD86-CTLA-4 pathways, suggesting a possible mechanism by which monocytes suppress CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity.

The scRNA-seq cohort included females and males at a 2:1 ratio, reflecting the known higher incidence of ME in women; all downstream detailed analyses used female subjects only to avoid sex-related confounds.

The authors note that SARS-CoV-2-reactive CD8+ T cells display features of exhaustion in severely ill Long COVID patients, and that SARS-CoV-2 antigen persistence has been observed after acute infection in LC, paralleling the T cell exhaustion phenotype found in ME.

Long COVID patients have been reported to have higher levels of antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins and latent viruses, suggesting viral persistence or reactivation could drive T cell exhaustion similar to that observed in ME.
In this ME cohort, 70% of cases reported sudden onset of illness, and all subjects were diagnosed prior to the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, meeting IOM and Canadian Consensus Criteria.
Whole-blood RNA sequencing revealed a distinct transcriptional profile in Long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
FEZF2 was found to be upregulated in Long COVID patients, a gene linked to neuronal development.
BRINP2 was found to be upregulated in Long COVID patients, associated with neuronal development and immune dysregulation.
HOXC12 was found to be upregulated in Long COVID patients, linked to hematopoietic disturbances.
ZFHX3, a gene involved in neuronal development, was upregulated in Long COVID/ME-CFS patients relative to controls.
RELN, encoding the Reelin protein, was notably elevated in Long COVID patients and is proposed as a potential biomarker due to its role in inflammation and neuronal function.
Immune cell profiling showed increased activated memory CD4+ T cells in Long COVID patients compared to controls.
Neutrophil levels were increased in Long COVID patients relative to controls, consistent with a chronic inflammatory state.
Regulatory T cell levels were decreased in Long COVID patients compared to controls.
Natural killer cell levels were decreased in Long COVID patients compared to controls.
Changes in cytokine and chemokine expression were observed in Long COVID patients, underscoring a chronic inflammatory state.
Olfactory receptor genes were uniquely upregulated in Long COVID patients, suggesting alternative non-olfactory roles for these receptors in immune or neuronal tissue.

Pathway analysis found upregulation of ribosomal RNA processing, amino acid metabolism, protein synthesis, cell proliferation, DNA repair, and mitochondrial pathways in Long COVID patients, indicating heightened metabolic and immune demands.
Long COVID patients showed a unique upregulation of olfactory receptor genes in whole blood, suggesting alternative, non-olfactory roles for these receptors.
Pathway analysis revealed upregulation of ribosomal RNA processing in LC patients, consistent with heightened protein synthesis demand.
Amino acid metabolism pathways were upregulated in LC patients, indicating heightened metabolic demand.
Protein synthesis pathways were upregulated in LC patients, reflecting increased cellular biosynthetic activity.
Cell proliferation pathways were upregulated in LC patients, indicating heightened cellular turnover or immune demand.
DNA repair pathways were upregulated in LC patients, suggesting increased cellular stress and genomic maintenance demands.
Mitochondrial pathways were upregulated in LC patients, indicating heightened metabolic demand.
VEGF signaling was downregulated in LC patients, suggesting impaired tissue repair capacity.
One proposed theory frames long COVID as a distinct neurological disease caused by direct viral neuroinvasion, apoptosis, and demyelination.
A second theory views long COVID as a systemic disease with neurological symptoms driven by virus-induced, prolonged cytokine and chemokine release and reactivation of latent viral infections.

A third theory conceptualizes long COVID as a somatoform disorder resulting from abnormal activation of the proinflammatory cytokine network leading to central nervous system sensitization, a psychoneuroimmunological mechanism.

The review identifies significant symptomatic and mechanistic overlap between long COVID and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, Gulf War syndrome, chronic Lyme disease, and somatic symptom disorder.
The authors conclude that despite extensive research, the pathomechanism of long COVID remains unknown and no reproducible disease-specific biomarker has yet been identified.

Treatment with ultrasound-assisted sweet corn cob polysaccharide selenium nanoparticles (U-SCPSeNPs) increased the activity/production capacity of Na+-K+-ATPase, Mg2+-ATPase, and Ca2+-ATPase in CFS mice, indicating improved cellular energy production.
U-SCPSeNPs treatment decreased SOD and MDA levels in CFS mice, reflecting a reduction in oxidative stress markers.
U-SCPSeNPs treatment increased CAT and GSH-Px levels in CFS mice, indicating enhanced antioxidant capacity.
U-SCPSeNPs treatment improved the diversity and abundance of gut microbiota in CFS mice.
U-SCPSeNPs treatment decreased the relative abundance of Firmicutes and increased the relative abundance of Bacteroidota at the phylum level in the gut microbiota of CFS mice.

Japanese patients with chronic fatigue syndrome and concomitant small heart syndrome had significantly smaller left ventricular chamber dimensions, stroke volume, and cardiac output compared with controls, even after indexing to body surface area.

In a cohort of 42 young CFS patients (62% also diagnosed with small heart syndrome), those with concomitant small heart syndrome had smaller LV chamber size, stroke volume, and cardiac index than controls and than CFS patients with normal heart dimensions, with improvement in these parameters during symptomatic remission.

Shalev et al. found that patients with positive tilt-table testing had significantly smaller LV end-systolic and end-diastolic areas and diameters along with significantly higher LV fractional shortening compared with controls or TTT-negative patients.

Mitzumaki et al. found no significant difference in cardiac geometry/function between RS patients induced by TTT alone versus those requiring isoproterenol, and unlike Shalev et al., LV contractility did not significantly increase in patients with positive baseline TTT.

Lee and colleagues found that RS patients had more vigorous myocardial contraction than TTT-negative patients but no significant difference in LV cavity size, suggesting a beta-adrenergic hypersensitive state rather than a preexisting small/empty ventricle as prerequisite for syncope.

Liu et al., using load-independent myocardial wall stress rather than fractional shortening, found that TTT-induced RS patients had a smaller LV and reduced myocardial contractility, suggesting multiple triggers rather than solely forceful contraction activate LV C fibers.

Yamanouchi et al. found a rapid reduction in LV end-diastolic volume during TTT as a trigger for syncope, with greater venous capacitance and reduced ejection fraction and stroke index in tilt-induced RS patients versus controls.
Kozlowski et al. observed a reduction in LV volumes during TTT overall but found no difference between TTT-positive and TTT-negative patients.

Folino et al. found that despite significant sympathetic activation, RS patients did not show a marked increase in ventricular contractility, but did show a more important reduction in left atrial contractility and a significant drop in left atrial and LV end-diastolic volumes during TTT.

Goel et al. using speckle tracking echocardiography found significantly lower endocardial longitudinal strain in TTT-positive RS patients versus controls, with non-significant trends toward smaller septal/posterior wall thickness and left atrial volume index.

Moon et al. showed that a small indexed left atrial volume (LAVI) is an independent predictor of reflex syncope during tilt-table testing, whereas LAVI ≥36 mL/m2 was not associated with fainting, and smaller LA anteroposterior diameter was seen in TTT-positive patients who fainted earlier.

Basanalan et al. found diminished left atrial ejection fraction and smaller left atrial volume in TTT-positive versus TTT-negative RS patients, supporting a role for decreased atrial contractility alongside reduced ventricular filling.

The Prevention of Syncope Trial 2 (POST2) did not meet its primary objective of demonstrating a 40% reduction in vasovagal syncope risk with fludrocortisone, but showed a significant effect after dose stabilization in post hoc multivariable and on-treatment analyses.

The ISSUE-3 double-blind, randomized placebo-controlled trial demonstrated a 32% absolute and 57% relative risk reduction in syncopal events with dual-chamber pacing with rate-drop response versus sensing alone in patients with recurrent syncope and cardioinhibitory response.

The SPAIN trial showed that dual-chamber closed-loop stimulation (DDD-CLS) pacing significantly improved quality of life compared to DDI simple mode, in addition to preventing syncopal events, in patients with cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope.

A 2018 meta-analysis found the estimated 3-year recurrence rate of vasovagal syncope was significantly higher in patients with positive tilt-table testing than those with negative TTT, identifying positive TTT as the only significant predictor of syncopal recurrence.
Two randomized trials of atenolol and propranolol did not demonstrate significant efficacy in reducing syncope episodes in vasovagal syncope patients.
Sheldon et al. reported no significant benefit of metoprolol in reducing recurrence of vasovagal syncope.

Isolated very low voltage QRS in frontal ECG leads and flat QRS loops on the frontal vectorcardiogram correlate with small LV end-diastolic diameter and low intravascular volume and have been shown to predict recurrent reflex syncope.

Cardioneuroablation, which performs selective endocardial denervation of ganglionated plexi to reduce excessive parasympathetic influence, has shown good results in treating vagal-mediated bradycardia and limited effects in preventing associated vasodilation, mainly studied in cardioinhibitory and mixed vasovagal syncope.
More than 90% of individuals with classical EDS (cEDS) carry heterozygous pathogenic variants in COL5A1 or COL5A2, the genes encoding type V collagen.
COL5A2 variants, which are generally missense/structural, may be associated with a more severe cEDS phenotype than COL5A1 variants.
Specific arginine-to-cysteine variants in the type I collagen gene COL1A1 can rarely cause a cEDS phenotype associated with an increased probability of vascular events.
In vascular EDS, glycine substitutions and splice-site/in-frame variants in COL3A1 are associated with more severe clinical manifestations than null/loss-of-function or non-glycine missense variants.

Glutamate-to-lysine substitutions in COL3A1 triple-helix Gly-Glu-Arg sequences have been reported in families with prominent classical-EDS-type skin features in addition to vascular EDS complications.
Several Arg>Cys variants in COL1A1, particularly p.Arg312Cys, have been reported to cause vascular fragility combined with a classical vEDS phenotype.
Cardiac-valvular EDS (cvEDS), a rare severe progressive valvular disease phenotype, is caused by biallelic null/loss-of-function variants in COL1A2.
Arthrochalasia EDS (aEDS) is caused by complete or partial loss of exon 6 of COL1A2 or COL1A1, which prevents N-propeptide cleavage and leads to congenital hip dislocation and extreme hypermobility.

A heterozygous missense variant in THBS2 has been proposed as a possible cause of classical-like EDS based on a multi-generation family and mouse model, but causality is not yet confirmed in additional families.
Complete loss of tenascin-X function due to biallelic null/loss-of-function TNXB variants causes TN-X-deficient classical-like EDS (clEDS type 1), reported in more than 50 individuals.
Heterozygous loss of TNXB was previously claimed to cause hypermobile EDS, but this association has not been confirmed, and population data indicate TNXB is haplosufficient (pLI=0, LOEUF=0.674).
AEBP1-related classical-like EDS (clEDS type 2) is an autosomal recessive condition caused mostly by biallelic null/loss-of-function variants in AEBP1, reported in more than 10 individuals.
Dermatosparaxis EDS (dEDS) is caused by biallelic null/loss-of-function ADAMTS2 variants, including a recurrent nonsense variant with 0.3% allele frequency in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.
Kyphoscoliotic EDS (kEDS) is caused by autosomal recessive deficiency of PLOD1 or FKBP14; a common 8.9 kb PLOD1 exon 10-16 duplication accounts for 30% of reported pathogenic alleles.

A recurrent FKBP14 frameshift variant (c.362dup) has a low general European allele frequency (0.086%) but accounts for up to 70% of pathogenic alleles among European FKBP14-kEDS patients, and FKBP14-kEDS is distinguished from PLOD1-kEDS by frequent hearing impairment.
Brittle cornea syndrome (BCS) is caused by biallelic pathogenic, mostly null/LoF, variants in either ZNF469 or PRDM5, and has been reported in more than 60 individuals.

Spondylodysplastic EDS (spEDS) is mostly caused by biallelic null/LoF variants in glycosaminoglycan linker-assembly genes B4GALT7, B3GALT6, or B3GAT3, and a founder B4GALT7 variant causes Larsen of La Réunion Island syndrome.
A spondylocheirodysplastic form of EDS is caused by biallelic, mostly null/LoF, variants in SLC39A13, encoding the zinc transporter ZIP13 expressed in bone, teeth, and connective tissue.

Musculocontractural EDS (mcEDS) is caused by deficiency of dermatan sulphate biosynthesis enzymes, mainly biallelic null/LoF variants in CHST14 (or less frequently DSE), reported in more than 70 individuals.

Myopathic EDS (mEDS) severity and inheritance pattern depend on COL12A1 variant type: dominant-negative missense variants cause autosomal dominant disease, while homozygous null/LoF variants cause recessive disease.

Periodontal EDS (pEDS) is caused by gain-of-function variants in complement genes C1S or C1R that trigger excess activation of the C1s serine protease, which degrades type I collagen, causing the connective tissue pathology.
