Null/loss-of-function variants or large multi-exon deletions in C1R or C1S do not cause pEDS, but in the biallelic state are possible causes of systemic lupus erythematosus instead.

Hypermobile EDS/hypermobility spectrum disorder (hEDS/HSD) together have an estimated incidence of up to 1 in 500, greatly exceeding the combined number of individuals with monogenic EDS types, and lack an identifiable genetic cause.

Individuals with hypermobile EDS can have debilitating systemic features including chronic musculoskeletal pain, chronic fatigue, sleep disturbances, dysautonomia, bowel disease of unknown mechanism, and depression, in addition to joint and skin manifestations.

Massively parallel sequencing of COL3A1 (and COL1A1), including deletion/duplication analysis, is expected to identify the causative pathogenic variant in more than 98% of individuals affected by vascular EDS.
Management of vascular EDS through a specialist expert service has been reported to have a favourable effect on patient survival.
Pharmacological therapy for vascular EDS includes blood-pressure-lowering medication such as Celiprolol, or combined therapy with a beta blocker and angiotensin II receptor blocker.
Women with vascular EDS have a reported 5.3% risk of death during pregnancy, warranting management in tertiary obstetric centres.
Rupture of medium-sized arteries has been reported as a minor diagnostic feature of PLOD1-related kyphoscoliotic EDS, supporting a need for cardiovascular surveillance.
A minority of individuals with PLOD1-related kyphoscoliotic EDS have been reported to experience scleral rupture after minimal trauma.

FKBP14-related kyphoscoliotic EDS differs from other kEDS subtypes in that skin fragility is often absent, while widespread follicular hyperkeratosis and congenital (sensorineural, conductive, or mixed) hearing impairment are common.
In arthrochalasia EDS, musculoskeletal features including fracture liability tend to be more severe in individuals carrying COL1A1 variants compared to COL1A2 variants.
Cardiac-valvular EDS is caused by bi-allelic loss-of-function COL1A2 variants that lead to mRNA decay.

In an expanded case series of cardiac-valvular EDS, core phenotype features included joint hypermobility of hands/feet (100%), skin hyperextensibility (100%), mitral valve insufficiency (83%), genua recurvata (66%), bilateral pes planus (66%), soft/doughy/thin skin (66%), atrophic scarring (50%), easy bruising (50%) and bilateral inguinal hernia (50%).
Foot abnormalities, particularly broad feet with brachydactyly, are very common (81%) in classical-like EDS caused by TNXB variants.

Individuals with TNXB classical-like EDS show tissue fragility including gastrointestinal rupture (16%), major vascular events (5%), and other fragility such as tracheal or nasal cartilage rupture (4%).
Hair thinning was present in 55% (6/11) of individuals with AEBP1-related classical-like EDS type 2, as reported by Angwin et al.

In a review of 15 individuals with AEBP1 classical-like EDS, arterial aneurysm/dissection occurred in 20%, aortic root dilatation in 13%, and bowel rupture in 13%, supporting the need for cardiovascular surveillance and caution with invasive procedures.

Periodontal EDS is caused by activation of the C1r complement subunit, which has collagenase-like function and may also lead to incomplete activation of the complement system, driving periodontal tissue destruction.

Brain imaging studies in adults with periodontal EDS have revealed white matter abnormalities in almost all who underwent imaging, usually without clear neurological symptoms though migraine and poor memory have been recorded.

Several heterozygous COL3A1 variants causing glutamic acid to lysine substitutions have been reported to cause an overlap phenotype of hyperextensible/fragile skin typical of classical EDS combined with generalised tissue fragility typical of vascular EDS.

Myopathic EDS has been reported in 25 individuals from 16 families, with autosomal recessive inheritance identified in two of those families, and shares clinical overlap with Bethlem and Ullrich congenital myopathies.

Dermatosparaxis EDS is extremely rare, with only 15 individuals reported in childhood (birth to 16 years) and one followed into adulthood, and is characterised by extreme skin fragility with congenital or postnatal skin tears and severe bruisability.

The HEDGE study is undertaking whole genome sequencing in 1000 adults fulfilling 2017 hypermobile EDS diagnostic criteria, but it is anticipated most will not have a monogenic cause, suggesting hEDS may have a multifactorial aetiology.
Dermatosparaxis-type EDS arises from mutations in the ADAMTS2 gene, which encodes procollagen I N-proteinase, leading to defective processing of type I procollagen into type I collagen.

The patient presented with redundant, lax, hyperextensible skin with a soft doughy texture and extreme fragility manifesting as generalized petechiae and subcutaneous hematomas, meeting major and minor clinical criteria for dermatosparaxis-type EDS.

Cardiovascular screening including duplex ultrasound and 12-lead ECG showed no evidence of aortic/iliac aneurysm, left atrial enlargement, or left ventricular hypertrophy suggestive of mitral valve prolapse.

Treatment with triamterene-hydrochlorothiazide (37.5-25 mg daily) controlled the patient's hypertension, with blood pressure improving from elevated diastolic readings to 112/64 and 117/60 mmHg at six- and 12-month follow-ups.

Joint hypermobility and instability in EDS, particularly of the knee, increase the risk of meniscal/ligamentous tears and predispose to osteoarthritis due to asymmetric joint loading during subluxation.
Changes in the quality or ratio of collagen and elastin in EDS alter arterial wall mechanics, and increased arterial elasticity may impair blood pressure control in EDS patients.
Bruising in EDS patients results from vessel wall fragility due to poor connective tissue support rather than abnormal platelet or coagulation function, and coagulation studies are typically normal.
Dermatosparaxis EDS is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in ADAMTS2, a very rare monogenic form of EDS.

Only fifteen individuals with dEDS had previously been reported in the literature, with the oldest previously reported at 19 years of age at follow-up, highlighting a lack of adult natural history data.
Adults with dEDS in this series exhibited extreme skin fragility resulting in iatrogenic injury.
Redundant skin folds in adults with dEDS often required surgical resection.
One or more individuals experienced severe complications following a gastric volvulus secondary to a diaphragmatic hernia.
Adults with dEDS in this series experienced multiple fractures.
Management recommendations include monitoring bone mineral density after low-impact fracture and/or post-menopause in adults with dEDS.
Management recommendations for adults with dEDS include thorough investigation of acute pain and careful consideration of skin closure techniques and manual handling.
A re-examination by Angwin et al. failed to confirm that duplication of the lamina densa on TEM is specifically associated with vascular EDS, contrary to an earlier report.
Hirose et al. found significant differences on skin TEM using cupromeronic blue staining of glycosaminoglycan chains between mcEDS-CHST14 patients and healthy controls.

Collagen flowers on TEM are almost invariably present in classical EDS but are not specific to cEDS, monogenic EDS, or even monogenic disease in general, as they also occur in OI and Ullrich muscular dystrophy.
A recent study confirmed higher variation (coefficient of variation) in collagen fibril diameter, due to many small fibrils, in genetically confirmed vascular EDS patients compared to controls.

Comparison of skin TEM across infants, vEDS patients, and adult controls showed similarly high COV in infants and vEDS patients, both significantly higher than adult controls, suggesting the high COV in infants is physiological whereas in vEDS it reflects ER stress-related unstable collagen bundle retention.
A study of 13 patients with PLOD1-related kyphoscoliotic EDS found variable fibril diameter and abnormal collagen fibre outline on TEM compared with controls.
Disorganised, kinked collagen fibres with a pathognomonic 'hieroglyphic' appearance on TEM are reported in dermatosparaxis EDS, caused by deficient ADAMTS-2 activity impairing N-propeptide excision.

In a series of four dermatosparaxis EDS patients, van Damme et al. found that the pathognomonic hieroglyphic EM pattern was not always present, with two cases instead resembling the arthrochalasia EDS pattern.

Redman et al. concluded that dilated rough endoplasmic reticulum on TEM, possibly reflecting the unfolded protein response, should be considered an abnormal finding supporting a diagnosis of vascular EDS or related connective tissue conditions.
Ishikawa et al. found rER dilatation present but less marked in high-COV individuals, with only mild or non-dilated rER in the low-COV group.

A heterozygous COL1A1 c.3790G>A splice-altering variant causing an OI-EDS overlap phenotype produced two mutant transcripts, one predicted to cause a truncated pro-alpha1(I) chain and functional haploinsufficiency, shown as markedly reduced type I collagen secretion on SDS-PAGE electrophoresis.

Angwin et al. reported that although no TEM findings were EDS-type specific, a higher percentage of abnormal skin biopsy findings occurred in individuals with a definitive genetic diagnosis (pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant) of monogenic EDS.
Heterozygous loss-of-function COL1A1 variants cause a 50% decrease in COL1A1 product, typically producing OI type 1 (mild non-deforming OI) through haploinsufficiency.
Homozygous, but not heterozygous, loss-of-function COL1A2 variants cause cardiac-valvular EDS.
Heterozygous triple-helical glycine substitutions in COL1A1/COL1A2 act via a dominant-negative mechanism and usually cause OI types 2-4, with severity depending on gene and variant position.
Triple-helical glycine substitutions and splice-site variants in COL3A1 act via a dominant-negative mechanism, significantly decreasing production of normal (pro)collagen type III by 87.5%.
COL3A1 loss-of-function variants cause a 50% reduction in collagen III production with clinical manifestation, reflecting haploinsufficiency.

Loss-of-function variants in either COL5A1 or COL5A2 cause classical EDS through haploinsufficiency, since type V procollagen cannot incorporate more than one proα2(V) chain, so a 50% reduction in proα1(V) halves normal collagen V amount.
An increased urinary ratio of deoxypyridinoline to pyridinoline collagen cross-links, measured by HPLC, is a highly sensitive and specific biomarker test for PLOD1-related kyphoscoliotic EDS.
Increased serum levels of GAG-free bikunin core protein, detected by Western blot, could serve as a biomarker for spondylodysplastic EDS.
Urinary disaccharide compositional analysis of chondroitin/dermatan sulfate chains could serve as a screening assay for musculocontractural EDS.
Specific arginine-to-cysteine substitutions in COL1A1, coding for the proα1(I) chain, have been reported to cause vascular EDS and can produce an abnormal electrophoretic pattern for type I collagen.

As reported since 1994, a normal collagen protein profile on SDS-PAGE electrophoresis does not exclude a diagnosis of vascular EDS, even though electrophoresis can show abnormalities in some affected individuals.
Among LBP patients, those with joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥4) were predominantly female compared to non-hypermobile patients.
Hypermobile LBP patients were on average 8.1 years younger than non-hypermobile LBP patients.
Hypermobile LBP patients had less severe lumbar disc degeneration (sum-score) than non-hypermobile LBP patients.
There was no overall difference in degenerative MRI findings (herniations, disc degeneration, spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis) between hypermobile and non-hypermobile LBP patients.
Hypermobile patients showed a non-significant tendency toward a higher number of anterolisthesis cases compared to non-hypermobile patients.
Hypermobile LBP patients had a greater lumbar lordosis angle than non-hypermobile patients in both supine and standing positions on weight-bearing MRI.
Hypermobile LBP patients had a greater sacral angle than non-hypermobile patients specifically in the supine position.
The change in lumbar lordosis and sacral angles between supine and standing positions did not differ between hypermobile and non-hypermobile LBP patients.
Joint hypermobility in LBP patients was not associated with increased back pain severity.
The sacral angle measured while standing did not differ significantly between hypermobile and non-hypermobile LBP patients.
The magnitude of change in lumbar lordosis and sacral angles between supine and standing positions did not differ between hypermobile and non-hypermobile LBP patients.
A sensitivity analysis adjusting for gender and age confirmed the primary findings regarding hypermobility and lumbar positional measures.
Joint hypermobility in LBP patients was not associated with increased severity of back pain, greater anterolisthesis grade, or more severe positional lumbar changes.
Genetic testing confirmed a pathogenic mutation in the COL3A1 gene, establishing a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS, type IV) in the patient.

A hyperaggregability study confirmed sticky platelet syndrome (SPS) type I, characterized by platelet hyperaggregability in response to both ADP and epinephrine, coexisting with vEDS in the same patient.

The authors note that platelet aggregability abnormalities have been documented in vEDS patients with significant variability, including subgroups showing prolonged bleeding times and reduced platelet aggregation responses, contrasting with the hyperaggregability seen in this patient's SPS.
The authors state that celiprolol is the only agent with proven efficacy in reducing vascular events in type IV EDS, though it was not administered to this patient.

The patient exhibited joint hyperlaxity/hypermobility, angioid streaks on ophthalmologic exam, and high myopia, phenotypic features considered alongside her vascular presentation in reaching the vEDS diagnosis.

Anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin (LMWH), instituted due to recurrent thrombotic events, was complicated by spontaneous haemorrhagic shock from a gluteal artery aneurysmal rupture, illustrating the treatment conflict between thrombotic and haemorrhagic risk in this dual-diagnosis patient.

The patient ultimately died from an irreparable dissection and rupture of the aortoiliac junction during an attempted embolization/stent procedure for a femoral pseudoaneurysm, representing the fatal outcome of coexisting vEDS and SPS.

Genetic testing revealed a COL3A1 gene abnormality (a missense mutation affecting a glycine residue), confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome after the patient developed multiple postoperative vascular complications.

Spontaneous carotid-cavernous fistula (sCCF) is the most frequent intracranial vascular arteriopathy complication in vEDS, with its reported frequency increasing from 2.4% to 9.8%, partly due to improved diagnostic rates.
sCCF in vEDS is more common in women (79.4%) than men, and among endovascular treatment cases reviewed since 2000, 83.3% of patients were women with a mean age of 38.3 years.

In this patient, arterial puncture during endovascular treatment for sCCF led to a hemorrhagic cascade including femoral puncture-site extravasation, retroperitoneal hematoma, hypovolemic shock, and later delayed vascular dissections and pseudoaneurysms in the iliac arteries remote from the puncture site, attributed to undiagnosed vEDS.

Endovascular angiography carries a 22% risk of morbidity and 5.6% risk of mortality in vEDS patients, and historically endovascular treatment mortality for sCCF in vEDS was reported as high as 58%, though a more recent review reported 0% mortality with advances in endovascular technique.

Celiprolol, a vasodilatory β1-blocker, has been reported to reduce cardiovascular and other serious events in vEDS patients by stimulating collagen production, and the authors suggest it may be useful preoperatively or after diagnosis to prevent delayed vascular events, though it was not used in this patient.
Heterozygous mutations in the SKI gene cause Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome, resulting in dysregulation of the TGF-beta signaling pathway and altered expression of TGF-beta responsive genes.

A patient initially suspected of having hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was reclassified as having Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome after identification of a heterozygous probably pathogenic SKI variant in the second mutational hotspot (Dachshund homology domain).

A second patient with a positive Marfan systemic score and no craniosynostosis or learning disabilities was ultimately diagnosed with Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome after identification of the same class of SKI variant.

One patient initially suspected of having hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was ultimately diagnosed with Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome after identification of a heterozygous probably pathogenic SKI variant.

The second patient, initially suspected of Marfan syndrome based on a positive Marfan systemic score and absence of craniosynostosis or learning disabilities, was instead diagnosed with Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome via identification of a SKI gene variant.

Patients with pathogenic variants at threonine 180 in the SKI Dachshund homology domain (hotspot group 3, n=11) showed absence of learning disabilities and less severe facial features compared to other SKI mutational hotspot groups.
Craniosynostosis and learning disabilities are described as the distinctive clinical features distinguishing Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome from Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes.

The clinical overlap between Shprintzen-Goldberg, Marfan, and Loeys-Dietz syndromes necessitates genetic testing to achieve an accurate molecular diagnosis and guide genetic counseling and clinical management.

A bacterial collagen-like protein engineered with a vEDS-associated Gly→Ser substitution in the integrin-binding site retained triple-helix structure with relatively modest functional perturbation compared to Gly→Arg.
The Gly→Arg substitution significantly reduced the global thermal stability of the collagen-like protein triple-helix compared to wild-type/Ser-substituted constructs.
The Gly→Arg substitution increased susceptibility of the collagen-like protein to trypsin digestion relative to Ser-substituted or wild-type constructs.
Gly→Arg substitution in the collagen integrin-binding site altered binding affinity to the integrin α2-inserted (α2I) domain compared to wild-type and Ser-substituted constructs.

Molecular dynamics simulations showed that Arg substitution caused notable structural bulging at the substitution site and disrupted interchain hydrogen bonds in the collagen triple-helix, distinct from the effect of Ser substitution.
Steered molecular dynamics simulations showed that Arg substitution significantly decreased the Young's modulus (a measure of stiffness/mechanical strength) of the collagen triple-helix.

The study demonstrates that bacterial collagen-like proteins are a viable model system for studying the mechanisms underlying vEDS-causing collagen-III mutations, and that Ser vs Arg substitutions differentially perturb structure/function in a manner consistent with observed clinical severity differences.

Downstreamer's height-associated key gene set showed substantial overlap with known Ehlers-Danlos syndrome genes, with 12 of the 20 currently known Ehlers-Danlos genes also prioritised as key genes for height.

Downstreamer identified additional height-associated key genes not currently known to cause Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or osteogenesis imperfecta, proposing them as candidate genes for interpreting variants of unknown significance in patients suspected of these connective tissue/skeletal disorders.

Height key genes prioritised by Downstreamer also overlapped with genes annotated to the gene ontology terms for extracellular matrix organisation and collagen fibril organisation, consistent with the connective-tissue relevance of these disorders.
A rare BMP6 missense variant (c.379G>A, p.Gly127Arg) was identified in the P01 family as a candidate for PEx, with low-to-moderate in silico prediction of a damaging effect.
A second, distinct BMP6 variant (c.720C>G, p.Phe240Leu) was identified in family P14, with in silico analysis supporting a potentially damaging effect.
A NOTCH3 variant (c.329G>A, p.Arg110His) identified in family P01 showed moderately elevated in silico scores supporting a damaging effect.
The CRTAC1 c.811C>T (p.Arg271Trp) variant, found in three affected members of family P02, did not segregate with the PEx phenotype because it was also present in an unaffected sister.
A BAZ1B variant (c.2134G>A, p.Asp712Asn) identified in family P03 was predicted in silico to be a tolerated, non-deleterious substitution.

A deep-splice GLG1 variant (c.2935-54T>C) in family P03 was predicted by SpliceAI to create a cryptic acceptor site causing inclusion of 51bp of intron 21, introducing a premature stop codon and likely nonsense-mediated decay in a gene intolerant to loss-of-function (pLI=1), despite a low CADD score.

In family P04, a COL5A1 5'UTR variant (c.-180C>A), a gene associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and fibromuscular dysplasia, segregated with the PEx phenotype but was classified as likely benign due to a low in silico damaging score.

A REST missense variant (c.70A>G, p.Met24Val) segregated with the PEx phenotype in family P02, present in the proband, affected father, and niece, and absent in unaffected mother and sister, although in silico analysis suggested the substitution is tolerated with limited damaging effect.

A novel SMAD4 missense variant, previously described as predisposing to thoracic aortic disease, was identified in affected members of family P02 and absent in unaffected members, though phenotypic features of known SMAD4-associated syndromes were not observed.

Across all ten multiplex PEx families studied by exome sequencing, no single shared candidate gene variant was found to be causative or strongly associated with pectus excavatum, supporting a complex, multifactorial genetic etiology rather than a universal monogenic cause.

Previously reported candidate genes GAL3ST4 (Wu et al.) and TINAG (Tong et al.) from other familial PEx exome studies were also observed in this cohort's affected probands but were deemed non-contributory, being common population variants or inherited from unaffected parents.
In families P06, P09, and P13, no variants in known cartilage-development or thoracic-aortic-disease genes were found to be strongly associated with PEx.
Halo-vest traction produced a 57% improvement in headache symptom scores in EDS patients with craniocervical instability.
Halo-vest traction produced a 71% improvement in brainstem function symptom scores.
Halo-vest traction produced a 55% improvement in cerebellar function symptom scores.
Halo-vest traction produced a 63% improvement in hearing symptom scores.
Halo-vest traction produced a 51% improvement in motor function symptom scores.
Halo-vest traction produced a 60% improvement in vision symptom scores.
Halo-vest traction produced a 46% improvement in cardiovascular function symptom scores.
Halo-vest traction produced a 53% improvement in sensory and pain symptom scores.
High cortical function symptoms improved by 54% after halo-vest traction, a statistically significant change.
Gastrointestinal function symptoms improved by 52% after halo-vest traction, a statistically significant change.
Bladder function symptoms improved by 52% after halo-vest traction, a statistically significant change.
Overall functional status measured by the Modified Karnofsky score improved by 30% after halo-vest traction, a statistically significant change.
Of the 21 EDS patients evaluated with halo-vest traction for craniocervical instability, 16 subsequently underwent definitive fusion surgery based on symptomatic improvement.
Skeletal (bone) age was significantly delayed relative to calendar age in adolescent female dancers.
Over half of the dancers reported an aberrant menstrual cycle, which was not related to LBP.
Scoliosis was not significantly related to low back pain history in the dancer cohort.
Generalized joint hypermobility was not significantly related to low back pain history in the dancers.
Dancers with a history of low back pain had started dance training approximately two years earlier than those without LBP.
Dancers with a history of low back pain showed significantly less hip internal rotation than those without LBP.
Dancers with a history of low back pain showed significant asymmetry in hip range of motion between sides.
Generalized joint hypermobility was not significantly associated with a history of low back pain in adolescent dancers.
Dancers with a history of low back pain began dancing approximately two years earlier than those without LBP.
Dancers with a history of low back pain had significantly less hip internal rotation range of motion than those without LBP.
Dancers with a history of low back pain showed asymmetrical hip range of motion compared to those without LBP.
During the intervention phase, two of three children showed reduced fatigue with the Pilates program.
One child showed improved strength in hip abduction (gluteus medius) and scapula adduction/rotation (rhomboideus major/minor) during the Pilates intervention phase.
One child showed improved Health Related Quality of Life during the Pilates intervention phase.
No improvements were seen in pain or postural control during the intervention phase.
During the early withdrawal phase after Pilates ended, all three children showed improved strength in at least two muscle groups.
During the early withdrawal phase, one child showed reduced fatigue, reduced worst-pain-in-last-week, and improved postural control (functional reach lateral).

Genome-wide expression profiling suggests that a subgroup of fibromyalgia patients shows low-level ('micro-') inflammation with upregulation of genes involved in antibacterial and innate immune responses, linked to high BMI and comorbid depression.
A set of 5 differentially expressed inflammatory genes has been proposed as potential biomarkers of a micro-inflammation fibromyalgia subtype.
Bacterial disease and gut dysbiosis are proposed as triggers of micro-inflammation in fibromyalgia.
Metabolic syndrome may be either a causative factor or a consequence of fibromyalgia.
Comorbid depression in fibromyalgia may be linked to gut dysbiosis and/or micro-inflammation via the gut-immune-brain axis.

No clear, reliable etiological biomarker for fibromyalgia has yet been identified, and the condition likely comprises multiple subtypes with distinct pathophysiological mechanisms requiring a multimodal, individualized treatment approach.
Cold stress (intermittent cold stress, ICS) induced fibromyalgia-like mechanical hyperalgesia in mice, with markedly reduced paw withdrawal thresholds compared to baseline.
Low-frequency 2 Hz electroacupuncture at ST36 significantly improved mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds compared to the FM group.
Sham electroacupuncture had no effect on mechanical thresholds, demonstrating acupoint specificity of EA's analgesic effect.
Cold stress induced thermal hyperalgesia, reducing paw withdrawal latency in the Hargreaves' test.
2 Hz electroacupuncture reduced thermal hyperalgesia by increasing paw withdrawal latency compared to FM mice, but sham EA further decreased latency.
Cold stress-induced fibromyalgia pain reduced CB1 receptor expression in the thalamus, which was restored by 2 Hz EA but further decreased by sham EA.
Phosphorylated PKA, PI3K, and PKC levels were increased in the thalamus of fibromyalgia mice and were reduced by 2 Hz EA but not sham EA.
Phospho-Akt, phospho-mTOR, phospho-ERK, and phospho-NF-κB were increased in the thalamus after fibromyalgia induction and normalized by EA but not sham EA.
CB1 expression decreased in the somatosensory cortex (SSC) two days after fibromyalgia induction, and this attenuation was reversed by 2 Hz EA but not sham EA.
Multiple pain-related kinases (pPKA, pPI3K, pPKC, pAkt, pmTOR, pERK, pNF-κB) were increased in the SSC of fibromyalgia mice and decreased by EA but not sham EA.
CB1 receptor activity decreased in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) after fibromyalgia induction and was increased by 2 Hz EA but not by sham EA.
Pain-related kinases were sequentially amplified in the ACC after fibromyalgia induction and improved by 2 Hz EA but not sham EA.
Intracerebroventricular injection of the CB1 agonist AEA significantly attenuated mechanical hyperalgesia in the fibromyalgia mouse model.
The CB1 antagonist AM251 abolished EA's analgesic effect on mechanical hyperalgesia, confirming that EA's effect is CB1-mediated.
Chemogenetic inhibition of SSC neurons via hM4Di DREADD activation with CNO significantly diminished mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia in fibromyalgia mice.
Injecting the CB1 agonist AEA into the SSC increased CB1 levels and reduced overexpressed pain-related kinases (pPKA, pPI3K, pPKC, pAkt, pmTOR, pERK, pNF-κB) in the fibromyalgia model.
Co-administration of AM251 with EA prevented the EA-induced increase in CB1 levels in the SSC, indicating EA's main effect is via CB1 receptor activation.
Chemogenetic inhibition of SSC layer 2/3 neurons significantly increased CB1 levels and reduced overexpression of pain-related kinases in both SSC and ACC.
Using the fixed-effects inverse variance weighted (IVW) method, genetically predicted depression was not significantly associated with increased risk of fibromyalgia.

Results were consistent across multiple sensitivity MR methods (maximum likelihood, weighted median, penalized weighted median, MR-RAPS, MR-PRESSO), all showing no significant causal effect of depression on fibromyalgia risk.
MR-Egger intercept analysis found no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy affecting the depression-fibromyalgia causal estimate.
Cochran's Q heterogeneity testing showed no significant heterogeneity among the genetic variant estimates used in the depression-fibromyalgia MR analysis.
The 42 SNPs selected as instrumental variables for depression showed F-statistics greater than 10, indicating no weak instrument bias in the MR analysis.
Prior literature reported increased Glx and lowered GABA in the insula of patients with fibromyalgia, a nociplastic chronic pain condition, forming the rationale for this study.
In the matched primary sample, Glx concentration in the right posterior insula cortex was significantly higher in patients with sickle cell disease compared to matched healthy controls.
The ratio of Glx to total creatine (tCr) in the posterior insula cortex was significantly higher in SCD patients than in matched healthy controls.
In a secondary analysis using the unpaired full sample of 24 SCD patients versus 19 healthy controls, Glx/tCr remained significantly higher in SCD patients.
Glx/tCr level in the posterior insula cortex correlated positively with the number of vaso-occlusive crises (VOCs) experienced in the prior 12 months.
Glx level in the posterior insula cortex correlated negatively with sensory sensitivity, measured by tonic pressure pain threshold in the gastrocnemius, in the SCD sample.
The unpaired full sample also showed a significant difference in sensory sensitivity between SCD patients and healthy controls.
Myo-inositol levels in the posterior insula were also found to be altered in SCD patients compared to healthy controls, though the specific direction was not detailed.
Clec12b is reported to alleviate mite-induced dermatitis in mice by regulating P2RX7-mediated mast cell activation.
Isobavachin reduced IgE/antigen-stimulated degranulation in bone marrow-derived mast cells.
Isobavachin decreased generation of the eicosanoids leukotriene C4 and prostaglandin D2 in IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cells.
Isobavachin reduced release of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6 from IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cells.
Isobavachin suppressed activation of the receptor-proximal tyrosine kinases Fyn, Lyn, Syk, and Lck that initiate FcεRI-mediated mast cell activation.
Isobavachin suppressed downstream signaling molecules including LAT, PLCγ1, AKT, MAPKs, and intracellular Ca2+ mobilization following the proximal kinase inhibition.
Isobavachin increased phosphorylation of SHP-1, strengthening its interaction with Syk, Lck, Fyn, and Lyn and causing their de-phosphorylation.
Genetic knockdown of SHP-1 reversed the inhibitory effects of isobavachin on mast cell activation and its associated signaling pathways, demonstrating SHP-1 dependence of the drug's mechanism.
Isobavachin suppressed LPS-stimulated production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and nitric oxide in macrophages.
Oral administration of isobavachin attenuated mast cell-mediated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) reactions in a mouse model.
PAFR mRNA expression in skin was significantly higher in CSU patients than in healthy controls.
Endothelial cell PAFR expression was observed exclusively in CSU patients and not in healthy control skin.
Serum PAF levels were elevated in CSU patients and were even higher in those who did not respond to H1-antihistamine treatment.
PAF-AH levels were reduced in CSU patients compared to healthy controls, and a lower PAF-AH/PAF ratio was observed in H1-antihistamine non-responders versus responders.
PAF-AH levels positively correlated with BMI and complement C3/C4, negatively correlated with urticaria duration, but neither PAF nor PAF-AH correlated with urticaria activity scores.

A large cohort of 283 CSU patients versus 111 healthy controls showed significantly increased serum PAF, whereas two smaller studies (<30 subjects per group) reported higher but non-significant PAF levels in CSU, likely due to inter-individual variability and PAF's short half-life.
Intradermal injection of PAF into human skin induces wheal, flare, and pruritus in a dose-dependent manner at doses of 10-100 ng.

Intradermal PAF injection caused an immediate (<5 min) increase in plasma histamine in both atopic and non-atopic individuals, with atopic subjects having double the baseline histamine level, and antihistamine treatment or prior histamine depletion significantly reduced PAF-induced pruritus, flare, and wheal.

Isolated human skin mast cells are unable to degranulate in response to PAF, whereas PAF induces histamine release from human lung mast cells and peripheral-blood-derived mast cells via the PAFR-coupled Gαi protein pathway shared with FcεRI signaling.
PAF induces mast cell degranulation in LAD2 human mast cell line and primary human lung mast cells, evidenced by beta-hexosaminidase and histamine release assays.

PAF induces histamine release from human basophils (enhanced by IL-3/GM-CSF), with no significant difference in histamine or LTC4 release between allergic and non-allergic donors, and this response is IgE-independent.
PAFR expression is significantly elevated in lesional skin of CSU patients at both mRNA and protein levels, localized primarily to epidermis and endothelium.

Platelet-derived PAF is sufficient to induce shock characterized by vascular leakage, tissue inflammation, and decreased core temperature in a systemic platelet activation mouse model, and both platelet-mediated mast cell degranulation and neutrophil priming effects were alleviated by a specific PAFR antagonist.

Peripheral blood platelet count is significantly higher in patients with moderate to severe CSU than in healthy individuals and those with mild CSU, and correlates significantly with CRP, a biomarker of CSU severity and antihistamine non-response.

Tryptase-positive/chymase-negative mast cells (MCT), which express PAFR, are significantly increased in CSU lesional skin compared to non-lesional CSU and healthy skin, while the main MCTC subpopulation does not differ between groups.
PAF induces IL-4 production in PBMCs from both healthy donors and CSU patients, and this IL-4 secretion enhances IL-6 secretion and activates Th2 cells.

PAF-AH expression is downregulated by microRNA-101-5p, which is released from endothelial cells and keratinocytes in response to IL-4 stimulation, providing a mechanism by which enhanced IL-4/IL-6 secretion in CSU skin prolongs PAF activity.
IL-4+ cells and Th2-initiating cytokines including IL-33, IL-25, and TSLP were significantly elevated in lesional CSU skin compared to non-lesional CSU skin and healthy controls.
Basopenia (reduced peripheral blood basophils) is significantly associated with higher urticaria activity scores and decreased responsiveness to antihistamine and anti-IgE treatments in CSU.

Carbamyl-PAF (10 µM) upregulated CXCR4 expression in HMC-1 human mast cell lines 6-24 h post-treatment while reducing DNMT1 for up to 48 h, suggesting PAF-induced epigenetic demethylation of the CXCR4 promoter.

PAF induces Th17 cell differentiation via Langerhans cell interactions, triggering IL-1β, IL-6 and IL-23 expression; elevated plasma IL-17 and IL-23 have been observed in CSU patients correlating with severity, and IL-23 is significantly higher in ASST-positive versus ASST-negative patients.

Local injection of PAF into rat paws induces spontaneous nociception and mechanical hypersensitivity, suggesting PAF sensitizes peripheral nerves to painful stimuli via mechanisms including IL-1β and TRPV1 activation and mast cell degranulation.

A double-blind, randomized, within-patient trial of topical PAF antagonist in atopic dermatitis patients showed significant reduction in pruritus severity during the first two weeks, without significant change in erythema, scaling, induration, or exudation.

Rupatadine inhibits PAF-induced mast cell degranulation in LAD2 cells and human lung tissue mast cells at 1-10 µM, whereas desloratadine shows no such effect and levocetirizine inhibits PAF-induced degranulation in LAD2 cells.

A randomized controlled trial found that combination treatment with antiplatelet drugs (cilostazol, dipyridamole) plus antihistamine up-dosing was more effective in reducing urticaria symptom severity than antihistamine up-dosing alone, particularly relevant to patients with signs of platelet activation such as elevated D-dimer.
Secukinumab, an anti-IL-17 monoclonal antibody, showed an 82% reduction in UAS7 scores after 3 months of treatment in a study of eight patients with severe CSU refractory to omalizumab.
A case series of three patients with antihistamine- and omalizumab-refractory CSU showed that anti-IL-23 treatment with tildrakizumab effectively improved urticarial symptoms and quality of life.

Dupilumab, which blocks IL-4 and IL-13, reduced itch, wheal, and urticaria activity scores over 24 weeks in patients with antihistamine-refractory CSU, though changes were not statistically significant in the omalizumab incomplete responder subgroup.

HSP10 was identified as a natural anti-PAF molecule that correlates with PAF-AH levels, prevents PAF-induced (but not FcεRI- or MRGX2-mediated) mast cell degranulation, reduces PAF-induced IL-4 production, and higher initial PAF-AH levels were associated with better urticaria control after 3 months of antihistamine treatment.
PAF stimulates IL-4 production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from both healthy donors and CSU patients, activating Th2 responses.
PAF-AH expression is downregulated by microRNA-101-5p released from endothelial cells and keratinocytes in response to IL-4 stimulation, prolonging PAF activity in CSU.
Th2-initiating cytokines IL-33, IL-25, and TSLP are elevated in lesional CSU skin compared to non-lesional skin and healthy controls.
A significant increase in IL-4+ cells was observed in lesional CSU skin compared to controls.
Basopenia (reduced peripheral blood basophils) is significantly associated with higher urticaria activity scores and reduced responsiveness to antihistamine and anti-IgE treatments.
PAF exposure upregulates CXCR4 expression in HMC-1 human mast cells via reduction of DNMT1 and consequent demethylation of the CXCR4 promoter.
TSLP and IL-31, elevated in CSU patients, induce basophil chemotaxis in vitro, potentially contributing to basophil skin infiltration and basopenia.
PAF stimulates cyclic AMP (cAMP) generation in normal human B lymphocytes in a time- and dose-dependent manner, and enhances IL-2- or IL-4-induced cAMP production.

PAF has differential effects on IgM synthesis in cytokine-stimulated B cells, downregulating IL-4-induced IgM secretion while increasing IL-2-induced IgM secretion; these effects were blocked by the PAFR antagonist CV-3988.
PAFR expression decreases 48 hours after LPS stimulation in human dendritic cells.
In a murine model, LPS-exposed dendritic cells produce PAF, which binds PAFR and enhances IL-10 and PGE2 synthesis, inducing a regulatory DC phenotype.

PAF induces Th17 cell differentiation via interactions with Langerhans cells, triggering immediate IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-23 expression in Langerhans cells and keratinocytes, which is blocked by PAFR antagonists plus anti-IL-6R/anti-IL-23.
Elevated plasma IL-17 and IL-23 levels have been observed in CSU patients, correlating with urticaria severity.
IL-23 levels are significantly higher in CSU patients with a positive autologous serum skin test (ASST) compared to those with a negative ASST.
PAF-induced pruritus in human skin is mediated primarily by an indirect, histamine-dependent mechanism rather than direct nerve activation.

Local injection of PAF into rat paws induces spontaneous nociception and mechanical hypersensitivity, suggesting PAF sensitizes peripheral nerves to painful stimuli, potentially via IL-1β and TRPV1 activation.

In a double-blind, randomized, within-patient trial in atopic dermatitis, topical PAF antagonist significantly reduced pruritus severity during the first two weeks, without significantly affecting erythema, scaling, induration, or exudation.
Rupatadine inhibits PAF-induced mast cell degranulation at concentrations of 1-10 µM in both LAD2 cells and human lung tissue mast cells.
Desloratadine shows no inhibitory effect on PAF-induced mast cell degranulation.
Levocetirizine inhibits PAF-induced mast cell degranulation in LAD2 cells.

A randomized controlled trial found that combination antiplatelet therapy (cilostazol, dipyridamole) with antihistamine up-dosing was more effective at reducing urticaria symptom severity than antihistamine up-dosing alone, suggesting benefit in patients with platelet activation signs like elevated D-dimer.
Secukinumab (anti-IL-17 monoclonal antibody) achieved an 82% reduction in UAS7 scores after 3 months in a study of eight omalizumab-refractory severe CSU patients.
Anti-IL-23 treatment with tildrakizumab effectively improved urticarial symptoms and quality of life in a case series of three antihistamine- and omalizumab-refractory CSU patients.

Dupilumab (anti-IL-4/IL-13) reduced itch, wheal, and urticaria activity scores over 24 weeks in antihistamine-refractory CSU patients, with improvement also seen in omalizumab incomplete-responders, though not statistically significant in that subgroup.
HSP10 was identified as a natural anti-PAF molecule showing significant correlation with PAF-AH levels, indicating a role in decreasing PAF activity.
HSP10 prevents PAF-induced mast cell degranulation and reduces PAF-induced IL-4 production, with the inhibitory effect being specific to PAF stimulation and independent of FcεRI or MRGPRX2 pathways.
Higher initial PAF-AH levels are significantly associated with better urticaria control after 3 months of antihistamine treatment.

In a double-blind, randomized, within-patient study, topical application of a PAF antagonist significantly reduced pruritus severity during the first two weeks in atopic dermatitis patients, without significant changes in erythema, scaling, induration, or exudation.
Rupatadine, an H1-antihistamine with PAF receptor antagonist activity, inhibited PAF-induced mast cell degranulation at concentrations of 1-10 µM in LAD2 cells and human lung tissue mast cells.
Unlike rupatadine, desloratadine showed no inhibitory effect on PAF-induced mast cell degranulation.
Levocetirizine inhibits PAF-induced degranulation in LAD2 mast cells.

A randomized controlled trial found that combination treatment with antiplatelet drugs (cilostazol and dipyridamole) plus up-dosed antihistamines was more effective in reducing urticaria symptom severity than up-dosed antihistamines alone.
Secukinumab, an anti-IL-17 monoclonal antibody, was effective in eight patients with severe CSU refractory to omalizumab, producing an 82% reduction in UAS7 scores after 3 months of treatment.
A case series of three patients with antihistamine- and omalizumab-refractory CSU found that anti-IL-23 treatment with tildrakizumab effectively improved urticarial symptoms and quality of life.

Dupilumab, which blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signaling, reduced itch, wheal, and urticaria activity scores over 24 weeks in patients with antihistamine-refractory CSU, though effects were not statistically significant in omalizumab incomplete responders.
Heat shock protein 10 (HSP10) was identified as a natural anti-PAF molecule that significantly correlates with PAF-AH levels, indicating a role in decreasing PAF activity.
Higher initial PAF-AH levels were significantly associated with better urticaria control after 3 months of antihistamine treatment.
HSP10 prevents PAF-induced mast cell degranulation, an inhibitory effect that is specific to PAF stimulation and not mediated by FcεRI or MRGPRX2 pathways.
HSP10 reduces PAF-induced IL-4 production, contributing further to its anti-PAF effects.
A single 40 mg dose of rupatadine in healthy volunteers reduced PAF-induced flares by 87% and PAF-induced platelet aggregation by 82% within 2 hours.

CSU patients show a higher prevalence of anti-HSP10 IgG autoantibodies compared to controls, suggesting that modulating this autoimmune reaction and increasing HSP10 production could be a therapeutic strategy.
Honeybee venom activated mouse cutaneous nociceptive-like C-fibers with an action potential discharge frequency similar to a maximally effective concentration of capsaicin.
Honeybee venom exerted a stronger stimulatory effect on chloroquine-sensitive C-fibers than on chloroquine-insensitive C-fibers.
Wasp (Vespula spp.) venom recapitulated the stronger activation of chloroquine-sensitive C-fibers relative to chloroquine-insensitive C-fibers seen with honeybee venom.
Pharmacological blockade of TRPV1 channels did not alter honeybee venom-induced C-fiber activation.

Melittin, a bee venom peptide component, reproduced the venom's differential activation of chloroquine-sensitive versus chloroquine-insensitive C-fibers, whereas apamin (another venom peptide) did not.
Activation of chloroquine-sensitive cutaneous C-fibers by bee venom occurred as a downstream consequence of mast cell activation/degranulation.
Melittin degranulated mast cells in mouse skin through a mechanism independent of both IgE-mediated signaling and the MrgprB2 receptor.
Genetically predicted higher HLA DR+ CD4+ absolute cell count was associated with increased risk of urticaria in the primary (IVW) MR analysis.
Genetically predicted higher CD45 expression on CD8br T cells was associated with increased risk of urticaria.
Genetically predicted higher HLA-DR expression on plasmacytoid dendritic cells was associated with increased risk of urticaria.
Genetically predicted higher proportion of CD8dim NKT cells among lymphocytes was protective against urticaria.
In reverse MR, genetically predicted urticaria was associated with a decreased proportion of CD8dim NKT cells among lymphocytes, suggesting the disease may itself alter this immune cell phenotype.
In an initial broader screen using IVW p<0.05, 31 of 731 tested immunophenotypes were nominally associated with urticaria risk, 18 increasing risk and 13 conferring protection.
In unadjusted analysis, higher serum MIG (CXCL9) levels were significantly associated with severe COVID-19, but this did not remain significant after correction for multiple testing.

In unadjusted longitudinal modeling, omalizumab treatment was associated with a significant decrease in IL-15 levels over time compared to placebo, but this was not significant after multiple-testing correction.

In unadjusted longitudinal modeling, omalizumab treatment was associated with a significant decrease in macrophage inflammatory protein-1 (MIP-1) levels over time compared to placebo, but this was not significant after multiple-testing correction.
Omalizumab did not significantly affect any of the other 25 cytokines measured in the panel compared to placebo.

After adjustment for multiple comparisons, no measured biomarker was significantly associated with COVID-19 disease severity, and no significant biomarker differences over time were attributable to omalizumab treatment.
No significant associations were found between disease severity and type II inflammatory cytokines, IFN-α, or markers of mast cell activation (including tryptase, CD63, and IgE).

In the parent CIAO trial (40 patients), omalizumab was associated with a 93% probability of reducing death or mechanical ventilation at day 14 compared to placebo, despite early termination due to waning recruitment.

In contrast to omalizumab's null effect on cytokines in this study, a prior dupilumab COVID-19 trial showed a probable clinical benefit accompanied by significant reductions in type II inflammatory cytokines such as eotaxin-3 and YKL-40 versus placebo.

Phase III trials (ASTERIA I, ASTERIA II, GLACIAL) showed omalizumab significantly outperformed placebo in reducing urticaria activity and itch severity in patients aged 12-75 with moderate-to-severe CSU unresponsive to antihistamines.
A meta-analysis of seven randomized controlled trials found that omalizumab at 300 mg every four weeks significantly reduced itch and wheal scores in CSU patients.

Baseline total serum IgE level is the most reliable predictor of omalizumab response in CSU, with non-responders typically having IgE levels below 40 IU/mL (sometimes below 20 IU/mL) and early responders generally above 70 IU/mL.
The ratio of week-4 to baseline IgE levels was found to be the best predictor of omalizumab response, with non-responders showing a significantly lower ratio than partial and complete responders.
Elevated serum soluble FcεRI (sFcεRI) levels are associated with a good response to omalizumab treatment.
Patients with type IIb autoimmune CSU, marked by IgG autoantibodies against IgE or FcεRI, tend to have more severe disease and respond less effectively to omalizumab.
A meta-analysis of 67 real-world studies found a 4% adverse event rate for omalizumab, consistent with the safety profile seen in clinical trials.

A multinational cohort study of 2325 patients across 14 centers in 10 countries found a drug survival rate of 76% at 1 year, decreasing to 39% at 7 years, with well-controlled disease the primary reason for discontinuation in 65% of cases.
A Polish retrospective cohort found that relapse after omalizumab discontinuation commonly occurred within 6 weeks, with each additional UAS7 point increasing relapse risk by 5.4%.
Phase III PEARL-1 and PEARL-2 trials of ligelizumab (a higher-affinity anti-IgE antibody) were halted because although superior to placebo, it did not significantly outperform omalizumab.
In the phase 3 LIBERTY-CSU CUPID Study A (n=138 biologic-naive antihistamine-refractory patients), dupilumab significantly reduced UAS7, pruritus, and urticaria scores at week 24 versus placebo.
A separate phase 3 study (LIBERTY-CUPID Study B, n=83, omalizumab-refractory patients) was discontinued because dupilumab did not achieve statistical significance for the primary endpoints.
A phase II randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial found canakinumab (150 mg SC) was not superior to placebo after 4 weeks, suggesting limited relevance of IL-1beta in CSU pathophysiology.
In 8 patients with antihistamine- and omalizumab-resistant CSU, secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) produced significant improvements in disease activity, reducing UAS7 by 55% at 30 days and 82% at 90 days.
In 3 omalizumab-refractory CSU patients, tildrakizumab (anti-IL-23) achieved good disease control in 2/3 patients at 4 weeks, with disease activity reduction ranging from 19% to 75% at 90 days.

Remibrutinib (BTK inhibitor) at 25 mg twice daily was particularly effective versus placebo in reducing itching and hives from the first week through week 12 in sgAH-refractory CSU patients, with phase III trials meeting all primary and secondary endpoints.

A double-blind placebo-controlled phase II trial found fenebrutinib (BTK inhibitor) effective in reducing disease activity in sgAH-resistant CSU, though a follow-up study was discontinued and some patients had reversible ALT/AST abnormalities.

In a phase 1b study of chronic inducible urticaria, a single IV dose of barzolvolimab (3 mg/kg) led to improvement by week 12 in disease control, quality of life, tryptase/SCF levels, and mast cell histopathology, with hair lightening and infusion reactions as notable adverse events.
Despite preliminary improvements in disease control seen with lirentelimab, the phase II CSU trial's primary endpoints were not met, and further development was discontinued.

Despite promising preliminary reports, a placebo-controlled RCT of benralizumab showed limited efficacy, leading to discontinuation of its CSU development program; a case report also described benralizumab worsening CSU in some cases.
At week 4, bilastine produced significantly greater improvement in urticaria symptoms and quality of life than levocetirizine and fexofenadine, with fewer somnolence side effects.
Increased (up to fourfold) doses of second-generation H1-antihistamines are associated with a higher risk of somnolence than standard doses (relative risk 3.28).
Cyclosporine combined with cetirizine was significantly more effective than placebo plus cetirizine in reducing CSU severity after 8 weeks.
A 2019 randomized prospective study of 80 antihistamine-refractory patients found azathioprine to be non-inferior to cyclosporine.
A randomized trial found hydroxychloroquine (400 mg/day) superior to placebo and to leukotriene receptor antagonists when added to fourfold-dose H1-antihistamines in antihistamine-refractory CSU.

Elevated D-dimer was associated with more severe CSU and antihistamine resistance, and in a pilot study, 5 of 8 patients with elevated D-dimer showed marked improvement with tranexamic acid plus nadroparin.

Ligelizumab, a second-generation anti-IgE antibody with much higher IgE affinity than omalizumab, outperformed placebo but failed to significantly outperform omalizumab in phase III trials, leading to discontinuation of the program.

UB-221, a high-affinity anti-IgE antibody that also promotes CD23-mediated downregulation of IgE production, was well tolerated with no serious adverse events in a phase I trial and is now in phase II recruitment.
Quilizumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting membrane-bound IgE, did not show any visible clinical improvement in patients with CSU.
In the phase 3 LIBERTY-CSU CUPID Study A, dupilumab significantly reduced UAS7, pruritus, and urticaria activity at week 24 in 138 biologic-naïve, antihistamine-refractory CSU patients.
In the phase 3 LIBERTY-CUPID Study B, dupilumab was discontinued due to lack of efficacy, not achieving statistical significance for primary endpoints in 83 omalizumab-refractory CSU patients.
A case report series indicated that 67% of patients maintained remission of CSU for up to 22 months after discontinuing dupilumab therapy, supporting its potential as a disease-modifying treatment.
Although a case report showed benralizumab benefit in severe chronic dermographism, a placebo-controlled RCT found limited efficacy, leading to discontinuation of the CSU development program.
Increased levels of Th2-initiating cytokines, including TSLP, have been observed in the lesional skin of CSU patients, supporting TSLP as a therapeutic target with tezepelumab.

MRGPRX2 is overexpressed in allergic and skin diseases such as CSU, and its downregulation reduces mast cell degranulation, with serum MRGPRX2 proposed as a potential biomarker of CSU activity, especially in treatment-naïve patients.

Novel computationally designed small-molecule MRGPRX2 antagonists inhibited both early and late phases of mast cell activation in vitro and in a mouse model of acute allergy and systemic anaphylaxis; two selective antagonists (EVO756, EP262) are now in clinical trials for CSU and CIndU.

The complement C5a/C5aR pathway, activated via the classical complement cascade and extrinsic coagulation pathway, contributes to mast cell degranulation in CSU and can be experimentally inhibited by the C5aR antagonist W-54011, though human studies are lacking.

Lirentelimab, an anti-Siglec-8 antibody that depletes eosinophils and silences mast cells, showed preliminary improvement in disease control but failed to meet primary endpoints in a phase II CSU trial, with further development deemed unlikely.

The Kit receptor (CD117) and its ligand stem cell factor drive mast cell differentiation, chemotaxis, maturation and survival; blocking this interaction (as in Kit/SCF-deficient mice and imatinib-treated patients) leads to significant reductions in mast cell burden.

A phase 1b open-label study of a single 3 mg/kg IV dose of barzolvolimab, an anti-Kit antibody, showed improvement by week 12 in disease control, quality of life, serum tryptase/SCF, and non-lesional skin mast cell counts in patients with chronic inducible urticaria.

BTK plays a central role in CSU pathogenesis via FcεRI-mediated mast cell/basophil activation and B-cell receptor signaling driving autoantibody production, making it a therapeutic target for antihistamine-refractory disease.

In a double-blind placebo-controlled phase II trial, the BTK inhibitor fenebrutinib effectively reduced disease activity in sgAH-resistant CSU patients, though reversible grade 2-3 ALT/AST abnormalities occurred and the follow-up study was discontinued.

Remibrutinib, an irreversible covalent BTK inhibitor, showed good clinical efficacy and favorable safety in phase II trials (10-200 mg/day) in sgAH-refractory CSU, with the 25 mg twice-daily dose reducing itch and hives from the first week through week 12, confirmed in phase III trials meeting all primary and secondary endpoints.
Rilzabrutinib, a reversible covalent selective BTK inhibitor effective in other autoimmune disorders, is being evaluated for CSU in a phase II trial, with results not yet available.
Tofacitinib (JAK1/3 inhibitor) reduced symptoms and was well tolerated in four CSU patients, and ruxolitinib (JAK1/2 inhibitor) also demonstrated efficacy in CSU treatment.
Cyclosporin in association with cetirizine was significantly more effective than placebo plus cetirizine alone in reducing CSU severity after 8 weeks of treatment.
Patients who responded well to cyclosporine had high baseline CRP levels before treatment in one study, although another study found no positive predictive factors of response.

An intensified combination protocol of omalizumab plus an immunosuppressant (most commonly cyclosporin) was proposed as safe and effective for recalcitrant CSU, particularly in patients with low baseline IgE levels.

Azathioprine was found non-inferior to cyclosporin in a 2019 randomized prospective study of 80 antihistamine-refractory CSU patients, and was previously shown effective at 150 mg/day in resistant patients and 50 mg/day in a single-blind RCT of autologous serum skin test-positive CSU.

A 2022 systematic review concluded methotrexate may help in recalcitrant or steroid-dependent CSU, but there is no evidence of its superiority to antihistamines as first-line molecules; it may be considered in omalizumab-resistant patients or combined with omalizumab, with a maximal dose of 25 mg/week.

In a double-blind placebo-controlled study, dapsone at 100 mg/day showed superior results to placebo in CSU patients who had failed antihistamine treatment, with augmented methemoglobin as the most important side effect.

A 2017 randomized single-blinded placebo-controlled trial found hydroxychloroquine (400 mg/day) superior to placebo and to leukotriene receptor antagonists when added to fourfold-dose H1-antihistamines in antihistamine-refractory CSU; the main adverse effect is retinopathy requiring periodic monitoring.

In an open-label uncontrolled trial, nine CSU patients poorly responsive to antihistamines and/or corticosteroids were successfully treated with mycophenolate mofetil at 1000 mg twice daily, with efficacy confirmed at 500 mg twice daily with progressive increments in a 2012 retrospective study.

Evidence for rituximab (anti-CD20 antibody) in recalcitrant CSU is contradictory, with some cases showing efficacy and others showing no benefit, and one case in which it triggered urticaria in a patient treated for pemphigus vulgaris.

A 2010 pilot study of 68 CSU patients found elevated D-dimer levels associated with more severe disease and resistance to antihistamines, with 5/8 elevated-D-dimer cases improving on tranexamic acid plus nadroparin; this correlation was confirmed in a 2021 Indian retrospective study.

Tranexamic acid in combination with nadroparin improved symptoms in patients with elevated D-dimer, based on the rationale that CSU involves activation of the coagulation cascade and fibrinolysis; nausea and diarrhea were the most common adverse events.

European guidelines recommend systemic corticosteroids (20-50 mg/day prednisone for up to 10 days) only as short-term rescue therapy for acute CSU exacerbations, not as first-line treatment, due to long-term side effects and evidence that early first-line use induces anti-H1 resistance and rebound effects on interruption.
Patients with small fiber neuropathy report lower physical and psychosocial quality of life compared to healthy individuals.
An identifiable underlying cause of small fiber neuropathy is present in 47% of cases, with the remainder classified as idiopathic.
Even the most potent analgesic pharmacotherapy achieves at most a 30-40% reduction in neuropathic pain, frequently accompanied by side effects.

Biopsychosocial factors—pain catastrophizing, pain-related fear, avoidance behaviour, and depressive mood—determine the degree of disability experienced in chronic pain, independent of pain intensity.
A meta-analysis found evidence supporting acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) for reducing disability and improving quality of life in chronic pain patients.

Diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy follows the international Besta criteria, requiring typical symptoms/signs combined with reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy and/or abnormal quantitative sensory testing thresholds.
In SFN patients, higher momentary physical activity was associated with an increase in subsequently reported pain intensity.
Higher momentary pain intensity was associated with an increase in subsequently reported physical activity, a bidirectional and counter-intuitive finding.
Pain catastrophic thoughts (item 'I want the pain to stop') significantly accounted for the association between physical activity and later pain intensity.
Fatigue significantly accounted for the association between physical activity and subsequent pain intensity in SFN.
An increase in cheerful mood significantly accounted for the association between pain intensity and subsequent physical activity.
An increase in anxiety significantly accounted for the association between pain intensity and subsequent physical activity.

Avoidance behavior ('I try to move less') was negatively associated with the pain intensity-physical activity relationship, decreasing as pain and activity increased, contrary to the classic fear-avoidance model.
Time-lagged analyses (±1.5h and ±3h) of pain intensity predicting physical activity, including affective states, showed no statistically significant associations.
Time-lagged analysis of physical activity predicting subsequent pain intensity showed no statistically significant association.
The overall frequency of peripheral neuropathy did not significantly differ between PSP and PD patients, occurring in roughly two-thirds of PSP patients and half of PD patients.
Among patients with neuropathy, PSP-PNP patients had a significantly shorter disease duration than PD-PNP patients.
PSP-PNP patients had significantly higher motor severity (MDS-UPDRS-III) scores than PD-PNP patients.
PSP-PNP patients had significantly higher Hoehn and Yahr disease staging than PD-PNP patients.
PSP-PNP patients had a significantly shorter duration of levodopa treatment than PD-PNP patients.
All patients with neuropathy in both PSP and PD groups had distal symmetrical sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy, with no pure motor axonal or demyelinating neuropathy observed.
Mixed (large plus small) fiber neuropathy was significantly more prevalent among PSP-PNP patients than PD-PNP patients.
Isolated small fiber polyneuropathy was observed exclusively in PD patients, seen in 21.3% of PD-PNP patients and none of the PSP-PNP patients.
All PSP-PNP patients had abnormal nerve conduction studies compared to only 78.7% of PD-PNP patients.
Median motor nerve conduction velocities in bilateral median and left ulnar nerves, although within normal limits, were significantly lower in PSP-PNP than PD-PNP patients.
Longer PD disease duration was independently associated with higher odds of developing peripheral neuropathy in PD patients on multivariate analysis.
No demographic or clinical characteristic was independently associated with peripheral neuropathy in PSP patients.

Prior work cited in the discussion found no difference in phosphorylated tau presence in sympathetic ganglia between healthy individuals and PSP subjects, suggesting normal aging rather than tauopathy drives neurofibrillary tangles in sympathetic ganglia.
One day after single prolonged stress (SPS), rats showed a significant acute increase in mean arterial pressure and heart rate compared to controls.
By day 7 post-SPS, MAP and HR were no longer significantly different between SPS and control rats, indicating the acute cardiovascular effects were transient.
AVP mRNA levels in the PVN were significantly upregulated 3.9-fold in SPS rats compared to controls.
AT1R mRNA levels in the PVN were significantly upregulated 1.6-fold in SPS rats compared to controls.
FOSL1 mRNA levels in the PVN, a marker of chronic neuronal activation, were significantly upregulated 1.6-fold in SPS rats compared to controls.
AVP immunoreactivity was selectively increased 2.1-fold in the magnocellular (Ma) subregion of the PVN in SPS rats, with no significant change in parvocellular or intermediocellular subregions.
AT1R and FOSL1 protein immunoreactivity were significantly increased across all PVN subregions, with notably greater upregulation in the parvocellular and intermediocellular (autonomic) regions.
SPS significantly increased mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) in all measured PVN subregions, with the greatest increases in parvocellular and intermediocellular regions.

mtROS enrichment was predominantly colocalized with AT1R- and FOSL1-expressing cells in the Pa and Me subregions, while colocalization with AVP-expressing cells was less prominent, suggesting oxidative stress is selectively linked to autonomic pathways rather than the neuroendocrine (AVP) pathway.
Aortic TNFα mRNA was significantly increased 2.6-fold in SPS rats compared to controls.
Aortic IL-1β mRNA was significantly increased 4.4-fold in SPS rats compared to controls.
Aortic iNOS mRNA expression was dramatically increased 37-fold in SPS rats compared to controls.
Aortic IL-6 and NF-κB mRNA levels were not significantly altered between SPS and control groups, suggesting selective rather than generalized inflammatory activation.
Aortic eNOS mRNA expression was significantly increased 2-fold in SPS rats compared to controls, suggesting altered endothelial function.
SPS rats showed an attenuated blood pressure response to the vasoconstrictor phenylephrine (PE) compared to controls, indicating impaired vascular smooth muscle reactivity.
SPS rats showed an attenuated blood pressure response to the vasodilator sodium nitroprusside (SNP) compared to controls, indicating impaired endothelium-independent vasodilatory reactivity.

During and after 40-minute restraint stress, SPS rats showed a significantly lower ΔMAP response during restraint and slower return of MAP to baseline afterward compared to controls, indicating disrupted adaptive cardiovascular responses to acute stress.
Spontaneous micronuclei counts were significantly higher in four Marfan syndrome (MFS) fibroblast cell lines than in radioresistant control fibroblasts.
Radiation-induced micronuclei assessed 24h after 2 Gy X-ray exposure were significantly higher in MFS fibroblasts than controls, but lower than in hyper-radiosensitive ATM-mutated cells.
Using a published MN-SF2 correlation and MFS prevalence data, the predicted SF2 for MFS cells was estimated at 15-25%, indicating moderate but significant cellular radiosensitivity.
Spontaneous (unirradiated) gamma-H2AX foci counts did not differ significantly between MFS fibroblasts and radioresistant controls.

Induced gamma-H2AX foci at 10 minutes post-irradiation were consistently lower in all four MFS fibroblast lines than in radioresistant controls, indicating impaired DSB recognition consistent with diminished ATM nucleo-shuttling (RIANS).
By 24h post-irradiation, gamma-H2AX foci counts (representing unrepaired DSB) were similar between MFS fibroblasts and radioresistant controls.
Nuclear phospho-ATM (pATM) foci at 10 minutes post-irradiation were significantly lower in MFS fibroblasts than in radioresistant controls, consistent with diminished RIANS.
By 24h post-irradiation, pATM foci counts were similar between MFS fibroblasts and radioresistant controls.
MRE11 foci kinetics were abnormal in MFS fibroblasts, with a peak at 4h post-irradiation that never reached the magnitude observed in radioresistant controls.
MRE11 foci remained detectable (non-zero) at 24h post-irradiation in all four MFS cell lines, suggesting persistence of DNA breaks and possible pro-inflammatory signaling.
MFS fibroblasts showed stronger cytoplasmic and nuclear FBN1 protein localization by immunofluorescence than control fibroblasts, both before and after irradiation.

Immunoblot of cytoplasmic extracts showed higher FBN1 protein expression in three MFS cell lines (GM21939, GM21972, GM21944) than in control cells before irradiation, with an unidentified extra band in most MFS lines.

Proximity ligation assay showed significantly more cytoplasmic ATM-FBN1 complexes in MFS fibroblasts than in radioresistant controls, before and after irradiation, supporting cytoplasmic ATM sequestration as a cause of diminished RIANS.

TGF-beta was abundantly expressed in both nucleus and cytoplasm of MFS fibroblasts by immunofluorescence, before and after irradiation, with a perinuclear pattern appearing in some cells after irradiation.
Immunoblotting of MFS cell extracts revealed an atypical two-band pattern for TGF-beta not seen in radioresistant controls, of unknown origin.

PLA confirmed cytoplasmic ATM-TGF-beta complexes in MFS fibroblasts with variable abundance across cell lines, higher before irradiation, further supporting cytoplasmic ATM sequestration as a mechanism of diminished RIANS.
ZOPRA treatment (zoledronate plus pravastatin) significantly decreased radiation-induced micronuclei counts at 24h in two of four MFS fibroblast cell lines (GM21944 and GM21972).
ZOPRA treatment significantly increased induced gamma-H2AX foci at 10 minutes post-irradiation in all four MFS fibroblast cell lines, indicating restored DSB recognition.
ZOPRA treatment increased pATM foci at 10 minutes post-irradiation in all tested MFS fibroblast cell lines, suggesting restoration of RIANS.

In prior work, ZOPRA treatment had no significant effect on micronuclei yields or on gamma-H2AX, pATM, and MRE11 foci kinetics in radioresistant control cells, supporting specificity of the ZOPRA effect to radiosensitive syndromes.
A prospective study found that a high-fiber diet of 24.3 g/day was associated with a 40% lower risk of developing Crohn's disease.
The low-FODMAP diet triggered a significant decrease in abdominal pain, bloating, and diarrhea in 72% of CD patients and 78% of UC patients in remission with IBS-like symptoms.

In a randomized controlled trial of 55 IBD patients, six weeks of a low-FODMAP diet reduced calprotectin levels, decreased disease activity, and improved quality of life compared with a standard diet control group.

A meta-analysis of six RCTs and sixteen non-randomized trials found low-FODMAP diet significantly reduced IBS Symptom Severity Scale scores and improved IBS quality-of-life scores in quiescent IBD patients.
Low-FODMAP diet use has been associated with dysbiosis, characterized by lower concentrations of Bifidobacteria, Akkermansia muciniphila, and Clostridium cluster XIVa.
In a Swiss IBD cohort study of 1254 patients, gluten-free diet users had significantly higher levels of depressive symptoms or anxiety, with no clinical benefit for disease evolution.

A cross-sectional study of 1647 IBD patients found that 65.6% reported digestive symptom improvement and 38.3% reported fewer/less severe flares on a gluten-free diet, with high adherence linked to significant fatigue reduction.

A prospective interventional trial found that 6 months of Mediterranean diet adherence in IBD patients reduced BMI, waist circumference, hepatic steatosis, CRP, and fecal calprotectin, correlating with improved disease activity.
A prospective cohort study of 83,147 volunteers (Swedish Cohorts) found higher Mediterranean diet adherence score was associated with reduced risk of Crohn's disease onset.

A review of 28 studies with 8168 adults found physical activity improved quality of life in seven studies, reduced fatigue scores in five studies, and improved sleep, digestive symptoms, and cardiorespiratory performance in IBD patients.
In a longitudinal cohort over 2 years, women who walked 9 hours per week had a 44% decreased risk of Crohn's disease onset.
A meta-analysis of nine RCTs (637 participants) found physical activity improved disease activity compared to controls, with the largest effect from a low-intensity walking program.

A randomized controlled trial in 60 adolescents/young adults with IBD in remission found short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy plus standard care significantly improved steroid-free remission rate at 52 weeks compared to standard care alone (93.1% vs 64.3%, p=0.01), with reduced depression scores.

In a rat model of chronic colon hypersensitivity, chitin glucan at human equivalent doses of 1.5-3 g/d for 12 weeks decreased visceral pain perception and reduced inflammation intensity by 50%, with full colonic mucosa regeneration in DSS-induced colitis.

In an open-label study of 120 IBS patients, 4 weeks of chitin glucan plus simethicone significantly improved abdominal pain in 67% of participants, with reduction in bloating and improved stool consistency.

A meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found B. coagulans and B. infantis probiotics significantly improved global symptom scores in IBS patients versus placebo, with B. coagulans ranking first for abdominal pain relief.

In an open-labeled post-marketing study of 33 IBS patients, B. longum 35624 supplementation significantly reduced the Total IBS Symptom Score by 43.4% from baseline, with over 60% of patients achieving clinically relevant improvement.

A pediatric real-world trial of 64 children/adolescents with IBS in Chile found B. longum 35624 for 12 weeks produced significant improvement in all IBS-SSS domains (p<0.0007), with 96.6% achieving clinically relevant improvement.

A randomized placebo-controlled trial in 330 IBS patients found significant improvement in IBS-SSS scores for L. acidophilus DDS-1 (-133.4±95.19, p<0.001) and B. lactis UABla-12 (-104.5±96.08, p<0.001) groups versus placebo.

A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 456 adults found significantly greater abdominal pain response with S. cerevisiae I-3856 versus placebo (45.1% vs 33.9%, p=0.017), with improved quality-of-life scores.

A multicenter open-label trial found that 12 weeks of 5g/day HMO (2'-FL and LNnT, 4:1) supplementation significantly improved abnormal stool consistency, IBS-SSS, and health-related quality of life across all IBS subtypes.

Galactooligosaccharide supplementation significantly enhanced fecal bifidobacteria and, at 3.5-7 g/day for 12 weeks, improved stool consistency, reduced flatulence and bloating, and improved anxiety scores.

In 636 constipation-type IBS patients, 36 days of a synbiotic combination significantly increased the 'no symptom' class from 3% to 26.7% for bloating and from 8.4% to 44.1% for abdominal pain, and improved stool frequency.
