Open surgical excision of the aneurysmal sac with primary continuous suture closure of the IVC neck resulted in an uneventful recovery and no recurrence or complications at 3-year follow-up.

An endovascular endograft approach was considered inferior to open surgery in this case because the aneurysm neck's proximity to the right renal vein risked inadvertent coverage of the renal vein ostium, and coil embolization was excluded due to the large neck size and risk of distal coil embolization to the pulmonary circulation.

A prior literature review of 54 IVCA cases through 2014 found type I (suprahepatic) aneurysms were most common (23 cases), followed by type III (infrarenal, without congenital anomalies, 21 cases), per the Gradman and Steinberg anatomical classification.
Sanger sequencing identified a likely pathogenic FBN1 variant (c.2364T>G, p.Phe788Leu) in the proband, leading to a diagnosis of Marfan syndrome.

Targeted NGS suggested a copy number deletion spanning SMAD3 exons 2-9, later confirmed by array-CGH as a ~510-560 kb heterozygous deletion at Chr15q22.33-q23, establishing a diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

Repeat NGS testing confirmed both the FBN1 c.2364T>G variant and the SMAD3 deletion in the proband and her older sister, establishing a definitive diagnosis of coexisting Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes within the same individuals.
Brain MRI screening performed as part of Loeys-Dietz syndrome workup revealed multiple cerebral aneurysms in the cavernous sinus segments of the bilateral internal carotid arteries in the proband.
The discussion, citing prior literature, states that Loeys-Dietz syndrome causes aortic dissection at an earlier age than Marfan syndrome, warranting earlier surgical intervention in LDS.
The discussion notes that Marfan syndrome is not commonly associated with cerebral aneurysms, whereas Loeys-Dietz syndrome is linked to a higher incidence of cerebral aneurysms.

The proband's sister, who carried both the FBN1 and SMAD3 mutations, developed acute Stanford type A aortic dissection soon after her ascending aortic diameter was measured at 45 mm, despite dissection risk generally being considered low below this threshold.

Standard short-read targeted NGS gene panel testing failed to detect the SMAD3 deletion, illustrating that array-CGH (or MLPA) is needed as the gold-standard method for CNV genotyping in hereditary thoracic aortic disease.

The authors suggest, drawing an analogy to double LDL receptor/PCSK9 mutations in familial hypercholesterolemia, that double mutations in different genes (here FBN1 and SMAD3) may result in a more severe HTAD phenotype than single mutations.
Citing prior literature, the authors state that comprehensive NGS-based genetic testing of HTAD-related genes has enabled identification of causative mutations in more than 80% of cases.
Reported COVID-19 illness was associated with a new abnormal heart rhythm occurring in the following 30 days compared to other time periods, though this was driven by only two participants.

There was no evidence of an increased rate of cardiovascular events other than new abnormal heart rhythm following COVID-19 illness, and this association could not be estimated due to no such events occurring within the follow-up window.

There was not a statistically significant increase in the rate of any cardiovascular event within one month after COVID-19 vaccination compared to other time periods, whether considering all CVEs, new abnormal heart rhythm alone, or other CVEs.

Vaccinated respondents reported cardiovascular events at a higher rate than unvaccinated respondents, but sensitivity analyses indicate this reflects confounding by older age rather than a causal vaccine effect.

The rate of expected adverse events (EAE) following COVID-19 vaccination among LDS, MFS, and vEDS respondents was not higher than that reported for the general population, with fatigue being the most common EAE across all three syndromes.

Symptoms suggestive of a possible allergic reaction (SSPAR) after COVID-19 vaccination occurred at similar rates across LDS, MFS, and vEDS respondents, and most were mild, self-limited, and unlikely to represent true IgE-mediated allergic reactions based on timing and lack of recurrence.

Contrary to the hypothesis that Loeys-Dietz syndrome patients (known to have increased susceptibility to allergic disease) would show elevated allergic-type reactions to COVID-19 vaccination, LDS respondents reported similar SSPAR rates to MFS and vEDS respondents.

Among vascular connective tissue disorder respondents, self-reported COVID-19 illness occurred in 37.3% of LDS, 25.6% of MFS, and 19.4% of vEDS respondents, with 98% treated at home and none requiring ICU admission.

The authors describe a proposed mechanism whereby SARS-CoV-2 infects vascular endothelial cells via the ACE2 receptor, causing endothelial cell damage/apoptosis and resultant endothelial dysfunction that promotes ischemia, inflammation, and a procoagulant state.

Background literature cited indicates that SARS-CoV-2 infection is associated with overexpression of VEGF, VEGF receptor 1 (Flt-1), ICAM-1, MMP-2, PDGF, TNFα, and TGFβ, factors implicated in aneurysm formation and progression in heritable vascular connective tissue disorders.

Background literature cited by the authors indicates COVID-19 mRNA vaccines had an initially reported higher rate of anaphylactic reactions (3.29-5.58 per million doses) compared to other vaccines (1.3 per million doses).
The most commonly reported cardiovascular event among survey respondents was new abnormal heart rhythm, accounting for 23 of the 89 total reported CVEs.
The patient met Brighton Criteria for hypermobility spectrum disorder with a Beighton Score of four plus arthralgia, soft tissue lesions, and Marfan-like habitus.

The patient was diagnosed with Raynaud's phenomenon presenting as painful, swelling, itching, blistering hands with cold white discoloration, occurring alongside HSD, a combination the authors state has not been previously reported.
Patellar instability testing showed significant lateral patellar movement, suggesting patellofemoral pain syndrome associated with increased patellar laxity linked to the patient's HSD.

Functional shoulder tests revealed type I and type II scapular dyskinesia with poor scapular humeral rhythm and scapular winging beyond 45° of abduction, indicating weak dynamic shoulder stability from the rotator cuff and serratus anterior.

Three sessions of physiotherapy (myofascial release, electrotherapy, manual therapy, Kinesio-taping, stretching, and home exercises) over three weeks in 2021 resolved the patient's left shoulder pain and improved posture, scapular positioning, rhomboid strength, and functional shoulder range of motion.

A biokinetic home-based exercise program (lower limb and core isometric/isotonic strengthening, mobility, and proprioceptive exercises) at 4x/week improved pelvic stability, squat mechanics, balance (mPCTSIB), and dynamic arch/shoulder stability at three-month follow-up, with the patient self-reporting ~80% adherence and improved overall body pain.
Hand and finger exercises performed in a lukewarm water basin during symptomatic Raynaud's flare-ups were reported by the patient to help control pain, stiffness, and hand discomfort during winter.
The patient was managed pharmacologically with Nifedipine to control Raynaud's phenomenon symptoms.

The authors describe reduced proprioception and kinesthesia in children with HSD, hypothesized to result from impaired mechanoreceptor feedback from ligaments, muscle spindles, and Golgi tendon organs, increasing risk of joint injury such as at the knee and shoulder.
Heterozygous deleterious null alleles and specific missense variants in the ERF DNA-binding domain are previously known causes of craniosynostosis.
The recurrent ERF missense variant p.(Tyr89Cys) is associated with Chitayat syndrome.

A de novo in-frame deletion (c.911_913del) removing the serine of the FSF motif of ERF was identified in a 10-year-old girl with microcephaly, multiple congenital joint dislocations, generalized joint hypermobility, and Pierre-Robin sequence.

Three additional individuals with de novo non-truncating ERF alleles in the same FSF motif (two with c.911_913del and one with missense c.907T>A) presented with developmental delay variably associated with microcephaly, Pierre-Robin sequence, and minor skeletal anomalies.
Protein affinity mapping and co-immunoprecipitation experiments showed that both FSF-motif variants impair the interaction between ERF and activated ERK1/2.

The proband with the de novo ERF c.911_913del in-frame deletion presented with generalized joint hypermobility and multiple congenital joint dislocations in addition to microcephaly and Pierre-Robin sequence.

The authors propose a new pleiotropic condition, termed MIDES syndrome, characterized by microcephaly, developmental delay and skeletal anomalies, expanding the known phenotypic spectrum of ERF-related disorders.
In animal models, metformin administration reduced pain sensitivity, suggesting a potential analgesic effect relevant to fibromyalgia.
Metformin improved mood-related behaviors in animal models, suggesting a possible mood-stabilizing effect relevant to fibromyalgia comorbid mood disturbances.
Metformin decreased levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β in animal models, supporting an anti-inflammatory mechanism potentially relevant to fibromyalgia.
Metformin was proposed to influence serotonin, norepinephrine, and glutamate levels, offering a potential mechanism for analgesic and mood-stabilizing effects in fibromyalgia.
Metformin has been shown to mitigate neuroinflammation and protect neural tissue in preclinical studies, a mechanism proposed as relevant to fibromyalgia pathophysiology.
Geraniol produced the strongest time-dependent elevation of mechanical pain thresholds in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia mouse model.
Linalool elevated mechanical pain thresholds in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia mouse model, with a weaker effect than geraniol.
α-Humulene elevated mechanical pain thresholds in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia mouse model.
β-Caryophyllene produced antinociceptive elevation of mechanical thresholds in the reserpine-induced fibromyalgia mouse model, though weaker than geraniol, linalool, or α-humulene.
Geraniol produced the strongest antinociceptive elevation of mechanical pain thresholds in the paw incision (post-operative) pain mouse model.

Pretreatment with the A2aR antagonist istradefylline blocked the antinociceptive effects of the terpenes in both the post-operative and fibromyalgia pain models, indicating the terpenes act through the adenosine A2a receptor.
Terpene treatment had no effect on hot plate latencies, indicating the antinociceptive effects were not due to non-specific motor impairment.

In the paw incision model of post-operative pain, terpene treatment (200 mg/kg ip) time-dependently elevated mechanical withdrawal thresholds, indicating antinociceptive activity distinct from the fibromyalgia model.
Among the four terpenes tested, geraniol produced the strongest antinociceptive effect, followed by linalool and α-humulene.

The study builds on prior work showing these same terpenes relieve chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy via A2aR, and extends this A2aR-mediated mechanism to post-operative and fibromyalgia pain models.
Small RNA-seq of whole blood identified 69 differentially expressed miRs in FMS patients compared with healthy controls, with 62.3% upregulated and 37.7% downregulated.

22 differentially expressed tRFs were identified in whole blood of FMS patients versus healthy controls, all of which were upregulated and derived exclusively from nuclear tRNA genes, predominantly 3′-tRFs and internal tRFs.
In keratinocytes, 41 differentially expressed miRs were identified between FMS and healthy controls, with 90.2% downregulated and 9.8% upregulated.

55 nuclear-genome-derived tRFs were differentially expressed in keratinocytes, with 54.5% downregulated (predominantly long 5′-tRFs from glutamate tRNAs, median 30nt) and 45.5% upregulated (shorter 3′-tRFs and internal tRFs, median 19nt).

A combined panel of all differentially expressed blood miRs discriminated FMS from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.88, and let-7i-5p, hsa-miR-148a-3p, hsa-miR-182-5p, hsa-miR-664a-3p, and hsa-miR-192-5p were the top single diagnostic candidates.

Combined blood tRFs distinguished FMS from healthy controls with AUC 0.77, while the single best tRF candidate tRF-21-WB8647O5D achieved AUC 0.78, followed by tRF-19-WB0Q37IO, tRF-16-9N1EWJ0, tRF-19-JMRPFQIX and tRF-22-WE884U1D2.
Blood hsa-miR-532-3p levels negatively correlated with widespread pain index (WPI) severity in FMS patients.
Blood hsa-miR-379-5p levels positively correlated with widespread pain index in FMS patients.
Blood hsa-miR-6855-3p negatively correlated with intraepidermal nerve fiber (IENF) subgroup severity in FMS.
Keratinocyte hsa-mir-25-5p levels positively correlated with widespread pain index in FMS patients.
Keratinocyte hsa-mir-92b-3p levels positively correlated with widespread pain index in FMS patients.
In keratinocytes, tRF-40-86J8WPMN1E8Y7Z2R levels positively correlated with severity of intraepidermal nerve fiber loss (skin denervation) in FMS patients.
Keratinocyte tRF-30-JZOYJE22RRN3 levels positively correlated with severity of intraepidermal nerve fiber loss in FMS patients.
qRT-PCR confirmed upregulation of hsa-miR-576-5p in whole blood of FMS patients compared with healthy controls, with even higher levels in women with major depression and physical pain (dCO).
qRT-PCR confirmed upregulation of hsa-miR-182-5p in whole blood of FMS patients versus healthy controls, with further elevation in the depression (dCO) group.
qRT-PCR did not confirm intergroup differences of hsa-miR-1976 between FMS and healthy controls, although it was significantly upregulated in the depression (dCO) group relative to both FMS and hCO.
qRT-PCR showed higher levels of blood TRF-20-40KK5Y93 in FMS patients compared with healthy controls.
hsa-miR-503-5p was markedly downregulated in keratinocytes from FMS patients compared with healthy controls, validated by qRT-PCR.

Pathway analysis of blood DE miRs predicted significant targeting of the FoxO signaling pathway, which includes hsa-miR-182-5p and hsa-miR-576-5p and is relevant to immune cell regulation of inflammation, oxidative stress, proliferation and apoptosis.
Keratinocyte DE miR target prediction identified the AMPK signaling pathway, adherens junction and focal adhesion as disease-relevant KEGG pathways in FMS.
Pathway analysis of blood DE tRF-predicted targets identified 5 KEGG pathways and 139 GO:BP terms, prominently involving mRNA metabolism, splicing and translation processes.

Keratinocyte tRF target pathway analysis highlighted focal adhesion, cell growth, morphogenesis of an epithelium, and positive regulation of epithelial cell migration as significantly enriched pathways in FMS.

Among screened predicted mRNA targets, cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1A (CDKN1A) showed a mild upregulation in FMS compared with healthy and disease controls, while other targets showed no relevant alterations.
The most frequent motif among upregulated blood tRFs (TCGAAYCCCGGCSKV, present in 24.2% of upregulated tRFs) predicted gene targets involved in membrane trafficking and neutrophil degranulation.

In keratinocytes, the most frequent motif among downregulated tRFs (KKSTMGTGGTTVKADTCCSKG, present in 34.4% of downregulated tRFs) predicted target pathways including membrane trafficking, protein localization to plasma membrane, and activation of GTPase activity.

Women with major depression and physical pain (dCO) showed elevated whole blood hsa-miR-182-5p and hsa-miR-575-5p levels compared with both FMS patients and healthy controls, suggesting distinct pathophysiology between FMS and depression.

The authors note that a previous study found no correlations between cardinal FMS symptoms and peripheral blood mononuclear cell-derived miRs, contrasting with the correlations found in this study's whole blood and keratinocyte analyses.
Across the clino-orthostatic protocol, fibromyalgia patients showed a significantly lower mean stroke volume than healthy controls.
Upon standing, stroke volume dropped more deeply in fibromyalgia patients than in controls, indicating an exaggerated hemodynamic response to orthostatic challenge.
Non-linear adaptive smoothing showed a slightly higher frequency of SV oscillation in FM patients (~5 cycles/min) than controls (~3.3–3.5 cycles/min) during the clino-orthostatic challenge.
Overall mean heart rate across the protocol was significantly lower in FM patients compared with healthy controls.
During the standing steady state, FM patients exhibited a higher heart rate level than controls with a blunted initial overshoot, resembling a POTS-like pattern.
Fast heart-rate oscillations occurred at a lower frequency in FM patients (~15.4–15.8 cycles/min) than in controls (~18.1–18.3 cycles/min).
Mean cardiac output was significantly lower in FM patients than controls across the protocol, with a stronger orthostatic drop on standing.
CO oscillation frequency was about twice lower in FM patients (~3.3–3.7 cycles/min) than controls (~6.7–7.4 cycles/min).

During standing, the compensatory relationship between stroke volume and pre-ejection period (Frank-Starling adherence) was significantly weaker in FM patients than controls, indicating impaired cardiac contractile compensation for reduced preload.
During lying posture, the SV-PEP (Frank-Starling) relationship did not differ significantly between FM and control groups.
Upon standing, systemic vascular resistance rose more strongly and to a higher steady level in FM patients than in controls, indicating greater reliance on vasoconstriction.
SVR oscillation frequency was about 1.7 times lower in FM (~3.9–4.0 cycles/min) than controls (~6.8–7.2 cycles/min).

During standing, the CO/SVR ratio was lower in FM patients than controls, indicating a relative bias toward vascular-resistance-based (afterload) rather than cardiac-output-based blood pressure regulation.
During lying posture, the CO/SVR balance did not differ significantly between FM and control groups.
Mean systolic blood pressure was significantly lower in FM patients than in controls across the protocol.
DBP oscillation frequency was about 1.7 times lower in FM patients (~2.4 cycles/min) than controls (~3.9–4.1 cycles/min).

On standing, the rise in pre-ejection period (reflecting decreased cardiac contractility) was smaller in FM patients than in controls, indicating an insufficient negative inotropic compensation for reduced central blood volume.

The authors propose that heightened systemic vasoconstriction during standing in FM patients aligns with neuroinflammation-driven central sensitization, a proposed key mechanism of fibromyalgia pathophysiology.

Authors note the observed FM hemodynamic pattern of blunted initial HR overshoot and elevated steady-state HR with reduced CO resembles patterns reported in POTS, renin-dependent hypertension, chronic fatigue syndrome, and functional abdominal pain.
BMI, which differed significantly between groups, was identified as a probable mediating covariate that reduced the observed group differences in SBP and DBP curves after adjustment.

Based on the observed hypovolemic/afterload-dependent BP regulation pattern in FM, the authors recommend avoiding diuretic-type antihypertensives (thiazide diuretics, mineralocorticoid receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, α1-blockers) in comorbid pain-hypertension patients, as these may worsen central hypovolemia and pain control.

Authors caution that vasodilatory antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct renin inhibitors, β-blockers, centrally acting α-agonists) might disrupt the vasoconstriction-based 'adaptation to pain' mechanism, potentially worsening pain unless combined with strategies to restore cardiac preload.

The authors suggest enhanced salt and water intake as a simple procedure to increase effective blood volume in individuals prone to blood volume contraction and afterload-dependent BP regulation, such as FM patients.

The study infers that most FM patients showed evidence of total body hypovolemia, causing them to miss the short-lived compensatory vasodilation/cardiac contractility mechanism seen in healthy controls upon standing.
Mast cells show relatively selective expression of the glutamate receptor ionotropic kainate 2 (GluK2) compared to other cell types.
The GluK2-specific agonist SYM2081 inhibited mast cell degranulation induced by MrgprB2 agonism in murine mast cells and human skin explants in vitro.
SYM2081 inhibited mast cell degranulation in vivo in mice following both intradermal and topical administration.
GluK2 agonism with SYM2081 suppressed expression of Mrgprb2 in mast cells based on transcriptomic analysis.
Transcriptomic and interpretable machine learning analyses revealed that GluK2 agonism coordinately downregulates a cellular program of genes associated with mast cell proliferation.
SYM2081 exposure reduced Ki-67 expression in mast cells, confirming suppression of mast cell proliferation both in vitro and in vivo.
SYM2081 exposure reduced BrdU incorporation in mast cells, confirming suppression of mast cell proliferation both in vitro and in vivo.

Differential expression and interpretable machine learning analysis of transcriptomic data from SYM2081-treated mast cells uncovered a previously unrecognized cellular program coordinately regulated by GluK2 agonism.
GluK2 agonism by SYM2081 suppressed the expression of Mrgprb2 in mast cells.
GluK2 agonism suppressed expression of genes associated with mast cell proliferation.
SYM2081 exposure reduced mast cell proliferation as evidenced by decreased Ki-67 expression both in vitro and in vivo.
SYM2081 exposure reduced mast cell proliferation as evidenced by decreased BrdU incorporation both in vitro and in vivo.
Pretreatment with SYM2081 reduced skin inflammation in a murine model of dermatitis.
Pretreatment with SYM2081 reduced skin inflammation in a murine model of rosacea.

Intratracheal DEP instillation in mice increased IL-33 expression within tryptase-positive mast cells and increased the number of IL-33+tryptase+ mast cells infiltrating the airway epithelium and sub-epithelial areas compared to vehicle-treated controls.
DEP stimulation of HMC-1 human mast cells induced IL-33 mRNA expression in a concentration-dependent manner.
DEP increased IL-33 protein expression in HMC-1 cells in a concentration-dependent manner as measured by immunoblotting.
DEP stimulation induced concentration-dependent release of IL-33 into the culture medium of HMC-1 cells as measured by ELISA.
DEP stimulation triggered nuclear translocation of AhR in HMC-1 cells, with cytosolic accumulation at 10 minutes and peak nuclear presence at 30 minutes.
siRNA knockdown of AhR or ARNT almost completely inhibited DEP-induced IL-33 mRNA and protein expression in HMC-1 cells, demonstrating AhR dependence of the response.
ChIP assay showed DEP increased binding of AhR and ARNT to the IL-33 gene promoter in HMC-1 cells, indicating direct transcriptional regulation.
DEP treatment induced time-dependent nuclear translocation of the NF-κB subunit p65 in HMC-1 cells.
DEP induced degradation of IκBα protein in HMC-1 cells, consistent with NF-κB pathway activation.
Pretreatment with the NF-κB inhibitor PDTC significantly inhibited DEP-induced IL-33 mRNA expression in HMC-1 cells.
Co-immunoprecipitation showed that DEP induced a physical interaction between AhR and NF-κB p65 in the nucleus of HMC-1 cells.
Inhibition of NF-κB with PDTC decreased DEP-induced AhR nuclear translocation, indicating NF-κB facilitates AhR nuclear entry.
DEP enhanced transmembrane migratory ability of HMC-1 mast cells, an effect blocked by AhR inhibitor CH223191 or anti-ST2 antibody, implicating the IL-33/ST2 axis in DEP-induced mast cell migration.
DEP induced HMC-1 mast cells to release the type-2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 in a concentration-dependent manner.
Anti-ST2 neutralizing antibody abolished DEP-induced release of type-2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 in HMC-1 cells, confirming the IL-33/ST2 axis mediates this response.
Mast cell infiltration, estimated by immune deconvolution, was significantly higher in expanded mouse skin than in control skin.
Mast cell infiltration score was positively correlated with Itgb5 expression in the integrated expanded-skin dataset.
Mast cell infiltration score was positively correlated with Igfbp2 expression in the integrated expanded-skin dataset.
M0 macrophage infiltration score was positively correlated with Tpm1 expression, while mast cell and regulatory T cell (Treg) scores were negatively correlated with Tpm1.
M2 macrophage infiltration score was positively correlated with Igf2 expression in the integrated dataset.
Immune cell infiltration correlation analysis showed mast cells were positively correlated with Tregs, while Tregs and mast cells were each negatively correlated with M0 macrophages.

Intersection of DEGs with EMT-related gene sets yielded 46 EMT-related DEGs (EMTRDEGs) between expanded and control skin, of which 28 were upregulated and 18 downregulated in the expanded group, enriched for ECM organization and elastic fiber formation pathways.
In the protein-protein interaction network of 23 hub genes, Notch1, Ncstn, Ctnnb1, and Psen1 showed the highest network connectivity, while Igfbp3, Sfrp1, Tnnt2, and Tpm1 showed the lowest.
A random forest diagnostic model based on five EMT-related genes (Itgb5, Tpm1, Sfrp1, Notch1, Igfbp2) predicted expanded versus control skin with perfect accuracy (AUC = 1).
The Wnt-β-catenin signaling pathway was significantly upregulated in stem cells from expanded skin compared with controls by single-cell GSVA.
TNF-α signaling via NF-κB was significantly upregulated in endothelial cells from expanded skin, while oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis were downregulated.
Single-cell analysis showed Igfbp2, one of the five diagnostic marker genes, was specifically expressed in fibroblasts among the skin cell populations.
Neutrophils were more abundant in the expanded skin group by single-cell analysis, whereas stem cells were more abundant in the control group.
The proportion of epidermal (epithelial) stem cells was significantly higher in expanded skin than in control skin.

KEGG pathway enrichment of the 23 hub genes showed enrichment in Notch, PI3K-AKT, and thyroid hormone signaling pathways, and GO enrichment highlighted insulin-like growth factor receptor signaling, consistent with roles in cell proliferation and ECM remodeling.
Mast cell density (MCD) was numerically highest in poorly differentiated OSCC followed by well- and moderately-differentiated OSCC, but the inter-group difference was not statistically significant.

Microvessel density (MVD), assessed by Masson's trichrome staining, decreased significantly with increasing OSCC tumour grade, being highest in well-differentiated and lowest in poorly-differentiated tumours.
Post-hoc pairwise comparison showed a significant reduction in MVD between moderately- and poorly-differentiated OSCC, while WDOSCC vs MDOSCC and WDOSCC vs PDOSCC differences were not significant.
Vascularity in poorly-differentiated OSCC and in normal buccal mucosa was significantly lower than in pyogenic granuloma (the positive control for angiogenesis).
Spearman correlation analysis found no significant correlation between mast cell density and microvessel density in OSCC tissue.
Mast cell density in the neurofibroma positive control was higher than in poorly-differentiated OSCC and in normal buccal mucosa negative control.

The authors interpreted their non-significant MCD findings as suggesting mast cells may not play a major role in OSCC tumour biology, or may be suppressed or show reduced infiltration with malignant onset, consistent with a possible tumour-suppressive role reported in other studies.

DRAM1 was identified via intersected DEG analysis and machine learning as a diagnostic biomarker upregulated in S. aureus bloodstream infection compared to controls in human and mouse GEO datasets and validated by RT-qPCR in a mouse infection model.
PSTPIP2 was identified as a diagnostic biomarker upregulated in S. aureus bloodstream infection across human and mouse datasets and confirmed by RT-qPCR in a mouse model.
UPP1 was identified as a diagnostic biomarker upregulated in S. aureus bloodstream infection across human and mouse datasets and confirmed by RT-qPCR in a mouse model.

DRAM1 expression was positively correlated with naive B cells and activated mast cells, and negatively correlated with NK cells and CD4/CD8+ T cells, based on CIBERSORT immune cell deconvolution in S. aureus bloodstream infection.

PSTPIP2 expression was positively correlated with M0 and M1 macrophages, naive B cells, and activated dendritic cells, and negatively correlated with NK cells and CD4/CD8+ T cells in S. aureus bloodstream infection.
UPP1 expression was negatively correlated with resting memory CD4 T cells and neutrophils in S. aureus bloodstream infection.

GO/KEGG functional enrichment of DEGs showed upregulated genes related to cytokine production and immune response activation and pathways including NOD-like receptor signaling, while downregulated genes were enriched for mononuclear/lymphocyte differentiation and Th1, Th2, and Th17 cell differentiation pathways.

In an independent validation dataset (GSE65088), DRAM1, PSTPIP2, and UPP1 were again significantly highly expressed in the S. aureus infection group with high AUC values, supporting their predictive accuracy.

In a mouse model of S. aureus (Newman strain) bloodstream infection, RNA-Seq and RT-qPCR confirmed significantly increased expression of DRAM1, PSTPIP2, and UPP1 in infected mice compared to controls, and this was replicated in a combined mouse dataset merging GSE33341-mouse data with the new infection model sequencing data.

The histamine-induced axon-reflex flare response showed good diagnostic accuracy for small fiber neuropathy relative to cold detection threshold on quantitative sensory testing, with an AUC of 0.82, sensitivity 67%, and specificity 70%.

The heat-induced axon-reflex flare response showed poor diagnostic accuracy for small fiber neuropathy relative to cold detection threshold on quantitative sensory testing, with an AUC of only 0.40, sensitivity 36%, and specificity 57%.
No significant correlation was found between the histamine-induced and heat-induced axon-reflex flare responses within the same participants.
Genetically predicted hypothyroidism was causally associated with an increased risk of diabetic polyneuropathy.
Genetically predicted hypothyroidism was causally associated with an increased risk of nerve root/plexus disorder.
Genetically predicted hypothyroidism was causally associated with an increased risk of carpal tunnel syndrome.
Genetically predicted hypothyroidism was causally associated with a decreased risk of polyneuropathies, suggesting a protective effect.
No causal relationship was found between genetically predicted hypothyroidism and small fibre neuropathy.
Genetically predicted autoimmune thyroid disease was a risk factor for diabetic polyneuropathy, with an extremely wide and unstable effect estimate.
Genetically predicted autoimmune thyroid disease was a risk factor for carpal tunnel syndrome.
Genetically predicted autoimmune thyroid disease appeared protective against polyneuropathies.
No causal relationship was found between genetically predicted autoimmune thyroid disease and nerve root/plexus disorder.
No causal relationship was found between benign pituitary gland/craniopharyngeal duct neoplasm and diabetic polyneuropathy.
No causal relationship was found between benign pituitary gland/craniopharyngeal duct neoplasm and carpal tunnel syndrome.
No causal relationship was found between benign pituitary gland/craniopharyngeal duct neoplasm and nerve root/plexus disorder.
No causal relationship was found between benign pituitary gland/craniopharyngeal duct neoplasm and polyneuropathies.
In an independent UK Biobank validation cohort, hypothyroidism showed a non-significant but directionally consistent positive association with nerve root/plexus disorder.
In an independent UK Biobank validation cohort, hypothyroidism showed a non-significant but directionally consistent positive association with carpal tunnel syndrome/surgery.
HAE type I is caused by SERPING1 mutations resulting in low antigenic and functional levels of C1 inhibitor protein, accounting for 85% of HAE-C1INH cases.
HAE type II results from SERPING1-related C1INH dysfunction with normal antigenic but low functional C1INH levels.
HAE with normal C1 inhibitor (HAE-nC1INH) is caused by mutations in genes other than SERPING1, including FXII, ANGPT1, PLG, KNG1, MYOF, or HS3ST6.
A newly described missense variant p.D239N in the DAB2IP C2-domain has been linked to HAE with normal C1 inhibitor.
Three CPN1 gene variants (c.533G>A, c.582A>G, c.734C>T) encoding the catalytic 55-kDa subunit of carboxypeptidase N have been associated with HAE with normal C1 inhibitor.
HAE-C1INH is autosomal dominant with 50% offspring inheritance risk, while 25% of patients carry de novo SERPING1 mutations.
In a French registry-based study of 101 pediatric HAE-C1INH/factor XII-mutated patients, 71% were classified HAE-I, 16% HAE-II, and 13% factor XII mutated.

Earlier age of first symptom onset is associated with a more severe disease course, with severe episodes occurring in 38.7% of children with first symptoms before age 5 versus 25% of those with later onset.

Symptomatic HAE-C1INH children (n=34) showed impaired quality of life compared to 64 healthy controls across total, school, and psychosocial PedsQL domains, worsening with more frequent and multisite attacks.
HAE-C1INH children (n=33) showed significantly higher state and trait anxiety scores on the STAI compared to 52 healthy controls (n=52), with anxiety inversely correlated with quality of life.
Children with HAE-C1INH suffer from alexithymia more frequently at a critical level than children with other chronic diseases, with alexithymia levels correlating with disease severity and stress.

Hereditary alpha tryptasemia, defined by increased TPSAB1 gene copy number, is a common autosomal dominant trait that can increase the frequency and severity of immediate hypersensitivity reactions, though most carriers are asymptomatic.
Combined measurement of serum/plasma C1INH function, C1INH protein, and complement C4 provides high diagnostic accuracy for HAE-C1INH, with C4 typically low even between attacks.
In the pediatric SPRING study, lanadelumab reduced the HAE attack rate by 94.8% from baseline (1.84 to 0.08 per month) in children aged 2-12 years over 52 weeks, with 76.2% remaining attack-free.
In the phase 3 HELP study, lanadelumab 300 mg every 2 weeks reduced mean monthly HAE attacks to 0.26 from a baseline of 1.97 (87% reduction), with 44% of patients attack-free, versus placebo.
In the phase 3 APeX-2 study, berotralstat 150 mg/day significantly reduced the monthly HAE attack rate to 1.31 versus 2.35 with placebo over 24 weeks.
In the phase 2 APEX-S adolescent safety study, berotralstat 150 mg/day over 48 weeks resulted in more than 70% of patients remaining attack-free with good tolerability.
In the OASIS-HAE study, donidalorsen (targeting prekallikrein) reduced mean HAE attack rate by 81% (4-week dosing) and 55% (8-week dosing) compared to placebo.

In the phase III VANGUARD study, garadacimab (a factor XII-inhibiting monoclonal antibody) reduced mean monthly HAE attacks to 0.27 versus 2.01 with placebo, a 91% reduction from baseline, without increased bleeding or thromboembolic risk.

In the phase 3 KONFIDENT crossover study, sebetralstat (oral kallikrein inhibitor) provided faster symptom relief, more frequent complete resolution, and decreased attack severity compared to placebo in adults and adolescents with HAE.

Non-specific mast cell activation causing angioedema typically shows normal tryptase levels, distinguishing it from mast cell activation syndrome, though pediatric diagnostic criteria for MCAS are not established.

Basophil-specific protease mRNAs (Mcpt8 and Prss34/Mcpt11) were expressed at higher levels in early-stage (3-week) bone marrow-derived cultures, when basophil-like cells are present, than in late-stage (7-week) cultures dominated by mast cell-like cells.
Basophil-like FcεRI+/c-kit- cells sorted from bone marrow cultures expressed significantly higher levels of Cebpa, Mcpt8, and Prss34 mRNA compared with mast cell-like FcεRI+/c-kit+ cells.

Mitf and Mcpt1 mRNA levels tended to be higher in mast cell-like cells than basophil-like cells but this was not statistically significant, and Cma1 (Mcpt5) mRNA levels did not differ between the two cell types.

Knockdown of Cebpa (reducing mRNA to ~30% of control) significantly decreased Mcpt8 and Prss34 mRNA levels while increasing Mitf mRNA, indicating C/EBPα positively regulates basophil-specific protease genes and suppresses Mitf.
Overexpression of C/EBPα in bone marrow cells significantly increased Mcpt8 mRNA and slightly increased Prss34 mRNA.
Treatment of early-stage bone marrow cells with the HDAC inhibitor trichostatin A (TSA) significantly decreased Cebpa, Mcpt8, and Prss34 mRNA levels, and decreased C/EBPα protein levels.
Treatment of late-stage bone marrow cells with the DNA methyltransferase inhibitor 5-aza-2-deoxycytidine increased Mcpt8 and Prss34 mRNA levels.

The degree of DNA methylation of the Prss34 promoter was significantly higher in mast cell-like cells than in basophil-like cells, suggesting promoter hypermethylation suppresses Prss34 expression in mast cells.
TSA treatment significantly enhanced Gata1 transcription and slightly increased Mitf mRNA, while repressing Spi1 mRNA.
Knockdown of Gata1 did not affect mRNA levels of Cebpa, Mcpt8, or Prss34, indicating GATA1 is not required for basophil-specific protease gene expression in this system.
Knockdown of Mitf caused a significant increase in Cebpa mRNA levels accompanied by a slight increase in Prss34 mRNA, suggesting MITF antagonizes C/EBPα-driven basophil gene expression.

Knockdown of Gata2 significantly reduced Mcpt8 and Prss34 mRNA levels without affecting Cebpa mRNA, and also reduced Mitf, Spi1, and Runx1 mRNA, indicating GATA2 positively and independently regulates basophil protease genes and other MC/basophil transcription factors.
Knockdown of Spi1 (PU.1) enhanced transcription of the Mcpt8 gene, and did not affect Runx1 KD's lack of effect on basophil protease genes.
Knockdown of Runx1 (targeting P1-Runx1) did not affect mRNA levels of Cebpa, Mcpt8, or Prss34, contrasting with a prior report that P1-Runx1 deficiency reduces basophil numbers in vivo.

Knockdown of Cebpa increased mRNA levels of Mitf, Gata1, and Gata2, while overexpression of Cebpa decreased Gata1 mRNA and slightly reduced Mitf mRNA, indicating reciprocal negative regulation between C/EBPα and mast cell-related transcription factors.

Treatment of bone marrow cells with recombinant TGF-β significantly increased Mcpt8 mRNA and slightly increased Prss34 mRNA, without significantly changing Cebpa or Gata2 mRNA levels, suggesting TGF-β signaling regulates basophil-specific protease genes independently of C/EBPα and GATA2.
TGF-β1 stimulation increased collagen deposition by pancreatic stellate cells in vitro.
Vitamin C stimulation increased collagen deposition by pancreatic stellate cells in vitro.
siRNA knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of ORAI1 with Synta-66 reduced collagen secretion in pancreatic stellate cells but had no effect in NIH-3T3 fibroblasts.
Physiological levels of vitamin C induced a drastic increase in intracellular calcium concentration in pancreatic stellate cells.
The ORAI1 inhibitor Synta-66 blocked the vitamin C-induced calcium influx in pancreatic stellate cells.
Orai1 protein was detected by immunohistochemistry in cancer-associated fibroblasts within fibrotic tumor tissue of a murine KPfC pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma model.

The authors developed and validated a high-throughput in vitro fibrosis assay using the collagen-binding peptide CNA-35-tdTomato as an optimized alternative to Sirius Red staining for quantifying collagen deposition.

In age- and sex-adjusted models, higher fasting insulin was positively associated with all functional somatic disorder delimitations.
In age- and sex-adjusted models, higher HbA1c was positively associated with all functional somatic disorder delimitations except irritable bowel.
No significant association was found between irritable bowel and HbA1c, unlike other FSD delimitations.
