Serum aspartic acid concentrations differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy women in both premenopausal and postmenopausal groups.
Serum glutamic acid concentrations differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy women in both premenopausal and postmenopausal groups.
Serum histidine concentrations differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy women in both premenopausal and postmenopausal groups.
Serum glycine concentrations differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy women in both premenopausal and postmenopausal groups.

The combination of menopause and fibromyalgia was associated with greater disruption of amino acid homeostasis than either menopause or fibromyalgia alone, suggesting increased risk of metabolic disorders.
TGF-β2 immunofluorescence intensity was significantly increased in the retina of Col4a3 knockout mice compared with wild-type mice.
TGF-β1 immunofluorescence showed a nonsignificant increase in the lens of Col4a3 knockout mice.
Immunopositive cells for CTGF were significantly increased in the cornea of Col4a3 knockout mice, with no apparent change in retina or lens.
Immunopositive cells for β-catenin were significantly increased in the cornea of Col4a3 knockout mice, with no apparent change in retina or lens.
No significant change in CTGF or β-catenin immunopositivity was observed in the retina or anterior lens of Col4a3 knockout mice.
Acta2 (αSMA) mRNA was significantly upregulated in the retina of Col4a3 knockout mice, showing a 6.8-fold increase relative to Tbp.
Col1a1 mRNA was significantly upregulated in the retina of Col4a3 knockout mice (1.8-fold increase).
Snai2 (Slug) mRNA was significantly upregulated in the retina of Col4a3 knockout mice (2.1-fold increase).
S100a4 (FSP-1) mRNA showed a nonsignificant 18.4-fold increase in the retina of Col4a3 knockout mice.
Snai1 (Snail) mRNA showed a nonsignificant 1.9-fold increase in the retina of Col4a3 knockout mice.
Twist1 mRNA showed a nonsignificant 3.6-fold increase in the retina of Col4a3 knockout mice.
Snai2 (Slug) mRNA was significantly upregulated in the cornea (anterior segment) of Col4a3 knockout mice (2.2-fold increase).
S100a4 mRNA showed a nonsignificant 2.8-fold increase in the anterior segment (cornea) of Col4a3 knockout mice.
Picrosirius red staining showed significantly increased collagen deposition in the corneal epithelium of Col4a3 knockout mice, but not in the retina, anterior lens, or other corneal substructures.
H&E staining revealed no evident histological differences, including lenticonus or cataracts, between wild-type and Col4a3 knockout mouse eyes at 25 weeks of age.
Collagen (IV) α3 protein, present in Bruch's membrane and the corneal endothelium (Descemet's membrane) of wild-type mice, was completely absent in Col4a3 knockout mouse eyes.

Collagen (IV) α4 protein, which colocalizes exclusively with α3 as part of the collagen (IV) α3α4α5 heterotrimer, was completely absent in Col4a3 knockout mouse eyes despite the Col4a4 gene itself not being knocked out.
The MFS mouse model used carries a heterozygous Fbn1 C1041G mutation, replicating the aortic root aneurysm phenotype associated with the most common human MFS mutation.
Aortic root diameters were significantly increased in both male and female MFS mice compared to age-matched wildtype controls, with no sex difference.
Genetic deletion of Cav1 did not alter aortic root growth or aneurysm formation in either male or female MFS mice.
ACh-induced initial vasorelaxation was significantly higher in Cav1KO and MFS/Cav1KO aorta than in CTRL and MFS aorta, indicating higher agonist-stimulated NO production when Cav1 is absent.
Maximal ACh-induced vasorelaxation (Emax) was significantly decreased in male MFS aorta compared to male CTRL, but not different between female MFS and female CTRL.
Emax values for ACh responses were significantly higher in female MFS mice than in age-matched male MFS mice.
Cav1 deletion significantly increased Emax values for ACh-induced vasorelaxation in both male and female MFS/Cav1KO mice compared to sex-matched MFS mice.
EC50 values for ACh responses were higher (reduced sensitivity) in male MFS aorta compared to male CTRL, with no difference between female CTRL and MFS.
Cav1 deletion enhanced ACh sensitivity (lower EC50) in male MFS/Cav1KO aorta but had no effect in female MFS/Cav1KO aorta.
In healthy mice, Cav1 deletion increased aortic relaxation in females but not males, showing a sex-dependent baseline effect of Cav1 loss.
High K+-induced aortic contraction was not different between male CTRL and MFS mice, but was significantly lower in female MFS versus female CTRL mice, a sex-dependent effect.
Cav1 gene deletion significantly reduced KCl-induced aortic contraction in both male and female MFS/Cav1KO mice, suggesting Cav1 regulates calcium entry in smooth muscle independent of sex.
Maximum PE-induced contractile force was significantly reduced in both male and female MFS aorta compared to sex-matched CTRL, with female MFS aorta showing lower contraction than male MFS aorta.
Cav1 ablation further reduced PE-induced contraction in male MFS/Cav1KO mice compared to male MFS mice, but had no effect in female MFS/Cav1KO aorta.
Pre-treatment with the NOS inhibitor L-NAME significantly increased PE-induced vasoconstriction in both male and female CTRL and MFS aorta, consistent with inhibition of endogenous NO.
L-NAME enhanced contractile responses to PE more strongly in MFS/Cav1KO aorta than in MFS aorta, in both sexes, indicating higher basal NO levels when Cav1 is absent, with a larger effect in females.

Pre-treatment with the specific iNOS inhibitor 1400W did not impact the Cav1KO-mediated decrease in aortic contraction in either male or female MFS/Cav1KO rings, indicating iNOS is not the source of the Cav1-deletion effect.
Pre-treatment of MFS aortic rings with the iNOS inhibitor 1400W increased PE-induced contraction, consistent with prior reports of elevated iNOS activity in MFS aortic tissue.
Aortic wall strength, measured by rupture point, was significantly decreased in both male and female MFS mice compared to sex-matched CTRL mice.

Cav1 deletion improved maximum aortic wall strength only in male MFS/Cav1KO mice, not in females, and similarly only in male CTRL/Cav1KO mice, indicating a sex-dependent effect of Cav1 loss on wall integrity.
Male MFS mice showed increased elastin fragmentation and decreased elastin fiber length in the aortic wall compared to male CTRL mice.
Cav1 deletion significantly improved aortic elastin structure in male MFS/Cav1KO mice, reducing elastin fragment count and increasing elastin fiber length.

Electron microscopy showed fewer open caveolae invaginations on endothelial cell membranes in MFS aorta compared to CTRL, and Cav1 knockout (CTRL/Cav1KO and MFS/Cav1KO) further reduced or abolished visible caveolae structures.
Loperamide reduced food intake 24 hours post-treatment by 38% in males and 44% in females compared to pretreatment baseline.
Loperamide reduced faecal output by 31% in males and 38% in females compared to pretreatment baseline, indicating slowed GI transit.
Loperamide-treated female rats showed 30% less total distance moved and 30% slower velocity in the open field test compared to controls, with no significant effect in males.
Loperamide reduced rearing frequency (exploratory behaviour) in female rats in the open field test, with no effect in males and no change in zone time preference for either sex.
In the elevated plus maze, loperamide-treated female rats spent 24% less time in the open arms compared to controls, indicating increased anxiety, with no effect observed in males.

Nine genes in the hippocampus were significantly decreased in expression in loperamide-treated female rats compared to controls, with no individual transcript-level differences detected in amygdala or prefrontal cortex, or in any brain region in males.

Gene set enrichment analysis identified 33 differentially expressed Reactome pathways in the hippocampus of loperamide-treated females, with immune-signalling pathways (TAK1, NOD1/2, CD28) upregulated and GABA synthesis/release/reuptake/degradation pathways downregulated.

In the prefrontal cortex of loperamide-treated females, seven Reactome pathways were differentially expressed, mostly upregulated, except MAP kinase activation and interleukin 17 signalling which were downregulated.
In the amygdala of loperamide-treated female rats, pathways related to ERK and NOD1/2 signalling showed increased expression compared to controls.

More than 200 genes in the proximal colon were differentially expressed between control and loperamide groups, with 145 genes altered in males versus 60 in females, showing sex-specific gut transcriptomic responses.
Caecal microbiota composition differed significantly between control and loperamide-treated rats in both sexes, with no significant sex difference or sex-by-treatment interaction.

At the family level, ten taxa differed significantly with loperamide treatment; most Firmicutes families (Lactobacillaceae excepted) were less abundant, while four Bacteroidetes families (Bacteroidaceae, Barnesiellaceae, Muribaculaceae, Tannerellaceae) were more abundant in loperamide-treated rats.
Loperamide increased the relative abundance of Bacteroides by 75% in males and 32% in females compared to controls.
Loperamide increased the relative abundance of Lactobacillus by 171% in males and 100% in females compared to controls.

Loperamide produced sex-specific functional shifts in the caecal microbiome, decreasing two-component quorum-sensing system genes in males and increasing xenobiotic and glutathione metabolism genes in females.

Loperamide administration reduced corticotropin releasing hormone receptor 2 (CRHR2) gene expression in the hippocampus of female rats compared to controls, potentially contributing to anxiogenic effects.

Integrated dataset analysis showed that time spent in the EPM closed arms (a marker of higher anxiety) positively correlated with expression of three hippocampal mitochondrial energy metabolism genes (Mt-cyb, Mt-atp6, Mt-co1).
EPM closed arm duration (anxiety) correlated with expression of three proximal colon genes involved in gut barrier and inflammation: Spink4, Muc2, and Reg4.

EPM closed arm duration (anxiety) positively correlated with abundance of Bifidobacterium, Barnesiella, and unclassified Odoribacteraceae, and negatively correlated with unclassified Paenibacillaceae and the KEGG hpnR (hopanoid C-3 methylase) pathway; these taxa were also positively correlated with hippocampal mitochondrial genes.

The behavioural and hippocampal gene expression effects of peripheral opioid receptor activation via loperamide were female-specific, whereas the loperamide-induced shift in caecal microbiome composition was not sex-specific and occurred rapidly within 48 hours of dosing.
taVNS significantly reduced abdominal pain (VAS score) compared with sham-taVNS after 4 weeks, with an 85% responder rate vs 10% in the sham group.
taVNS significantly reduced overall IBS symptom severity (IBS-SSS total and subscores) compared with sham at week 4.
taVNS significantly improved quality of life (IBS-QOL score) compared with sham-taVNS at week 4.
taVNS improved stool consistency (BSFS) and bowel movement frequency (SBM and CSBM) compared with sham-taVNS.
taVNS increased vagal (parasympathetic) activity and decreased sympathetic activity as measured by heart rate variability, compared with sham.
taVNS significantly reduced anxiety (HAMA) and depression (HAMD) scores compared with sham-taVNS at week 4.
taVNS improved rectal sensation, lowering the threshold volume for the rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR) and raising thresholds for first sensation and desire to defecate compared with sham.
Serum acetylcholine levels were significantly increased after taVNS treatment compared with baseline and with sham-taVNS.
Serum nitric oxide levels were significantly decreased after taVNS treatment compared with baseline and with sham-taVNS.
taVNS altered gut microbial composition, with significant changes in the phyla Campylobacterota and Patescibacteria before and after treatment, without changes in overall alpha or beta diversity.
The genus Bifidobacterium was significantly increased in the gut microbiota of IBS-C patients after taVNS treatment.
Fecal levels of acetic acid, butyric acid, and propionic acid were significantly higher after taVNS treatment compared with baseline in IBS-C patients.
Fecal levels of 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, anthranilic acid, and L-tryptophan were significantly decreased after taVNS treatment compared with baseline in IBS-C patients.

Abdominal pain (VAS) score correlated positively with abundances of Bifidobacterium, Paramuribaculum, and Mucispirillum, and with levels of 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, acetic acid, propionic acid, and butyric acid in taVNS-treated IBS-C patients.

taVNS was well tolerated with no significant difference in adverse events (ear skin rash, dizziness, palpitation, intolerable diarrhea) compared with sham-taVNS, and no abnormal laboratory findings were observed.
NRG1 expression was decreased in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus of Zucker diabetic fatty rats, coinciding with weakened gastric motility.
ChAT expression was reduced in the DMV of ZDF diabetic rats alongside decreased NRG1 and weakened gastric motility.
AAV-mediated NRG1 overexpression microinjected into the DMV enhanced gastric motility and increased vagal nerve discharge frequency in diabetic rats.
AAV-NRG1 upregulated acetylcholine and α7nAChR expression in the gastric body, which mitigated gastric inflammation.

The beneficial effects of AAV-NRG1 on gastric motility and inflammation were partially reversed by vagotomy or pharmacologic antagonism of α7nAChR, indicating dependence on the vagus nerve and α7nAChR signaling.
Among 1,511 survey respondents, 8.87% attributed tinnitus onset to COVID infection, 9% to long COVID, 37.19% to COVID vaccination, and 44.94% had pre-existing tinnitus unrelated to COVID.
Median age differed significantly across the four groups, with the pre-existing tinnitus group being significantly older than each of the three COVID-associated tinnitus groups.
The pre-existing tinnitus group had the highest proportion of male respondents and hearing loss but the lowest rates of depression and anxiety among the four groups.
The long COVID group had the highest rates of hyperacusis, depression, and anxiety among all four groups.
Individuals reporting tinnitus associated with COVID infection had significantly decreased odds of also reporting hyperacusis, after adjusting for age and gender.
Individuals reporting tinnitus associated with COVID vaccination had significantly increased odds of also reporting anxiety, after adjusting for age and gender.

Individuals reporting tinnitus associated with COVID vaccination had significantly decreased odds of also reporting hearing loss, contrasting with prior clinic-based studies linking vaccination-related SSNHL with tinnitus.
Reporting tinnitus associated with long COVID did not significantly change the odds of reporting hearing loss, hyperacusis, depression, or anxiety.

Among 679 respondents with pre-existing tinnitus, 43.3% reported a change (mostly worsening) in tinnitus attributed to COVID infection, long COVID, or vaccination, but no examined factor significantly predicted these changes.

Tinnitus severity (TFI score) was significantly higher in all three COVID-associated tinnitus groups compared with the pre-existing tinnitus group, with the long COVID group showing the highest median score.
In the COVID infection group, gender, hearing loss, and anxiety significantly predicted tinnitus severity (TFI score) in a multiple regression model explaining 27.1% of variance.
In the long COVID group, only hyperacusis and depression significantly predicted tinnitus severity (TFI score) in a regression model explaining 27.9% of variance.

In the COVID vaccination group, age, hearing loss, hyperacusis, depression, and anxiety were all significant predictors of tinnitus severity (TFI score), with the regression model explaining 26.1% of variance.

In the pre-existing tinnitus group, age, gender, hearing loss, hyperacusis, depression, and anxiety were all significant predictors of tinnitus severity (TFI score), with the regression model explaining 25.6% of variance.
The authors identified ten symptoms most specifically associated with COVID-19 that met both statistical and clinical significance thresholds, used to define post-COVID condition (PCC).

PCC was classified into four subtypes: ENT (smell/taste/hearing), cardiopulmonary (dyspnea, postural tachycardia, chest tightness/pressure), neurological (brain fog, difficulty communicating), and mild fatigue.
Postural tachycardia was identified as one of the ten symptoms most specifically associated with COVID-19, contributing to the definition of the cardiopulmonary PCC subtype.
Infection with the original Wildtype SARS-CoV-2 variant carried the highest risk of any PCC, with risk decreasing progressively through Alpha, Delta to Omicron.
Participants with multiple COVID-19 infections had a higher risk of any PCC compared to those with a single infection.
Severe acute COVID-19 requiring hospitalization was associated with markedly increased risk of PCC, especially the cardiopulmonary subtype.
Full vaccination and booster doses against COVID-19 were associated with significantly lower risk of developing PCC across all subtypes compared to no or partial vaccination.

Age had heterogeneous, non-linear effects on PCC risk: those 55-75 years had lower risk than 45-55 reference, those over 75 had increased risk, while younger participants had higher risk of neurological and fatigue subtypes.
Female sex was associated with increased overall PCC risk and increased risk of cardiopulmonary, neurological, and mild fatigue subtypes, but lower risk of the ENT subtype.
Overall PCC risk increased with greater socioeconomic deprivation.
Risk of PCC and all subtypes increased monotonically with increasing BMI, with the strongest effect on the cardiopulmonary subtype.
Adherence to a healthy lifestyle was consistently associated with lower risk of PCC overall and across subtypes.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) was one of the most significant comorbidities related to PCC risk, with the strongest effect specifically on the cardiopulmonary subtype.
Pre-existing depression was strongly associated with increased risk of PCC, particularly the neurological subtype.
Chronic kidney disease was the only comorbidity not significantly associated with the neurological PCC subtype, in contrast to all other studied comorbidities.
The neurological PCC subtype had the strongest adverse impact on physical function among all subtypes, particularly on ability to concentrate.
Cardiopulmonary PCC subtype had the second-strongest impact on physical function, notably day-to-day work capacity.

A higher number of coexisting PCC subtypes was associated with progressively worse physical and mental health impacts, with those having all four subtypes showing the largest odds of functional impairment.
Gastrointestinal and musculoskeletal symptoms, commonly reported in EHR-based studies, were not significantly associated with PCC in this self-reported data cohort.

Feeling hot/cold and other typical acute COVID symptoms (sore throat, cough, nausea, appetite decrease) were inversely associated with PCC in this cohort, contrasting with their prior classification as core PCC symptoms.

Using LASSO regression building on the 2023 model, eleven symptoms (postexertional malaise, fatigue, brain fog, dizziness, palpitations, change in smell or taste, thirst, chronic cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, and sleep apnea) contributed to the updated 2024 Long COVID research index.
The optimal score threshold on the 2024 Long COVID research index to identify highly symptomatic LC was a score of 11 or greater.

The 2024 index classified 20% of participants with known prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and 4% of those without known prior infection as having likely LC, similar to the 21% and 5% classified using the 2023 index.
The 2024 index introduced a new 'possible LC' category, classifying 39% of participants with known prior SARS-CoV-2 infection as having possible LC.
Cluster analysis of participant symptoms identified 5 distinct Long COVID subtypes that were associated with differences in quality-of-life measures.
Nearly half of the Long COVID sample met PHQ-9 criteria for clinically significant depressive symptoms, a rate higher than previously reported in the literature.
The large majority of participants reported poor sleep quality on the PSQI, exceeding previously reported rates in Long COVID literature.
Anxiety prevalence in this Long COVID sample was consistent with rates reported elsewhere in post-COVID literature.
Almost all participants reported some degree of subjective cognitive decline relative to their prior baseline functioning.
Higher neuroticism scores were significantly associated with greater subjective cognitive decline (total effect).
The effect of neuroticism on subjective cognitive decline was significantly mediated by psychological distress (composite anxiety/depression score).
Once psychological distress was accounted for, neuroticism had no significant direct effect on subjective cognitive decline, indicating full mediation.
Higher conscientiousness scores were significantly associated with less subjective cognitive decline (total effect), consistent with a protective role.
The protective effect of conscientiousness on subjective cognitive decline was significantly mediated by (lower) psychological distress.
Once psychological distress was accounted for, conscientiousness had no significant direct effect on subjective cognitive decline, indicating full mediation.
Anxiety and depression scores were highly correlated, supporting their combination into a single composite psychological distress index.
Among Long COVID patients reporting a chronic comorbidity, fibromyalgia was the most commonly reported specific comorbid condition.

The study sample was predominantly female, consistent with literature indicating women are diagnosed with Long COVID roughly three times more often than men, potentially reflecting sex differences in immune response.
IL-6 is described (via cited literature) as a central mediator in the development of neuropsychiatric symptoms observed in Long COVID patients.
GBA1-associated Parkinson's disease patients (GBA-PD) showed a greater burden of autonomic symptoms than idiopathic PD (I-PD) patients as measured by the SCOPA-AUT questionnaire.
Cardiovascular autonomic function testing revealed worse parasympathetic (cardiovagal) scores in GBA-PD patients compared to I-PD patients.
Sympathetic autonomic indexes and the degree of cardiac sympathetic (noradrenergic) binding were comparable between GBA-PD and I-PD patients.
Heart rate variability analysis showed lower vagal modulation in the GBA-PD group compared to I-PD.
Overall, GBA-PD patients show a cardiovascular autonomic profile dominated by cardiovagal (parasympathetic) dysfunction relative to I-PD.
Most ME/CFS patients show diminished muscle strength as measured by hand grip and quadriceps strength testing.
Lower hand grip strength measured early after infection was associated with persistence of symptoms in long COVID patients.
Exercise testing in ME/CFS and PCS shows limited exercise capacity, early anaerobic metabolism, mitochondrial dysfunction, and reduced oxygen extraction.
Diminished muscle strength correlated with blood markers of hypoperfusion in ME/CFS patients and with markers of inflammation in PCS patients.

In PCS, endothelial dysfunction and capillary-microvascular perfusion disturbance involve inflammatory capillary wall changes, impaired red blood cell deformability, possible microclots and high vasoconstrictor tone.
Later-stage muscle biopsy studies in PCS/ME-CFS showed no more capillary obstructions or microclots (seen earlier in disease), no viral reactivation, and only mild inflammation.
SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein was detected equally in patients and in healthy controls with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection, arguing against a persistent viral role in muscle pathology.
SARS-CoV-2 RNA could not be detected in muscle tissue in a non-exercise biopsy study of PCS patients.
Muscle biopsies from patients showed fewer capillaries, thicker capillary basement membranes and increased numbers of CD169+ macrophages compared with expected normal tissue.
In the exercise biopsy study, skeletal muscle capillary-to-fibre ratio, capillary density, and intracellular/circulating lactate were not different between PCS patients and controls.
Post-exercise muscle biopsies in ME/CFS showed evidence of tissue necrosis and increased numbers of glycolytic fibres, indicating exercise-induced muscle damage.

Increases in the skeletal muscle proteins TPM4, TMOD3 and CALM2 in extracellular vesicles were strongly correlated with higher myalgia levels after exercise in ME/CFS patients, suggesting mild muscle damage.

mRNA sequencing of muscle biopsies showed sex-specific mitochondrial gene expression changes in ME/CFS: males showed downregulated mitochondrial and hexose metabolism with upregulated fatty acid beta oxidation, while females showed downregulated mitochondrial and fatty acid metabolism.
Electron microscopy of ME/CFS skeletal muscle showed preferential damage to subsarcolemmal mitochondria compared with interfibrillary mitochondria.
A 23-Na-MRI study found elevated intracellular sodium in skeletal muscle of ME/CFS patients, negatively correlating with handgrip strength, depending on muscle type and rest/exercise state.
Unlike skeletal muscle, studies of mitochondrial function in peripheral blood immune cells of ME/CFS patients have shown inconsistent results.
Genomic DNA analysis of muscle mitochondria from ME/CFS patients found that all patients carried variants in mitochondrial genes, though of uncertain clinical significance.
Sera from PC-ME/CFS patients showed increased anti-endothelial cell autoantibodies and different functional effects on endothelial cells compared with PCS.

PCS sera enhanced release of vascular remodelling molecules and significantly promoted angiogenesis in vitro compared to PC-ME/CFS sera, suggesting a compensatory pro-angiogenic response absent in ME/CFS.
Endothelial dysfunction and elevated endothelin-1 levels were found in both PCS and PC-ME/CFS patients, indicating a role for hypoperfusion.
Retinal microvasculature imaging using OCT angiography showed retinal vascular damage 138 days after acute infection in hospitalized long COVID patients.
In PCS patients studied on average 15 months after infection, there were no long-term structural signs of retinal microvascular damage, suggesting healing.
GPCR autoantibodies correlated with fatigue, cognitive function and impaired microcirculation, predominantly in PCS patients fulfilling ME/CFS criteria.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and joint hypermobility are cited as risk factors for developing ME/CFS and are associated with vascular disease.
Mast cell hyperactivity and dysfunction of the ion channel TRPM3 are proposed as additional risk factors for ME/CFS.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition by pyridostigmine (Mestinon) is proposed to improve perfusion by enhancing cardiac preload and output in ME/CFS.

Skeletal muscle proteins tropomyosin TPM4, tropomodulin TMOD3 and calmodulin CALM2 were increased in extracellular vesicles after exercise in ME/CFS patients and strongly correlated with higher post-exercise myalgia.

mRNA sequencing of muscle biopsies revealed sex differences: males showed downregulated mitochondrial and hexose metabolism genes with upregulated fatty acid beta oxidation, while females showed downregulated mitochondrial and fatty acid metabolism genes, with no difference in blood immune cell mitochondrial function.
A study analysing genomic DNA from muscle mitochondria of ME/CFS patients found that all patients had variants in mitochondrial genes, though of uncertain significance.

Autoantibodies to G protein-coupled receptors were associated with symptom severity in PCS, with fatigue, cognitive function and impaired microcirculation correlating with GPCR autoantibody levels predominantly in PCS patients fulfilling ME/CFS criteria.

Sera from PC-ME/CFS patients had increased anti-endothelial cell autoantibodies and reduced angiogenic potential compared with PCS sera, which promoted angiogenesis in vitro, suggesting a compensatory pro-angiogenic mechanism absent in PC-ME/CFS.

Endothelial dysfunction and elevated endothelin-1 were found in both PCS and PC-ME/CFS patients, but a paradoxical association of reactive hyperaemia index with age, blood pressure and BMI, plus diminished angiopoietin-2 in PCS, suggested distinct vascular pathomechanisms between the two conditions.
Retinal microvasculature imaging by optical coherence tomography angiography showed retinal vascular damage 138 days after acute infection in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
In PCS patients assessed on average 15 months after infection, there were no long-term structural signs of retinal vascular damage, suggesting the microvascular disturbance heals over time.
Studies of circulating microRNAs in ME/CFS provide evidence for impairments in exercise hyperaemia, angiogenic adaptations to hypoxia, antioxidant defences and mitochondrial function.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and joint hypermobility are risk factors for ME/CFS and are associated with vascular diseases.
Mast cell hyperactivity and dysfunction of the ion channel TRPM3 are suggested as additional risk factors for ME/CFS.

Genetic risk factors for severe and fatigue-dominant long COVID overlapping with ME/CFS were identified by combinatorial analysis, including genes regulating mitochondrial, vascular and muscle function.
Acetylcholine esterase inhibition by pyridostigmine (Mestinon) has the potential to improve perfusion by enhancing cardiac preload and output in ME/CFS.
The guanylate cyclase activator vericiguat induces vasodilation via directly stimulating cGMP in a nitric oxide mimetic manner and is being tested in a registered trial.
Immunoadsorption, which transiently removes autoantibodies, improved symptoms in two-thirds of patients and normalized diminished endothelial function in observational studies.
An aptamer-based approach designed to neutralize GPCR autoantibodies (BC007) is currently being tested in a multicentre phase II trial.

Studies of mitochondrial function in peripheral blood immune cells of ME/CFS patients have shown inconsistent results, in contrast to consistent findings of mitochondrial dysfunction in skeletal muscle.
Reduced erythrocyte deformability was found to impair capillary flow, and capillary rarefication was reported in two studies contributing to malperfusion in ME/CFS and PCS.

The majority (91%, 488/534) of ME/CFS patients with a normal HR-BP response during tilt had an abnormally large reduction in cerebral blood flow, averaging -29%, accompanied by a mean cardiac output reduction of -28%.

A minority (9%, 46/534) of ME/CFS patients had a %CBF reduction (-5%) and %CO reduction (-13%) during tilt that fell within the normal range of healthy controls, with no significant difference from HCs.

In patients with an abnormal %CBF reduction, the relationship between %CO reduction and %CBF reduction was nearly 1:1 (slope 0.971, R2=0.762, p<0.001), unlike the near-flat relationship seen in patients with normal %CBF reduction or the modest relationship in healthy controls.
In ME/CFS patients with a %CBF reduction in the normal range, the regression slope between %CO reduction and %CBF reduction was not significantly different from zero (slope 0.076, R2=0.014, p=0.438).

In healthy controls, the relationship between %CO reduction and %CBF reduction was only marginally significant (slope 0.171, R2=0.114, p=0.018), and this slope was significantly different from the near-1:1 slope in the ME/CFS group with abnormal %CBF reduction (p<0.001).

Multiple regression analysis in the abnormal-%CBF-reduction ME/CFS subgroup showed that %CO reduction was the strongest predictor of %CBF reduction (unstandardized B=0.959), with the overall model explaining 78% of the variance.
PETCO2 reduction contributed only marginally to predicting %CBF reduction in the multivariate model (p=0.011), just above the study's conservative significance threshold of p<0.01.
Tilt duration was inversely, though only weakly, associated with %CBF reduction in multivariate analysis (unstandardized B=-0.063, p=0.003).
Disease severity (per ICC criteria) was significantly higher in the ME/CFS subgroup with abnormal %CBF reduction compared to the subgroup with normal %CBF reduction.
Significantly more males were present in the ME/CFS subgroup with a %CBF reduction in the normal range compared to the subgroup with an abnormal %CBF reduction.

The near 1:1 relationship between %CO and %CBF reduction in most ME/CFS patients, rather than the compensatory vasodilation seen in healthy controls under high orthostatic stress, suggests endothelial dysfunction of the cerebral vasculature as a dominant mechanism.

Citing prior work, the authors note that compression stockings improved both cardiac index and cerebral blood flow, and orthostatic intolerance symptomatology, in ME/CFS patients compared to those without compression stockings.
In a subgroup of patients with worsening symptoms on repeat testing (25 of 71), %CBF reduction worsened from an initial -6% (in the normal range) to -25%, well beyond the abnormal cut-off of -15%.
Among the abnormal-%CBF-reduction subgroup with adequate PETCO2 data (440/488, 90%), 43% had an end-tilt PETCO2 below 30 mmHg, a higher proportion than in the other groups.
Supine and end-tilt heart rate were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients with an abnormal %CBF reduction compared to healthy controls, despite both groups having a normal HR-BP classification.
End-tilt cardiac output was lowest in the ME/CFS subgroup with abnormal %CBF reduction compared to both the normal-%CBF-reduction subgroup and healthy controls.

Tilt duration was significantly shorter in ME/CFS patients with an abnormal %CBF reduction compared to patients with a normal %CBF reduction and compared to healthy controls, reflecting earlier termination due to worsening symptoms.
Screening of 402 patients meeting criteria for post-infectious ME/CFS found that 47% had elevated β2 adrenergic receptor autoantibodies above the healthy control 90th percentile.
Immunoadsorption produced a significant mean 17.75-point increase in SF-36 physical functioning four weeks post-treatment, with a large effect size.
The improvement in SF-36 physical functioning persisted at a statistically significant level of 12.81 points six months after immunoadsorption, though it declined somewhat from the peak.
70% (14/20) of patients were classified as responders to immunoadsorption, defined by a ≥10-point increase in SF-36 physical functioning at four weeks.
Serum IgG levels dropped by a mean of 79% during the five-session immunoadsorption course.
Serum IgA levels dropped by a mean of 68% during the immunoadsorption course.
Serum IgM levels dropped by a mean of 76% during the immunoadsorption course.
β2 AR-AB levels declined by a mean of 77% in parallel with total immunoglobulin depletion during immunoadsorption.
Baseline β1 AR-AB levels correlated positively with an immune symptom score reflecting lymph node pain, throat pain, and flu-like symptoms.
Baseline β2 AR-AB levels correlated positively with the immune symptom score at baseline.
Baseline M3 AChR-AB levels correlated positively with the immune symptom score.
Baseline M4 AChR-AB levels correlated positively with the immune symptom score.
SF-36 energy/fatigue scores improved by up to a mean of 19 points, peaking two months after immunoadsorption, indicating reduced fatigue.
SF-36 pain domain scores improved by up to a mean of 22.63 points, peaking two months after immunoadsorption, indicating reduced pain.

Autonomic symptom burden, measured by the total COMPASS-31 score, decreased significantly by a mean of 12.23 points one month after immunoadsorption, with particular improvement in orthostatic, secretomotor, and gastrointestinal domains.
Both frequency and severity of post-exertional malaise, measured by the DSQ-PEM, significantly decreased after immunoadsorption and remained decreased through six months.
Fatigue Severity Scale scores decreased significantly by a mean of 4.9 points one month after immunoadsorption.
Bell disability score improved significantly at several timepoints post-treatment, with a maximum mean increase of 5.18 points at month two.

In female patients, repeat handgrip strength measured after a 60-minute rest period improved significantly by a mean of 20% six months after immunoadsorption, indicating better recovery from muscle fatigue.

Among female patients, those who responded to immunoadsorption had significantly higher baseline maximum handgrip strength than non-responders, suggesting less severe baseline muscular/mitochondrial impairment predicts treatment response.
Endothelial function, measured as reactive hyperemia index, did not significantly change six months after immunoadsorption.

A second cycle of immunoadsorption in seven patients who had relapsed again improved SF-36 physical functioning at four weeks, similar to the first cycle, though it plateaued rather than exceeding prior gains.
One patient developed an internal jugular vein thrombosis as a catheter-related complication of vascular access for immunoadsorption; no other severe adverse events occurred.
No significant differences in age, symptom severity, disease duration, or baseline β2 AR-AB level were found between responders and non-responders to immunoadsorption.
A novel heterozygous frameshift deletion in ADCK1 (p.Asn280fs) was identified in a 35-year-old Japanese woman with chronic fatigue syndrome, confirmed by cDNA sequencing.
Introduction of oral 5-aminolevulinic acid with sodium ferrous citrate (5-ALA/SFC) resulted in significant improvements in the patient's daily activities, mobility, and psychosocial functioning.
Prior standard treatments including modafinil, methylphenidate, levocarnitine, and ubiquinone failed to relieve the patient's chronic fatigue symptoms.
Prior model-organism and cell studies show that ADCK1 deficiency causes developmental disabilities, mitochondrial dysfunction, increased reactive oxygen species, and apoptosis.
The multicomponent intervention group showed significantly higher light, moderate-to-vigorous, and total physical activity time compared to the control group at 3-month follow-up.
The intervention group showed significantly reduced sedentary (sitting) time compared to controls at 3-month follow-up.
The intervention group demonstrated significantly greater lower-body strength (sit-to-stand test) compared to controls after the intervention.
The intervention group showed significantly better cardiorespiratory capacity, measured as distance walked and perceived exertion on the 6-minute walk test, compared to controls.
Although trends toward improvement were noted in sedentary time and hand grip (upper-body) strength in the intervention group, these changes did not reach statistical significance.

A generalized linear model showed that participation in the Synchronize+ intervention significantly influenced changes in physical activity and cardiorespiratory capacity after adjusting for sociodemographic, clinical, and comorbidity variables.
Age was significantly associated with outcomes for muscle strength and 6-minute walk test distance in the adjusted regression model.
No significant baseline differences were found between the intervention and control groups in sociodemographic, clinical, comorbidity, movement behavior, or health outcome variables.
Among the study sample, 55.9% of fibromyalgia patients also had a concomitant diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome.
The Synchronize+ program was reported to produce improvements in sedentary time, sleep time, lower- and upper-body strength, and aerobic capacity among participants overall.
Resting heart rate was higher in both the functional somatic syndrome (fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue syndrome) and stress-related syndrome groups compared to healthy controls.
Resting skin conductance level was higher in both patient groups (FSS and SRS) than in healthy controls, indicating increased sympathetic tone.
Resting heart rate variability was lower in both the FSS and SRS groups compared to healthy controls.
Patients with functional somatic syndromes (fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue syndrome) showed a larger skin conductance response to psychosocial stress than healthy controls.
Heart rate increased less during the psychosocial stress tasks in both the FSS and SRS patient groups compared to healthy controls.
Heart rate showed a smaller reduction during the post-stress recovery period in both patient groups compared to healthy controls, indicating impaired autonomic recovery.
HRV during the recovery periods after stress tasks was lower in both patient groups compared to healthy controls.
There were no significant differences in peripheral skin temperature levels or responses between the FSS, SRS, and healthy control groups.
Resting heart rate was higher in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome (as part of the functional somatic syndromes group) compared to healthy controls.
Resting skin conductance level was higher in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome (within the FSS group) than in healthy controls.
Resting heart rate variability was lower in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome (within FSS group) compared to healthy controls.
Patients with functional somatic syndromes (including chronic fatigue syndrome) showed a larger skin conductance response to psychosocial stress than healthy controls.
Heart rate increased less during psychosocial stress in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome (within FSS group) compared to healthy controls, indicating blunted sympathetic reactivity.
Heart rate showed a smaller reduction during the recovery period after stress in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome (within FSS group) compared to healthy controls.
Heart rate variability during the recovery period after stress was lower in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome (within FSS group) compared to healthy controls.
Delayed gastric emptying was highly prevalent in both HSD/hEDS and non-HSD/hEDS patients, with similar rates between groups (85% vs. 94%).
Overall abnormal antroduodenal manometry was not significantly more prevalent in HSD/hEDS patients compared with non-HSD/hEDS patients.
Enteric dysmotility alone was significantly less common in HSD/hEDS patients than in non-HSD/hEDS patients.
Bursts, a neuropathic enteric motility pattern, were observed significantly less frequently in HSD/hEDS patients than in non-HSD/hEDS patients.
In multivariable logistic regression, the presence of enteric dysmotility alone was associated with a lower likelihood of having HSD/hEDS.
Patients with HSD/hEDS had a significantly lower BMI than non-HSD/hEDS patients.
HSD/hEDS patients had a significantly higher use of enteral feeding than non-HSD/hEDS patients.
BMI was not significantly associated with the presence of bursts on binary logistic regression.
The predominant referred gastrointestinal symptom (nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, excessive fullness) did not differ significantly between HSD/hEDS and non-HSD/hEDS patients.
Molecular testing identified a COL5A2 mutation (exon 29, c.1977G>A) in the patient, confirming a genetic diagnosis of classical EDS.

The patient developed a spontaneous Stanford B aortic dissection in his 70s, representing what the authors describe as the first documented case of aortic dissection associated with a COL5A2 mutation.
A cited systematic review of 112 papers covering 467 patients with non-vascular EDS found that 17% of individuals developed vascular complications.
In the same systematic review, 3% of patients with non-vascular EDS experienced more than one vascular complication.
Spontaneous or traumatic haematomas were the most frequent vascular complication among non-vascular EDS patients in the cited review, occurring in 53% of cases.
Following haematomas, intracranial haemorrhage (18%), arterial dissections (16%) and aneurysms (5%) were the next most frequent vascular complications reported in non-vascular EDS.
In the cited review, classical EDS patients with COL5A1 mutations had haematomas (subcutaneous, epidural, spinal, scalp, stomach wall) in up to 3% of cases.
Prior published case reports of aortic/iliac artery dissection in classical EDS involved patients aged 39 and 42 years, all carrying COL5A1 mutations.
Celiprolol, a beta-blocker, has been shown to delay vascular complications in vascular EDS, though this has not been demonstrated in classical EDS subgroups.
Desmopressin has anecdotal reports of use to treat and prevent bleeding in vascular EDS, but is not extensively studied.
Elevated D-dimer in acute heart failure has been associated with increased stroke incidence and may serve as a biomarker for predicting stroke risk to guide anticoagulation decisions.

The patient's persistent right hemidiaphragm elevation with basal atelectasis was attributed to diaphragmatic eventration secondary to tissue laxity from EDS, without evidence of diaphragmatic rupture.

Visceroptosis, a rare complication involving displacement of abdominal viscera, is described as occurring in hypermobility-type EDS and can present with chronic abdominal pain, dyspepsia, bloating, dysmotility, constipation, or bowel obstruction.
The patient's history of spontaneous haemothorax at age 30 was considered a hallmark feature indicating vascular predisposition in his classical EDS.
The patient's significant smoking history (30 pack-years) was considered to have adversely affected his vascular risk and tissue fragility despite absence of hypertension or family history.
Fatigue severity, measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale, was significantly higher in the hEDS group compared with the MFS group.
A significantly higher proportion of hEDS patients met the clinical threshold for fatigue on the FSS compared with MFS patients.
Daily persistence of fatigue was far more common among hEDS patients than MFS patients.
Depression scores (PHQ-9) were significantly higher in the hEDS group than in the MFS group.
Insomnia severity (ISI) scores were significantly higher in the hEDS group than in the MFS group.
Cardiovascular disease was significantly more prevalent among MFS patients than among the overall sample/hEDS patients.
Among the subset with cardiovascular disease, heart valve dysfunction and aortic aneurysms were the most prevalent conditions, especially among MFS patients.
Joint diseases and scoliosis were notably more frequent among hEDS patients compared with those with other diagnoses.
Ongoing psychotherapy was significantly more prevalent among hEDS patients than MFS patients.
Antidepressant medication use was significantly more common in the hEDS group than in the MFS group.
Insomnia medication use was significantly more common in the hEDS group than in the MFS group.
Time since diagnosis was significantly longer among MFS patients than hEDS patients.
The temporal pattern of fatigue throughout the day was more evenly distributed in hEDS patients, aligning with their higher insomnia (ISI) scores.

In the combined MFS/hEDS sample, disease type, sex, participation in psychotherapy, depression (PHQ-9) and insomnia (ISI) scores were significant predictors of fatigue severity, explaining 54.9% of variance.
In the MFS subgroup, depression (PHQ-9) score was the significant predictor of fatigue, with the model explaining 43.0% of variance.
In the hEDS subgroup, both depression (PHQ-9) and insomnia (ISI) scores were significant predictors of fatigue, with the model explaining 47.4% of variance.

Comparative analysis of regression models indicated that insomnia severity (ISI) has a substantially stronger influence on fatigue in hEDS patients than in MFS patients, whereas depression (PHQ-9) has a relatively stable influence across both conditions.

Participation in psychotherapy showed a differential (opposite-direction or disparate magnitude) effect on fatigue between the MFS and hEDS groups, appearing more influential in the overall combined sample than within the MFS subgroup alone.
A patient with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and AML achieved deeper remission after treatment with oral azacitidine.
Finite segment analysis shows that hypermobility of the upper cervical spinal segments increases mechanical loading on the spinal cord.
Greater atlanto-axial rotation and lateral translation are associated with increased spinal cord stress and higher rotation with compromised vertebral artery patency.
The central canal is estimated to be 5-9 cm longer during trunk flexion compared to extension, with greater posterior than anterior length change.
Nerve roots stretch up to 1 cm during rotation of adjacent vertebrae.

In patients with EDS and tethered cord syndrome, the filum terminale shows abnormal elasticity, collagen fibril changes, and inflammatory cell invasion, while the myodural bridge shows swelling, disruption, and altered collagen fibril orientation.
Increased cardiac-synchronous pulsatility of the cervical spinal cord, along with altered antero-posterior cord displacement during cervical movement, was noted in EDS patients without CSF leak.
Electron microscopy of EDS patients identified structural changes in the myodural bridge, including fibril swelling and loss of integrity in fiber arrangements.
In idiopathic intracranial hypertension, MRI studies show reduced compliance of the spinal canal.
In spontaneous intracranial hypotension, the intrathecal spinal canal shows increased compliance to infused fluid, and venous distension is noted intracranially and within the spinal canal.
MR elastography studies in spontaneous intracranial hypotension show increased stiffness in periventricular brain regions and decreased stiffness around the cerebellum and frontal lobe.

Dysautonomia has approximately twice the diagnosed prevalence of MCAS in EDS, which the authors attribute partly to healthcare access inequities and diagnostic delay rather than true prevalence differences.
With comorbid dysautonomia and mast cell activation syndrome, the odds of having EDS increase by 32-fold.
Dysautonomia has been found to mediate the statistical association between hypermobility, chronic pain, and neurodivergence.

POTS is commonly diagnosed in EDS, can cause headache and cervical/thoracic pain via reduced tissue perfusion, and is also associated with spontaneous intracranial hypotension, upper cervical instability, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

Reduced cerebral perfusion with compensatory upright tachycardia occurs in many EDS individuals, attributed to increased vascular compliance permitting dependent blood pooling and disordered autonomic regulation.

In one SIH cohort, 24% of patients had non-positional headache and 16% had orthostatic symptoms persisting after up to 2 hours of upright posture, indicating classic orthostatic headache is not a reliable diagnostic feature.
Spinal MRI fails to detect CSF-venous fistulae, which represent an estimated 50% of spinal CSF leaks, contributing to diagnostic delay and misdiagnosis.

Studies consistently show normal or high spinal CSF opening pressure in patients with confirmed CSF leaks, making opening pressure an unreliable biomarker for a leak despite diagnostic criteria still referencing low opening pressure.
Shorter duration of pre-operative symptoms is the strongest predictor of favorable outcomes for surgical repair of CSF leaks.

EDS is clinically associated with idiopathic intracranial hypertension and extracranial cerebral venous outflow obstruction, with EDS patients showing lower CSF opening pressure and co-occurring immunological and neurological signs not present in controls.
One study found that 54% of hypermobile patients also had symptoms of thoracic outlet syndrome.
Approximately 90% of thoracic outlet syndrome cases are neurogenic in type.
In hypermobile athletes, electromyography shows myopathic or mixed neuropathic-myopathic patterns, which researchers link to possible primary CNS impairment.
Patients diagnosed with occult tethered cord syndrome show filum terminale abnormalities including reduced elasticity, collagen fibril abnormalities, and inflammatory cell invasion.

Surgical release of the filum terminale produces similar symptomatic improvements in patients diagnosed with occult tethered cord syndrome compared to those with classic tethered cord syndrome with a low-lying conus.
A recent study identified three phenotypic clusters within hypermobile EDS, with one cluster showing a notably increased rate of neurological pathologies.
EDS predisposes patients to higher rates of venous compression syndromes involving peripheral vascular structures.
Compression of the proximal internal jugular vein between the styloid process and C1 lateral mass has been described in association with EDS and with intracranial hypertension.
Electrical stimulation of the filum terminale has been shown to activate paraspinal musculature, indicating a proprioceptive/motor role for this structure.
Animal models suggest that contraction of the obliquus capitis inferior (via the myodural bridge) increases intracranial pressure during neck motion.

Co-occurring upper cervical instability with Chiari Malformation morphology is proposed to increase myodural bridge muscle activity, reducing dural compliance at the foramen magnum and potentially converting benign Chiari malformation into symptomatic disease, which may also explain failure of decompression surgery in some patients.
Compression of the proximal internal jugular vein between the styloid process and C1 lateral mass has been described in association with EDS and linked to intracranial hypertension.
In hypermobile athletes with thoracic outlet syndrome, electromyography shows myopathic or mixed neuropathic-myopathic patterns, which researchers link to possible primary CNS impairment.

Hypermobile Chiari malformation patients show altered craniocervical junction morphometrics on upright imaging that are reversible with cervical traction or return to supine posture, differing from non-hypermobile Chiari patients, potentially explaining failure of decompression surgery alone to resolve symptoms.
Weight loss has a positive effect on idiopathic intracranial hypertension, an effect proposed to be moderated by reductions in intra-abdominal pressure.
Venous sinus stenosis is a common finding in patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension despite the 'idiopathic' label, with venous sinus stenting proposed as a treatment.

An association has been reported between EDS, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and extracranial cerebral venous outflow obstruction, with EDS patients having lower opening pressure and co-occurring immunological and neurological signs and symptoms not present in controls.

Reduced cerebral perfusion with compensatory tachycardia in the upright posture is common in EDS, attributed to increased vascular compliance permitting dependent blood pooling and disordered autonomic neural regulation.

POTS may cause headache and pain in the cervical and thoracic region, attributed to reduced vascular perfusion of tissues in the cranial and upper trunk regions, and is also associated with SIH, UCI, and IIH.

Nutcracker compression of the left renal vein can result in backflow via collateral circulation into the spinal epidural veins, as shown in cadaver and animal studies and observed in clinical practice with EDS patients.

Surgical release of the filum terminale in patients diagnosed with occult tethered cord syndrome (no low-lying conus) has been reported to produce similar improvement as surgery in patients with classic tethered cord syndrome (low-lying conus).
A recent study identified three phenotypic clusters within hypermobile EDS, with one cluster showing a notably increased rate of neurological pathologies.

Peripheral nerve entrapments, subluxations, and polyneuropathies (e.g., carpal tunnel, cuboid syndrome, median arcuate ligament syndrome, superior mesenteric artery syndrome, May-Thurner, nutcracker compression) are common but underdiagnosed in EDS/hypermobility and can transmit aberrant mechanical forces to the neuraxis.
PET scans have detected inflammation in extradural tissues surrounding spinal CSF leak sites, potentially due to pro-inflammatory properties of extradural CSF or dural tissue damage.
Shorter duration of pre-operative symptoms is the strongest predictor of favorable outcomes for surgical repair of spinal CSF leaks, supporting calls for earlier, more aggressive treatment.

Pathogenic COL3A1 variants, most frequently glycine missense substitutions and splice-site variants causing exon skipping, cause vEDS through a dominant-negative mechanism disrupting collagen III assembly.
Null COL3A1 variants causing premature termination and nonsense-mediated decay lead to haploinsufficiency, reducing total collagen III protein production by 50%.
A total of 18 clinical events (arterial rupture, GI perforation, other organ rupture) were recorded in 13 of 63 children (20.6%) with vEDS, occurring between birth and 17 years of age.
Events were observed more frequently in males than females and in index cases versus relatives, though these differences did not reach statistical significance.
Gastrointestinal events (predominantly bowel perforations) were the most common event type in childhood, occurring in 6 children at a median age of 13 years.
Minor diagnostic criteria for vEDS, particularly excessive bruising and thin translucent skin, were present in the vast majority of children in this cohort.

Congenital defects, including talipes, congenital hip dislocation, amniotic band sequence, and congenital heart defects, were found in 22.2% of the cohort, higher than expected in the general population.
Premature birth occurred in over half of the cohort with available data, and preterm premature rupture of membranes occurred in 12.7%.

Developmental delay, including delayed motor development, speech/language delay, and global developmental delay, was noted in nearly a fifth of the cohort, with global delay linked to traumatic premature births.
The majority of vEDS diagnoses in childhood (55.5%) were initiated due to positive family history and familial genetic testing, rather than clinical events.

In children without a positive family history or event, easy and/or excessive bruising was the most common trigger for referral leading to vEDS diagnosis, sometimes after initial suspicion of non-accidental injury.

Glycine substitutions in the triple helical domain of COL3A1 (Group 1) were the most frequent variant type and accounted for the majority of childhood events, particularly when glycine was replaced by bulkier, more destabilising amino acids.

Individuals with haploinsufficiency-causing COL3A1 variants (Group 5) showed fewer minor diagnostic criteria and no childhood events, supporting a milder disease course associated with this variant class.
Three nonsense substitutions located in the terminal exon of COL3A1, which escape nonsense-mediated decay and do not cause haploinsufficiency, were associated with no childhood events.
Under cardiovascular surveillance, new cardiovascular abnormalities (aneurysm, valve prolapse, vessel dilation) were identified in 7 of 53 children under review, with the youngest detection at age 6.
Celiprolol, a beta-blocker, was the primary blood pressure lowering medication offered to children with vEDS, used in 30 of 34 treated individuals, started at a median age of 12.53 years.
In one individual, the angiotensin receptor blocker losartan was prescribed in combination with celiprolol to manage systemic hypertension.

Genetic analysis identified 47 unique COL3A1 variants across 63 individuals, predominantly located in the triple helical domain, with the majority inherited (mostly maternal) and 12 confirmed de novo.
A post-mortem molecular diagnosis of vEDS was made in a male who died at age 14 from lethal aortic rupture, highlighting under-ascertainment of pediatric vEDS through lethal presentation.

At least 8 individuals diagnosed with vEDS in childhood experienced events between ages 18-25, of whom 4 had lethal vascular events, consistent with prior reports of increased early death risk in young males with vEDS.
About 57% of both parents and patients had heard of EDS prior to the patient's diagnosis.

Parents most commonly learned about EDS from a medical provider or family member (26%), whereas patients most commonly learned about EDS from a parent or another diagnosed patient (22%), and more patients than parents heard about EDS via social media (18% vs 10%).
Most parents (67%) and about half of patients (49%) reported being only 'somewhat comfortable' with their understanding of EDS after diagnosis.
The biggest reported barriers to parental comfort with EDS knowledge were lack of knowledge (47%), lack of educational materials (42%), and lack of confidence in provider knowledge (42%).
The biggest reported barriers to patient comfort with EDS knowledge were lack of knowledge (57%) and lack of educational materials (32%).
Most parents (72%) and 62% of patients reported being 'somewhat comfortable' with identifying and managing EDS symptoms.

Parents' top barriers to comfort with EDS symptoms were uncertainty about which symptoms are EDS-related (51%), lack of confidence in provider knowledge (45%), and lack of educational materials (38%).
Patients' top barriers to comfort with EDS symptoms were lack of knowledge (37%), lack of educational materials (32%), and uncertainty about which symptoms are EDS-related (32%).
Access to online EDS educational materials increased after diagnosis compared to before diagnosis for both parents (43% to 76%) and patients (30% to 43%).
After diagnosis, 42% of parents and 33% of patients reported they were either not given educational materials at their medical visit or were unsure if they had been given any.
Prior to EDS diagnosis, parents' top concerns and clinical needs were musculoskeletal care (66%), primary care for EDS (58%), education about EDS (45%), and gastrointestinal care (41%).

After diagnosis, parental concerns increased across categories including new concerns about mental health (46%) and multidisciplinary care (46%), alongside continued concerns about musculoskeletal care (66%), education (60%), primary care (55%), and GI care (45%).
Prior to diagnosis, patients' top concerns were musculoskeletal care (57%), education about EDS (35%), and mental health care (34%).
After diagnosis, patient concern about long-term outcomes increased and became a top-3 concern (37%), alongside continued musculoskeletal (54%) and education (47%) concerns.

A substantial minority of parents had a personal EDS diagnosis (20%) or suspected undiagnosed EDS (30%), and 51% reported 1-3 other family members with EDS, consistent with the known female predominance and heritability of EDS.
A higher-than-typical proportion of patients (13%) identified as gender diverse, which the authors note is consistent with prior reports of gender diversity being more common among EDS patients.
At baseline, prevalence of pain (6% of children) was not related to joint mobility category.
At baseline, children in the 'mobile' group (Beighton 5–6) completed significantly more shuttle run laps and had higher estimated VO2Max than children with normal mobility.
At baseline, the mobile group had significantly greater physical health functioning QoL scores than children with normal mobility.
At baseline, pain-related activity limitations (CALI-21) did not differ significantly across the three joint mobility categories.
At baseline, total physical activity score (PAQ-C) did not differ between joint mobility groups.
Reported pain decreased across the three annual measurements regardless of mobility group, falling from 6% in year 1 to 2.8% in year 2 and 0% in year 3.
Functional activity limitations (CALI-21 scores) declined significantly (improved) over the three measurements, with a similar pattern across all mobility groups and no time-by-group interaction.
Longitudinally, children with hypermobility had significantly lower overall physical activity levels than children with normal mobility, the only outcome showing a consistent group difference.
Children with normal mobility engaged more in spare-time physical activity than children with generalized joint hypermobility.
Physical education class activity levels were significantly lower in hypermobile children compared with normally mobile children, though this measure declined for all groups over time.
By the end of the longitudinal follow-up, total shuttle run laps no longer differed between mobility groups, in contrast to the baseline advantage seen in the mobile group.
Estimated VO2Max declined significantly over the three-year period for all children, with no differences between mobility groups by the end of the study.
Overall quality of life increased significantly across the three annual measurements, with no difference between joint mobility groups.

Physical health QoL scores showed a significant time-by-group interaction, with distinct patterns of change across the three mobility groups (normal mobile improved between measurements 1 and 3, mobile group declined between 1 and 2, hypermobile group improved between 2 and 3).
Emotional QoL declined significantly over time (more negative emotions reported), particularly between measurements 1 and 2, with no difference between mobility groups.
Social QoL showed neither a group effect, a time effect, nor a time-by-group interaction across the study.
School functioning QoL increased significantly over the study period, indicating fewer school-related problems over time, with no difference between mobility groups.
BMI increased significantly over the three-year study period across all children, with no difference between mobility groups and no time-by-group interaction.

In patients without hypermobility (Beighton score 0) undergoing hip arthroscopy for FAIS, capsular closure versus nonclosure of the periportal capsulotomy showed no difference in mean 2-year postoperative patient-reported outcome score change.

Both the capsular closure and nonclosure groups achieved statistically significant improvements in all patient-reported outcome measures at 2 years postoperatively, except for the SF-12 Mental Component Summary which remained unchanged.

Rates of achieving minimal clinically important difference, patient acceptable symptom state, and substantial clinical benefit thresholds were similar between closure and nonclosure groups across all patient-reported outcomes.
The first case-control study found markedly reduced IENFD in the lower and upper leg skin of women with FMS compared with healthy and disease (depression) controls.
A meta-analysis of 20 articles covering 903 patients with FMS confirmed that IENFD is reduced in about 50% of women with FMS.
Electron microscopy revealed a reduced mean axon diameter of unmyelinated fibers in FMS compared with SFN and healthy controls, present at all biopsy sites including distal, proximal leg and finger.

In a study of 117 women with FMS, IENFD was significantly reduced at different biopsy sites in 63% of patients with FMS, compared with 10% of those with major depressive disorder plus pain and 18% of healthy controls.

Patients with FMS showed reduced pressure pain thresholds (indicating gain of nociceptive function) compared with healthy volunteers.

Two nVNS studies investigated effects on fibromyalgia symptoms in a combined 138 subjects.
One nVNS study examined effects on chronic low back pain in a small sample of 22 subjects.

The author argues that persistent central sensitization, proposed as the core mechanism of nociplastic pain, lacks compelling evidence of occurring autonomously without ongoing noxious or neuroinflammatory input.
Misdiagnosis in chronic pain conditions has been reported to occur in 40% to 80% of cases, frequently involving overlooked neural compressive disorders.

CRPS type I, despite being classified as non-neurogenic and often cited as nociplastic, has been shown in histological studies to be associated with peripheral nerve changes similar to nerve-injury-based CRPS type II.
Fibromyalgia, often described as the prototypical nociplastic pain condition, has been associated with underlying neural pathology in multiple studies.

Widespread pain in fibromyalgia is not truly generalized but tends to localize to circumscribed body areas, which may correspond to distinct innervation patterns rather than diffuse central dysfunction.

Trigger points, seen in fibromyalgia, non-specific low back pain, and neck pain, have anatomically been linked to sites of neural entrapment where nerves enter muscles alongside a 'perforating triad' of nerve and vessels through fascial openings.

Structural brain changes detected by neuroimaging in fibromyalgia, CRPS type I, migraine, non-specific neck pain, non-specific low back pain, and irritable bowel syndrome are proposed to result from peripheral neural damage and consequent reduced afferent input, rather than representing a primary central pathology.

Opioids are not recommended as treatment for either nociplastic or neuropathic pain, a similarity in treatment guidance that the author interprets as suggesting a shared, possibly neuropathic, underlying nature.
Opioids can worsen both neuropathic and nociplastic pain, potentially due to opioid-induced neurotoxicity and neural damage.

Brain neurochemical alterations, such as glutamate/glutamine (Glx) and GABA levels, found in nociplastic pain patients are not specific to nociplastic pain, as similar changes occur in neural injury-induced neuropathic pain.

Fatigue-only symptoms co-occurring in fibromyalgia may be explained by selective vulnerability of motor nerve fibers relative to sensory fibers, similar to neuralgic amyotrophy presenting with motor but not sensory symptoms.

Non-symptomatic hypersensitivity has been detected in pain-free areas of some fibromyalgia patients, which the author suggests may reflect posture-related neural damage and central interconnections rather than pure central sensitization.

An acute-to-basal serum tryptase ratio of ≥1.685 is a sensitive and specific marker confirming mast cell mediated anaphylaxis.
