Colonic mast cell infiltration showed a non-significant trend toward increase in endometriosis animals compared to sham and naïve groups.
Ileal mast cell density was significantly increased in endometriosis animals compared to naïve controls.
Colonic GFAP immunoreactivity, a marker of enteric reactive gliosis, was significantly increased in endometriosis animals compared to naïve and sham groups.
No significant difference in colonic S100B expression was observed among naïve, sham, and endometriosis groups, despite the increase in GFAP.

No statistically significant difference in colonic α-7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor expression (integrated density or percentage area) was found between endometriosis animals and controls, despite elevated GFAP and macroscopic damage.
The proportion of αSMA-positive macrophages in BAL was increased at six months post-COVID-19 compared to healthy controls.
TGFβ mRNA and protein levels in BAL were elevated at six months post-COVID-19 compared to controls.
CTGF mRNA and protein levels in BAL were elevated at six months post-COVID-19 compared to controls.
Galectin-1 concentrations in BAL showed a time-dependent increase over the 1-, 3-, and 6-month follow-up and correlated significantly with pro-fibrotic markers.
Galectin-3 concentrations in BAL showed a time-dependent increase over the 1-, 3-, and 6-month follow-up and correlated significantly with pro-fibrotic markers.
The study proposes that galectins-1 and -3 contribute mechanistically to fibrotic progression after COVID-19 and could serve as therapeutic targets.
Of the 51 systematic reviews characterized for the Evidence Gap Map, 42 yielded inconclusive findings regarding the clinical effectiveness of homeopathy.
Among seven systematic reviews rated high-quality by AMSTAR-2, reliable primary studies reported positive or potentially positive results for homeopathy in fibromyalgia.
Among the seven high-quality (AMSTAR-2) systematic reviews, reliable primary studies reported positive or potentially positive results for homeopathy in irritable bowel syndrome.

Among the seven high-quality (AMSTAR-2) systematic reviews, reliable primary studies also reported positive or potentially positive homeopathy results for otitis media, diarrhea, respiratory infections, menopausal syndrome, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children.
Genetic testing identified a TGFBR1 mutation in the patient, confirming a diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
The patient presented with a 53-mm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) as the primary manifestation of LDS, atypical since AAA is a rare complication of LDS.

The patient had multiple peripheral arterial aneurysms and dilatations, including a 20-mm left subclavian artery aneurysm, a 16-mm right superior gluteal artery aneurysm, and superior mesenteric artery dilatation, consistent with reports that most LDS patients with aortic disease also have peripheral aneurysms.

Pathological examination of the resected aneurysm wall showed diffuse myxomatous changes, fragmentation of elastic fibers in the tunica media, and cystic medial necrosis, consistent with connective tissue disorder pathology.

The right superior gluteal artery aneurysm was successfully treated with endovascular coil embolization, followed by open surgical repair of the AAA using a quadrifurcated prosthetic graft, with an uneventful postoperative course.

Guidelines suggest surgical intervention for aortic root dilatation exceeding 40 mm in patients with TGFBR1 mutations who exhibit high-risk features; the patient's 40-mm aortic root dilatation was identified as the next likely treatment target.
TYMP protein expression (IHC staining score) was significantly higher in human AAA vessel walls than in healthy donor aortas.
TYMP mRNA levels were significantly increased in AAA vessel walls compared to healthy aortas by qPCR.
Tymp-/- mice had a markedly lower incidence of Ang II/Western-diet-induced AAA than wild-type mice.
Chronic Ang II infusion significantly increased diastolic abdominal aortic diameter in WT mice.
TYMP deficiency abolished the Ang II-induced increase in aortic diastolic diameter observed in wild-type mice.
Elastic fiber integrity (EVG staining) was better preserved in Tymp-/- aortic walls compared to the disorganized, broken elastic fibers seen in WT AAA walls.
Overexpression of TYMP in VSMCs (C2 cells) significantly increased secreted MMP2 activity compared to control (PC) cells.
Intracellular MMP2 protein levels were reduced in TYMP-overexpressing (C2) VSMCs, consistent with increased MMP2 secretion.
MMP2 mRNA expression was significantly increased in TYMP-overexpressing VSMCs.
Primary VSMCs from Tymp-/- mice showed markedly decreased MMP2 mRNA expression and activity compared to WT VSMCs.
Tipiracil, a selective TYMP inhibitor, dose-dependently reduced MMP2 expression at the mRNA, protein, and activity levels in VSMCs.
Plasma cytokine/chemokine array showed elevated levels of multiple proinflammatory mediators in WT mice compared to Tymp-/- mice, many previously implicated in AAA formation.
IL-1α levels were significantly lower in WT (TYMP-expressing) mouse plasma compared to Tymp-/- mice.
TIMP1 (an endogenous MMP inhibitor) levels were significantly lower in WT (TYMP-expressing) mouse plasma compared to Tymp-/- mice.
TNF-α stimulated MMP2 secretion in VSMCs, an effect further augmented by TYMP overexpression.
TYMP did not exhibit a synergistic effect with Ang II in regulating MMP2 production/activation, and Ang II alone did not influence constitutive MMP2 production/activity in VSMCs.
In situ zymography of aortic sections showed that TYMP deficiency substantially decreased in vivo MMP activity in the aortic wall.
VSMCs cocultured with TYMP-expressing (WT) platelets proliferated less than VSMCs cocultured with Tymp-/- platelets, indicating platelet-derived TYMP inhibits VSMC proliferation.
Overexpression of TYMP in VSMCs significantly increased constitutive AKT phosphorylation at Ser473.
Human AAA tissue showed strong p-AKT staining, indicating increased AKT activity compared to healthy aorta.
TGFβ1 expression was significantly upregulated within human AAA vessel walls compared to healthy donor aorta.
TGFβ1 expression positively correlated with TYMP expression in human AAA samples, particularly within VSMCs.
TYMP overexpression increased TGFβ1 protein and mRNA expression in VSMCs, independent of Angiotensin II stimulation.
The TSP1 type-1 repeat domain (TSR) induced a significantly greater time-dependent increase in CTGF expression in TYMP-overexpressing VSMCs than in control cells.

TSR dose-dependently increased AKT phosphorylation and MMP2 activity in WT VSMCs, and this was blocked by the TGFβ1 inhibitor SB431542, indicating a TSP1/TGFβ1-AKT-MMP2 signaling axis; the same treatment paradoxically decreased AKT phosphorylation in Tymp-/- VSMCs without corresponding MMP2 change.

Single-cell RNA-seq of nasal polyp mast cells from AERD patients identified six clusters (two MCTC, two MCT, a transitional cluster, and a proliferating cluster) distinguished by core protease and receptor transcripts.

TGF-β target transcripts (SKIL, SMAD7, LDLRAD4) and ITGAE were significantly elevated in transitional and MCT clusters in vivo, and basal epithelial cell TGFB1/TGFB2 transcripts were upregulated in CRSwNP relative to CRSsNP.
Cell-surface αVβ6 integrin, which activates latent TGF-β, was significantly increased on epithelial cells from CRSwNP and AERD nasal polyps relative to CRSsNP.

SMAD2/3 phosphorylation was significantly higher in the epithelium than the parenchyma of CRSwNP tissue, with similar levels in epithelium and subepithelium, indicating an epithelial TGF-β-rich niche.

TGF-β1 treatment of PB-derived mast cells caused time-dependent transcriptional changes, differentially regulating 414 genes at 24 hours, 1013 at 6 days, and 1903 at 7 weeks, with a core 149-gene signature altered at all time points.
A core set of 149 TGF-β1-regulated genes included upregulation of IL4R, SIGLEC6, and LTC4S and downregulation of CMA1, CTSG, and MRGPRX2 across all treatment durations.

Culturing CD34+ progenitors under mast cell-differentiating conditions with TGF-β1 for 7 weeks significantly reduced intracellular chymase and CTSG protein compared to differentiation without TGF-β1, producing MCT-like cells.

Withdrawal of TGF-β1 from differentiated PB-MCTs or primary nasal polyp MCTs for two weeks led to increased intracellular chymase, whereas primary MCTCs remained chymase-stable regardless of TGF-β1 exposure, demonstrating one-way granular plasticity.

In epithelial cell/mast cell cocultures, blocking TGF-β receptor kinase signaling with LY2109761 increased intracellular chymase in PB-MCT in a dose-dependent manner, while coculture with epithelial cells alone maintained the chymase-low MCT phenotype without exogenous TGF-β.

TGF-β1 treatment for 6 days dose-dependently downregulated MRGPRX2 surface expression on PB-MCTCs and significantly reduced their degranulation in response to MRGPRX2 ligands compound 48/80 and substance P, while PB-MCTs showed minimal MRGPRX2 expression and abolished degranulation to these ligands.
Removal of TGF-β1 from PB-MCT culture media for 2 weeks increased MRGPRX2 surface expression, indicating that continued TGF-β signaling is required to maintain MRGPRX2 suppression.
Despite TGF-β1 altering FcεR1 pathway transcripts, it did not change FcεR1α surface expression on PB-MCTC nor IgE-mediated degranulation between PB-MCT/PB-MCTC or TGF-β1-treated vs untreated PB-MCTC.

Following IgE crosslinking or IL-33 activation, PB-MCTs preferentially secreted IL-5, IL-10, CCL4, and VEGF, while PB-MCTCs preferentially secreted IL-13 and CSF1, mirroring transcript differences seen in polyp MCT versus MCTC clusters in vivo.
TGF-β1 upregulated transcripts for ALOX5, ALOX5AP, LTC4S, and PTGS1 (COX-1) at 6 days and 7 weeks, and enhanced production of cysteinyl leukotrienes and PGD2 following IgE activation.

The COX-1-specific inhibitor SC560 significantly reduced FcεR1-induced PGD2 synthesis in both PB-MCT/MCTC and TGF-β1-treated/untreated groups, while COX-2 inhibitor SC236 only marginally decreased PGD2 in TGF-β1-treated cells, indicating TGF-β1-driven COX-1 upregulation as the dominant driver of MCT PGD2 production.
Primary nasal polyp MCTs generated significantly more cysteinyl leukotrienes than MCTCs ex vivo following anti-IgE activation and trended toward higher PGD2 production per cell.

Reanalysis of an ulcerative colitis scRNA-seq dataset showed intestinal epithelial mast cells were enriched for MCT-associated transcripts and the TGF-β developmental signature, while lamina propria mast cells were enriched for MCTC-associated and inflammatory transcripts, supporting a cross-tissue role for TGF-β in MCT differentiation.

Despite transcriptional upregulation, intracellular CPA3 protein was lower in PB-MCT versus PB-MCTC, while extracellular CPA3 and tryptase β2 were significantly elevated in PB-MCT culture supernatants relative to PB-MCTC, indicating active secretion rather than intracellular storage.
Serum H3Cit levels were significantly higher in SLE patients with arthralgia compared to those without arthralgia.
Serum H3Cit levels were significantly higher in SLE patients with reduced complement component C4 compared to those without.
H3Cit levels showed a weak negative correlation with leukocytosis in SLE patients.
H3Cit levels showed a weak negative correlation with reduced complement component C3 levels in SLE patients.
H3Cit levels showed a weak positive correlation with anti-double stranded DNA antibody levels in SLE patients.
H3Cit assay showed diagnostic utility (AUC 0.709) for differentiating SLE patients with arthralgia from those without.
H3Cit assay showed strong diagnostic utility (AUC 0.813) for differentiating SLE patients with seizures from those without.
H3Cit assay showed diagnostic utility (AUC 0.746) for differentiating SLE patients with hepatomegaly from those without.
H3Cit assay showed diagnostic utility (AUC 0.662) in differentiating SLE patients with reduced complement C4 levels from those without.
IBS was one of the two most commonly discussed comorbidities in fibromyalgia social media conversations, with 16,663 mentions.
Arthritis was the most frequently mentioned comorbidity in fibromyalgia social media conversations, with 40,916 mentions.
Fibromyalgia and IBS were both reported as triggered by dietary choices with flares occurring simultaneously, though few posts explicitly discussed shared dietary triggers.
Massage therapy was the most frequently discussed treatment for fibromyalgia on social media, with 7009 mentions, despite not being endorsed by current clinical guidelines.
Meditation, acupuncture and mindfulness were the next most discussed fibromyalgia treatments after massage, with 5090, 3778 and 2936 mentions respectively.
Pharmacologic treatments discussed for fibromyalgia included NSAIDs, amitriptyline, anti-epileptic drugs, cyclobenzaprine and SSRIs, with mention counts ranging from 1154 to 2301.
Cognitive behavioral therapy was mentioned 1051 times as a fibromyalgia treatment on social media.
Stress and anxiety were reported as the most common triggers for fibromyalgia symptom flares, with patients describing that emotional stress or anxious situations intensified pain and fatigue.
Weather, temperature and air quality (rain, cold, extreme heat, humidity, pollution) were reported as significant triggers for fibromyalgia flares.
Gluten and wheat were the most frequently reported dietary triggers of fibromyalgia symptom flares.
Sugar, dairy and lactose were also frequently reported to worsen fibromyalgia pain and fatigue, and carbohydrate/keto diets were noted as difficult to balance to avoid flares.
Caffeine was reported as a paradoxical factor: patients relied on it to manage fatigue, but it could also trigger symptom exacerbation.
Patients reported that maintaining adequate vitamin D levels through supplementation and monitoring plays a role in managing fibromyalgia symptoms.
Magnesium supplements and magnesium baths were commonly reported by patients to help ease muscle pain and reduce flare intensity.

Patients with fibromyalgia reported symptoms across six key areas: pain, fatigue/sleep disturbance, mental health, unexpected sensations (numbness, cramping, spasms, restless legs), cognition, and sensory sensitivities (touch, light, noise, weather).

Vaccines were reported by some patients as a trigger for fibromyalgia flares, though there was no evidence of strong anti-vaccine sentiment in the community, and COVID-19 infection was also linked to flare-ups with patients often unable to distinguish fibromyalgia, vaccine side effects, or viral effects.

There was an increase in fibromyalgia-related social media conversations in March 2020, attributed by the authors to the COVID-19 pandemic, mirroring a similar increase seen across all medical conditions.

Patients described interacting with multiple medical professionals (up to five) for fibromyalgia, most frequently psychotherapists (7713 mentions) and therapists (7081 mentions), alongside frustration with providers over lack of acknowledgement and minimization of symptoms.

Peer support groups were generally viewed positively as a nonjudgmental forum for discussing pain and emotions, though they could also be perceived as draining, contrasting with family members and medical providers who were seen as less understanding.

Patients hospitalised during the first COVID-19 wave had significantly higher adjusted odds of experiencing one or more long COVID symptoms across all time points compared with those hospitalised in the second wave.
First-wave hospitalisation was also significantly associated with higher odds of one or more long COVID symptoms across all time points when compared with the third wave.
First-wave hospitalisation was strongly associated with persistent dyspnoea across all time points compared with the second wave.
First-wave hospitalisation was significantly associated with persistent dyspnoea across all time points compared with the third wave.
At each individual follow-up point (3, 6 and 12 months), first-wave patients had significantly higher adjusted odds of dyspnoea than second-wave patients.
At each individual follow-up point (3, 6 and 12 months), first-wave patients had significantly higher adjusted odds of dyspnoea than third-wave patients.
Unadjusted proportions of patients reporting one or more long COVID symptoms trended higher in the first wave at 3, 6 and 12 months but were not statistically significant between the three waves.
Dyspnoea had the highest raw prevalence at all follow-up time points among first-wave patients compared with second- and third-wave patients.
Among 24 assessed symptoms, alopecia, sleeping disorders and headaches (at 3 months) and numbness (at 6 months) were more prevalent in first-wave patients in addition to dyspnoea.
The average number of the 24 assessed long COVID symptoms per patient at 3, 6 and 12 months did not differ significantly between the three waves.

Among first-wave patients, those treated with ciclesonide, hydroxychloroquine sulfate or lopinavir/ritonavir did not have significantly different rates of one or more long COVID symptoms or dyspnoea at 3, 6 or 12 months compared with untreated patients, despite having more comorbidities and severe disease, suggesting these medications had minimal impact on long COVID.

Baseline and acute clinical characteristics differed significantly across waves: third-wave patients were older with more hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, oxygen therapy, ICU admission, thromboembolism and renal damage, while second-wave patients were younger with fewer comorbidities and complications.

First-wave patients had the highest proportion requiring intubation and had more ground-glass opacities, consolidation, bacterial infections, heart failure and liver damage during acute hospitalisation, which the authors propose may explain their higher long COVID symptom burden via lung tissue damage and pulmonary fibrosis.
Both PCC and ME/CFS patients showed significantly higher fatigue levels than healthy controls, with no difference between the two patient groups.
COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores differed significantly between patients and healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients showed numerically the lowest electrochemical skin conductance (palms) followed by PCC and HC, but the difference was not statistically significant.
Small fiber neuropathy symptoms (SFNSL) differed significantly across groups, with ME/CFS reporting the most symptoms, followed by PCC and then HC.
Heat detection thresholds were significantly impaired in PCC patients compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients exhibited lower N amplitude in Contact Heat Evoked Potentials compared to healthy controls.
Corneal small fiber density, branch density, fiber length, total branch density, fiber area, fiber width, and fractal dimension did not differ significantly between PCC, ME/CFS, and HC.
The number of dendritic cells in the corneal subbasal plexus did not differ significantly between patients and healthy controls.
Corneal subbasal plexus small fiber tortuosity was significantly worse in both ME/CFS and PCC patients compared to healthy controls.
Corneal nerve fiber tortuosity was the best variable discriminating PCC patients from healthy controls in ROC analysis.
Heat detection latency (CHEPs N latency) was the second-best discriminator between PCC patients and healthy controls.
Corneal nerve fiber tortuosity best discriminated ME/CFS patients from healthy controls.
When PCC and ME/CFS patients were combined, fiber tortuosity remained the main discriminator versus healthy controls, followed by CHEPs N latency.
Pupillary light reflex parameters (diameter, latency, contraction/dilation speed, recovery time) did not differ significantly among PCC, ME/CFS, and HC.
Deep breathing (parasympathetic) and Valsalva maneuver (sympathetic) test results did not differ significantly among the three groups.

Tilt table test responses differed significantly in ME/CFS patients compared to PCC and HC, with 30% of ME/CFS patients meeting criteria for Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS), while none of the PCC patients or HC met these criteria.
In PCC patients, more small fiber neuropathy symptoms correlated with higher fatigue levels and more autonomic symptoms.
In PCC patients, lower corneal fiber density correlated with a greater number of autonomic symptoms.
In PCC patients, longer disease duration correlated with worse cold detection thresholds on QST.
In PCC patients, increased pupillary dilation velocity correlated with more autonomic symptoms on COMPASS-31.
In ME/CFS patients, more neuropathic symptoms were associated with more autonomic symptoms, higher fatigue, and longer disease duration.
In ME/CFS patients, higher electrochemical skin conductance in hands correlated with shorter disease duration, and better ESC in hands correlated with lower fatigue.

In ME/CFS patients, higher electrochemical skin conductance in the feet was associated with greater corneal small fiber density, and lower ESC (feet and hands) was associated with longer blood pressure recovery time during the Valsalva maneuver.
ME/CFS patients had a significantly longer disease duration than PCC patients.
Tomas et al. reported that reduced maximal mitochondrial respiration best differentiated PBMC mitochondrial function between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Nguyen et al. found no statistically significant difference in resting mitochondrial respiration of NK cells between ME/CFS patients and matched healthy controls.
NK cell mitochondria in ME/CFS patients showed a significantly reduced ability to increase glycolytic flux compared with healthy controls.
Missailidis et al. reported significantly reduced ATP synthesis by Complex V in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, alongside increased expression of many mitochondrial proteins, potentially compensatory.

Lawson et al. found mitochondrial ATP unchanged but non-mitochondrial ATP increased in CFS, with ATPB protein expression significantly increased, suggesting an ATP-utilisation rather than production defect.
Ciregia et al. found ATPB and aconitate hydratase (ACON) upregulated in CFS saliva samples, and combining both markers yielded a diagnostic biomarker with 85% sensitivity, 72% specificity, AUC 0.793.

Missailidis et al. combined abnormal mitochondrial respiratory function, elevated TORC1 activity, and increased 48-hour lymphocyte death rate into a multi-parameter logistic regression biomarker with near-100% sensitivity/specificity and AUC 0.98.
Castro-Marrero et al. found decreased levels of Coenzyme Q10 and ATP, alongside increased lipid peroxidation, in PBMCs of CFS patients compared with healthy controls.

Kavyani et al. found kynurenine and the kynurenine/tryptophan ratio significantly increased in ME/CFS patients, correlating with symptom severity, while several downstream metabolites (3-HK, 3-AA, QUIN, PIC) were decreased.
Simonato et al. reported an increased kynurenine/tryptophan ratio but, in contrast to Kavyani et al., found kynurenine itself decreased and 3-HK increased in ME/CFS.
Russell et al. reported lower kynurenine/tryptophan ratios and reduced 3-HK in CFS cohorts compared to controls, contradicting both Kavyani et al. and Simonato et al.

Kashi et al. proposed a mathematical 'IDO metabolic trap' hypothesis in which damaging IDO2 mutations combined with tryptophan-induced IDO1 inhibition trap cells in a state of reduced kynurenine and NAD+ production, potentially underlying ME/CFS pathology.

Independent replication attempts by Tomas et al. found no significant differences in the commercially marketed Mitochondrial Energy Score (ATP Profile Test) between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls in neutrophils and PBMCs.

Yagin et al. used explainable AI/machine learning on metabolomics data and identified C-glycosyltryptophan, oleocholine, cortisone, and 3-hydroxydecanoate as discriminative metabolites, achieving 98% accuracy and AUC 0.99 for ME/CFS classification.
Naviaux et al. targeted 612 plasma metabolites and identified disturbances across 20 biochemical pathways, achieving sex-specific diagnostic accuracies of 94% in males and 96% in females.
Huang et al. applied machine learning to NMR metabolomic data in a large UK Biobank-scale sample and identified nine NMR biomarkers plus 19 baseline characteristics diagnosing ME/CFS with AUC = 0.83.

Xu et al. used single-cell Raman spectroscopy, confocal microscopy and AI profiling of PBMCs to differentiate ME/CFS from healthy controls and MS disease controls with 91% accuracy, and to distinguish mild/moderate/severe ME/CFS with 84% accuracy.

González-Cebrián et al. found Raman spectral profiles of plasma extracellular vesicles differentiated severe ME/CFS from healthy controls with AUC 0.7, improving to AUC 1.0 with a partial least squares-discriminant model.
Fletcher et al. identified IL-4, IL-5, LTα, and IL-12 as significantly elevated in an all-female CFS cohort compared with healthy controls, with good individual ROC AUCs.
Landi et al. and Groven et al. found IL-4 significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients compared with controls, contradicting other studies reporting IL-4 elevation.

Breen et al. found that comparing four multiplex cytokine kits (and multiple lots of the same kit) across six laboratories produced significant lot or laboratory effects for every one of 13 cytokines tested, indicating a major source of irreproducibility in cytokine biomarker research.

Hornig et al. found a multi-centre study showed markedly different immune signatures in early (<3-year) ME/CFS with elevated pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines, while long-duration (>3-year) cases showed the same cytokines lower than in healthy controls, correlating more with illness duration than severity.
SNP and genotype analysis identified 17 SNPs in acetylcholine receptor genes significantly associated with ME/CFS, nine of which were in mAChR M3 (CHRM3).

Autoantibodies against muscarinic acetylcholine receptors M1, M3, and M4 were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared with controls, though similar autoantibodies are also seen in myasthenia gravis.
Thirteen SNPs significantly associated with ME/CFS were identified in TRP ion channel genes, nine of which were located in TRPM3.
Immunophenotyping showed TRPM3 ion channel expression is significantly reduced in NK cell subsets but significantly increased in CD19+ B-cell subsets in ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
Whole-cell patch clamp showed the amplitude of pregnenolone sulphate-induced TRPM3 currents was significantly reduced in isolated NK cells from ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls.
Low-dose naltrexone (LDN) is used to treat pain in ME/CFS attributed to opioid peptide deficiency and excess pro-inflammatory cytokines, with 73.9% of patients reporting symptom improvement.
Genotype analysis of DNA from whole blood identified 17 SNPs in acetylcholine receptor genes significantly associated with ME/CFS, nine of which were located in mAChM3 (CHRM3).
Autoantibodies against the M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared with controls.

Autoantibodies against M3 and M4 muscarinic acetylcholine receptors were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared with controls, but specificity is questioned because such autoantibodies also occur in myasthenia gravis.
Thirteen SNPs significantly associated with ME/CFS were identified in TRP ion channel genes, with nine located within TRPM3 and others in TRPC4 and TRPA1.

TRPM3 surface expression was significantly reduced on NK cells but significantly increased on CD19+ B-cell subsets in ME/CFS donors compared with healthy controls, with impaired TRPM3 activity in NK cells.

Whole-cell patch clamp showed that the amplitude of TRPM3 currents after pregnenolone sulphate stimulation was significantly reduced in isolated NK cells from ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
In vitro treatment of ME/CFS NK cells with naltrexone hydrochloride for 24 hours restored TRPM3 channel activity and TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ influx to levels similar to healthy controls.

Low-dose naltrexone taken by ME/CFS patients for pain was reported to improve symptoms in 73.9% of patients, and TRPM3 channel function in NK cells of patients taking LDN resembled that of healthy controls.
Increased expression of the sensory ion channel TRPV1 has been identified in ME/CFS.
Balinas et al. found a significant increase in surface expression of TRPM2 and CD38 on NK cell subsets in ME/CFS versus healthy controls, with reduced baseline natural killer cell cytotoxicity.

Du Preez et al. found significantly higher co-localisation of TRPM7 with actin following NS8593 treatment and significantly decreased natural killer cell cytotoxicity in ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.

Gravelsina et al. reported significantly increased plasma autoantibody concentrations against mAChM4R and β2-adrenergic receptor in ME/CFS versus healthy controls, though the mAChM4R difference was not significant when restricted to women.

Sasso et al. found reduced amplitude of pregnenolone sulphate-induced TRPM3 currents in post-COVID-19 patients versus healthy controls, with no significant difference between ME/CFS and post-COVID-19 groups, and both groups were resistant to ononetin treatment compared to controls.

Nguyen et al. (2016) found significantly decreased TRPM3 surface expression on CD19+ B cells and CD56bright NK cells, and decreased cytoplasmic Ca2+ in CD19+ lymphocytes following streptavidin/thapsigargin stimulation and 2-APB-stimulated CD56bright NK cells in ME/CFS versus healthy controls.

Nguyen et al. (2017) found reduced TRPM3 expression in unstimulated CD56bright CD16dim NK cells but no difference in Ca2+ flux, while pregnenolone sulphate-stimulated NK cells showed significantly increased Ca2+ flux in ME/CFS versus healthy controls; no differences were found in CD56dim CD16+ NK cells.

Esfandyarpour et al. found that after hyperosmotic challenge with 200 mM/L NaCl, ME/CFS PBMC impedance rose markedly above baseline (unlike healthy controls, which returned to and remained at baseline), with substantial increases in impedance magnitude and phase components.

Cross-suspension experiments showed that ME/CFS PBMCs suspended in healthy control plasma produced a healthy-control-like impedance pattern, while healthy control PBMCs suspended in ME/CFS plasma produced an ME/CFS-like pattern, indicating a plasma-borne factor contributes to the phenotype.

Fluge et al. reported that muscle cells incubated in ME/CFS plasma produced more lactate than when incubated in healthy control plasma, and another group found ME/CFS plasma decreased oxygen concentration in healthy muscle cells, supporting a plasma-borne pathological factor.

Martinez-Rodriguez et al. found that at 1.36 kHz following 1M NaCl hyperosmotic challenge, real and imaginary impedance values were approximately 15% higher in ME/CFS PBMCs than healthy controls, but no significant difference was found at 154 kHz.
Groven et al. found no difference in the cytokines and chemokines investigated between ME/CFS and fibromyalgia patients, questioning cytokine profiling specificity.
Despite symptom overlap, Khaiboullina et al. found evidence of different immune profiles in ME/CFS compared with Gulf War Illness.

Reale et al. identified serum IL-1β and IL-17 pro-inflammatory cytokines to be elevated in both ME/CFS and multiple sclerosis compared with controls, indicating overlap that limits specificity, though Hornig et al. identified a distinct immune signature able to differentiate MS from ME/CFS.
Jensen et al. reported that autoantibodies in ME/CFS have enzymatic activity which may cause demyelination in some individuals with ME/CFS.
ME/CFS affects two to four times more women than men, potentially due to differences in sex hormones and sex chromosomes.

Esfandyarpour et al. first attempted to measure impedance in whole blood rather than isolated PBMCs but found no reliable or repeatable patterns, favoring PBMC isolation despite added processing time.

Esfandyarpour et al. found that after fresh samples, one-week liquid nitrogen storage and 24-hour room temperature storage were the next best-preserving conditions for the ME/CFS impedance biomarker pattern, though attenuated compared with fresh samples.
During a modified 1-minute elevated arm stress test (EAST), 62 of 64 participants (97%) developed at least one local upper limb/shoulder symptom such as fatigue, pain, paresthesias, or heaviness.

The EAST provoked systemic symptoms (lightheadedness, overall fatigue, racing heart, cognitive fogginess, nausea) in 41% of the 64 participants, a phenomenon not previously described in the TOS literature.
Combining local and systemic responses, 63 of 64 participants (98%) had an overall abnormal EAST result.
The median time until onset of the first local (upper limb) symptom during the EAST was 20 seconds.

Among the 41% who experienced systemic symptoms during EAST, the median onset occurred at 30 seconds; overall median time to systemic symptom onset could not be calculated because more than half of participants never developed one.
Joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥4) was present in 58% of the study sample of chronic-fatigue patients with arm symptoms.
42% of the study sample (27/64) had been diagnosed with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

The time to onset of local upper limb symptoms during EAST did not differ between participants with joint hypermobility (Beighton 4-9) and those without (Beighton 0-3), with a median of 20 seconds in both groups.
The EAST was abnormal far more often (98%) than the upper limb neurodynamic test 1 (ULNT1) (43%) when both were performed on the same day in 63 patients.

Among 64 patients with chronic fatigue and arm symptoms, 46 (72%) met criteria for POTS (one of whom also had NMH), and 17 had orthostatic intolerance symptoms without hemodynamic abnormalities; all but one had some form of orthostatic intolerance.
Among patients with an abnormal ULNT1, the median elbow extension angle at symptom onset was 145 degrees (range 90–160, IQR 140–160), below the normal cutoff of 170 degrees.

The authors identified 58 genes that overlap between SLE differentially expressed genes and ME/CFS-associated genes (from DEGs plus DisGeNET/GeneCards), representing candidate shared fatigue-related targets.
GO and KEGG enrichment of the 58 overlapping genes showed strong enrichment for innate immune and inflammatory pathways, including LPS, TNF, IL-8, IFN-γ, IL-1β, and MHC-II related processes.
PPI network analysis (STRING/Cytoscape, cytoHubba MCC and MCODE) of the 58 overlapping genes identified five key hub targets shared between SLE and ME/CFS: IL1β, CCL2, TLR2, STAT1, and IFIH1.
IL-1β concentration is significantly correlated with fatigue symptoms during the acute phase of ME/CFS, according to cited prior literature.
CCL2 (MCP-1) concentration correlates with fatigue symptoms and its expression is elevated in blood samples from ME/CFS patients per cited prior studies.
TLR2 activation may be linked to pathophysiological mechanisms of immune-related chronic fatigue across various diseases, per cited literature.
STAT1, a key IFN-α/β and IFN-γ signaling molecule, is upregulated in SLE per cited literature.
Increased IFIH1 (MDA5) expression in SLE patients promotes type I interferon and cytokine production, impacting disease onset and severity, per cited literature.
In SLE patient samples, correlation analysis among the five key targets revealed a significant negative correlation between STAT1 and IL-1β expression.
ROC analysis using an independent SLE dataset (GSE211700) showed STAT1 and IFIH1 had superior diagnostic discriminatory performance, while TLR2 and CCL2 had moderate performance.
ROC analysis using an independent ME/CFS dataset (GSE128078) showed IL1β, TLR2, STAT1, and IFIH1 had moderate diagnostic discriminatory ability.

Single-cell RNA-seq of SLE (GSE135779) and ME/CFS (GSE214284) peripheral blood samples showed that key target expression concentrated in monocytes, with IL1B and STAT1 particularly elevated in CD14+ monocytes.

Two-thirds of participants who had PCS at phase 1 continued to have persistent PCS roughly 17 months after acute infection, at the phase 2 clinical assessment.
Obesity prevalence was higher among patients with persistent PCS than among individuals with continued recovery.

Fatigue was the most prevalent symptom cluster among persistent PCS patients, with prevalence estimates varying by assessment method from 67.6% (symptom questionnaire) up to 92.1% using the CFQ-11 fatigue-case threshold.
Post-exertional malaise lasting more than 14 hours was reported by 35.6% of patients with persistent PCS.
A symptom profile compatible with ME/CFS was found in 11.6% of patients with persistent PCS.
Among persistent PCS patients, those with PEM reported more symptoms overall than those without PEM, particularly pain syndromes, confusion and dizziness.

Validated questionnaires for fatigue, cognition, anxiety, depression and sleep quality strongly discriminated persistent PCS from continued recovery, with the CFQ-11 fatigue scale showing the highest discriminative accuracy.
Persistent PCS patients had markedly higher COMPASS-31 dysautonomia scores than recovered individuals, with over 40% scoring in the moderate-to-severe dysautonomia range.
Nearly half of persistent PCS patients reported orthostatic symptoms upon standing, compared with only 7.5% of recovered controls.
Comparison of SF-12 scores between phase 1 and phase 2 in the same PCS patients showed no improvement in physical quality of life and a significant decline in mental quality of life.
Persistent PCS patients had significantly lower MoCA cognitive screening scores, with one-third scoring below the cutoff for mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment versus 18.9% of recovered controls.

Group differences on the SDMT and TMT-B cognitive tests remained statistically significant after adjusting for fatigue and depression scores, while the MoCA difference was attenuated to non-significance, indicating objective cognitive deficits (processing speed, executive function) are not fully explained by mood or fatigue.
Maximal handgrip strength was significantly lower in patients with persistent PCS than in recovered controls.
Reduced exercise capacity, defined as VO2max below 85% of predicted, was far more prevalent among persistent PCS patients than among recovered controls.

Ventilatory inefficiency, measured as the VE/VCO2 slope during exercise testing, was significantly higher in persistent PCS patients than in controls, with more cases exceeding increased/abnormal thresholds.
Diastolic dysfunction (grades 1-2) was numerically more common in persistent PCS but the difference was not statistically significant after adjustment for confounders.
Left ventricular ejection fraction, diastolic filling ratios (LV-E/e', LV-E/A) and pro-BNP levels did not differ between persistent PCS and control groups, arguing against central cardiac limitation.
FEV1, FVC and resting SpO2 were statistically significantly lower among persistent PCS patients than controls, though the absolute differences were small and airflow obstruction rates were similar.

Most laboratory biomarkers, including inflammatory and coagulation markers, did not differ significantly between persistent PCS and controls after adjustment for BMI and smoking, though CRP, HbA1c and D-dimer were significantly elevated before adjustment.
No significant differences in cortisol, ACTH or DHEA-S levels were found between persistent PCS patients and controls, arguing against hypocortisolism/adrenal insufficiency as a major driver of PCS.
Resting echocardiographic parameters including LV-EF, LV-E/e', and LV-E/A did not differ significantly between patients with persistent PCS and recovered controls.
Pro-BNP blood levels were not different between patients with persistent PCS and controls with continued recovery.

A higher crude prevalence of grade 1-2 diastolic dysfunction was seen in persistent PCS (30.9%) versus continued recovery (21.9%), but the difference was not statistically significant after adjustment for confounders.
CRP levels were significantly higher in patients with persistent PCS before adjustment for BMI and smoking, but this and other laboratory markers showed no significant difference after adjustment.
HbA1c was significantly higher in patients with persistent PCS before adjustment, but not after adjustment for BMI and smoking.
D-dimer levels were slightly elevated in individuals with persistent PCS in unadjusted analysis, consistent with prior reports, but were not significant after adjustment.
No significant differences in cortisol, ACTH or DHEA-S levels were found between persistent PCS and controls, arguing against hypocortisolism/adrenal insufficiency as a major contributor to PCS.

Classical pathway complement haemolytic activity (CH50) did not differ between persistent PCS patients and controls, arguing against increased complement turnover as a mechanism, though individual complement components were not measured.

EBV reactivation prevalence was 13% overall, with no elevated risk of EBV reactivation among patients with persistent PCS versus recovered individuals, and no significant association between elevated EA-D IgG or EBNA IgG antibodies and PCS.

Prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 N antibodies and levels of S1 spike antibodies did not differ significantly between persistent PCS and controls, with S1 antibody levels appearing to be driven by vaccination rather than PCS.

Using an ultrasensitive antigen assay, SARS-CoV-2 spike antigen was not detected in plasma from 100 persistent PCS patients or 100 controls, arguing against ongoing viral antigen persistence as a driver of PCS.

RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 RNA was negative in all tested stool samples from 156 persistent PCS patients and 103 recovered controls, allowing an estimate that true PCR positivity prevalence in persistent PCS 17 months after infection is ≤1.9% with 95% certainty.

Patients with persistent PCS and PEM lasting >14 hours showed substantially worse symptom burden across sleep, depression, anxiety, perceived stress, subjective cognition and fatigue, and worse neurocognitive test results, than those without PEM.

Patients with persistent PCS and PEM showed reduced handgrip strength, lower SpO2, lower peak heart rate, higher VE/VCO2 slope, and reduced VO2max compared with persistent PCS patients without PEM, with a higher proportion having VO2max <85% of target (41.0% vs 32.5%).
SF-12 health-related quality of life scores in patients with PCS showed no improvement between phase 1 and phase 2, with a slight worsening in the mental component subscale.
CFQ-11 (fatigue), PSS-10 and SF-12 scores all discriminated persistent PCS from continued recovery with high discrimination (AUC >0.8), with CFQ-11 having the highest AUC (>0.90).

Maximal handgrip strength was significantly lower in patients with persistent PCS (40.2 kg) than in recovered controls (42.5 kg), and was lower in women than men and inversely correlated with body fat and BMI.
Resting heart rate, breathing reserve, respiratory rate, and systolic/diastolic blood pressure did not differ significantly between persistent PCS and recovered subgroups.

Lower educational status, no medical care for the acute infection, full-time employment at phase 1, and no recent specialist consultation or rehabilitation participation were independently associated with higher odds of improvement from PCS in adjusted logistic regression.
Among initially recovered individuals, lower educational status and secondary SARS-CoV-2 infection since phase 1 were associated with higher odds of worsening (developing new symptoms) by phase 2.

SARS-CoV-2 vaccination had no measurable association with improvement or worsening of PCS status between phases, and age, sex, and inter-phase time were also not significantly associated with status change.

FVC was slightly but significantly reduced in patients with persistent PCS compared with controls (95.9% vs 99.1% predicted), a small but noteworthy difference possibly attributable to respiratory muscle weakness.
The odds of abnormal neurocognitive and cardiopulmonary test results in persistent PCS were higher for female than male participants, but the difference reached significance only for the TMT-B test.

The 2023 International Ehlers-Danlos Consortium criteria introduce the concept of hypermobility spectrum disorder for children and adolescents and state that adult hEDS clinical criteria should not be applied before biological maturity.
There is currently no genetic marker specific to the hypermobile type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS), making differentiation from benign joint hypermobility difficult in pediatric patients.
Once a child has finished growing, specialized reassessment applying the 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria is recommended to confirm or exclude the hEDS diagnosis.
Average ULF HRV power density was lower on high-GI-symptom days compared with low-symptom days.

Aggregated F-tests comparing high- vs low-symptom days showed the strongest ratio of statistically significant results in the VLF (~76%) and ULF (~92%) frequency domains, suggesting these bands are most associated with GI symptom expression.
Contrary to expectation, the LF/HF ratio was higher on low-symptom days than high-symptom days, an unexpected pattern that the authors note contradicts anticipated sympathetic/parasympathetic shifts.
At the population level, there was no statistically significant difference in overall HRV mean or variance between high- and low-GI-symptom days across any frequency domain except ULF power density.
A difference in average LF-band HRV power density was observed between low- and high-GI-symptom days, consistent with baroreceptor-related autonomic dysfunction previously reported in hEDS.

The study cohort reported high daily symptom burden, with fatigue, pain, and brain fog showing the highest mean severity scores among the symptom domains assessed.

hEDS patients with comorbid POTS have increased GI diagnoses and symptoms, including IBS and functional gastroduodenal disorders, compared with POTS-negative hEDS patients (cited from prior literature).
