Whole-exome sequencing with confirmatory Sanger sequencing identified a heterozygous pathogenic COL3A1 mutation, establishing the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the patient.
The patient with vEDS developed a large left MCA-territory hemorrhagic infarct, an uncommon and life-threatening cerebrovascular complication of the disorder.
The patient had a low Beighton score of 2/9, indicating only mild joint hypermobility, yet this did not rule out a diagnosis of vEDS given other clinical and vascular findings.

Segregation analysis in the patient's family demonstrated an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern of the COL3A1 mutation, consistent with the typical genetic mechanism of vEDS, in the context of a consanguineous (first-cousin) marriage.

Acute management of the hemorrhagic infarct included mannitol for intracranial pressure reduction and deliberate maintenance of systolic blood pressure at 160-180 mmHg for 72 hours, alongside potassium and antibiotic therapy.

Because vEDS has no curative treatment, the patient's long-term care plan focused on a tailored physical therapy regimen, avoidance of high-risk activities, blood pressure control, and regular cardiovascular monitoring to reduce recurrent vascular risk.
Vascular EDS is described as the rarest and most severe EDS subtype, affecting an estimated 1 in 50,000 to 1 in 200,000 individuals, with a reported median survival age of 48 years.
The patient was found to carry biallelic pathogenic variants in CHST14 (p.Phe209Ser and p.Pro281Leu), confirming diagnosis of mcEDS-CHST14.

Laparotomy was preferred over laparoscopic surgery for the hysterectomy to minimize blunt tissue trauma and pneumothorax risk associated with laparoscopic port insertion and higher inspiratory pressures in a patient with mcEDS.

Prophylactic administration of plasma-derived factor VIII concentrate containing von Willebrand factor before and after surgery was considered effective in preventing massive operative bleeding in this mcEDS-CHST14 patient.
Despite prophylactic hemostatic treatment, the patient experienced postoperative wound dissection and delayed wound healing with subcutaneous fluid accumulation persisting for 1.5 months.

Despite systemic connective tissue fragility, intraoperative manipulation of the internal genitals revealed no fragility or tendency to hemorrhage, suggesting internal organs are not prone to bleeding in this condition.

The patient developed endometrioid endometrial carcinoma grade 1, FIGO stage IA, at age 33, which is considered young-onset, in the setting of obesity and oligomenorrhea, marking the first reported case of malignancy in mcEDS-CHST14.

The authors hypothesize that dermatan sulfate-containing proteoglycans decorin and biglycan, known to change distribution in mouse endometrium under estrogen/progestin, may be abnormally distributed in the endometrium of mcEDS-CHST14 patients, potentially contributing to endometrial morphological/functional abnormality.
A prior survey found that 95.5% of people with hypermobility self-report falling at least once per year, with some falling more than once per week.
Across multiple studies, postural sway was greater in people with joint hypermobility compared to non-hypermobile individuals.
There is some evidence that people with symptomatic hypermobility sway more than people with asymptomatic hypermobility.
When balance was stressed by removing vision or reducing surface stability, postural sway increased further in people with hypermobility.
When the head was placed in extension, a position challenging visual, proprioceptive and vestibular systems together, sway increased more in symptomatic hypermobile people than in healthy controls.
One study did not find a significant difference in postural sway between people with symptomatic hypermobility and healthy controls, contrasting with other studies.
One study found no correlation between balance performance and degree of hypermobility as measured by the Beighton score.
The review highlights that increased fear of falling can itself lead to increased rates of falling, though direct evidence in hypermobility populations is limited.

95% of relatively young adults with hypermobility reported falling within a year, a rate comparable to or exceeding the 50% annual fall rate reported for people aged 80 and above in UK government guidance.
During prolonged standing, only antero-posterior sway was increased in people with symptomatic hypermobility compared to both asymptomatic hypermobile individuals and non-hypermobile controls.
When visual and vestibular systems were challenged, both mediolateral and antero-posterior sway were greater in people with symptomatic hypermobility than in healthy controls.
Two studies stressing proprioception via eyes-open/eyes-closed sway comparisons found greater sway in people with symptomatic hypermobility than in healthy controls.
Vestibular system testing via neck extension during quiet standing showed greater sway in both symptomatic and asymptomatic hypermobile individuals compared to healthy controls.

The review notes that postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), along with muscle weakness and poor proprioception, has been suggested as a factor contributing to reduced balance in people with hypermobility.
The review found that protected characteristics such as ethnicity were rarely recorded across the included studies on hypermobility, balance and falls.

Classification of hypermobility varied across studies, with the Beighton score often used alone (without complementary systems such as Brighton criteria or Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder criteria) and inconsistent cutoff values applied.

Of the 19 included studies, only two were small randomised controlled trials, ten used case-control designs, and four used cross-sectional designs, indicating an overall low level of evidence in this field.
Individuals with generalised anxiety disorder had a markedly higher prevalence of joint hypermobility syndrome than the non-clinical comparison group.
Prior literature cited in this paper reports markedly higher odds of anxiety among hypermobile individuals.
Anxiety severity (BAI score) did not differ significantly between participants with and without HMS, either within the anxious group or the non-anxious group.
Anxious (GAD) participants showed significantly greater activation than non-anxious participants in the left amygdala and right mid insula while viewing emotional faces.

Participants with HMS showed reduced activation compared to non-HMS participants in the left inferior frontal gyrus, precuneus, left pre-SMA, right posterior and left anterior mid cingulate gyrus, and left supramarginal gyrus while viewing emotional faces.
Although a main effect of HMS was found in the right mid insula, post-hoc HMS versus non-HMS comparisons were not statistically significant for this region.
There was a significant interaction between HMS and anxiety status in the left amygdala, left hippocampus, right paracingulate gyrus and right mid insula during emotional face viewing.
Within the HMS group, anxious participants showed greater activation than non-anxious participants in the left amygdala and right paracingulate gyrus.
The interaction effect of HMS and anxiety in the left hippocampus was not significant in post-hoc testing.
Among anxious participants, those with HMS showed greater activation than those without HMS in the right paracingulate gyrus and right mid-insula.
Activation in the left anterior insula was more positively correlated with Beighton hypermobility score in anxious participants than in non-anxious participants.
Activation in the left putamen was more positively correlated with anxiety severity (BAI score) in participants with HMS than in those without HMS.
Functional connectivity between the left amygdala and left precuneus during emotional face viewing was greater in participants with HMS than in those without, irrespective of anxiety status.

An interaction between HMS and anxiety severity was found in insula functional connectivity with the right supramarginal gyrus and occipital cortex, but this did not survive correction for multiple comparisons in post-hoc testing.
Functional connectivity analyses seeded on the left inferior frontal gyrus did not reveal any statistically significant effects related to HMS or anxiety.
EDS patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty had a significantly increased risk of all-cause revision compared to non-EDS patients.
EDS patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty had a significantly increased risk of instability or frank dislocation compared to non-EDS patients.
EDS patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty had a significantly increased risk of aseptic loosening compared to non-EDS patients.
EDS patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty had a significantly increased risk of all-cause revision compared to non-EDS patients.
EDS patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty had a significantly increased risk of instability compared to non-EDS patients.
EDS patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty had a significantly increased risk of periprosthetic fracture compared to non-EDS patients.
EDS patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty had a significantly increased risk of wound complications/hematoma compared to non-EDS patients.
There was no significant difference in medical complication rates between EDS and non-EDS patients following total joint arthroplasty.
Patients with EDS undergoing THA or TKA showed no significant difference in rates of medical complications compared to non-EDS patients.
EDS patients did not show a significantly increased risk of periprosthetic joint infection following TJA compared to non-EDS patients.
EDS patients did not show a significantly increased risk of hospital readmission following TJA compared to non-EDS patients.
Patient-reported outcome measures after TJA were similar between EDS and non-EDS cohorts and showed significant improvement compared to preoperative baselines.

The 129S6/SvEvTac genetic background dramatically improves survival of Col3a1G938D/+ vEDS mice compared with the C57BL/6 background, which shows a median survival of ~60 days due to spontaneous aortic rupture.

Aortic wall architectural abnormalities (elastin fiber breaks, decreased wall thickness, reduced collagen content) were present in vEDS aortas on both BL6 and 129 backgrounds despite markedly improved survival in the 129 background.

Passive biaxial mechanical testing showed increased circumferential stretch and stress at 120 mmHg in BL6 vEDS aortas relative to controls, but this difference was not observed in the 129 background, though the differences were modest.
Activation of ERK1/2 and PKC was accentuated in the descending thoracic aorta of BL6 vEDS mice, whereas activation of these pathways in 129 vEDS aortas did not differ from wild-type littermates.
A genome-wide significant locus on chromosome 11 was linked to protection from aortic rupture in mixed BL6/129 vEDS mice, with the single 129 allele substantially decreasing odds of early death.
Male vEDS mice in the mixed-background cohort were significantly more likely than female vEDS mice to be categorized with a severe (early death) phenotype.
Among candidate genes within the linked region, Map2k6 was identified as the most likely modifier gene, harboring a missense variant (p.G76E) predicted to affect protein function.

Immunoblot analysis showed increased phospho-p38α (Thr180/Tyr182) levels in aortas from 129-background mice relative to BL6, independently of Col3a1 genotype, consistent with intrinsically higher M2K6 activity in 129 mice.

Biallelic loss of Map2k6 in previously protected 129 vEDS mice rendered them vulnerable to vascular rupture in both sexes, while Map2k6 deletion alone did not affect survival of control (non-vEDS) 129 mice.
Map2k6 haploinsufficiency (Col3a1G938D/+ Map2k6+/-) was sufficient to increase death in male but not female 129 vEDS mice, paralleling the sex dimorphism seen in F1 vEDS survival.
BL6 vEDS mice with only one copy of Map2k6 exhibited complete prenatal or perinatal lethality, with no surviving pups observed past postnatal day 1.
Map2k6-deficient 129 vEDS mice showed increased PKC and ERK phosphorylation along with decreased p38 phosphorylation compared with Map2k6-intact protected 129 vEDS mice.

The descending thoracic aorta of vulnerable 129 Map2k6-deficient vEDS mice showed reduced PP1 phosphatase activity relative to protected 129 Map2k6+/+ vEDS mice, supporting a model where M2K6-activated p38 promotes PP1-mediated dephosphorylation of PKC/ERK.

Overall serine/threonine phosphatase activity, largely attributable to PP1 (~70% of activity), was higher in 129-background aortas compared with BL6-background aortas at 2 months, regardless of Col3a1 genotype.

Treatment with the PKC inhibitor ruboxistaurin for 4 months fully rescued the vulnerable phenotype of Map2k6-deficient 129 vEDS mice, achieving 100% survival compared with 50% survival in placebo-treated mice.

Pharmacological inhibition of p38 with SB203580 significantly decreased survival in BL6 vEDS mice without affecting BL6 control mice, indicating a protective role of p38 activity against vascular rupture.

In contrast to BL6 mice, treatment with an equivalent or doubled dose of the p38 inhibitor SB203580 did not affect risk of vascular rupture in 129 vEDS mice, and PKC/ERK phosphorylation was unaffected in this background.

Concomitant treatment with the MEK inhibitor cobimetinib rescued the elevated aortic rupture risk caused by p38 inhibition in BL6 vEDS mice, supporting antagonistic roles of MAP2K6/p38 and PKC/ERK pathways.

The FVB mouse strain, known to be resistant to β-aminopropionitrile–induced vascular rupture, also carries the same protective Map2k6 c.G227A allele, suggesting broader relevance of Map2k6 to other models of aortic dissection.

Light and transmission electron microscopy showed fragmented elastic fibers throughout the aortic elastic lamina in the LH1 (PLOD1 Gly678Arg) mutant horse compared to intact fibers in wild-type aorta.
TEM of LH1 mutant tendon showed looser collagen fibril packing and occasional disorganized "cauliflower"-shaped fibril profiles compared to WT tendon, resembling deformities seen in human EDS skin.
In LH1 mutant skin, most collagen fibrils showed normal D-period banding, but occasional fibrils displayed misaligned D-periods appearing as radial twists along the fibril axis.

On SDS-PAGE, pepsin-extracted collagen I from LH1 mutant skin migrated slightly faster than WT collagen I, closely resembling the electrophoretic pattern of CypB mutant collagen I, suggesting impaired post-translational modification.
Amino acid analysis of skin collagen I showed that hydroxylysine content was drastically reduced in LH1 mutant collagen compared to WT.
Proline hydroxylation levels (3-Hyp, 4-Hyp, unmodified Pro) in skin collagen I were unchanged between LH1 mutant and WT horses.

The horse studied carried a known PLOD1 point mutation (c.2032G>A, p.Gly678Arg) that causes Warmblood Fragile Foal Syndrome (WFFS), an autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder affecting skin and joints.

In humans, mutations in LH1/PLOD1 are known to cause kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and one human EDS-causing mutation coincides with the horse mutation at a conserved glycine residue in the LH1 carboxyl terminus.

Mutation in PPIB, encoding cyclophilin B (a collagen triple-helix proline isomerase), causes Hereditary Equine Regional Dermal Asthenia (HERDA), a distinct autosomal recessive skin disorder in Quarter Horses used here as a reference comparator.

Because elastin lacks hydroxylysine residues, the authors note that observed aortic elastin damage in the LH1 mutant is unexpected and may reflect a secondary effect or an uncharacterized role of LH1 in elastin biosynthesis.

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is described as a rare vascular disorder with an estimated prevalence of about 12 per 100,000 individuals, predominantly affecting women (about 85% of cases) aged 18 to 65 years.
Men and African Americans with FMD tend to present with more severe vascular manifestations (dissections, aneurysms) compared to women and Caucasians.

The differential diagnosis for FMD includes Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, and polyarteritis nodosa, since these conditions can present with similar vascular abnormalities requiring careful distinction via imaging.
CT angiography revealed a giant saccular aneurysm of the right cavernous carotid artery measuring 31.6 x 28.4 mm in a 74-year-old woman initially evaluated for suspected DVT.

Additional imaging abnormalities included a small saccular aneurysm of the left cavernous carotid artery, fusiform dilation of the humeral artery, a 'Bud's pearl sign' in small head/neck arteries, and extensive cervical arterial tortuosity, consistent with FMD.

Abdominal/pelvic imaging showed a hypoplastic left iliac vein with extensive venous collateral formation, a venous anomaly that may predispose to DVT despite standard treatment for a prior DVT episode.
Renal imaging revealed small caliber renal arteries with small caliber accessory renal arteries, consistent with FMD arterial involvement.

The patient was managed conservatively without anticoagulation therapy (to minimize aneurysm rupture risk) and showed favorable clinical improvement on follow-up, while interventional embolization of the giant intracranial aneurysm was planned by a multidisciplinary team.

FMD is typically diagnosed via imaging (CT, MRI, angiography) showing a characteristic 'string of beads' appearance from alternating arterial stenosis and aneurysmal dilatation, along with arterial tortuosity and small caliber arteries.

The patient showed no clinical signs of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (e.g., skin hyperextensibility, facial features) or Marfan/Loeys-Dietz syndrome, ruling these connective tissue disorders out as the cause of his isolated myxomatous aortic valve degeneration.
A cited cohort study reported familial myxomatous valve degeneration mapped to the Xq28 chromosomal region, associated with an imbalance between extracellular matrix synthesis and degradation.

Histopathological examination of the excised valve confirmed myxomatous degeneration, characterized by collagen fiber fragmentation in the fibrosa layer and acid mucopolysaccharide accumulation in the spongiosa layer.

Myxoid degeneration of uncertain origin affects an estimated 5% to 10% of valves in developed countries and predominantly occurs in individuals in their sixth and seventh decades of life, unlike this 37-year-old patient.

Intraoperative findings revealed rupture of both the right coronary and non-coronary cusps from their annular attachment in a tri-leaflet myxomatous aortic valve, a presentation the authors describe as unique and not widely reported.

Because extensive rupture of both cusps precluded repair, the patient underwent aortic valve replacement with a 23 mm TTK Chitra mechanical valve, with an uneventful postoperative course and good recovery on follow-up.
Microbiological culture of the excised valve cusp showed no bacterial growth, and there were no vegetations on echocardiography, ruling out infective endocarditis as the cause of valve rupture.

Normal Anti-streptolysin O titers and C-reactive protein along with absence of history/signs of rheumatic fever ruled out rheumatic heart disease, the most common cause of aortic regurgitation in India, as the etiology in this patient.
Joint hypermobility prevalence in the general population ranges from 5% to 40% in children and 10% to 20% in adults.
The combined estimated prevalence of hypermobility spectrum disorder and hypermobile EDS is 19 per 10,000 people.

Across all Delphi participants, the single highest-ranked research priority was how to prevent disability, pain, and poor quality of life associated with musculoskeletal comorbidities of symptomatic generalized joint hypermobility.

People with symptomatic generalized joint hypermobility report a broad range of musculoskeletal issues including acute and chronic pain, fatigue, joint instability, soft tissue injury, muscle weakness, balance issues, joint proprioception difficulties, movement dysfunction, and pelvic floor dysfunction.

Consumers with lived experience prioritized treatment and prevention research questions, whereas health care professionals and researchers prioritized service-impact and utilization questions such as clinical practice guidelines.
A cited study found that inadequate health care provider education/awareness of EDS may contribute to diagnostic delay.
Earlier diagnosis of generalized joint hypermobility-related conditions has been associated with fewer disease complications.
A cited study of knowledge and confidence in diagnosing EDS found that baseline knowledge and confidence were low across health care professional disciplines.

Among 210 final consolidated research questions from the Delphi round 1, treatment-related questions were the most common category (38%), followed by etiology (17%), service-impact/utilization (16%), diagnosis (14%), prognosis (5%), prevention (5%), and meaning (5%).
Beighton Score values were significantly higher in girls than boys in this pediatric hypermobility cohort.
Generalized joint hypermobility (BS>6) was significantly more frequent in girls (60.8%) than boys (40%).
The concave (C) sitting posture was the most common atypical sitting position among hypermobile children, followed by W, F, and S positions.
Most children were never able to sit in the S and F positions, whereas W and C positions were most often achievable currently or in the past.
Occasional joint dislocations and subluxations occurred in a notable subset of hypermobile children, half of whom had the highest Beighton Scores.
Among children who always exhibited the ability to sit in S, W, F, or C positions, females showed higher prevalence across all four positions.

The authors note that other studies report an association between joint hypermobility and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and ADHD, supporting the need for early identification of hypermobility signs in these populations.
Prior literature cited in this paper indicates that joint mobility (hypermobility trait) decreases with increasing age even within a narrow age range in children.

Among patients with generalized joint hypermobility, those who underwent ACL reconstruction with hamstring tendon autograft had a nearly 5-fold higher rate of second ACL rupture after return to sport compared with those who received bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft.

Graft rupture alone was more common in the hamstring tendon autograft group than the bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft group at 12 months, 24 months, and longest available follow-up, with no graft ruptures occurring in the BPTB group at any time point.
Participants with FM required a significantly lower thermode temperature than healthy controls to reach the same calibrated moderate pain level, indicating greater heat pain sensitivity.
Despite requiring a lower calibrated temperature, FM participants' pain ratings to the last heat contact were not significantly different from HC ratings.

The descending NRM→C6 dorsal horn connectivity was consistently stronger in magnitude and inhibitory (negative) in FM participants regardless of pain condition, whereas this inhibitory effect was not observed in HC.
Twelve of eighteen significant network connections identified had lower magnitude connectivity (DB) values in FM compared to HC.

At the start of every fMRI run, BOLD signal in nearly all analyzed brain/brainstem regions showed an initial rise that was approximately twice the magnitude in FM participants compared to HC, sustained for the remainder of the run.
Sustained pupil area during fMRI runs was approximately 25% larger on average in FM participants compared to healthy controls, consistent with heightened autonomic arousal.
No difference in the magnitude of the initial BOLD rise was detected between participants taking SNRIs and those who were not, arguing against a simple noradrenergic reuptake explanation.
The magnitude of the initial BOLD rise was not related to individual pain sensitivity (high/medium/low stratification) or to run number, indicating it does not diminish with familiarity.
The AC-IC connectivity strength differed between FM and HC groups when variations in COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores were accounted for.
The AC-PC connectivity strength differed between FM and HC groups when variations in state anxiety (STAI-Y-1) scores were accounted for.
The IC-HG connection showed the strongest ANCOVA significance, varying in relation to COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores across groups.
The AC-FOrb connectivity varied with Pain Catastrophizing Scale Magnification subscores in a manner that differed between FM and HC groups (interaction effect).
The AC→IC connectivity value was lower in FM than in HC, meaning excitatory input from AC produces less output signaling from IC in FM compared to HC.
Excitatory input from the thalamus to the hypothalamus produced reduced output signaling from the hypothalamus in FM compared to HC, and was also reduced in HC during noxious stimulation.

The size of the initial BOLD signal rise was related to state and trait anxiety (STAI-Y-1/Y-2) scores across regions including insular cortex, nucleus accumbens, amygdala, hypothalamus and thalamus, with the relationship exaggerated in FM compared to HC.

A study found decreased amplitude of diurnal cortisol changes and a blunted cortisol awakening response during the first month post-mTBI, with cortisol anomalies associated with symptom severity and neurocognitive testing results.

Chronic pituitary dysfunction is commonly observed following mTBI, with up to 40% of patients displaying hormone production anomalies even years after injury, most commonly growth hormone and ACTH deficiencies.
A trial of growth hormone replacement therapy in mTBI patients with deficiencies resulted in improved symptoms and changes in brain morphology and connectivity.

Multiple studies show atypical cytokine levels in acute and chronic phases following mTBI with variable direction of change, and elevated acute-phase cytokines predicted development of persisting post-concussive symptoms in one study.

In a randomized controlled trial, internet-delivered CBT-I for six weeks in mTBI veterans showed significant Insomnia Severity Index improvement versus sleep education control at end of treatment, but the difference was not significant at 3-month follow-up due to control group improvement.

A randomized controlled trial of clinician-administered CBT-I in adults with concussion history found 81% of completers had clinically relevant improvement (≥7-point drop) on the Insomnia Severity Index.

A randomized controlled trial of 6 weeks of CBT-I in concussed adolescents with persisting symptoms showed significant improvements in insomnia ratings and modest improvement in post-concussive symptoms versus treatment as usual.

A case series of CBT-I in 11 TBI patients (mild to severe) showed clinically and statistically significant reductions in total wake time (average 53.9% reduction) and improved sleep efficiency from 77.2% pretreatment to 87.9% post-treatment and 90.9% at 3-month follow-up.

Early participation in physical exercise after pediatric concussion reduced the prevalence of persisting symptoms at one month post-injury (25% vs 43%) in a large multicenter prospective cohort of over 2,413 children and adolescents.

A randomized controlled study of six weeks of aerobic training in mTBI patients more than two years post-injury showed improvements in post-concussion symptoms, quality of life, depression, anxiety, and fatigue compared to control.

In a controlled study of the Buffalo graduated sub-symptom threshold exercise program for adults with persisting post-concussion symptoms (1-71 months post-injury), approximately 72% of those who completed the program (41 of 57) returned to full functioning in daily activities.

Higher volumes of vigorous activity (72 min/day) in the first 3 days post-injury were associated with longer recovery times in youths with sports concussion compared with moderate volumes (36.9 min/day), illustrating an overexertion risk.

A randomized controlled trial in Taiwan of heart rate variability biofeedback (resonant frequency breathing) training in acute adult mTBI patients showed improved executive functioning, processing speed, and verbal memory, reduced post-concussive symptoms, and reduced anxiety, depression, and irritability, with large effect sizes at 12-week post-test.
PTSD symptom prevalence in a study of over 1000 mTBI patients was approximately 20% at both 3 and 6 months post-injury.

Orthostatic intolerance is a highly prevalent complaint in patients with persisting symptoms following concussion, typically related to altered autonomic control of the baroreflex and peripheral vasculature causing reductions in brain blood pressure.
Standard orthostatic vital signs as a standalone test may have poor sensitivity to detect orthostatic intolerance following concussion.

The number of previous concussions correlates with psychiatric symptoms, limbic system anomalies, and indicators of chronic inflammation impacting neurotoxic metabolites implicated as risk factors for psychiatric disturbance.
Retired American football players' accrued concussion burden correlates with increased prevalence of hypertension in later life, which may increase risk for late-life cognitive decline.
Two-sample Mendelian randomization found that genetically predicted higher copper levels were associated with increased fibromyalgia risk.
Two-sample Mendelian randomization found that genetically predicted higher iron levels were associated with decreased fibromyalgia risk, suggesting a protective effect.
Mendelian randomization found no significant causal association between calcium, zinc, folate, or vitamin B6 levels and fibromyalgia risk.

In multivariate MR adjusting for selenium as a potential confounder, both the positive association of copper with fibromyalgia risk and the negative association of iron with fibromyalgia risk remained statistically significant and independent.
In multivariate MR, selenium levels showed no significant association with fibromyalgia risk after adjustment for copper and iron.

The authors propose that excess copper promotes oxidative stress in fibromyalgia via the Fenton reaction, in which cuprous ions catalyze conversion of hydrogen peroxide into damaging hydroxyl radicals.

The authors hypothesize that iron deficiency reduces serotonin transporter density and disrupts dopamine D2 receptor function/reuptake, potentially explaining impaired natural analgesia and heightened pain perception in fibromyalgia.

The Rome Foundation Working Team notes that fibromyalgia, headaches, gynaecological and urological conditions, sleep disturbances and fatigue commonly overlap with disorders of gut-brain interaction, and this overlap affects patient management and outcome.
Reserpine treatment in mice induced periorbital mechanical allodynia (PMA), modeling a migraine-like symptom within the fibromyalgia model.
Antimigraine drugs alleviated the reserpine-induced periorbital mechanical allodynia in mice.
Reserpine-treated mice showed increased endoneurial macrophage density in trigeminal nerve tissue, indicating neuroinflammation.
Oxidative stress markers were increased in trigeminal nerve tissues of reserpine-treated mice.
Selective silencing of TRPA1 in Schwann cells attenuated both reserpine-induced periorbital mechanical allodynia and trigeminal nerve neuroinflammation in mice.
Selective silencing of TRPA1 in sensory neurons reduced periorbital mechanical allodynia but did not affect trigeminal nerve neuroinflammation, indicating cell-type-specific roles of TRPA1.

In reserpine-treated mice, Schwann cell TRPA1 promoted NADPH oxidase 1 (NOX1)-mediated reactive oxygen species generation and increased macrophage density in the trigeminal nerve, sustaining periorbital mechanical allodynia.
In mouse models of FcεRI-dependent mast cell activation, scratching was required for the development of skin inflammation.
Scratching-induced skin inflammation required activation of pain-sensing nociceptors.
The neuropeptide substance P was required for scratching-induced cutaneous inflammation.
The mast cell receptor MrgprB2 was required for scratching-induced cutaneous inflammation, implicating direct neuropeptide-driven mast cell activation.
Scratching increased cutaneous inflammation and enhanced host defense against superficial Staphylococcus aureus skin infection.
Mechanical scratching of keratinocytes (HaCaT) generates ROS that activates TRPA1 on tryptase-presenting mast cells in atopic dermatitis.
TRPA1 on mast cells is activated by keratinocyte-derived ROS, linking epidermal oxidative stress to dermal mast cell activation in atopic dermatitis.
Administration of a free radical scavenger inhibited mast cell activation and type II inflammatory response, alleviating itching and skin lesions in the AD model.
A TRPA1 inhibitor suppressed mast cell activation and type II inflammatory response, reducing itching and skin lesions in the AD mouse model.
Combined ROS scavenging and TRPA1 inhibition together can inhibit the itch-scratch cycle, suggesting a potential dual-target therapeutic strategy for AD.

MMCS is a newly proposed diagnostic category for patients with clonal/atypical bone marrow mast cells (KIT 816 mutation and/or aberrant CD2/CD25 expression) who do not meet WHO criteria for systemic mastocytosis or full MCAS criteria.
KIT D816V/816 mutations were significantly less frequent in MMCS patients compared with ISM patients.
Aberrant CD2 expression on mast cells was significantly less common in MMCS than in ISM or BMM patients.
Baseline serum tryptase levels were significantly lower in MMCS patients compared to both ISM and BMM patients.
Anaphylaxis was significantly more prevalent in MMCS patients compared to ISM patients, but not significantly different from BMM patients.
The overall number of MCA symptoms was much lower in MMCS patients compared to ISM patients.
Musculoskeletal symptoms, flushing, and malaise were significantly less frequent in MMCS compared to both ISM and BMM.
Osteoporosis prevalence was numerically higher in MMCS than ISM and BMM but the difference was not statistically significant.

Hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HαT) prevalence did not differ significantly between MMCS KIT 816+ and KIT 816- subgroups, and was not higher than in typical mastocytosis, suggesting HαT alone does not explain the high anaphylaxis prevalence in MMCS.

Most MCA symptoms including anaphylaxis did not differ significantly between MMCS patients with and without KIT 816 mutation, except gastrointestinal symptoms and flushing which were more frequent in KIT-negative patients.
H1 antihistamine use at diagnosis was significantly lower in MMCS patients compared to ISM patients, consistent with lower overall symptomatic medication needs.

Over a median follow-up of 4.7 years, no MMCS patient progressed to systemic mastocytosis, developed additional MCAS criteria, or died, though none underwent repeat bone marrow biopsy absent clinical worsening.

MMCS is a predisposing condition for allergy, particularly hymenoptera venom allergy, and MCA symptoms, independently of KIT mutation status; over half of MMCS patients were referred for allergy or idiopathic anaphylaxis alone.
Patients with MMCS were diagnosed at a significantly older age than patients with ISM.
Time from symptom onset to diagnosis was significantly shorter in MMCS compared to ISM, likely due to the acute, severe nature of anaphylactic presentations prompting earlier workup.

Prior studies cited suggest that 14% and 5% of patients presenting with idiopathic or severe anaphylaxis respectively may have an underlying clonal mast cell disease, supporting the hypothesis that MMCS is underdiagnosed.
Tcd A increased intestinal permeability in an in vitro Caco-2/HT-29 coculture monolayer model.
Tcd A promoted β-hexosaminidase release in a bone marrow-derived mast cell degranulation model, indicating direct mast cell activation.
In OVA-sensitized mice, oral co-exposure to 4 μg Tcd A during challenge increased OVA-specific IgE levels compared to allergy alone.
MCPT-1, a marker of mucosal mast cell activation, was increased in sensitized mice orally exposed to Tcd A during OVA challenge.
Flow cytometry showed that Th1 cell populations were reduced in Tcd A-exposed, OVA-sensitized mice.
Flow cytometry showed that Treg cell populations were reduced in Tcd A-exposed, OVA-sensitized mice.
ELISA showed higher IL-5 induction in Tcd A-exposed, OVA-sensitized mice, indicating a Th2-biased immune response.
Histological jejunum staining showed that villus injury was aggravated in Tcd A-exposed, OVA-sensitized mice.
Mast cells from AD patients showed significantly higher 5-LO mRNA expression than mast cells from healthy volunteers in non-stimulated and cytokine-stimulated conditions.
FLAP mRNA expression was significantly higher in AD patient mast cells than HV mast cells across non-stimulated and stimulated conditions.
IL-13 stimulation significantly reduced 5-LO and FLAP mRNA expression only in mast cells from healthy volunteers, not in AD patient mast cells.
5-LO and FLAP mRNA expression levels in AD patients showed only a weak, non-significant correlation with disease severity (SCORAD).
Histamine significantly up-regulated LTC4S mRNA expression in healthy volunteer mast cells, an effect mainly mediated via the H4 receptor.
The H4R-selective antagonist JNJ7777120 blocked histamine-induced up-regulation of LTC4S mRNA in healthy volunteer mast cells, confirming H4R mediation.
Histamine also significantly increased LTC4S mRNA expression in mast cells from AD patients.
IL-4 and IL-13 significantly up-regulated LTC4S mRNA expression in mast cells from both HVs and AD patients, with IL-4's effect more pronounced in AD patients.
Histamine and IL-4 significantly increased CysLT release from mast cells of both healthy volunteers and AD patients.
IL-13 significantly increased CysLT release only in mast cells from healthy volunteers, not from AD patients.
In preliminary experiments, FcεRI cross-linking induced strong CysLT release from mast cells, which was further moderately enhanced by histamine pre-stimulation, suggesting a synergistic effect.
Preliminary data suggest higher CysLT release in AD patient mast cells compared to healthy volunteer mast cells, both at baseline and after histamine stimulation.
Histamine significantly up-regulated CysLT1R mRNA expression in mast cells from both HVs and AD patients, mainly via H1R signaling.
Direct H1 receptor agonist stimulation significantly up-regulated CysLT1R mRNA only in mast cells from AD patients, not in HV mast cells.
IL-4 and IL-13 up-regulated CysLT1R mRNA expression only in mast cells from AD patients, not in mast cells from HVs.
Histamine, mainly via H1R, significantly up-regulated CysLT2R mRNA in HV mast cells, with a non-significant trend in AD patient mast cells.
IL-4 up-regulated CysLT2R mRNA expression to a greater degree in AD patient mast cells than in HV mast cells.
IL-13 significantly up-regulated CysLT2R mRNA expression in AD patient mast cells but not in HV mast cells.
Baseline (non-stimulated) and IL-4-stimulated CysLT2R mRNA expression levels were significantly higher in AD patient mast cells compared to HV mast cells.
Baseline CysLT2R mRNA expression showed a moderate-to-strong positive correlation with AD severity (SCORAD), though this did not reach statistical significance.
Baseline H2R mRNA expression was significantly higher in AD patient mast cells compared to HV mast cells.
Baseline H4R mRNA expression was significantly higher in AD patient mast cells compared to HV mast cells.
Of 217 patients evaluated for suspected histamine intolerance (HIT), 77 (35.5%) were confirmed as HIT based on symptom improvement with a low-histamine or elimination diet.
Among patients voluntarily tested, serum DAO levels were below the reference limit in 74% overall and in 82% of confirmed HIT patients.

A logistic regression model using BMI, HIT symptom frequency score, meal-attributed symptom onset, and number of nontolerated foods significantly distinguished HIT presence/absence, yielding an ROC AUC of 0.76.
Adding DAO concentration as a predictor to the logistic regression model improved discrimination of HIT, increasing the AUC to 0.794.
Among 36 confirmed HIT patients with detailed longitudinal data, symptom severity progressed through stages, with Stage 2 in 42%, Stage 3 in 47%, and Stage 4 in 11% of patients.
Patients experienced multiple distinct symptom recurrence timelines over several days, with most (44%) experiencing all four described timeline types.

96% of HIT patients reported absence of most or any symptoms during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy, hypothesized to result from a large placental increase in serum DAO compensating for impaired DAO/HNMT function.

A high proportion of confirmed HIT patients reported family history of similar symptoms: 70% had a relative with diarrhea/headache, 51% had a relative on dyspepsia medication, and 17% had a family member with diagnosed HIT, supporting a genetic basis.

Sixty-six percent of surveyed HIT patients reported feeling more energetic on an empty stomach, and 87% could already associate intermittent symptoms with meals at first interview, with 62% reporting highest symptom intensity in the late afternoon/evening after main meals.

Patients with possible mast cell activation (MCA; n=41) had significantly higher average counts of gastrointestinal, neurological, and respiratory symptoms, overall symptom severity score, and total complaints, along with more frequent nausea and vomiting, compared to the remaining confirmed HIT patients without suspected MCA (n=36).
Suspected HIT patients had significantly more frequent primary care visits for upper respiratory symptoms than non-HIT patients, with a median of six visits versus two.
21% of confirmed HIT patients reported sensitivity to medications known to act as DAO blockers, such as clavulanic acid and acetylcysteine.
A few confirmed HIT patients had elevated urinary histamine and N-methylhistamine, which according to global Consensus-2 criteria could support a concurrent diagnosis of idiopathic MCAS.

Cited literature indicates HIT is associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis, with overabundance of histamine-secreting bacteria and reduced beneficial gut bacteria such as Ruminococcus and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii.
Cited literature reports that dietary interventions including low-histamine diets and DAO supplementation reduce histaminogenic gut bacteria and increase beneficial species such as Roseburia spp.
Following implementation of a low-histamine or elimination diet, confirmed HIT patients showed significant reductions in symptom frequency and subjective severity scores.
Most confirmed HIT patients maintained dietary adherence at follow-up: 94% still followed a diet, with 61% on an elimination diet and 32% on a low-histamine diet.

Following a dietary mistake, HIT symptoms typically emerged after an average of 1.1 hours; sudden lethargy accompanied symptoms in 52% of patients, symptom severity varied with food quantity in 68%, and intercurrent illness exacerbated symptoms in 88% of applicable cases.
Overall mood improvement following dietary intervention was reported by 38% of confirmed HIT patients.
A theoretical possibility of mast cell activation (MCA) was considered in 41 of 77 confirmed HIT cases, based on recurring sore throat with prolonged common-cold-like symptoms or flushing.

On average, confirmed HIT patients had 4.3 of 5 organ systems affected and reported 21 of 62 possible symptoms on the questionnaire, with a mean of 38.8 out of 110 total positive questionnaire responses.
IL-4 concentration in nasal lavage fluid was significantly higher in nasal polyp (NP) mice than in control mice.
IL-5 concentration in nasal lavage fluid was significantly higher in NP mice than in control mice.
Mast cell tryptase (MCT) in nasal lavage fluid was significantly elevated in NP mice compared to control mice, indicating increased mast cell degranulation.
Inotodiol treatment significantly reduced nasal lavage fluid concentrations of IL-4, IL-5, and mast cell tryptase compared to untreated NP mice.
mRNA expression of Th2/Th1/Th17-associated cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13, IL-17A, IFN-γ) in nasal mucosa was significantly elevated in NP mice compared to control mice.
Inotodiol treatment reduced the elevated mucosal mRNA expression of IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13, IL-17A, and IFN-γ seen in NP mice, with effects broadly similar to dexamethasone.
Mucosal mRNA expression of IL-6, IL-1β, IL-25, and IL-33 (alarmins/pro-inflammatory cytokines) was significantly higher in NP mice than in control mice.
Inotodiol treatment reduced mucosal mRNA expression of IL-6, IL-1β, IL-25, and IL-33 compared to untreated NP mice.
Mucosal mRNA expression of chemokines CCL1, CCL2, and CXCL2 was significantly higher in NP mice than in control mice.
Inotodiol treatment reduced mucosal chemokine (CCL1, CCL2, CXCL2) mRNA expression relative to untreated NP mice.
Inotodiol treatment did not significantly reduce the number of nasal polyps compared to untreated NP mice, whereas dexamethasone did.
Epithelial thickness in the nasal mucosa was significantly reduced by inotodiol and dexamethasone treatment compared to untreated NP mice.
Eosinophil infiltration in nasal mucosa was significantly reduced by inotodiol and dexamethasone treatment compared to untreated NP mice.
The number of goblet cells was significantly reduced by inotodiol and dexamethasone treatment compared to untreated NP mice.
Toluidine blue staining showed more pronounced mast cell degranulation in the NP group than other groups, although total mast cell numbers did not differ between groups.

Tryptase expression by immunofluorescence in nasal mucosa was significantly lower in inotodiol- and dexamethasone-treated NP mice compared to untreated NP mice, indicating suppressed mast cell activation.
Inotodiol (5-10 µg/mL) did not significantly increase apoptosis in PBMCs from CRSwNP patients compared to medium alone, whereas dexamethasone (1 µM) significantly increased apoptosis.
Lactate dehydrogenase assay showed no cytotoxicity of inotodiol or dexamethasone at the tested concentrations in PBMCs.
Cleaved caspase-3 expression was significantly higher in EoL-1-derived eosinophils treated with inotodiol (10 µg/mL) than in those treated with media alone, indicating induction of apoptosis.
Apoptosis-related proteins TRAILR2, Fas, Bax, and phosphorylated p53 were increased in EoL-1 eosinophils after inotodiol treatment compared to before treatment.
The number of apoptotic (cleaved caspase-3+/Siglec-F+) eosinophils in nasal mucosa was significantly higher in inotodiol- and dexamethasone-treated ECRS mice than in untreated NP mice.

In dispersed nasal polyp cells (DNPCs) from CRS patients stimulated with staphylococcal enterotoxin B, inotodiol treatment significantly increased the number of apoptotic eosinophils compared to media alone.
IL-13 production after SEB stimulation was significantly suppressed in inotodiol-treated DNPCs harvested from ECRS patients.

The authors cite prior literature that inotodiol inhibits NF-κB activation, thereby reducing transcription of inflammatory genes, as a proposed mechanism relevant to their observed suppression of IL-6 and IL-1β.

The authors cite a prior study reporting that 13 weeks of daily 20 mg/kg inotodiol (95% purity) in mice caused no organ abnormalities, mortality, changes in lipid metabolism, hematological/biochemical parameter alterations, or liver toxicity.
LDH assay showed no cytotoxicity from inotodiol or dexamethasone at the concentrations tested in PBMCs.
